10331-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This volume gathers weekly numbers of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, a London miscellany of the 1820s. Each Saturday issue, priced at two pence, mixed engravings, short essays, and curious facts for a broad middle-class readership. No single author wrote it; editors and contributors filled every page.

One number describes Kingston's new bridge in detail, from its five stone arches to its cost and opening in July 1828. Other pieces treat towns, inventions, history, and odd customs in the same light style. Readers get a lively window into what literate Londoners read for pleasure in 1828.
10332-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This volume of The Mirror, a London weekly miscellany, gathers numbers from the summer of 1828, including the issue of August 2. Each number, priced at two pence, mixed engravings, verse, and short prose for general readers. Editors and many contributors shared the work, so no single author owns it.

One long piece treats All-Souls' Church in Langham Place, built by Nash in 1822 to 1825, and mocked in song and satire for its queer proportions. Other items cover towns, arts, and curious facts. Readers get a lively, illustrated glimpse of London taste and talk in 1828.
10475-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This volume of The Mirror, a London weekly miscellany, includes the number of August 9, 1828, with an engraving of Regent Bridge in Edinburgh. Each Saturday number, priced at two pence, mixed pictures, verse, and short prose for general readers. Many hands wrote it, under editors who prized variety and curiosity.

The lead piece praises Edinburgh, queen of the North, and its New Town, built since 1769, with a grand entrance across Calton Hill begun in 1814. Other items treat towns, arts, and wonders in the same light style. Readers get a lively, illustrated glimpse of British taste in 1828.
10572-manners-makyth-man-ship-s-company-:
W. W. Jacobs often let a night-watchman tell his tales, and "Manners Makyth Man," from Ship's Company, is one of those yarns. The watchman grumbles about play-acting, which he calls a silly game of dressing up, and then explains how a wish to do good to others left him a laughingstock. Sailors on the Lizzie and Annie spread the story through every nearby pub.

The tale turns on pride, a prank gone wrong, and the sting of being laughed at by workmates. Young Ted Sawyer, mate of the Lizzie and Annie, sets the trouble in motion. Readers get a comic monologue in Thames-side speech, funny on its own and typical of Jacobs's way of letting ordinary working men tell their own stories.
10719-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction was a cheap weekly miscellany for British readers, and this volume holds its numbers from late 1828. The issue of December 6, 1828, priced at two pence, opens with an engraving of the Arch of Constantine at Rome and a supplement of poetical gems after Turner. Architecture, painting, and verse share the pages.

Each number mixes short articles, stories, poems, and pictures for family reading. The Mirror aimed to bring art, history, and entertainment to readers of modest means. Modern readers get a lively sample of popular print culture in the age before cheap newspapers.
10730-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary number of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, volume twelve, number 344, sold for two pence in 1828. It opens with a view of Ehrenbreitstein on the Rhine, its shattered wall still proud after war, with verses from Byron's Childe Harold. A "Spirit of the Annuals" feature follows, sampling the year's gift books.

The Mirror mixed engravings, poetry, and short prose for family readers of modest means. This number shows that formula at work: a famous fortress, fine verse, and literary gossip. Readers get a small, vivid slice of popular reading in Regency England.
10792-keeping-up-appearances-sailor-s-kn:
W. W. Jacobs closes Sailors' Knots with "Keeping Up Appearances," the twelfth tale of 1909, on superstition. The night-watchman, coaxing a one-eyed black cat that used his trousers as a napkin, declares everybody superstitious. Men who stole a cat's supper would act foolish for life, and one man who killed a black cat saw its ghost whenever he drank.

The watchman scratches the cat's ears as he moralizes, half fond of the beast and half afraid of it. Jacobs turns a common sailor belief into gentle comedy. Readers get a brief, charming finale to the collection, funny on its own and a fitting farewell to the watchman.
10845-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for September 20, 1828, volume twelve, number 332, leads with Anne Hathaway's cottage. The engraving, one of Mr. Rider's views illustrating Shakespeare's life, shows the Shottery cottage where the poet's wife is said to have lived with her parents, about a mile from Stratford-upon-Avon.

Rider's note weighs what is known of the humble house, inside and out. The Mirror offered such literary pilgrimages to readers who might never travel. Modern readers get a small, pretty piece of Shakespeare tourism, from the age when his birthplace first drew crowds.
11210-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for November 1, 1828, opens with Nelson's Monument at Liverpool. The bronze monument by Richard Westmacott, erected in the Liverpool Exchange Buildings and completed in October 1823, cost about nine thousand pounds in subscriptions, weighs upwards of twenty-two tons.

On Westmoreland marble, four emblematic captives at the pedestal base allude to Nelson's victories, with four bronze bas-reliefs of his great naval actions between them. The principal group shows Nelson, Victory, and Death, with his country mourning and his navy eager to avenge him. Nelson rests one foot on a conquered enemy and the other on a cannon, receiving a fourth naval crown on the sword held in his left hand. The penny weekly mixes engravings, antiquarian notes, and verse.
11264-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The August 16, 1828 Mirror opens at Rosamond's Well and Labyrinth at Woodstock, Oxfordshire, with engravings from correspondents' sketchbooks. Drayton's Elizabethan description is quoted for the vaults, arched and walled. winding within one another so Rosamond might escape by secret issues, and Scott's novel Woodstock is credited with reviving interest in the spot. Tradition places fair Rosamond's surrender to Queen Eleanor on the bank above the well.

The article adds few words of its own, trusting history and poetry to carry the place. That restraint is characteristic of the Mirror's antiquarian pieces. Readers interested in the Rosamond legend will find here a compact survey of its sources, from Drayton to Scott.
11267-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated August 23, 1828, this Mirror number leads with an ancient plan of Oxford Castle. tracing the site from Alfred and Harold Harefoot through Offa's walls to Robert D'Oiley's Norman castle of 1071. Antiquarian authorities including Hearne, Leland, Dugdale, and Camden are weighed, and the plan itself is explained for readers. Shorter pieces follow on the intellectual cat, stanzas for music, and trout binning in Westmoreland.

The issue is typical of the Mirror's antiquarian streak, giving ordinary readers a guided tour of a famous place with footnotes. An excursion to Rievaulx and Byland abbeys and to Laurence Sterne's home at Coxwold extends the travel theme. Together the pieces show how history reached a popular audience in 1828.
11281-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 4, 1828 Mirror leads with the United Service Club-House at the angle of Charles Street and Regent Street, built for officers of the army and navy. The article admires the club's purpose, leisure with dignity in peacetime, while judging architect Robert Smirke's exterior cold and rigid. save for a bas-relief of Britannia distributing laurels to her sons by land and sea. Turtle, venison, and claret in the cellars get a wry mention.

Shorter items complete the number in the weekly's usual miscellany. The club-house piece doubles as architectural criticism and social comment on post-Waterloo London. Readers interested in clubland or Regent Street will find a contemporary verdict, flattering neither building nor luxury.
11282-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 18, 1828 Mirror leads with Richmond Palace, from a very old drawing of Henry VII's rebuilding, noting that few visitors appreciate its antiquarian importance beside poets Pope and Thomson. The article traces Sheen manor from Edward I through Edward III's death there in 1377. Queen Anne's death in 1394 and Richard II's destruction of the palace in grief, Henry V's restoration, and Henry VII's 1492 tournament and rebuilding after the 1499 fire.

Most visitors, the article jokes, prefer the Star and Garter's cellars to poetry. The palace history corrects that indifference with a royal chronology. For Thames-side historians, the number offers a compact account of Richmond before its palace vanished almost entirely.
11312-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 8, 1828 Mirror opens at Great Milton, a picturesque Oxfordshire village near Thame, presented as the family seat of the Miltons, ancestors of the epic poet. The article traces the family through a forfeited estate in the Wars of the Roses, a grandfather who disinherited his Protestant son. A scrivener father in London, eminent in music and classical scholarship, whose sons were John the poet and Christopher the judge.

Johnson's life of Milton supplies much of the detail, quoted and paraphrased for weekly readers. The village engraving anchors a literary pilgrimage in print. For Milton enthusiasts, the number shows how the poet's origins were packaged for a popular audience in the 1820s.
11320-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The September 13, 1828 Mirror urges Londoners to make a pilgrimage to Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace, and leads with Charlecote Hall, a venerable mansion on the Avon about four miles from Stratford. The article calls Charlecote one of the Shakespearean relics, worth visiting alone or with a garrulous old guide, and quotes Milton's lines on sweetest Shakespeare warbling native wood-notes wild.

Shorter pieces follow in the weekly's miscellany, but Charlecote carries the number. The piece shows the Mirror promoting literary tourism decades before it became an industry. Readers can still use it as a contemporary guide to how Shakespeare's country was presented to ordinary visitors.
11336-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 25, 1828 Mirror opens with the Cheese Wring in Cornwall. a pile of stones venerable amid storms and changes of religion, sent by a correspondent with remarks on Cornwall's early importance. The article claims Cornwall as the Cassiterides, citing the Abbé de Fontenu on Phoenician tin trade before the Trojan war, Homer on tin, and Ezekiel's Tarshish as the source of Tyrian metals. Herodotus confesses ignorance of the tin islands, the writer notes.

The Cheese Wring thus becomes a gateway to ancient trade history, with legend hallowing the stones for surrounding peasants. Shorter items follow. For Cornish antiquaries, the number shows how local pride recruited classical authorities to prove Cornwall's ancient fame.
11362-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The July 12, 1828 Mirror continues its illustrated ramble in Regent's Park with Clarence Terrace, named for the Lord High Admiral and designed by Decimus Burton. The terrace joins a center and two wings of the Corinthian order by colonnades of Ilyssus Ionic order. A rusticated basement, a drawing-room and chamber story, and an elegant entablature and balustrade. Bold central columns and classic pilasters draw particular praise.

The article calls Clarence Terrace the park's smallest terrace, yielding to none in picturesque effect and harmonious design. Shorter items follow. For Regent's Park historians, the number adds another contemporary judgment to the series, admiring Burton's variety within a classical vocabulary.
11370-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The August 30, 1828 Mirror leads with the new church building at Staines, on the Exeter road. a town rich in antiquarian associations: the London Stone, an ancient bridge repaired with three Windsor oaks in 1262, and Stukeley's Via Trinobantica. The article tours the road from Kensington and Hammersmith through Brentford, Hounslow, and Bedfont, with inns where Quin. Johnson, and Shenstone lingered, before reaching the old Gothic church with lancet windows, disfigured by churchwardens' repairs.

The new church replaces that old building, and the article welcomes the change while recording what was lost. Shorter items follow. For Thames-valley historians, the number preserves Staines as coaching-age travelers knew it.
11386-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 20, 1828 Mirror continues its European cities series with Naples, situated on hills encircling a gulf sixteen miles broad and long, called Crater by Neapolitans. One part rises in amphitheatre form over Pausilippo, St. Ermo, and Antignano hills; the other extends east over level territory, villas succeeding one another from the Magdalen Bridge to Portici. Naples, the article insists, is among the most beautiful and delightful cities on the globe, despite lacking Rome's art.

The series began with London and paused for contemporary subjects, a delay the editor jokes about. Shorter items follow. For travel readers, the number offers Naples as a coup d'oeil, a city best seen whole from its bay.
11389-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The September 6, 1828 Mirror asks why the English are not a musical people, quoting Massinger's Roman Actor as its motto. The article admits England has no national music like the Welsh, Irish, or Scots, its music being a mere raree-show stolen from every European nation. yet notes the king plays violoncello delightfully, an Academy of Music exists, and an Italian theatre burns managers' fingers, witness Mr. Ebers losing forty-seven thousand pounds. Pepys shows Italian singers arriving under Charles II.

The English Opera House, playing mostly foreign music, earns praise for transplanting continental compositions. The essay is witty and self-deprecating, a common Mirror mode. For music historians, it preserves a contemporary debate about national taste that long outlived the 1820s.
11404-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 29, 1828 Mirror leads with the Admiralty Office in Whitehall, a commanding pile with few pretensions to architectural beauty. built by Ripley under George II on the site of Wallingford House, adjoining the Horse Guards. Brick-built with advancing wings, it centers on a lofty Ionic portico of four columns bearing an anchor in bold relief, housing lords commissioners' offices and a handsome hall. A semaphore telegraph on the roof signals principal ports.

The most tasteful portion, the article says, is Adams's stone screen facing the street, chaste and pleasing, with naval emblems and ancient vessels. Shorter items follow. For naval historians, the number gives Whitehall's Admiralty as contemporaries saw it, functional and symbolic at once.
11405-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 22, 1828 Mirror leads with the Council Office and Board of Trade buildings at Whitehall. a new splendid range by architect John Soane, adapted partially from the Temple of Jupiter Stator in Rome. The article quotes the Athenaeum's verdict that, despite the finest site, unlimited expense, finest materials. Richest order of antiquity lavishly employed, the whole is a failure, poor or at best something less than grand. Soane kept only column and entablature details.

The piece moves from the Druids' temple at Avebury, its last engraving, to Whitehall, celebrating variety. Shorter items follow. For architectural critics, the number preserves a sharp contemporary judgment on Soane's most prominent government work.
11406-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary Mirror number for 1828 surveys the Spirit of the Annuals for 1829, opening with an engraving of Vicenza. The editor's table glitters with caskets of song and tale in silken sheen and burnished gold, seven of nine in watered silk bindings. Silk enough for seventy thousand copies to stretch five miles from Hyde Park Corner to Turnham Green, by a lady friend's calculation. Contents, Miss Jane Porter says of heroines, are transcendently beautiful.

The survey begins with the parent stock, the Forget-Me-Not, and promises exquisite specimens. Its delight in gift books as social bonds, intertwining hands and hearts, is characteristic. For publishing historians, the number documents the annual craze at its most glittering.
11408-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 13, 1828 Mirror leads with Old Covent Garden, copied from a Hollar print showing the garden about Charles II's time, before filth and vegetable odours polluted its area. Originally the Westminster abbot's convent garden, extending to St. Martin's church, it passed from Edward VI to Protector Somerset, then to the Bedford family. Francis, Earl of Bedford, began clearing old buildings in 1634 and forming the square, executed by Inigo Jones, though only north and part of east sides were completed.

A handsome dial, gravel, and rails once ordered the area, with market booths only along Bedford House's wall. The most striking object is Jones's original St. Paul's church. Shorter items follow. For London historians, the number traces Covent Garden from monastery garden to market square.
11420-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplement to volume twelve of the Mirror completes the volume in 1828, with the editors noting six years and twelve volumes. or sessions, without recess, always a house, hoping for re-election by constituents in the republic of letters. Their approbation, they say in Puff's phrase from The Critic, is the air they breathe. Economy of plan and a spirit of curiosity, encouraging readers to wonder, are credited for success through six years' fluctuations.

Sterne is quoted on curiosity as the number closes. The supplement lists the volume's usual contents: essays, narratives, memoirs, sketches, topography, tales, anecdotes, extracts, poetry, journals, discoveries, and domestic hints. For Mirror collectors, this sheet is the volume's farewell, self-conscious and grateful.
11445-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 27, 1828 Mirror leads with Barber's Barn in Mare Street, Hackney, an ancient mansion built about 1591 on ground called Barbour Berns. Colonel John Okey, a regicide charged with compassing Charles I's death, held the house at his attainder. his forfeited interest passed to the Duke of York, who gave it to Okey's widow in 1663. Okey, seized in Holland with Berkestead and Corbett in 1662, was executed at Tyburn, among the last regicides punished capitally.

Later the grounds became a nursery under John Busch, visited in spirit by Catherine II's interest. The article moves from treason to horticulture in one house's history. For Hackney historians, the number preserves a mansion where national drama and local gardening meet.
11528-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 15 November 1828, priced at twopence, opens at Abury in Wiltshire, called the most extensive Druid ruin in the county. The writer counts its great outer circle, its two smaller circles, and the ditch around them, and notes how much modern damage had already levelled.

The rest of the number keeps the same pattern of short, illustrated notes: places, antiquities, and natural facts, each given in a few pages. For a reader today it preserves both the site as it looked in 1828 and the plain way such ruins were then described.
12132-three-at-table-the-lady-of-the-bar:
Ghost talk in a coffee room leads into Three at Table, a quietly eerie story from W. W. Jacobs Lady of the Barge. A sailor of thirty years at sea, who claims only one unpleasant incident of the kind, tells of a night in the English countryside.

Fresh home from China, the young sailor finds his uncle house closed and takes shelter with an old man and woman in a lonely cottage. Dinner, they say, will seat three: the couple and their son. The guest senses a third presence he cannot see, and the meal grows stranger by the minute. Jacobs leaves the horror half-spoken, trusting the reader to feel what the narrator will not name.
12212-the-third-string-odd-craft-part-12:
Love, says the night watchman who narrates The Third String, has caused as much mischief as drink, and ought to have its own teetotal ribbon. The tale, from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft, proves the point through Ginger Dick, a red-haired sailor lodging in Wapping.

Ginger falls for Miss Tucker and must face Bill Lumm, a prizefighter who claims her too. Ginger, fined five pounds for street fighting, insists on a proper Thursday afternoon bout, combining business with pleasure. The comedy turns on sailor vanity, jealousy, and the gap between boasting and fighting. Jacobs keeps the tone broad, but the story also notes how quickly affection turns to possessiveness.
12438-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 11 October 1828, this Mirror number opens with Lavenham Church in Suffolk. Lavenham, once eminent for cloth, held eight or nine cloth-halls and rich clothiers, while the De Veres, Earls of Oxford, held the manor from Henry I to Elizabeth. A charter from Edward III let its tenants pass toll-free through England.

Manufacturing fame had dwindled, the article notes, to spinning woollen yarn and making calimancoes and hempen cloth. The Mirror pairs such local history with engraving and anecdote, for twopence a week. This number shows the miscellany's method: a church, a town and a vanished trade, told briefly for readers who liked learning in small, pictured pieces.
12873-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, July 19, 1828, this Mirror number opens at Columbia College, praising London's new drive to become a seat of learning. A large academy, colleges near completion, and subscriptions pouring in from across the empire mark what the writer calls grand strides in national learning. Swift's Tale of a Tub supplies a witty motto.

Later pages turn to travel and animal tales, including a voyage with a panther fed on parrots after pirates boarded the ship and left the crew near starvation. The mix of learning news and lively anecdote is typical of the weekly. The issue gives a pleasant glimpse of London reading in 1828.
13955-the-sunny-side-of-diplomatic-life-:
Lillie de Hegermann-Lindencrone recalled diplomatic life from 1875 to 1912 in this memoir, published in 1914. She follows posts in Washington, Rome, Stockholm, Paris, and Berlin, with portraits and facsimiles. An alphabet of a diplomat opens the book with witty advice. Illustrations include Mrs. U. S. Grant and Sarah Bernhardt.

At a dinner for the diplomatic corps, she sat between the German minister and Sir Edward Thornton, opposite the president. Such scenes fill the memoir with gossip, ceremony, and character. Hegermann-Lindencrone writes as an insider who enjoyed society. Her sunny view stresses charm over crisis. The book offers a lively record of courts and embassies.
13968-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume nine of Edmund Burke's Works, published by John C. Nimmo in 1887, prints articles of charge against Warren Hastings. Presented to the Commons in April and May 1786, articles seven to twenty-two cover contracts, presents, and later charges. Rights of Fyzoola Khân, treaties of Lall-Dang and Chunar, and demands for horse follow.

Burke's prosecution of Hastings, late governor-general of Bengal, shaped impeachment history. A passage on merchants' opinion, twenty per cent on prime cost as agent's pay, shows the detail. The volume preserves Burke's legal and moral argument. It suits students of empire and oratory. Burke's coat of arms fronts the edition.
14582-the-war-with-the-united-states-a-c:
William Wood's chronicle of the War of 1812, volume fourteen of the Chronicles of Canada, was published in Toronto in 1915. Wood wrote for general readers under editors George Wrong and H. H. Langton.

Chapters weigh opposing claims and forces, then follow Brock at Detroit and Queenston Heights, Beaver Dams, Lake Erie, Châteauguay, Lundy's Lane, and Plattsburg. Wood notes Tecumseh's brother, the Prophet, defeated at Tippecanoe, and the British joy at Michilimackinac. The book is a clear, Canadian telling of a war both sides claimed. Wood's volume balanced British and American viewpoints fairly.
15043-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
This first volume of Edmund Burke's collected works, issued in London in 1887, gathers his early writings and speeches. It opens with his Vindication of Natural Society, a satire on the ills of artificial society, and moves to his famous Inquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful, with a discourse on taste.

Later pieces take up a short ministry, the state of the nation, and the causes of political discontent in Britain. Together they show Burke's mind forming: sharp prose, deep feeling for order, and a critic's eye for power. The volume is the natural starting point for readers new to one of Britain's great political writers.
15087-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
One weekly issue of a London miscellany, dated September 1828, gathers short pieces on art, science, travel, and odd news from Britain and abroad. Engraved views head several items, and brief notes fill the gaps between longer essays. Its tone is light and curious, aimed at a general reader with an hour to spare.

Inside, an opening piece asks what the round towers of Scotland and Ireland were built for, weighing old claims about sacred fires against plain facts of stone and site. Other items range from church history to natural wonders, with poems and letters mixed in. Read as a whole, the issue shows what educated readers in 1828 found strange, amusing, and worth debate.
15198-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
This second volume of Burke's collected works, issued in London in 1887, gathers his speeches and letters on America. It opens with his 1774 speech on American taxation, followed by Bristol speeches and his 1775 plea for conciliation with America. A 1777 letter to the sheriffs of Bristol continues the argument.

Later pieces take up Irish trade, parliamentary reform, and economical reform of the civil establishments. Together they show Burke urging restraint, justice, and reform before revolution hardened positions. Readers of political history will find the volume essential to understanding Burke and the American crisis.
15450-against-home-rule-the-case-for-the:
S. Rosenbaum edited this 1912 volume against Irish Home Rule, with an introduction by Sir Edward Carson and a preface by A. Bonar Law. Contributors include Arthur Balfour, Austen Chamberlain, Walter Long, George Wyndham, Lord Charles Beresford, and many other Unionist members of Parliament. Frederick Warne published it in London and New York.

Essays divide into historical and critical parts. Balfour writes a note on Home Rule and a historical retrospect, while Cave treats the constitutional question, Chamberlain the finance, and Amery the colonial analogy. Later essays take up courts, land, and empire. The book is a party case made in public: a coordinated argument that union, not a Dublin parliament, best served Ireland and Britain on the eve of the Home Rule crisis.
15700-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
This fourth volume of the works of Edmund Burke, in twelve volumes, was published in London in 1887 by John C. Nimmo, with a Burke coat of arms as frontispiece. The volume gathers Burke's writings on France and Ireland from the revolutionary years, when the old Whig defended tradition against revolution. Eight pieces run from a letter to a member of the National Assembly to remarks on the policy of the allies.

Contents include an appeal from the new to the old Whigs, letters on the penal laws against Irish Catholics, and a letter to Sir Hercules Langrishe on Roman Catholics in Ireland. Hints for a memorial, thoughts on French affairs, and heads for consideration on the present state of affairs follow. The opening letter, dated 1791, answers objections to Burke's book on French affairs. The volume shows Burke at his most prophetic: revolution as a threat to order, property, and faith.
15701-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
The fifth volume of Edmund Burke's collected works, issued by John C. Nimmo in London in 1887. Burke, the great Whig orator and writer, speaks here from the heart of the French Revolution years. The volume gathers pamphlets and letters from 1793 to 1795, when Britain watched France with fear and anger. Nimmo's twelve-volume set aimed to give Burke whole to a new age.

Contents include observations on the minority in the last session of Parliament in 1793, and a preface to Brissot's address to his constituents. A letter to William Elliot on Lord Fitzwilliam closes the main run. Burke defends order, faith, and slow reform against revolutionary haste. The volume shows his late style at full power: learned, fierce, and rich in historical warning.
15702-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
This sixth volume of the works of Edmund Burke, in twelve volumes, was published in London in 1887 by John C. Nimmo, with a Burke coat of arms as frontispiece. The volume gathers letters on peace with revolutionary France, on Ireland, and on the American war, spanning 1773 to the 1790s. Burke's correspondence shows a statesman arguing across three crises of empire and revolution.

Contents open with a fourth letter on proposals for peace with the regicide directory of France, with preliminary correspondence. Letters to the Empress of Russia, to Sir Charles Bingham on the Irish absentee tax, and to Charles James Fox on the American war follow. A letter to the Marquis of Rockingham, with addresses to the king and British colonists, treats the American contest and a proposed secession of the opposition. Letters on Catholic relief in Ireland close the set.
16292-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume seven of Edmund Burke's Works, published in London by John C. Nimmo in 1887 as part of a twelve-volume set, gathers fragments and notes of speeches in Parliament. Contents include his speech on the Acts of Uniformity in February 1772. A bill for relieving Protestant dissenters in March 1773 follows. A motion on repealing acts on religious opinions after a Unitarian petition in May 1792 closes the set. The Middlesex election speech of 1771 follows.

A bill for shortening parliaments in 1780 and a motion for a committee to inquire into the state of the nation complete the opening contents. Burke's oratory on religion, representation, and reform fills the volume. Students of British politics will find essential, first-hand parliamentary prose.
17332-history-of-egypt-from-330-b-c-to-t:
Rappoport's twelfth volume of Egyptian history turns to modern Egypt, from Crusades to khedives. Fatimite caliphs, Saladin, Damietta, Beybars, and Mamluks lead to Turkish misrule and Napoleon's invasion. The Pyramids, Nelson's fleet victory, Kleber's murder, and the French surrender give way to Mehemet Ali, the Mamluk massacre, and reforms under Ismail.

Arabi's revolt, the Mahdist rising, Gordon's death, and Kitchener's campaign close the road to English control and later prosperity. Rappoport writes in clear, sweeping prose for general readers. Modern Egypt's long story, from Crusader castles to Khedival palaces, finds a full, readable volume here.
18161-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume eight of the works of Edmund Burke was printed in London in 1887 by John C. Nimmo, as part of a twelve-volume set. Burke, the great Irish statesman and orator, here turns his fire on British rule in India.

The volume holds the ninth report of the Commons committee on India, dated June 1783, with notes on Bengal trade, silk, opium, and salt. Later parts charge Warren Hastings with designs to ruin the Rajah of Benares, and with wrongs to the princesses of Oude. It is a weighty, historic indictment, and a key text for students of empire and Burke.
18192-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume ten of the works of Edmund Burke was printed in London in 1887 by John C. Nimmo, as part of a twelve-volume set. This volume holds Burke's speeches in the impeachment of Warren Hastings, late governor-general of Bengal.

The speeches open on February 18, 1788, and run through the spring of 1789, on the sixth article of charge and more. Burke, the great orator, lays out Hastings's alleged wrongs in India with fire and moral force. The volume is a landmark of parliamentary eloquence, and a key text for students of empire, law, and Burke's mind.
18218-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume eleven of the works of Edmund Burke was printed in London in 1887 by John C. Nimmo, as part of a twelve-volume set. This volume carries the Hastings impeachment forward, with reports and speeches from 1794.

It opens with a Commons report on the Lords' journals in the Hastings trial, with remarks answering Lord Thurlow. Burke's speech in general reply follows, from May 28 through June 5, 1794. The volume closes a great trial in Burke's voice, full of law, rhetoric, and moral fire. It is essential reading for students of Burke, of Parliament, and of empire.
18315-the-works-of-the-right-honourable-:
Volume twelve of Edmund Burke's works, published in London by John C. Nimmo in 1887, closes the twelve-volume set. The volume continues Burke's speeches in the impeachment of Warren Hastings, late governor-general of Bengal, with his speech in general reply. Burke's coat of arms fronts the book, and a general table of contents and index close it.

The reply runs across five days in June 1794. It opens on Saturday, June 7, and continues June 11, 12, and 14. It closes on Monday, June 16. Readers get Burke at his most sustained: a prosecution speech that sums a long trial, charges misrule in India, and defends the duty of empire to govern justly.
2112-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle reaches the First Silesian War in this volume, as Frederick invades Silesia in December 1740 and wakes a general European war. Book Twelve opens with a long geography of Silesia, its mountains, rivers, and shape. Silesia, rich and disputed, tempted every neighbour, which is why Frederick struck first.

From Crossen toward the Jablunka Pass, Carlyle follows armies and diplomacy through the spring of 1741. The volume marks the turn from prince to warrior king, and it shows Carlyle at his most detailed on campaigns and ground. Carlyle's geography chapter, long as it is, helps a reader follow armies across a complex map.
24095-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated May 12, 1920, the weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, gathers a week of British satire, jokes, and cartoons. Punch, long the country's leading comic paper, mixed short paragraphs, mock reports, and drawings that poked fun at politics, fashion, and daily life. The issue opens with Charivaria, its column of brief, sharp news jokes.

Inside, readers find quips on the King's yacht Britannia returning to service, smoking breaks in Massachusetts factories, and an eclipse of the moon that passed without a hitch. Music-hall audiences, press letters, and the small absurdities of postwar life all come in for teasing. The issue is a lively snapshot of Britain in the spring of 1920, laughing at itself as normal life resumed.
24904-golden-days-for-boys-and-girls-vol:
Golden Days for Boys and Girls, volume thirteen, number fifty-one, dated November 12, 1892, shows a Philadelphia weekly for young readers at its best. Its publisher, James Elverson, promised good, pure fiction, puzzles, a letter box, and an exchange column, with artistic pictures through the issue.

One continued story turns on New Orleans in wartime. A messenger brings word that the enemy fleet has reached the passes of the Mississippi. Gentlemen who opposed dealing with Lafitte change their minds and accept his offer to help defend the city. Ads for Sapolio soap fill the margins. The issue gives a lively taste of boys' papers in the 1890s.
27812-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-january-:
Joseph R. Buchanan's January 1888 Journal of Man, volume one, number twelve, opens with an essay on the pursuit of truth, arguing that loyalty to truth matters more than success in formulating it. Other pieces define occultism and discuss psychic phenomena.

The miscellany ranges from the ancient Iberians and the star dust of the universe to photography, phylloxera, falling rents, and Dorothea Dix, with methods of studying the brain and readers' responses. The issue captures Buchanan's late-career blend of science, psychical research, and reform. Buchanan compares loyalty to truth to daylight, opening all avenues between mind and nature.
3088-original-short-stories-volume-12:
The Child opens volume twelve, a widower's honest love tested by a second marriage. Lemonnier, a widower with one child, loved his wife devotedly with tender, exalted love, without a slip, through their married life. A good, honest, simple, sincere man without suspicion or malice, he falls in love with a poor neighbor, proposes, and is accepted, making a comfortable living. The volume adds A Country Excursion, Rose, Rosalie Prudent, Regret, A Sister's Confession, Coco, A Dead Woman's Secret, A Humble Drama, Mademoiselle Cocotte, The Corsican Bandit, and The Grave.

A sister's confession tells of an artillery non-commissioned officer, Joseph Varambot, who stayed two summer months and flattered a girl into love. The volume closes Maupassant's series with domestic tragedy.
30939-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume twelve of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds one novel, The Master of Ballantrae, and its front shows Stevenson dictating to Mrs. Strong in his study at Vailima.

Early chapters give summaries of events during the master's wanderings, then the master's wanderings from the memoirs of the Chevalier de Burke. Later chapters turn to persecutions endured by Mr. Henry and an account of all that passed on the road home. It is a dark tale of two brothers, loyalty, and revenge, told with Stevenson's usual vigor and Scottish color.
3562-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This twelfth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers Napoleon in 1814, the year of his first abdication. Bourrienne, his former private secretary, follows the collapse of the empire as allied armies entered France, Paris fell, and the emperor gave up his throne. The volume belongs to the older Project Gutenberg Napoleon series, produced by David Widger.

The narrative moves from desperate defense to negotiation and exile. Marshals, ministers, and foreign envoys bargain over a fallen ruler's fate, while Napoleon weighs abdication against abdication for his son. Bourrienne gives the fall from the inside, with the bitterness of a man who had served the rise. The volume suits readers reaching the first end of the story.
3579-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's twelfth and last volume brings his recollections to their close, covering the emperor's final fall and farewell. He describes the last days at Fontainebleau, the abdication, and the parting from the household that had served Napoleon for years. Servants who had dressed him, fed him, and traveled with him now watched him leave for exile.

The volume reads as a servant's farewell to a master and to a way of life. Constant defends his loyalty and records small last kindnesses that official histories miss. Readers finishing the series will find a moving, personal end to the story of Napoleon's private life, told by the man who stood at his door.
3592-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This twelfth volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters eighteen through thirty one of Book Two. They treat giving the lie, liberty of conscience, and the claim that we taste nothing pure. Other essays cover idleness, posting, ill means used to a good end, Roman grandeur, counterfeiting sickness, thumbs, cowardice as the mother of cruelty, seasons, virtue, a monstrous child, and anger.

Montaigne writes on conscience and lying with the wars of religion in view, defending freedom of thought while doubting human certainty. Small chapters on thumbs and on feigned sickness sit beside large ones on Rome and virtue. The volume suits readers who want Montaigne's range in one place, from a body part to the fate of empires.
3912-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau opens his twelfth and final book with the work of darkness in which he has lived enveloped for eight years. Blows reach him without his perceiving the hand that directs them. Shame and misfortune fall of themselves, and the authors of his ruin make the public an unwitting accomplice. He cannot name the directing hand or assign causes, only state effects, since the primitive causes already stand in earlier books.

Losses crowd the close. His lord marshal speaks of a testament, and Rousseau refuses any place in it. The best of women and mothers, weighed down by years and misery, quits this vale of tears. He hopes his name will never appear in any friend's will. Readers who reach the end will find a man convinced of conspiracy and worn down by it, still insisting on truth.
5286-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this twelfth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are The Monks of Catalonia and The Cradle. The first opens among monks in Catalonia, whose generous attentions to wife and maid leave youthful minds sweetly fascinated.

La Fontaine's irony is at work throughout, as monks work in the holy vineyard and youthful, easy minds fall into their net. Readers get two bawdy, anticlerical tales in the author's lightest manner, where piety and appetite prove hard to tell apart in this volume.
5528-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-12:
While Rustem prepares their journey with a practiced guide's care in the twelfth volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile, Mary comforts her governess and Mandane. Mary had entrusted Rustem with the jeweller's gold. She explains that Rustem's journey aims to save Paula's life. Meanwhile a fresh trial goes forward in the Court of Justice, and this time Orion stands accused.

The volume runs two plots at once: a rescue journey and a courtroom accusation, each raising the stakes for Paula and Orion. Ebers keeps the personal and legal threads tight. Readers get a tense, double-stranded stretch of the romance, where a journey and a trial race each other.
5541-a-thorny-path-volume-12:
Caracalla's evening meal has ended, and his friends have never seen the gloomy monarch in so mad a mood, in the twelfth volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. The high priest of Serapis and Dio Cassius the senator stay away from table. The priest of Alexander, the prefect Macrinus, and favorites such as Theocritus crowd around him, drinking his health and wishing him joy of his glorious revenge.

The volume shows a court celebrating a day's violent work, comparing it with deeds from legend and history. Ebers writes the feast as moral darkness. Readers get a chilling stretch of the romance, where congratulations follow revenge.
569-the-complete-works-of-brann-the-icon:
The twelfth and final volume of Brann's collected works closes the set with pieces written near the end of his stormy career in Waco. Newspaper reports, recollections, and controversies around Brann himself fill much of the book. Brann was shot in Waco in 1898, a death that made the final volume a memorial as well.

Accounts of friends, rivals, and a shooting tragedy give the volume a darker cast than the earlier satires. Read after the first volumes, it shows how a career built on attack ended in violence, and why Brann became a legend. The closing pieces show friends and foes alike reckoning with a career cut short by violence.
5914-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Dorothea's wit carries chapters thirty through thirty-two of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter thirty treats the address displayed by the fair Dorothea, with other pleasant and amusing matters, after the curate ceases speaking and Sancho confesses his master's deed. Chapter thirty-one offers the delectable discussion between Quixote and Sancho, and chapter thirty-two what befell the knight's party at the inn.

Readers watch Dorothea, as Princess Micomicona, steer Quixote toward home with courtesy and invention. The chapters favor dialogue and inn comedy, as Sancho's honesty and Quixote's courtesy collide. This part suits readers following the rescue plot, since Dorothea's address proves that fiction, kindly used, can lead a madman gently homeward.
6661-waverley-novels-volume-12:
Volume twelve of Scott's Waverley Novels, in the Abbotsford edition, holds Count Robert of Paris, Castle Dangerous, and My Aunt Margaret's Mirror, with the author's last corrections, prefaces, and notes. An illustration shows Hereward resisting a Greek assassin, and a verse from Don Juan opens Count Robert with a view of Asian shores, cypress groves, and high Olympus.

Scott sent the Castle Dangerous introduction from Naples in 1832, while no second-edition note for Count Robert has been found among his papers. The volume thus closes the great series with late, varied tales. Waverley Novels, volume twelve, is a fitting end shelf for Scott lovers.
6828-the-works-of-henry-fielding-vol-12:
Volume twelve of Fielding's works, edited by George Saintsbury, holds Miscellanies, volume two: The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great and other writings. The Author's Farce, The Tragedy of Tragedies, Pasquin, a satire on the times, an essay on conversation, The True Patriot, and Covent-Garden Journal pieces all appear, with a portrait by Hogarth.

Fielding's wit, satire, and stage craft shine in these shorter works, which show the novelist as a man of the theatre and the press. Saintsbury's edition frames them with care. Volume twelve is a rich, varied close to Fielding's collected works, for lovers of eighteenth-century satire.
7597-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part twelve of The Caxtons is domestic comedy at its gentlest, as a scholar's household settles into the old Tower. The father's books arrive by wagon and fill their new apartment, bedchamber and two lobbies included. That quiet settling matters more than any plot turn: a library finding its rooms again. Lytton loves his Caxtons most when they are simply at home.

The move completes the family's Hegira, with all taking roost in the Tower. The duck arrives under Mrs. Primmins's wing and reconciles herself to the old stewpond. Beside that pond, the father finds a walk to replace his lost peach-wall and makes acquaintance with respectable carps, which let him feed them after he has fed himself. A duck resettled, fish for company, and a father content: the part asks for nothing grander.
7670-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-12:
George takes up a hard mission in Book Twelve of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? His uncle Alban sends word of Lionel's hopes for Sophy under Darrell's roof, and of a plan to clear William Losely's name from a stain of crime. George must deal with Jasper Losely on terms that end future shame.

Caroline Montfort's pride also takes center stage, as she weighs whether to humble herself once more for Darrell's sake. The closing book ties love, honor, and family name together, and asks what price peace is worth when the past will not stay buried.
7683-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
A gloomy forest pool under an autumn moon opens the final book of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Harold, subtitled The Battle of Hastings. Pollard oaks and beeches, dwarfed by lopping, stand as crooked marks of age and man's waste, while deer, hares, and bats stir in the dark glades.

Then the battle itself breaks: Norman archers hold firm, English ranks rush down and leave a gap, and William gallops through as Odo cries that saints wheel their steeds. Harold rallies in the breach. The volume ends Saxon England in blood, noise, and a king's last stand.
7713-my-novel-volume-12:
The Caxton family gathers for the close in Book Twelve of Edward Bulwer Lytton's My Novel, like a chorus round an altar, unsure how the skein will unravel. Mrs. Caxton fears Violante was deceived like a heroine of Camilla, while her husband jests that such girls ought to die young.

Captain Roland protests: the story already grows out of a grave, and Nora's tale needs no more tombs. Randal, bound for Lansmere, fears his secret name Fairfield will betray his birth from Nora. The final book ties kinship, shame, and fate into a long-awaited ending.
7726-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-12:
Edward reaches St. Albans in the final book of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The Battle of Barnet. Joy fills Westminster sanctuary, terror fills London, and a timid mayor feigns illness while deputies flee, leaving power to Ureswick the Yorkist recorder.

The Archbishop of York parades poor King Henry through Cheapside to St. Paul's, but news of Edward brings on one of Henry's fits from childhood. On the field, Oxford draws off cavalry, yet Montagu charges downhill crying his name against D'Eyncourt and Say. The Wars of the Roses reach a bloody close.
7748-the-parisians-volume-12:
Winter and famine settle on Paris in the final book of Lytton's The Parisians, after a sortie on November 30 and hard fights on December 2. Hopes that Trochu would break the iron ring fade as Ducrot explains a retreat across the Marne and Moltke reports the Loire army beaten.

Even after a failed sortie at Le Bourget on December 21, Parisians joke about defeat and predict triumph. In dreadful days the worst and best of the city show together, unnoticed in rich times. The closing volume ends a tale of siege, love, and national pride.
8640-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
Number 321 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, number 321, dated Saturday, July 5, 1828, opens with Eaton Hall in Cheshire, seat of Earl Grosvenor. The magazine praises the mansion as a princely Gothic pile, built to house a nobleman famed for supporting the fine arts. An engraving accompanies the account, in the Mirror's usual mix of picture and short essay.

Inside, readers of 1828 found the miscellany they expected: sketches, anecdotes, curiosities, and instructive scraps, all for twopence. The Mirror was a staple of early Victorian popular reading, cheap, illustrated, and wide-ranging. This single number gives a neat snapshot of what ordinary readers browsed on a Saturday morning. From country houses to odd facts, before the age of the daily newspaper picture.
9484-georgian-poetry-1911-1912:
Georgian Poetry 1911-1912 gathers new English verse from just two years, chosen by its editor to show a fresh age of poetry. The book claims English verse was gaining new strength and grace, and that few readers had time to track each new volume. Poets inside include Rupert Brooke, John Masefield, G. K. Chesterton, and John Drinkwater. The book was dedicated to Robert Bridges.

Poems range across country scenes, town life, love, war, and craft, in plain, musical forms. The editor admits the choice is narrow by design, and leaves out many fine poets outside the two-year span. A reader gets a snapshot of a poetic moment on the edge of war, and a first taste of names that soon shaped English verse.
9929-the-great-events-by-famous-historia:
Volume twelve of The Great Events by Famous Historians continues a chronological history of the world told in the words of great writers. Edited on a plan drawn from scholars of America and Europe, the series presents important events as complete narratives, linked by short introductions.

This volume draws on voices such as Daniel Defoe, John Evelyn, Thomas Carlyle, and François Xavier Garneau, with chronologies, bibliographies, and indexes to guide readers. The method lets readers hear history from those who lived near it. It is a rich, browsable history for curious general readers.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Ulysses Grant, the successful soldier turned president, fills this seventh volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Without the civil war, the volume notes, Grant would likely never have reached the presidency. His services in that struggle won him the gratitude of the republic. The volume prints his messages and papers as chief executive.
a-thorny-path-volume-12:
A Thorny Path ends in Volume 12 of the novel by Georg Ebers, at a dinner where cruelty is toasted like wine. Ebers shows Caracalla's friends crowding the table, drinking his health, and praising the day's revenge as greater than any deed in legend or history. The emperor, half drunk, declares that only now has he dared to be fully himself, judge and executioner in one person.

Chapter XXXIV lets the courtiers argue over the count of the slain in Alexandria, each guess wilder than the last, while the one man who saw it all stays absent. Caracalla rewards the largest claim with loud delight. Ebers offers no comfort here: flattery, wine, and wounded pride have turned a city festival into mass murder, and the throne room calls it glory.
against-home-rule-the-case-for-the-union: Simon Rosenbaum edits a unionist case against Home Rule, gathering leading opponents of Irish self-government in a single volume. Contributors including Arthur Balfour, Austen Chamberlain, and Walter Long argue that the Union protects law, trade, and the empire. Published in 1912, the book is a clear record of the arguments deployed as the Home Rule crisis reached its height.
agricola-de-re-metallica-1912:
Georgius Agricola wrote De Re Metallica in Latin in 1556. Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover gave it English dress in 1912. Hoover was a mine man long past when he took up the task. The book is the great text on mines and metal work of its age.

Twelve books tell of shafts, pumps, ores, and the smelt of each metal. Fine wood cuts show the craft at work, gear by gear. Agricola writes from years at the mines of Bohemia. The Hoover dress, with its rich notes, made the book a prize of the trade.
annales-cambriae-ingram-1912:
The Annales Cambriae, or Annals of Wales, are a Latin chronicle kept year by year in medieval Wales. James Ingram translated them into English in 1912. Most entries are bare lines about kings, battles, and deaths, the plain record of a small nation's memory.

Two short entries changed literary history. One notes Arthur's victory at Badon in 516, where he carried a cross into battle. Another records Camlann in 537, where Arthur and Medraut fell. From those stark lines grew centuries of argument about whether Arthur lived at all. The whole Arthurian tradition leans on this spare chronicle.
arxiv-2509-00112:
Nupoor Thakur and Navinder Singh Bathinda review the statistical mechanics of paraparticles in 2025. Quantum theory sorts particles into fermions, which exclude each other from the same state, and bosons, which do not. Two exceptions exist: anyons in flat systems, and paraparticles in any dimension, which follow a broader exclusion rule of their own.

The review lays out the base theory of paraparticle statistics from a 2025 source work and extends it. A key step derives a formula for the heat capacity of paraparticles in a set case. Heat capacity, the heat needed to raise temperature, could give an experimental handle to detect such particles. A clear detection path would test if paraparticles are real.
arxiv-2509-00312:
Xintao Xia and Yumou Qiu build a new way in 2025 to judge a treatment's mean effect when many background traits are tracked at once. The mean effect says what a treatment changes on the whole. To find it, one must model each person's chance of being treated, called a propensity score. A single such model can be wrong when the group mixes sources with distinct rules for who gets treated.

Their method weights the data so background traits balance out, and it blends many working score models at once. A wider set of check terms and a tuned outcome model fix the bias left by rough balance. The end result is a score with a key trait: small model flaws do not skew it to first order. The stated range for the effect stays valid if any one score model is right.
arxiv-2509-00512:
David Chinellato leads six authors in total, with Michael Lisa, Willian Serenone, Chun Shen, Jun Takahashi, and Giorgio Torrieri, in simulating proton-argon collisions event by event. The collisions are central and asymmetric, one side much lighter, and use a fixed target, where a beam hits a still target.

Chinellato and his co-authors look for vortex rings, swirling ring-shaped flow patterns, that may form from the early lengthwise flow profile. They give predictions for how such rings would appear in polarization measures, spin alignment measures, for Lambda hyperons, heavy particles used as probes. Their predictions complement an earlier study and can be tested in future fixed-target runs at the LHCb experiment.
arxiv-2509-00712:
Raghunath Sahoo, with two co-authors, Kangkan Goswami and Suraj Prasad, uses machine learning to identify leptons from heavy-flavor decays in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Heavy-flavor hadrons, particles with heavy quarks, probe the early stages of collisions, but measuring their semi-leptonic decays is resource-intensive and leans on event generators.

Sahoo and his co-authors train an XGBoost model on events generated by PYTHIA8 at the collision energy stated in the record. Inputs are displacement measures and pseudo-rapidity, a direction measure. The model reaches ninety-eight percent accuracy for heavy-flavor decay electrons and almost one hundred percent for muons, offering an independent identification method for precision studies.
arxiv-2509-00812:
Samuel Punch and Krishnendu Guha introduce NADGO for cloud quantum services. Such services can leak circuit structure and timing. Leaks come through scheduler metadata and latency patterns. Interference from co-tenants on shared hardware is another channel. NADGO is a scheduling and obfuscation stack against such leaks.

It enforces privacy with per-interval limits on information leakage. It pads traffic with structured cover traffic based on t-designs. A particle filter randomizes timing to mask queue patterns. A routing method spreads subcircuits across heterogeneous backends. A leakage estimator watches each interval, with a kill-switch for breaches. The prototype runs on a four-qubit superconducting tile. It keeps leakage within budget in normal operation. Abort rates stay below one percent of intervals.
arxiv-2509-00912:
Jianpei Geng leads a team of fourteen authors on spin defects in a layered nitride. The defect is the negatively charged boron vacancy in hexagonal boron nitride. It is a promising tool for quantum sensing in two dimensions. It offers ultimate proximity to target samples. Its practical sensitivity is limited by weak light emission, though.

The team reports emission enhanced up to thirty times in suspended regions. Supported regions on a substrate emit far less by contrast. Key spin properties are well preserved in the bright regions. They include resonance contrast, linewidth, and spin lifetime. Further tests link the gain to local deformation in the sample. Suspended regions deform more, breaking local symmetry. That activates optical transitions that are otherwise weak or forbidden.
arxiv-2509-01012:
Aamod Khatiwada, with two co-authors, introduces diverse unionable tuple search in data lakes. Unionable table search finds tables that can add rows to a query table. Data lakes hold many copies and versions of tables. The most unionable tables may thus be near duplicates of the query. They may add little new information for the user.

The team defines the problem of finding diverse unionable tuples instead. Tuples should differ from those already in the query table. An extensive analysis of diversity algorithms reveals a gap. Their DUST algorithm addresses it with clustering-based diversification. A novel embedding model represents unionable tuples better than rivals. On real data lake benchmarks, DUST is over six times faster than the best baseline. It is also more effective at diversifying results.
arxiv-2509-01412:
Chain-of-thought reasoning lets language models show their steps, but plain text traces are hard to check or steer in high-stakes work. Kaviraj Pather, with six co-authors, presents Vis-CoT, a framework that turns a linear reasoning trace into an interactive graph. Users can see the logical flow, spot flawed steps, and act on them directly.

Within the graph, users prune wrong paths and graft in new premises of their own, shifting the work from passive watching to active collaboration. On two benchmarks, a math word problem set and a strategy question set, Vis-CoT raised final-answer accuracy by up to twenty-four points over non-interactive baselines. A user study also found large gains in felt usability and trust. The authors present the tool as a practical path to more reliable model reasoning.
arxiv-2509-01812:
Kuan-Cheng Chen leads four co-authors in testing quantum learning for spotting intrusions in drone swarms. Drone fleets face fast motion, shifting traffic, and rare attack cases that skew training data. The team uses a simulated set of network flows covering five attack types. Three quantum methods face strong classic rivals under the same prep and noise rules.

Quantum kernels and hybrid trained networks do best when data are scarce and patterns bend sharply. Deeper quantum networks suffer training trouble, while classic convolutional networks win when data are plentiful. The study weighs encoding choices, circuit depth, qubit counts, and shot noise. Code and data splits are public so others can repeat the work.
arxiv-2509-02312:
Zsolt Lángi and Sára Lengyel wrote a 2025 geometry note on curves whose chords grow as points move apart along the curve. Four points in order must satisfy a simple rule: the outer pair sits no closer than the inner pair.

Back in 1994, Rote settled a conjecture by Larman and McMullen for the ordinary plane, bounding curve length by a fixed multiple of endpoint distance. Lángi and Lengyel extend that sharp bound to normed planes, where distance follows a strictly convex rule rather than the usual one. Their proof studies involutes, curves traced by unwinding a taut string. Related extreme-value problems close the note, widening a classic result.
arxiv-2509-02412:
Wenhao Chen, Morris Chang, Witawas Srisa-an, and Yong Guan present a 2025 software testing paper on generating event sequences for Android apps. Apps react to taps and inputs, and varied screen designs make thorough testing within a time budget hard.

Their APEX framework uses concolic execution, which runs an app with real inputs while also tracking symbolic constraints. That process reveals how data shapes screen transitions, so event choices can be prioritised during exploration. The same engine both builds sequences and steers the search through the interface more systematically. Experiments show the generated sequences reach high code coverage. They also hit specific target behaviours that model-based generators often miss, which matters for finding input-dependent bugs.
arxiv-2509-02512:
Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata, Jie Ye, and Murali Emani present a 2025 machine learning systems paper on shrinking mixture-of-experts models, which split work among many expert subnetworks. Such models strain memory when deployed, especially in combined vision-language systems.

Their MoPEQ method assigns a different bit width, the number size used in storage, to each expert after training. Sensitivity is judged by a Hessian trace approximation, a curvature-based score, rather than by how often an expert fires. Similar experts are clustered to protect accuracy. Tests on vision-language benchmarks with several DeepSeek and MolmoE models kept accuracy competitive while cutting memory sharply against uniform precision. A broader study varies two, three, and four bit settings across layers and models.
arxiv-2509-02612:
Leire Benito-Del-Valle and six co-authors wrote a 2025 computational pathology study asking whether synthetic images help classify atypical dividing cells, a rare class in the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Real atypical examples are heavily outnumbered by normal ones.

Two backbones were compared: a ConvNeXt model pretrained on general images, and a histopathology vision transformer trained by self-supervision. The team generated extra atypical examples to balance classes, then trained with real data alone versus real plus synthetic. Five-fold validation gave both backbones strong ranking scores. The general model peaked slightly higher, while the domain model varied less between folds. Synthetic balancing brought no consistent gain. On a hidden out-of-distribution test slice, the general backbone led on ranking score.
arxiv-2509-02812:
Zixuan He, Charalambos D. Charalambous, and Photios A. Stavrou present a 2025 control theory paper on decision problems where the controller should learn as little as possible about the system it steers. The cost is directed information flowing from the controlled process to the control process, capped stage by stage.

Exact solutions use a continuous information state, and discretising that space is prohibitively expensive. The authors build a truncated rollout method with an offline phase, where a base policy is fitted over a shorter horizon, and an online phase of lookahead minimisation at run time. Both phases carry convergence guarantees. A numerical example shows lower costs than an earlier policy approximation, with observed computing effort compared for each phase. The approach suits privacy- or communication-limited control.
arxiv-2509-03012:
Uddeshya Upadhyay proposed a 2025 framework, shortened to UT3, for helping depth-estimating software adapt while it works. Robots and self-driving systems use neural networks to judge distance from a single camera. Those networks falter when lighting, weather, or place shifts away from training conditions.

A known remedy retrains the network briefly on each new input, but repeated passes make answers slow. Upadhyay adds an uncertainty check, an estimate of how unsure the network is, to decide which inputs deserve that extra training. Users can also set how often adaptation runs by picking key frames. On a depth estimation task the method matched standard adaptation quality while cutting response time sharply. That balance suits robots with tight speed and hardware limits.
arxiv-2509-03812:
Shadeeb Hossain and two co-authors focus on combining extended reality with AI for remote STEM education and assessment in a 2025 research paper. Extended reality places students in simulated worlds, while adaptive AI can tailor tasks to each learner. Their design is a gamified virtual training space built around immersive, adaptive, hands-on learning.

Rollout runs in four phases: topic introduction, building parts, fault introduction with correction, and finally generative AI driven scenarios. Security and privacy receive a defence-in-depth treatment across client, middleware, and backend layers. Measures include role-based access control, strong AES encryption, multi-factor authentication, and compliance with GDPR or FERPA rules. Risks specific to immersive systems are named directly, from sensor exploitation to virtual harm. Mitigations are embedded at design stage rather than bolted on. Adoption barriers are discussed honestly, from technical complexity to cost and scarce security expertise.
arxiv-2509-03912:
Dazhi Zhou and twenty-three co-authors report, in a 2025 research paper, a huge reservoir of thermal energy in a young galaxy protocluster, seen when the universe was 1.4 billion years old. In today's clusters, most ordinary matter sits as hot gas between galaxies. Simulations predict that gas in younger clusters should be cooler and still gathering, so early heating was expected to be modest.

Using ALMA, the team observed the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect in protocluster SPT2349-56. That effect gauges how hot gas boosts passing cosmic background photons, leaving a dip that measures thermal energy and pressure. The protocluster packs at least thirty dusty star-forming galaxies and three active nuclei into a small region. Its signal implies thermal energy around ten to the sixty-first power ergs, roughly ten times what a settled gas cloud could hold. Substantial heating, the authors conclude, can happen far earlier than theory expects.
arxiv-2509-04312:
Jonathan Meddaugh and one co-author, Elyssa Stephens, study systems whose near-miss paths can be shadowed by tiny sets in a 2025 mathematics paper. In dynamics, a pseudo-orbit is a path with small errors at each step, and shadowing means a real path stays close to it. Here the tracing object is a small-diameter set, a tight cluster of points, whose size stays within a fixed bound. The authors ask which systems enjoy this stronger tracing property.

Two large families qualify: mixing sofic subshifts, symbolic systems built from labeled graphs, and surjective systems with the specification property. In those cases, clusters of just two points suffice. A broader class called subshifts of quasi-finite type also qualifies, widening the result.
arxiv-2509-04512:
Edoardo Pinzuti and two co-authors study how model size affects emotional safety judgments in a 2025 research paper. Systems used near mental health conversations must classify content as safe, unsafe, or borderline, and tag risks across a six-category scheme. Their data set merges several human-authored mental health collections, over fifteen thousand samples, with emotion reinterpretation prompts generated through ChatGPT. Four LLaMA models, from one to seventy billion parameters, were compared under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned conditions.

Bigger models performed best on average, especially on the nuanced multi-label task and without examples. Light fine-tuning, though, lifted the smallest model to rival larger ones in several data-rich categories, while needing under two gigabytes of memory. Private, on-device safety screening looks feasible.
arxiv-2509-04812:
Asset pricing models try to explain returns using risk factors whose strength changes with conditions. Hongyi Liu proposes a deep learning model for that task in a solo-authored 2025 finance paper. The model, called SNAP, is a pseudo-Siamese network that lets alpha, beta, and factor risk premia depend on firm characteristics and macroeconomic states.

A long short-term memory network stores long-term dependencies among informative features. Applied to monthly United States stock returns across five decades, the model beats benchmarks on out-of-sample prediction and Sharpe ratio in the author's tests. Mispricing errors from the model also build an arbitrage portfolio with significant reported alphas.
arxiv-2509-05112:
Writing test cases for software-defined vehicles by hand is slow, and generative artificial intelligence may automate much of it. Denesa Zyberaj, lead author with seven co-authors, present such an approach in a 2025 automotive software paper. Language and vision-language models turn requirements written in natural language, plus system diagrams, into structured Gherkin test cases.

Vehicle signal definitions are standardised through a common specification model, easing integration with testing tools. Generated tests run inside an open, vendor-neutral playground environment. A child presence detection case shows large reductions in manual effort in their evaluation. Human intervention is still needed, a limit the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2509-05412:
What counts as a physical state in gravity is untangled by Jesse Held and Henry Maxfield in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Gravity's constraints make its Hilbert space, the space of quantum states, unusually subtle, especially the rule for measuring overlap between states.

Using simple one-dimensional and reduced models, the authors compare two definitions: states killed by the constraint operators, and states identified up to an equivalence relation. An inner product built by group averaging links the two views and, they argue, is the correct one. A popular alternative inner product can fail to be positive, which they trace to a bad gauge choice. The BRST formalism then organises all these equivalent constructions.
arxiv-2509-06412:
Comparing the research of whole institutions, not just counting papers, is what the Compare framework does, in a 2025 paper led by Moritz Staudinger with five co-authors. The flood of new papers makes it hard to spot overlaps, gaps, and who does what best. Older tools give counts or summaries of single papers, not side-by-side judgments.

Compare answers a user's own questions by pulling from live online sources and citing what it finds. It works at two levels: whole institutions, or single papers. The authors show it in use for groups that need to map their place in a field. They stress that the point is judgment backed by sources, not one more score.
arxiv-2509-06512:
Tiny kinks called jogs can drag on moving dislocations in nickel, and Wu-Rong Jian and two co-authors model that effect in a 2025 materials paper. Dislocations are line defects whose motion shapes how metals harden under strain. Larger-scale models still lack a good way to include jogs.

Molecular dynamics simulations, which track atoms directly, cover many jog shapes, stresses, and temperatures. At low stress, jogged edge dislocations move in a heat-activated, nonlinear way and face a higher energy barrier than straight ones. Oddly, the speed curves for one jog shape at different temperatures all cross at a single point, which separates heat-driven motion from phonon drag. The authors turn this into a simple three-part mobility law with few, meaningful parameters for use in bigger simulations.
arxiv-2509-06912:
Streaming data through a relay without losing packets to bursts of erasures is given optimal codes by Zhipeng Li and two co-authors in a 2025 information theory paper. The network has three nodes: source, relay, and destination. Within any window set by a delay limit, each of the two links can erase a burst of packets up to a known length.

An earlier construction reached the best possible code rate only when the larger burst length divided a certain remainder. The authors construct codes achieving the optimal rate under a different, broader condition relating the delay to the two burst lengths. That condition covers cases the earlier divisibility requirement missed. The result enriches the family of rate-optimal streaming codes for three-node relay networks, a setting that models real-time communication through an intermediate hop where delay is capped.
arxiv-2509-07412:
Zhen Tian and 9 co-authors develop a risk-aware decision framework for self-driving cars in 2025. Proximal policy optimization, or PPO, is a reinforcement learning method that learns driving by trial and error. Standard PPO trains slowly on long driving sequences and can learn poorly, which in driving terms means collisions. Fixed model-based methods, by contrast, struggle with events no one foresaw.

The improved PPO adds a risk-aware mechanism that highlights areas where collisions may occur, plus a risk-attention network that focuses the model on those areas in camera images. A balanced reward function adjusts payoffs with the number of nearby vehicles, encouraging efficient exploration. A safety-assisted mechanism adds a further guard. The authors report the package learns safer driving than plain PPO, aiming at the weak training and low efficiency that held it back.
arxiv-2509-07512:
Naming chemicals and materials inside scientific text is essential work, but labeling enough examples by hand is expensive. Zihan Chen and 4 co-authors present ALLabel in a 2025 research paper. ALLabel helps large language models do entity recognition, the task of spotting named items in text. It picks which examples are worth annotating, in three stages, using different active learning strategies in sequence.

The chosen examples become demonstrations that teach the model through in-context learning. Across three specialized domain datasets, ALLabel beat all baselines under the same annotation budget. Labeling only a small share of each dataset matched the performance of labeling everything. Ablation tests confirm each stage contributes. The result matters for labs that need accurate entity extraction but cannot afford massive annotation campaigns.
arxiv-2509-07712:
COVID-19 vaccines cut deaths sharply, yet many people refused or delayed their shots. Wajid Ali and 5 co-authors model that hesitancy mathematically in a 2025 research paper. Their model follows how people move between three groups over time: vaccinated, willing but unvaccinated, and refusing. Social interaction drives the movement between groups.

The authors fit the model to United States survey data at state and national level. They estimate the rates at which opinions change. They then test how politics, age, and education shift those rates. State political affiliation, age, and schooling all shaped vaccination opinions strongly. The findings show why one national message fits poorly. Public health campaigns can use such models to target the groups whose views are actually movable.
arxiv-2509-07812:
A stop-rotor aircraft takes off like a helicopter, then locks its rotor into a wing for fast forward flight. Kristan Hilby and Ian Hunter present SPERO, a working example, in a 2025 research paper. The concept promises efficiency in both modes, ideal for farm monitoring, search and rescue, and delivery. Aerodynamic and stability conflicts between the modes have blocked it for decades.

SPERO uses a flipping, latching wing and a five-rotor layout. An active center-of-pressure mechanism and thrust-vectored counterbalances keep it stable. An eleven-state flight controller coordinates the shape changes and control changes together. The craft achieved stable transitions in both directions, a first for this class. Beyond the prototype, the authors offer a general design and control framework. Other builders can use it for future stopped-rotor drones.
arxiv-2509-07912:
Eddy Pariguan and 1 co-author apply a classic counting algorithm to quantum-style products of symmetric functions in a 2025 combinatorics paper. The Robinson-Schensted-Knuth algorithm, known as RSK, matches sequences with pairs of tableaux, grid diagrams that encode structure. Quantum symmetric functions extend a familiar algebraic family with an extra deformation.

After reviewing the combinatorial foundations, the authors connect the quantum product with transportation polytopes, geometric objects borrowed from logistics problems about moving goods between sources and destinations. The star product of symmetric functions gains a concrete combinatorial reading.
