Bridges of this kind help algebraists compute with abstract products by counting visible configurations instead, and they often reveal structure that pure algebra hides.
arxiv-2509-08412:
Strong magnetic fields force optimal shapes toward roundness, prove Vladimir Lotoreichik and Léo Morin in a 2025 mathematical physics paper on shape optimisation. The objects optimised are eigenvalues of the magnetic Laplacian, which govern quantum particles confined to a planar domain in a uniform field. A disk is the natural champion, and the question is whether rivals can beat it.

Asymptotic bounds show that any bounded, simply connected domain beating the disk's eigenvalue must see its Fraenkel asymmetry, a measure of non-roundness, shrink to zero as the field grows. Matching results cover domains with a magnetic field on the boundary operator as well. Symmetry emerging in a limit is a recurring miracle in optimisation; here it is proved, not assumed.
arxiv-2509-08912:
Lingyao Li and 3 co-authors characterize user reported risks of language models in the wild in a 2025 paper. Most risk research is lab based and far from daily use. The team instead studies Reddit discussions about seven major chatbots.

Risks are mapped through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, a national guide for AI risk. Valid and reliable is the most mentioned concern, but each product shows a distinct risk fingerprint. Some brands link more to privacy, others to safety or fairness. Rare risks appear as nuanced trade-offs, while common ones feel like direct personal harm. User centered study is urged.
arxiv-2509-09012:
If dark matter particles decay or annihilate in dwarf galaxies, telescopes should see the glow, but predicting its brightness needs the right geometric factors. Fedor Bezrukov, Dmitry Gorbunov, and Ekaterina Koreshkova compute those factors in a 2025 research paper. They start from dark matter profiles fitted to stellar observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies. The fitting solves the Jeans equation, which links star motions to the gravity they feel.

The authors calculate factors for decay and for several annihilation modes. Their analysis newly allows the dark matter velocities to be anisotropic, pointing preferentially in some directions. They finish with simple scaling formulas using only a galaxy's distance, size, and stellar velocity spread. Those formulas apply to any galaxy an observer cares about. Sharper factors mean gamma-ray non-detections translate into tighter, more honest limits on dark matter's nature.
arxiv-2509-09112:
Zhaoxi Zhang and 7 co-authors show character-level perturbations disrupt language model watermarks in a 2025 paper. Watermarking embeds detectable signals in generated text for copyright and misuse detection. Prior removal studies used large edits, suggesting removal is hard.

Small character edits like typos, swaps, deletions, and look-alike letters change tokenization, so one edit can affect several tokens. That makes them far more effective under strict threat models with limited detector access. A genetic algorithm guided attack further improves removal with few black box queries. Defenses face a dilemma, since a suitable perturbation can bypass any fixed defense. An adaptive compound attack defeats tested defenses.
arxiv-2509-09212:
Amir Ivry and 2 co-authors give new scores for audio source separation in a 2025 paper. Listeners judge separation by ear, but lab scores often miss what people hear. Leakage from rival talkers and warping of the target voice both matter, and they trade off.

Two scores split those faults. Fake warps of each clean voice are made, then all sounds are encoded by a pretrained model and mapped with diffusion maps. One score tracks self warp, the other tracks leakage from other sources. Error bounds and confidence ranges are derived for both. On English, Spanish, and music mixes, the scores place first or second of eighteen in matching human ratings.
arxiv-2509-09312:
Clément Contet and 2 co-authors explain tournament solutions with minimal supports in a 2025 paper. Tournaments model pairwise dominance between candidates, alternatives, or teams. Explaining why a candidate wins under a given rule is the goal, in a certified way.

A minimal support is a smallest sub-tournament where the candidate is guaranteed to win no matter how the rest is completed. That acts as an abductive explanation, answering why the winner wins. Six common rules are studied, including top cycle, Copeland, Borda, and maximin. Smallest support sizes are determined, with polynomial algorithms for all but one rule, which proves NP-complete. Supports yield compact, intuitive explanations.
arxiv-2509-09512:
Choosing the best machine learning pipeline for a dataset is itself a learning problem. It feeds on records of past runs. Cynthia Moreira Maia and 3 co-authors built such a record collection, called PIPES, in a 2025 research paper. The popular OpenML repository, they found, lacks pipeline diversity. Its preprocessing steps cluster on a few fashionable techniques, leaving the sample badly skewed.

PIPES instead runs a designed grid: thousands of pipelines covering all combinations of chosen techniques per pipeline stage. The pipelines were applied to hundreds of datasets. Records include timings, predictions, performance, and even error messages. That completeness lets meta-learning researchers model failures as well as successes. The collection is public and built to expand. Better algorithm selection saves every practitioner the compute now burned on brute-force pipeline searches.
arxiv-2509-09712:
Talha Tahir, writing alone in this 2025 study, asks whether a small open-weight language model can learn to deliver Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. That is a form of talk therapy used for several mental health conditions. Training data came from synthetic therapy transcripts written by a larger model. Two post-training methods were compared, supervised fine-tuning and odds ratio policy optimization, each with and without a step of written reasoning.

Four trained versions were tested in simulated therapy sessions and scored on therapy fidelity and empathy by a judge model tuned on human ratings. The odds ratio approach clearly beat fine-tuning and the base model on both scores. Written reasoning helped the fine-tuned models but added nothing for the stronger method.
arxiv-2509-09812:
Xiuzhen Ye and 1 co-author design watchers for nonlinear systems from data alone in a 2025 control paper. An observer reconstructs a system's hidden state from its outputs, a basic need in monitoring and control. Their route first lifts the nonlinear behaviour into a higher-dimensional space where an approximate linear model fits, built through extended dynamic mode decomposition over a chosen dictionary of functions.

That lift always leaves a mismatch, so the authors bound the error from both sides: a fixed part from the finite dictionary and a random part from sampling. Observer gains are then computed through matrix inequalities that guarantee a chosen error decay rate or disturbance tolerance despite the mismatch. Numerical trials confirm the design works and adapts flexibly to different demands.
arxiv-2509-09912:
Changjia Zhu and 5 co-authors put a language model in the reviewer's chair in a 2025 study of academic peer review. Submissions keep rising while expert reviewers tire, so model assistance tempts every venue. The team graded GPT-5-mini against human reviewers on 1,441 papers from two major machine learning conferences, comparing scores, strengths, and weaknesses through calibrated prompts and topic analysis.

The model padded marks for weaker papers yet tracked human judgement closely on strong ones. Hidden instructions planted inside submitted PDFs were also tested as a prompt injection risk. Broad malicious orders barely moved the reviews, but narrow, field-specific plants did twist particular aspects, a split result that captures both the promise and the peril of automated reviewing.
arxiv-2509-10012:
Richard Matthias Hartisch and 3 co-authors optimise soft robot fingers inside a simulator in a 2025 robotics paper aimed at high-speed connector assembly. A finger's give is a design choice that decides whether a plug seats cleanly or jams when parts arrive slightly off position. Trying shapes on real hardware is slow, and flat simplified models cannot score a whole insertion task, so the team designs against task success inside dynamic contact simulation instead.

Tuning the structured finger's geometry and stiffness in that virtual bench widened the window of starting positions the robot could tolerate, more than doubling it. The winning design was then built and checked on a real robot using standard benchmark board tasks. Simulation-led tuning of softness, the authors argue, is ready for contact-rich work.
arxiv-2509-10112:
Ndidi Bianca Ogbo and 2 co-authors model how institutions can buy better coordination in this 2025 paper. Promises made before people act can support cooperation, but only if people join in and keep their word. Institutions hold limited budgets for rewards and punishments, and must split them between drawing people in and policing those who signed up.

Using evolutionary game theory, the authors track how strategies spread through a population under different budget splits. Rewards beat punishments for producing coordination, across the cases studied. The best results came when money was divided sensibly between encouraging participation and checking compliance. The findings speak to any program, such as a technology rollout, that needs wide, coordinated adoption to work.
arxiv-2509-10212:
Alisa Rieger and 2 co-authors set out a research vision for web search on emerging topics in this 2025 paper. Breaking news and fast-moving subjects have thin, shifting information behind them. Search results on such topics can be wrong, biased, or planted, yet people rely on them to form opinions while events are still unfolding.

The authors argue that search systems should help users learn, notice that a topic is still changing, and form views responsibly. They pose three guiding questions: what the current situation looks like, what such systems must do, and how to build them. For each question they point to relevant studies and likely methods, and they close with the challenges the program will face.
arxiv-2509-10612:
Star formation shuts down inside galaxy clusters, and Simon B. De Daniloff and colleagues quantify that quenching in this 2025 astronomy paper, part three of the GLACE survey of the rich cluster ZwCl 0024.0+1652. Using multi-object spectroscopy from the OSIRIS instrument on the Gran Telescopio Canarias, they measured emission lines for one hundred seventy-three galaxies at redshift about 0.4.

For ninety-eight star-forming galaxies they derived the relation between stellar mass and star formation rate. About thirty-five percent show suppressed star formation, versus eleven percent outside the cluster. Suppressed galaxies concentrate in the cluster's infall region, especially one infalling structure, while star-forming ones favor the outskirts. The pattern supports a delayed-then-rapid picture: galaxies keep forming stars for a while after falling in, then shut down quickly. Total cluster mass, notably, did not drive the effect.
arxiv-2509-11812:
Giuseppe Meneghini, Samuel Brem, and Ermin Malic follow excitons through a moiré landscape. This 2025 condensed matter paper treats stacked semiconductor layers. A slight twist or mismatch lays a repeating moiré pattern over interlayer excitons. These bound electron-hole pairs can now be watched directly. Theory for their motion in space and time lagged behind.

The authors build a predictive many-body model for one material. It tracks how excitons move and settle across time, space, and momentum. The moiré pattern and the odd band shape are both inside. Flat bands usually trap excitons. Here they speed the spread instead. A bottleneck in energy relaxation keeps excitons hot. Hot excitons travel. Twist angle becomes a dial for exciton transport.
arxiv-2509-12012:
Invisible momentum is precious data at the Large Hadron Collider, and the CMS Collaboration presents DeepMET in 2025, a neural-network estimator for missing transverse momentum. Whatever escapes the detector unseen, neutrinos in the standard picture and possibly dark matter particles beyond it, unbalances the visible momentum sum.

DeepMET learns a weight for every reconstructed particle from its properties, then adds up the weighted transverse momenta and flips the sign. Against the estimators CMS currently uses, the network sharpens resolution by roughly a tenth to a third across many final states. It also trains more easily and holds up better as extra proton collisions pile into the same event, a practical virtue at a busy collider.
arxiv-2509-12212:
Power grid researchers lack test networks to share, because real grids are sensitive and hard to anonymize. Xinyu He and seven co-authors offer PowerGrow in 2025, a generator that invents realistic grids together with the load patterns that run on them, keeping both halves physically plausible.

The method splits the joint problem into stages: first a feasible layout, then time-varying loads, then the remaining attributes. A graph diffusion process builds the structure while an autoencoder compresses load curves for stable training. Generated grids pass power flow checks at a very high rate and survive single-component outage tests better than earlier diffusion models.
arxiv-2509-12312:
Galaxies shaped like the letter X in radio light may hide two giant black holes at once. Prajnadipt Ghosh and fifteen co-authors test that idea in 2025 using double-peaked narrow emission lines, a spectral fingerprint that can betray two active nuclei orbiting in one galaxy.

Among nearly two hundred X-shaped radio galaxies with survey spectra, about three in ten show the double peaks, far above the rate in ordinary galaxies. Line diagnostics say both peaks are almost always powered by active nuclei, implying a very high chance of true dual systems. Companion galaxies in a third of cases point to mergers as the trigger.
arxiv-2509-13112:
Weiming Feng, Zelin Li and Pan Peng solve dominant linear systems in 2025 by reading only a sliver of the input. Dominant rows outweigh off-row sums, a trait in many network flows. Full solves waste time when one entry is all that is needed.

Random methods return one entry within a set error. They need just a small part of the matrix and right side. A matching lower bound proves one factor cannot be cut. Past work needed symmetric forms; the new path covers broad strict and some loose cases. A key use speeds opinion reads in the Friedkin and Johnsen model.
arxiv-2509-13212:
Evan Williams, Peter Carragher and three co-authors extend the BEND influence frame to webgraphs in 2025. Web link graphs shape what search lifts or buries. Analysts lacked shared counts for moves that warp those graphs at scale.

New counts score community moves in BEND terms for link graphs. Two small graphs with SEO-boosted Kremlin-aligned sites test face validity. Scores improve over base BEND in graph settings. The counts give a standard way to log warp attempts via search tactics. Teams can now compare cases in one tongue across studies and track campaigns over time with shared terms.
arxiv-2509-13312:
Zijian Li, Xin Guan and ten co-authors structure web evidence in 2025 with WebWeaver for open deep research. Agents must fuse vast web data into trusted reports. Static pipes split planning from gathering, and bulk drafting drags in noise and false cites.

A planner agent loops gathering with outline revision, tied to an evidence bank. A writer agent drafts section by section, pulling only cited evidence per part. Long-context strain and cite errors fall. Top marks land across three deep research benchmarks. Human-like looping proves key to trusted, well-built reports.
arxiv-2509-13412:
Francisca Espinoza-Rojas, Nathalie Themessl and Saskia Hekker study in 2025 forty asteroseismic binaries in Kepler data, where two pulsing stars share one light curve. Bound pairs would fuse seismology with orbital dynamics for precise stellar traits. Synthesis foresaw near two hundred such pairs; few were found.

Global pulse parameters for both stars are estimated per pair. Gaia matches use spectral peak guesses. Bound tests weigh projected split, parallax fit, and orbital speed gaps. Most pairs prove chance alignments. Two wide pairs fit bound traits with fair odds. Eleven more look like unresolved binaries. Follow-up spectra must confirm the two benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-13512:
The CMS Collaboration reports new particle physics measurements in a 2025 paper from the Large Hadron Collider at CERN. The team studied collisions that produce a top quark and an antiquark together with a W boson, a rare process whose details test the standard model of particle physics.

Using proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS detector, the collaboration selected events with two or three leptons plus jets, including jets from bottom quarks. It measured production rates across many kinematic variables and also measured the leptonic charge asymmetry, the imbalance between positive and negative leptons. The normalized rates match standard model expectations well, while the absolute rates run somewhat high, in line with earlier results.
arxiv-2509-13812:
Yun-Zhi Shen and three co-authors analyze gamma rays around the supernova remnant Kes 78 in a 2025 astrophysics paper, using nearly seventeen years of Fermi-LAT telescope data. Two cataloged sources in the region turn out to be better described as extended sources, and one of them, called E2, lines up with the middle-aged remnant.

E2 was detected at high significance across a wide energy band, and its spectrum fits a curved log-parabola shape. Modeling points to hadronic emission, gamma rays from protons smashing into the dense molecular gas around the remnant, as the dominant source. Part of the glow may instead come from a newly discovered pulsar in the region, whose spectrum also fits a radiation model for spinning neutron stars.
arxiv-2509-14012:
Tamara Lenhard, Andreas Weinmann, and Tobias Koch improve drone detection in cluttered scenes in a 2025 computer vision paper. Generic detectors such as YOLO shine on clean backgrounds. They fade when a small drone hides against tangled scenery or camouflage. Contrast between object and background is weak there.

Their system, YOLO-FEDER FusionNet, fuses ordinary object detection with camouflage object detection features. The features come from the FEDER architecture. The new iteration upgrades the training data with large-scale photo-realistic synthetic scenes plus a small real set. It reworks the feature fusion and tests several YOLO backbones. Adding intermediate FEDER features, especially from one module, with a stronger backbone gave the best configuration. The false negative rate fell by up to about thirty-nine points. Mean average precision rose sharply over the original baseline.
arxiv-2509-14112:
Muqsit Azeem, Jan Kretinsky, and Maximilian Weininger extend sound value iteration to simple stochastic games in a 2025 verification paper. Value iteration computes winning odds or expected payoffs in Markov decision processes and games. Plain iteration gives no certificate of its own accuracy. The sound version fixes that with rigorous lower and upper bounds. It converges faster around probabilistic cycles. Yet it covered neither stochastic games nor models with end components.

The technical heart is handling end components, regions the play can never leave. They need different treatment than in earlier literature. The authors extend the algorithm to both missing cases and add several tweaks. They test a prototype build. Experiments show the potential of the approach on systems whose chance-driven cycles defeat simpler methods.
arxiv-2509-14312:
Andreas Karch and Merna Youssef study energy loss in open holography in 2025, where a quantum theory is linked to an outside bath. Holography maps that setup to gravity with a boundary that lets energy pass through. The joined system is simple enough to calculate in detail.

Karch and Youssef work out how much energy crosses the boundary, expressed as a transmission coefficient. They find a novel duality that swaps weak and strong coupling to the bath. They also quantify loss through quasinormal modes, the ringing tones at which the system settles. Those results give a clean baseline for dissipation, meaning gradual energy loss, in open systems that can be treated with holographic methods.
arxiv-2509-14512:
Zhan Cao and three co-authors explore Laughlin charge pumping in 2025 at junctions of topological materials, where slow change drives exact charge transfer. Pumping has revealed how single materials are classified topologically. Junctions of unlike topological phases remain largely unexplored.

Their junction sandwiches a chiral topological superconductor between two quantum anomalous Hall insulators. A slowly varying magnetic flux drives the pump. With only chiral Dirac modes, one flux quantum moves one unit of charge. When chiral Majorana modes join in, fractional flux steps suffice to pump a unit charge. The fractional step is set by the mode interplay. Pumping signatures could let experimentalists detect elusive Majorana modes through charge counting.
arxiv-2509-14612:
Makarand Diwe, P B Sunil Kumar and Pramod Pullarkat report experiments in 2025 where swimming bacteria push membrane tubes into giant vesicles, soft lipid bubbles used as cell models. Bacteria were chosen to have no sticking interaction with the membrane. Pushing alone shapes the tubes.

Once formed, tubes trap the bacteria inside and persist, protruding into the vesicle. Tube pairs interact and settle into stable bound pairs that orbit each other. Persistent bacterial pushing likely maintains the tubes against membrane tension. Rotation may be stabilised by a mix of pushing and membrane forces, the authors speculate. Active matter inside soft compartments creates structures no equilibrium system would hold, a lesson for synthetic cell design.
arxiv-2509-14712:
Seunguk Yu and three co-authors study offensive language judgement in 2025 on contemporary Korean political discourse. Offensive language shifts quickly, yet detectors are often trained and tested on outdated data. Generalisation to unseen current text is rarely measured, especially for Korean.

A large new data set of current political text anchors the study. Three refined judgement methods, each a representative detection approach run under strong conditions, label the data without a ground truth. Agreement patterns are probed with a leave one out strategy, and pseudo labels serve as a stand in truth for scoring. Disparities among methods show how fragile a single detector verdict is on fast moving political speech.
arxiv-2509-14812:
Yonghong Huang uses orbifold Hilbert schemes to compactify two-dimensional Hitchin systems in a solo 2025 algebraic geometry paper. Hitchin systems are integrable systems built from Higgs bundles, and the cases treated here correspond to five affine Dynkin types. Compactifying means adding well-behaved boundary points so the geometry becomes complete.

The construction yields four rational elliptic surfaces that carry a natural circle-like group action. Huang lists their singular fibers and relative minimal models in a summary table. Remarkably, all four surfaces arise from the second Hirzebruch surface by repeated blow-ups, a standard way of refining a surface. The proof shows orbifold Hilbert schemes are connected, smooth, and projective under suitable conditions, and uses the Hilbert-Chow morphism to resolve the coarse moduli spaces.
arxiv-2509-14912:
Kangdi Wang and five co-authors present a music reconstruction model built around human hearing in a 2025 audio paper. Variational autoencoders compress audio for large generative systems, but open models often ignore how ears actually perceive sound. The result can be weak phase accuracy and a poor stereo image.

Their model applies a K-weighting perceptual filter before computing the training loss, so errors are judged the way listeners hear them. Two new phase losses target stereo coherence and precise phase behavior through its frequency and delay derivatives. Magnitude is supervised across mid, side, left, and right channels, while phase is supervised on the stereo pair. At standard music sampling rates, the model beats leading open-source rivals across many metrics, with clear gains in stereo quality.
arxiv-2509-15012:
Duncan J. Bowden leads a team of twenty authors using a rare double gravitational lens to measure cosmology, in a 2025 astronomy paper. In a double-source-plane lens, one galaxy bends light from two background sources at different distances. The geometry depends on the matter density and on dark energy's equation of state, making such systems independent cosmological probes.

The team models one system from the AGEL survey in detail and derives constraints under two standard cosmologies. Alone, the system gives broad but usable values for both parameters. Adding two earlier double-source-plane lenses makes the largest galaxy-scale sample used this way so far, and sharpens the dark energy measurement noticeably. Combining the lenses with cosmic microwave background data tightens things further, showing the method's promise as samples grow.
arxiv-2509-15312:
Jonas C. J. Zatsch and five co-authors prepare and measure photonic qubits on a silicon chip for quantum network nodes in a 2025 quantum photonics paper. Quantum networks need nodes that process information locally and ship it efficiently between sites. Silicon-on-insulator photonics suits the job because telecom-wavelength photons travel through existing fiber with low loss.

Their chip runs in both directions, preparing arbitrary single- and two-qubit states and performing full quantum state tomography on up to two qubits. Bell states prepared on chip and coupled into fibers exceed ninety-seven percent fidelity. The team also distributes entanglement between nodes by preparing a two-qubit cluster state at one node and tomographing it at the other. The demonstration packages state preparation, analysis, and networking in one integrated device.
arxiv-2509-15512:
Daniela Calvetti leads a team that focuses an inverse problem on the part that matters. Many tasks ask for a whole set of unknown values when only a few are needed. Extra unknowns, called nuisance parameters, can cloud the answer. The team call their fix spotlight inversion, since it lights the part of interest and leaves the rest in shadow.

Their method uses angled projections to cut or shrink the sway of the extra unknowns in a linear model. They show it at work in two cases. One shrinks a large mesh model of a curved equation. The other is local X-ray scanning, where only a small region of the full target is lit. Both cases support the approach.
arxiv-2509-15612:
Yiru Zhang leads a team that picks one voice out of a crowded room. Their task is to write down what a named target speaker says amid overlapping talk. Large audio language models have opened new paths for this task. Yet much room to grow remains inside those models.

The team add two training ideas: step by step reasoning traces and reward based fine tuning. They first build a data set of reasoning traces for the task. The model trains on plain data, then on the traces, then with rewards on chosen data. Tests show clear gains in accuracy from both added stages. The plan suits a task that needs deep listening and speaker sorting.
arxiv-2509-15912:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Francesco Sannino, and Jessica Turner argue that a predicted particle has been hiding in plain sight. The Standard Model's electroweak sector has a trait that implies a light pseudoscalar state, which they call eta W. Such a state would normally suggest a new particle in the spectrum. The trio say none is needed.

They identify the state with one specific blend of the lowest energy states of hydrogen and antihydrogen atoms. The mix has odd parity under a charge and mirror flip, matching the state's traits. In other words, known atoms in a quantum blend already form the predicted object. The claim is compact and testable in principle. It reframes a supposed new particle as a known system in disguise.
arxiv-2509-16312:
Layered graphene under a sideways electric field can host a flat energy band where electrons barely move, a ripe setting for superconductivity. Ming-Rui Li and three co-authors study a minimal model of this system, nicknamed the Berry Trashcan for its flat bottom and steep walls. Under short-range attraction, they find exact ground states with a swirling paired form.

The swirl's handedness locks to the model's Berry curvature, and exact results match computer checks on binding and spectra. The model's algebra mirrors one built for quantum scars. Among its cousins, only this point stays realistic, which makes chiral pairing look natural here.
arxiv-2509-16412:
Robot teams that guard a person in a ring formation cannot keep that ring through a narrow doorway. Zihao Deng and seven co-authors build STAF, a method that lets a team split into subteams, pass tight spots, and reform. Three learning layers handle the split, the coordination between subteams, and each robot's own motion and collision dodging.

Tests in simulated and real indoor and outdoor settings show the team keeps its guard role through hard scenes. The split-and-reform skill is new for such formation work. Results point to robot teams that adapt their shape to the place, not the other way around.
arxiv-2509-16512:
Memory chips that switch resistance with voltage could power brain-like computing at far lower energy than today's designs. Md Tawsif Rahman Chowdhury, Alireza Moazzeni, and Gozde Tutuncuoglu study such devices built on tantalum oxide, comparing layers rich in oxygen with layers starved of it. At atomic scale, defects and ion motion form and break the tiny filaments that set each state.

The team maps which conduction paths dominate and how oxygen balance shifts endurance, spread between cycles, and the number of stable levels. Their bottom-up guidelines link material recipe to device behavior, a practical aid for designing efficient memory.
arxiv-2509-16712:
Mingyang Han and Chunqin Zhou study least-energy solutions on a sphere in a 2025 math paper. Their equation is a super form of a classic one from surface geometry. It carries positive weight functions that shape where solutions can live. The pair first derive a global identity that limits what solutions can do.

That identity extends a known barrier result for a related problem. The team then sort all least-energy solutions when the weights are constant. Non-trivial solutions exist when a spectral value tied to the weights stays below one. The work sharpens the map of when such curved-space equations admit real answers.
arxiv-2509-17112:
Alexander Wang, Chris Donahue, and Dhruv Jain sync music to workout intensity in real time in a 2025 paper. Music can boost drive and performance during exercise. Their system, RISE, rearranges a user's own music so high-energy segments land on hard intervals. It estimates intensity as the workout unfolds and reshuffles segments to match.

A lab study with a dozen participants compared the system with a plain playback baseline. Intensity estimates stayed accurate under the rearrangement. Many users recalled moments when the alignment helped them push through. Adaptive soundtracks could make solo training feel coached, without a trainer present.
arxiv-2509-17212:
Federico Stella, Nicolas Talabot, Hieu Le, and Pascal Fua wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on turning distance fields into surface meshes. An unsigned distance field stores, for each point in space, its distance to the nearest surface. Such fields suit open surfaces well, but reading a clean mesh out of them is hard, most of all when the data is fine and noisy.

Older tools decide each small cube on its own, so they miss surface where the field is vague or noisy and leave holes. The authors' network works in passes instead. Each pass spreads word of found surface, distances, and slopes to farther neighbors, and later passes fix errors. On varied three-dimensional models, the method gave fuller and more accurate meshes than rivals. It also held up at fine resolutions where older methods fail.
arxiv-2509-17412:
Zvi Bern and six co-authors compute how two heavy bodies scatter under gravity in a simplified theory. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in maximal supergravity, a cleaner cousin of Einstein gravity, at fifth order in Newton's constant. The true target is the same math in general relativity, where the integrals are far harder.

The team seeks the part of the scattering angle due to potential gravitons, with second-order self-force effects included. Their tools mix scattering amplitudes, effective field theory, and multi-loop integration by parts and differential equations. The answer comes out as a series around the static limit, which dodges hard special functions. Along the way, terms tied to Calabi-Yau integrals cancel in a striking fashion, while one part obeys a Heun equation. The series for the master integrals carries over to general relativity itself.
arxiv-2509-17512:
A. Chakraborty, Vaibhav Katyal, and B. K. Sahoo compute clock-grade traits of three atomic ions. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets the singly charged ions of calcium, strontium, and barium, all alkaline earth metals used in precision clocks. The traits in play are electric dipole polarizabilities and quadrupole moments of the clock states.

The team uses relativistic coupled-cluster theory and stresses the role of triple excitations, where three electrons correlate at once. Including them proves vital for high-precision values. The pattern of correlations in the quadrupole moments also differs from an earlier study once higher angular momentum orbitals enter. To check trust, they compare computed energies, hyperfine constants, and lifetimes with lab values for three isotopes. Joining the math to measured hyperfine data yields nuclear quadrupole moments that depart from the values in the literature, a result spectroscopists will want to test.
arxiv-2509-17712:
Geonho Bang and seven co-authors teach radar-camera car perception from a LiDAR teacher. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a cost story: radar plus camera is cheap, but its 3D detection trails LiDAR systems. Temporal fusion and knowledge distillation have chipped at that gap, yet motion blur in time and sensor-specific errors remain under-treated.

Their framework, RCTDistill, distills across modalities with three modules. One transfers range and azimuth knowledge while respecting radar's uneven errors in those directions. A temporal module aligns past radar-camera features with present LiDAR features, countering moving-object misalignment. A region-decoupled module passes relational knowledge so features stay discriminative. Together they refine the bird's-eye view maps the student model reasons over. The authors report a student that closes much of the gap to its LiDAR teacher while keeping the cheap sensor suite.
arxiv-2509-18012:
Natalie Behague, Debsoumya Chakraborti, and Jared Leon find how lopsided a loop's colours can be in a dense graph. Their 2025 paper rests on a classic result by Dirac: a graph where each point links to at least half the rest holds a full loop. Colour the edges in a few hues, and one hue must show up oft on some loop.

Past work set a floor for that count at a fixed density. The team pins the best such floor for each density in a broad range. The floor is the least of three terms, each set by density and hue count. Random graph results extend the tale.
arxiv-2509-18112:
Sheng Wong and 3 co-authors bench many model types at reading fetal heart traces before birth. Their 2025 study is the first broad test of its kind for this task. Past work used tailor-made models for the traces, with few checks against broad modern models.

Thousands of short traces feed more than fifteen models, from niche to language based. Tuned language models won most rounds across data levels. When a key womb signal was missing, niche models held up better. The wins cost far more compute, the team notes. Real use must weigh score gains against that run cost.
arxiv-2509-18812:
Neutrino oscillation is a textbook effect: neutrinos switch flavor as they travel. Anca Tureanu challenges the standard account of that effect in this 2025 paper. The usual theory treats each neutrino as a coherent blend of states with different masses. Production and detection, on that view, handle flavor states directly.

Tureanu argues that every line of support for that picture, from the uncertainty principle to wave packet models, in fact implies something else. On her reading, neutrinos are produced as statistical ensembles of mass states. Ensemble members do not interfere, so the blend picture cannot explain oscillation. She notes that oscillation in vacuum can still be framed in theories that take the outgoing states as massless flavor neutrinos. The paper is a dissent aimed at the foundations of a settled topic. It asks the field to re-examine a core assumption.
arxiv-2509-19212:
Multimodal language models that see images as well as text often misjudge safety: they refuse harmless requests or miss risks that are plain in the picture. Zheyuan Liu and six co-authors introduce SafeCoDe, a decoding method that steers generation toward context-aware safety without retraining the model. It works with any model of this kind and adds little weight. The first stage contrasts the real image with a blurred, noised version to spotlight tokens that depend on visual context.

The second stage blends scene-level reasoning with token-level adjustment, shaping refusals to match the predicted safety verdict. Across several model families and safety benchmarks, SafeCoDe improved refusal behavior where refusal was warranted and reduced needless refusals. Helpfulness on ordinary tasks was preserved. The authors present the method as a practical patch for a persistent gap in multimodal safety alignment.
arxiv-2509-19412:
Turning musical content into a readable printed score, called engraving, is essential wherever a human will play the music, yet software has barely touched it. Emmanouil Karystinaios and two co-authors formalize engraving for piano music as a bundle of interlocking subtasks. Their system, EngravingGNN, is a graph neural network that handles all of them at once from quantized symbolic input. It predicts voice connections, staff assignments, pitch spelling, key signature, stem direction, octave shifts, and clef signs.

A post-processing pipeline turns those predictions into print-ready files in the MusicXML and MEI formats. On two contrasting piano corpora, Japanese pop and romantic-era repertoire, the unified model scored well across every subtask. Specialist systems each cover only a slice of the job. The authors argue that one shared encoder with light task-specific heads is a scalable route to full automatic engraving.
arxiv-2509-19812:
Synthetic voices can now clone a person well enough to fool family, so tracing a clip's origin matters. Yang Cui and three co-authors build PKDMark, a speech watermarking method that stays light enough for daily use. Signal-processing watermarks are fast but fragile. Deep learning watermarks are sturdy but heavy.

Their route trains a strong teacher model on an invertible network design. A compact student then absorbs the teacher's skill through staged distillation. The student keeps robustness while shedding much of the computing cost. Watermarks that survive editing yet run cheaply could ship inside real synthesis products. Provenance tools are a frontline defense against voice fraud. The paper tries to close the gap between lab-grade protection and deployable cost.
arxiv-2509-20212:
Konrad Janik and Peter Benner wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on learning physics-preserving simulators. Hamiltonian systems describe much of classical mechanics, from planets to molecules. Their measurement data often arrives at uneven time steps. Existing neural integrators that respect the physics, though, are trained on fixed step sizes.

The authors extend one such family, HenonNets, to handle adaptive time steps. Their new architecture, T-HenonNets, stays symplectic by construction, so it respects the geometry of the physics. They also extend it to systems driven by outside forces that change with time. Universal approximation theorems cover both new designs for separable systems. The paper also explains why non-separable systems resist this approach. Numerical experiments probe how well the theory holds in practice.
arxiv-2509-20512:
Lab knowledge evaporates into chat scrollback, and Sangwook Lee and four co-authors build a chatbot to catch it in a 2025 arXiv paper. University research groups coordinate over chat platforms where hard-won answers vanish in the stream. Documentation could preserve them, but upkeep is tedious and searching is painful. Formative interviews confirmed the memory problem across labs.

Their system, CHOIR, is a language-model chatbot with four functions: answering questions from documents, sharing answers for discussion, extracting knowledge from conversations, and helping update documents. Four labs used it for a month, with twenty-one members asking one hundred seven questions and directors updating documents thirty-eight times. A privacy tension emerged: private questions hid documentation gaps from directors. Students also struggled to turn personal experience into general documentation. The authors derive design lessons for privacy-aware lab memory.
arxiv-2509-20612:
Robots that keep learning new skills can break the older plans built on those skills. Daehee Lee and four co-authors present a fix in a 2025 paper on skill incremental learning for embodied agents. Their framework, called SIL-C, keeps skills and the policies that use them compatible as skills improve.

SIL-C uses a two-way lazy learning mapping between what a policy expects and what a skill now does. The mapping updates the link as skills change, so downstream policies gain from better skills without retraining. The authors report gains in policy reuse and generalization across tasks. The paper was selected as a NeurIPS 2025 spotlight.
arxiv-2509-20712:
Training large language models with reinforcement learning depends on keeping exploration alive. Zhenpeng Su and seven co-authors study that balance in a 2025 paper accepted for ACL 2026. Their algorithm is called CE-GPPO, short for coordinating entropy via gradient-preserving policy optimization.

Popular methods based on proximal policy optimization clip updates and throw away gradient signals from unlikely tokens. The authors show those discarded tokens quietly steer how entropy, the spread of the model's choices, evolves during training. Their method restores those gradients while still clipping in a controlled way. The goal is steadier exploration without losing training stability. The paper speaks to anyone fine-tuning reasoning models with policy optimization methods.
arxiv-2509-20812:
Gravitational-wave detectors use squeezed light to beat quantum noise, but the squeezing angle must change with frequency. Yohei Nishino examines a teleportation-based way to apply such filters in a 2025 physics paper. The approach builds on a recent proposal using cascaded quantum teleportation.

Earlier work showed teleportation can mimic filters placed before the squeezed light enters the detector. Nishino asks whether it can also mimic filters placed after detection. With perfect teleportation, he shows the answer is yes. With realistic imperfections, the sensitivity ends up close to the pre-filtering scheme instead. The study clarifies what teleportation can and cannot add to future detector designs, where filter cavities are costly and lossy.
arxiv-2509-20912:
Multimodal models can give the right answer for the wrong visual reason. Tianrun Xu and eight co-authors tackle that faithfulness problem with DeFacto, a 2025 framework for thinking with images. The goal is answers backed by correct visual evidence, not lucky guesses.

DeFacto trains with three complementary setups: ordinary positive examples, counterfactual variants, and random masking. An automatic pipeline finds the image regions a question depends on and edits them to build counterfactuals, yielding a dataset of one hundred thousand examples. If the evidence changes, the answer must change too. Training this way teaches the model to tie its conclusions to what it actually sees, improving evidence-answer consistency.
arxiv-2509-21512:
Competing magnetic links on a honeycomb lattice create frustration that can suppress ordering. Carlos Batista and 2 co-authors study the first and second neighbour Ising model there in a 2025 paper. First neighbours interact ferromagnetically, second neighbours antiferromagnetically. Their tool is correlated cluster mean field theory, adapted for competing links. Magnetization, energy, entropy, and specific heat are all estimated.

The ferromagnetic transition temperature falls toward zero as frustration nears its maximum. Thermodynamic quantities indicate only non stop phase transitions in the range studied. Short range correlations are also tracked by the method. Critical temperatures and transition types agree well with recent Monte Carlo model runs. The paper validates the cluster mean field approach for frustrated honeycomb magnets. The method is cheap to run, so it can scan many settings fast and flag where full sims are worth the cost.
arxiv-2509-21612:
Pooling data across agents makes federated learning sample fast, but each contribution costs its giver. Ariel Procaccia and 2 co-authors model those incentives game theoretically in a 2025 paper. Data differs by source: what an agent gains depends on which agents supplied the samples, not only on the count. Agents aim to hit a hit rate threshold at minimal personal cost. Uncoordinated play produces pathologies.

Pure equilibria may be missing entirely, and the best of them can cost far more than cooperation. The cost minimizing contribution vector is analysed and shown NP-hard to compute. A polynomial time linear program achieves a logarithmic approximation instead. A pay what you contribute rule, paying each agent its sample cost, pairs with that program. Together they steer collaboration toward fast outcomes.
arxiv-2509-21712:
People set privacy limits differently when an AI agent shares information on their behalf. Bingcan Guo and 3 co-authors elicit those limits in a 2025 study. General privacy norms miss context dependent trade offs in disclosure. Their approach probes limits through a discriminative task. Communication roles and delegation settings vary between subject groups in the design.

Hundreds of limits were collected from participants across many scenarios. Communication roles sharply influenced sensitivity to disclosure granularity or identifiability, depending on whose information was shared. AI delegation heightened sensitivity to disclosed identifiers, as did individual need for privacy. The analysis reveals how delegation shifts personal limits. Aligning AI systems with human privacy preferences is the wider goal. When a tool speaks for a user, the line for what may be shared can move, and this work maps that move.
arxiv-2509-21912:
Steering a generative model toward wanted outputs, called guidance, is easy to state and hard to do exactly for discrete data like text. Zhengyan Wan and five co-authors present an exact route in this 2025 paper, published at ICLR 2026. Existing guidance for discrete flow matching leans on a first-order approximation. In discrete spaces that shortcut can stray far, since values jump instead of sliding.

The authors derive the exact transition rate for the target distribution, given a trained discrete flow model. Their guidance then needs only one forward pass at each sampling step, a clear efficiency gain. The frame is broad: older guidance methods appear inside it as special cases. It also applies directly to masked diffusion models, a close cousin. Tests cover energy-guided simulations and preference alignment for image generation from text and for multimodal understanding, where the method performed well.
arxiv-2509-22012:
Samanyu Tirumala and five co-authors build a fast simulation tool for tungsten, the metal favored for the walls of fusion reactors. Inside a reactor, tungsten faces intense radiation plus a plasma of helium and hydrogen. Those light gases gather into tiny defect clusters that change the metal over time. Following that evolution needs large molecular dynamics simulations, which need a fast and faithful interaction model.

The team fitted an empirical potential of the embedded-atom type for the three elements together. The fitting targets quantum-level calculations of the formation energies and swelling volumes of small gas-filled defects. With the new potential, they built a thermodynamics-based model that predicts the energetics of gas-filled voids in the metal. Molecular dynamics runs with the potential confirmed the model's predictions. The tool is meant for studying how reactor tungsten ages under irradiation and gas exposure.
arxiv-2509-22112:
Jingrui Ye and seven co-authors present a model that generates three-dimensional objects together with their surface materials. Industry demand for 3D assets is growing, and recent large reconstruction models can build shapes quickly from generated views. Those models, though, output colored surfaces with lighting already baked in, so the assets cannot be relit in a new scene. Real use needs the material itself: base color, roughness, and metalness.

The team's Large Material Gaussian Model starts by fine-tuning a multi-view diffusion model that produces material images, guided by depth and surface-direction maps. From those views, a Gaussian representation carries each material channel alongside the geometry, in step with a two-dimensional splatting scheme. The rebuilt point cloud can then be rendered under fresh lighting maps for dynamic relighting. In experiments, the generated materials looked better than baselines and modeled materials more faithfully.
arxiv-2509-22712:
Zihan Wei and Tapabrata Chakraborti fight demographic bias in skin lesion classifiers by normalizing skin tone. Models trained on unbalanced data can favor certain races, ages, or genders. Most fixes trade accuracy for fairness, help one attribute only, or sit outside the learning process. Their method estimates each image's skin tone type with the Individual Typology Angle. Tones are then adjusted toward target tones to balance the data, with augmentation on top.

A meta-learning framework prunes network channels jointly with that balancing. Inner loops prune local channels; outer loops reweight each sensitive attribute by group variance. On the ISIC2019 data set, fairness improved across several attributes at once, with little accuracy loss.
arxiv-2509-22812:
Kai Zhang and 3 co-authors add a self-correction step to reinforcement learning for chest X-ray reports. Writing these reports needs sharp image reading, temporal reasoning, and precise text. Fine-tuning alone does not target clinical accuracy directly. Their algorithm, EditGRPO, mixes on-policy exploration with off-policy guidance. During training rollouts, it injects sentence-level corrections into the model's own drafts.

That mixed approach eases the classic exploration dilemma and wasteful sampling of reinforcement learning. Applied to a mid-size vision-language model, it beat both fine-tuning and plain GRPO on clinical metrics across four data sets. Gains grew larger on unseen data sets, which suggests strong out-of-domain generalization.
arxiv-2509-23412:
When machines grade essays, their written reasons can be compared with human reasons for the same scores. Haowei Hua, Hong Jiao, and Dan Song run that comparison on a large-scale test. Several large language models, GPT-4o and Gemini among them, grade the essays. Scoring accuracy is measured with standard agreement statistics. Rationale similarity is scored by cosine similarity on text.

Embeddings of the rationales also get clustered to find thinking patterns. The study hunts causes of scoring inconsistency between human and machine raters. Findings aim to clarify how each side reasons about quality. Better rationale checks could improve trust in automated scoring.
arxiv-2509-23512:
Factories that run jobs through the same machine order face a classic scheduling puzzle. J. A. Alejandro-Soto and 2 co-authors bound how fast such a permutation flowshop schedule can finish. Using a matrix form of the problem, they derive an upper bound on the makespan and a general way to build lower bounds. The lower-bound route solves a min-max or max-min expression over sets of paths.

For one family of path sets, that expression can be solved in polynomial time when some parameters stay bounded. On the Taillard and VRF benchmark sets, the method improved most bounds on record. The upper bound also sharpens counts of possible makespan values and supports progress on a conjecture of Taillard.
arxiv-2509-23712:
Payment fraud hides inside streams where both the order of events and the gaps between them carry clues. Gholamali Aminian and 10 co-authors built FraudTransformer, a GPT-style sequence model shaped for transaction streams. A dedicated time encoder embeds absolute timestamps or gaps between events. A learned positional encoder keeps the relative order of the stream intact.

On an industrial data set with tens of millions of transactions and side events, the model beat four strong classical baselines, including gradient boosting tools. It also beat transformer variants missing either the time or the position part. On held-out data it posted the best AUROC and PRAUC scores.
arxiv-2509-23912:
Combining logics by fibring has a neural twin, and nobody had proved the two truly correspond. Ouns El Harzli and 4 co-authors close that gap. Fibring modal logics merges countable families of logics into one fibred language with shared semantics. Fibring neural networks, inspired by it, lets one trained network's activations set another network's weights, whose outputs feed back in.

The authors formalize fibred models compatible with fibred networks. From the correspondence they derive non-uniform expressiveness results for graph neural networks, graph attention networks, and transformer encoders. Their longer aim is to read the logical theories networks learn with the tools of computational logic.
arxiv-2509-24012:
Forecasting how a model's score on generative tasks will grow with training is harder than tracking its loss. Rylan Schaeffer and 3 co-authors propose three pretraining scaling laws for pass-at-k on generative evaluations, such as math solving and software tasks. The laws use pretraining compute, model size plus tokens, or the log likelihood of gold reference solutions. The sampling count k itself acts as a lever that shifts the scaling behavior.

The gold-likelihood law stayed stable across about five orders of magnitude, far longer than the other two. All three predicted comparably overall. The authors also prove the compute law is the compute-optimal envelope of the size-and-tokens law.
arxiv-2510-00112:
A. Comastri and a team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper on black holes found by the James Webb Space Telescope. Many of these early active galaxies shine in infrared light yet vanish in X-rays. That X-ray weakness is a puzzle, since growing black holes usually glow in both. The team stacked deep Chandra telescope data to hunt for a faint shared signal.

They combined data on 50 type-1 and 38 type-2 active galaxies in two deep sky fields. For the type-2 group, a signal finally appeared in the hardest X-ray band. The pattern fits gas so thick that only the most piercing X-rays escape. The type-1 group stayed silent even after stacking, deepening the mystery around it. The work suggests at least some early black holes hide behind near-total blankets of gas.
arxiv-2510-00412:
Gwangyong Gwon wrote this 2025 mathematics paper proving that a natural question about polynomial maps has no algorithmic answer. Start a polynomial dynamical system at an integer point and iterate it forever. The orbit either runs on endlessly or eventually falls into a repeating loop. Gwon asks whether any program could always decide which fate a given system meets.

The proof starts from Turing machines and their eventual periodicity, itself shown undecidable here. That undecidability then transfers to orbit finiteness for systems on infinite tuples of integers. No algorithm can settle the question in general, however cleverly it is built. Results like this map the hard boundary between dynamics and computation theory. They warn that long-term prediction questions can be impossible in principle, not merely hard in practice. The paper is short, but its conclusion is absolute.
arxiv-2510-00512:
Yuanfang Xiang and Lun Ai published this 2025 paper on predicting how cells respond when genes are perturbed. Such predictions test our mechanistic grasp of the cell, yet data and curated knowledge often disagree. Noise, wrong labels, and gaps make naive integration brittle. Their framework, ALIGNED, fuses neural learning with symbolic knowledge under abductive learning.

The system aligns predictions against both the data and the knowledge base at once. A balanced consistency score grades that double agreement fairly. Knowledge itself gets refined systematically when the data keeps overruling it. In tests, ALIGNED beat leading methods on the balanced consistency measure. It also rediscovered biological relationships that experts recognize as meaningful. The authors argue the approach moves past black-box prediction toward transparent, evolving biological understanding. Future extensions could plug in protein interaction or metabolic networks as the knowledge side.
arxiv-2510-00612:
Jan Korbel, Remah Dahdoul, and Stefan Thurner published this 2025 paper modeling elections as a physics phase transition. Voters feel two forces: neighbors who think alike, and the pull of two rival campaigns. The setup maps exactly onto a classic random-field magnet model. The authors ask when campaign money tips the whole electorate into polarization.

Past a critical spending level for both parties, local influence stops mattering. Outcomes then mirror the campaigns' shares of aligned voters, regardless of the totals spent. A hysteresis band appears where incumbency, not spending, decides the result. Calibrated on United States House elections from nineteen eighty to twenty twenty, the threshold lands near one point eight million dollars. Races crossing that line surged in twenty eighteen and twenty twenty. The model reads recent polarization as a spending-driven regime change.
arxiv-2510-00712:
Mphako-Banda, Kriel, and Alochukwu introduce a new graph colouring parameter in this 2025 arXiv paper on discrete mathematics. Proper colourings forbid any edge joining two vertices of the same colour, and the chromatic number counts the fewest colours needed. Their k-defect number relaxes that rule in an edge-centred way: it is the smallest number of colours in a colouring with exactly k monochromatic edges, nicknamed bad edges. Setting k to zero recovers the chromatic number.

The authors establish basic properties of the parameter and derive bounds for trees, cycles, and wheels. They generalize several classical chromatic-number results to the framework. A curious feature emerges: for some graphs and positive k, no colouring achieves exactly k bad edges, however many colours are allowed. They map impossible ranges for bipartite and complete graphs, and they pose open questions on bounds for other graph families.
arxiv-2510-00912:
Hofmann and Tholen generalize Lawvere's notion of Cauchy completeness to normed categories in this 2025 arXiv paper on category theory, dedicated to Robert Paré. Lawvere's 1973 insight read metric spaces as categories enriched over the extended real half-line. Completeness of a metric space then became representability of adjoint distributors, which for ordinary categories is the idempotent-split property. Lawvere also sketched normed categories, enriched over normed sets, and the two threads were never joined.

The authors join them for any commutative quantale in place of the half-line. Their main theorem characterizes Lawvere completeness for categories enriched over normed sets over that quantale. They also improve recent results on normed convergence of Cauchy sequences in two major examples. Concrete corollaries show that categories of Lawvere metric spaces under natural norms are Cauchy cocomplete. The paper closes a conceptual gap that had stood since Lawvere's paper.
arxiv-2510-01112:
Desmond and Ramsey argue that astrophysics should move from correlation to causation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Galaxy studies usually link properties statistically, then test theories against those links. Correlations alone cannot say which properties drive which, in what direction, or whether hidden confounders fake a link. Causal discovery, a method common in genomics and epidemiology, is built to recover exactly that structure, yet astronomy barely uses it.

The authors adapt a hybrid causal discovery algorithm for astrophysical data and test it on mock catalogues, reaching about ninety percent accuracy. They then apply it to roughly half a million low-redshift galaxies from the NASA Sloan Atlas. The recovered causal graph supports a hierarchical, mass-driven picture of galaxy evolution. It also separated physical mechanisms that pure correlation analysis leaves degenerate, showing the method's added value.
arxiv-2510-01312:
Saad updates the reference tables that track how quark and lepton properties change with probing energy. Couplings and masses are not constants; they run with scale, and model builders need their values everywhere. Fresh particle data with smaller uncertainties motivated a full recomputation.

Side-by-side results use the previous and newest datasets so readers can see what shifted. Values appear for the standard model at a ladder of benchmark scales. The supersymmetric extension gets extra tables at unification scales for several parameter choices. Builders of theories beyond the standard model can test their ideas against the refreshed numbers. Smaller uncertainties in the newest release came from reduced systematic estimates. Mixing parameters run alongside the couplings in the tables. Threshold corrections from supersymmetric loops get an approximate treatment. Grand-unified scales anchor the highest benchmark column. Reference data quietly enables theory testing.
arxiv-2510-01612:
Panchumarthi and co-authors build a question-answering system that writes long, evidence-based answers to biomedical questions. Medical readers need explanations, not one-line verdicts, and the literature grows too fast to read directly. Their framework pairs retrieval with a generator fine-tuned for the biomedical domain.

Specialized embeddings and a fast index fetch candidate passages from the literature. Three re-ranking strategies compete to pick the best context before synthesis. On a standard biomedical test set, the full system beat baselines across several overlap measures. Careful retrieval plumbing, more than model size, drove the gains. BioBERT embeddings speak the vocabulary of biomedical text from the start. Re-ranking decides which evidence the generator actually sees. Parameter-efficient tuning keeps the domain adaptation affordable. Long-form answers can cite their way to trust. Clinicians need synthesis across papers, not snippets from one. Retrieval quality caps answer quality.
arxiv-2510-01912:
Ai, Cai, Zhang, and Yang rebuild hyperspectral images from compressed snapshots in this 2025 computer vision paper. Hyperspectral cameras record a full spectrum at every pixel, which makes them costly and slow. Compressive systems like CASSI capture a coded mixture instead, and software must undo the damage. Fine spectral detail is exactly what reconstruction tends to lose.

Their network, FMU, embeds a flow-matching generative prior inside a deep unfolding framework. Unfolding keeps the interpretability of an optimization algorithm, while flow matching supplies learned image knowledge. A new mean velocity loss enforces global consistency on the learned flow. The authors say this is the first use of flow matching for this reconstruction task. Experiments on simulated and real data beat existing approaches clearly. Gains were strongest for filter-based systems and real CASSI acquisitions.
arxiv-2510-02112:
Jeong and Tae lower the regularity bar for the Vlasov-Poisson equation in this 2025 analysis paper. The equation tracks a plasma or galaxy as a distribution over position and velocity, coupled to its own electric field. Well-posedness theory asks which initial data launch exactly one solution. Rougher data are more physical, but the equations may misbehave there.

The authors prove local well-posedness in Sobolev spaces with surprisingly low smoothness. In dimensions three and up, data slightly above the halfway threshold suffice. The initial distribution needs compact support in velocity, a mild physical condition. Data outside every high-integrability Lebesgue space are still allowed, a genuine extension. Velocity averaging, which smooths the density, powers the argument. The threshold improves on what scaling alone would suggest. Kinetic theorists gain room to start from realistic, irregular distributions. The result sharpens the boundary between solvable and ill-posed for a canonical model.
arxiv-2510-02212:
Zhao, Liang, Tang, Yao, and Kallus train diffusion language models to reason better and faster in this 2025 paper. Masked diffusion models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, but reinforcement learning for them is awkward. Their likelihoods resist the tractable forms policy optimization wants. The framework, DiFFPO, routes around that with surrogate policies.

Surrogates trained by off-policy reinforcement learning approximate the true diffusion policy with usable likelihoods. A two-stage likelihood approximation, corrected by importance sampling, sharpens that estimate further. The generalized algorithms gain sample efficiency and task performance over prior baselines. A second idea trains the sampler itself: the model learns to set its own inference threshold per prompt. That exploits the multi-token prediction these models naturally offer. Speed then adapts to difficulty instead of following a fixed schedule. Diffusion language models get both sharper reasoning and cheaper decoding from one training scheme.
arxiv-2510-02412:
Sienicki and Sienicki dispute a claimed loophole in Bell theorem reasoning. Their 2025 comment examines a model built on hierarchical arithmetics. Changing arithmetic changes how probabilities combine across levels. That formal starting point is sound, they grant. A mapping must translate probabilities between the levels. The target paper fixes that mapping by importing the Born rule. It also imports a standard quantum distance measure. Both tools come from the very theory under challenge. Quantum correlations then appear because they were built in.

The comment calls the result a hybrid framework. It mixes classical probability inside each measurement context with exotic rules across contexts. Bell theorem assumes classical probability throughout its scope. A model that drops that premise sits outside the theorem. It therefore cannot count as a genuine counterexample. Engineered agreement is not new physics. The critique defends careful premise checking in foundations debates.
arxiv-2510-02512:
Tian, Ganguly, and Macdonald retrieve ready made query variants instead of generating them. Their 2025 information retrieval paper improves query performance prediction. Predicting whether a search will succeed guides system choices. Variant queries with similar needs can sharpen that prediction. Generated variants may drift off topic or hallucinate. The team retrieves variants from a large training query set instead. A second hop through shared relevant documents widens recall. Those two hop variants track the target information need closely. Experiments ran on the TREC Deep Learning benchmarks from two years.

Retrieved variants beat the best generated variant methods clearly. Gains reached about twenty percent on neural ranking models. MonoT5 was one of the rankers showing the benefit. Real query logs make the approach practical for deployed systems. Not every target query finds good variants, they note. Coverage limits remain for rare information needs. Retrieval offers a grounded alternative to synthetic variants.
arxiv-2510-02912:
Zou and co-authors trim the visual load of multimodal language models. Such models turn images into long strings of visual tokens. Long strings make every answer slower and costlier. Pruning drops tokens, but common methods chase the flashiest spots. They keep near-duplicate tokens around a few highlights. Under heavy pruning, accuracy falls off a cliff. Their framework, HoloV, takes a wider view.

HoloV splits the token budget across spatial crops of the image. Each region keeps a fair share of its tokens. The kept set thus covers the scene as a whole. The method plugs into existing models without retraining. Tests spanned many tasks, model designs, and pruning levels. HoloV beat the best prior methods across that range. One model kept nearly all its skill after losing most tokens. Only about one token in nine survived that cut.
arxiv-2510-03512:
Tackney and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper comparing ways to fill missing outcomes in randomized clinical trials. Trials lose data when patients skip visits or drop out, and analysis must guess the gaps fairly. The team ran two simulation studies that mimic real trial data with nonlinear patterns and skewed repeated measures. They compared complete case analysis, standard imputation, predictive mean matching, and machine learning imputers such as random forests and boosted ensembles of trees.

Without treatment and covariate interplay, complete cases gave trustworthy answers in their runs. Machine learning imputers sometimes cut error in nonlinear settings but broke down in others, with biased effects or wrong standard errors. A popular matching method also misbehaved under its default settings. Filling data separately by treatment arm fixed several failures when interplay was present. Trial statisticians get a clear warning: flexible imputers need checking, not blind trust.
arxiv-2510-03612:
Jiang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper showing that AI web agents can be steered by editing a listing's picture and text. Such agents rank products and pick content for users, so a seller who biases the pick gains advantage. The attack assumes no insider access: the adversary edits only their listing, with no view of the agent's internals. Their method pairs image perturbations with wording that exploits biases baked into models by human feedback training. The team tested agents built on commercial and open vision language models.

The attack beat single channel baselines on movie and shopping tasks. Manipulation succeeded in up to seventy one percent of attempts. Detection stayed low: models hunting for manipulation caught about a quarter of cases. The results span proprietary and open agents, so the weakness looks structural rather than vendor specific. Platforms deploying shopping agents need defenses before steering becomes a marketing trick.
arxiv-2510-04112:
Pan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a numerical scheme for gas flows that gravitate toward themselves. Self-gravitating Euler equations model star formation and supernova remnants, but their time-dependent gravitational potential makes structure preservation hard. A good scheme should hold a polytropic equilibrium exactly and conserve total energy, in several dimensions without assuming spherical symmetry. The authors build a local discontinuous Galerkin method achieving both at high order.

Well-balancing comes from splitting the potential into equilibrium and perturbation parts, with a modified numerical flux and source discretization. For energy conservation, they rewrite the energy equation in conservative form and design the energy flux through the weak formulation. Two- and three-dimensional tests verify shock capturing, high-order accuracy, exact balance, and energy conservation. Structure-preserving methods matter because small energy leaks corrupt long astrophysical simulations.
arxiv-2510-04212:
Qiu and Yao present this 2025 arXiv paper explaining a notorious failure of low-precision transformer training with Flash Attention. Low-precision formats cut memory and boost speed, so labs push attention into BF16 and feed-forward layers even lower. Yet one long-standing configuration reliably ends in catastrophic loss explosion. The authors give the first mechanistic account of why.

Inside the attention mechanism, representations collapse toward similar low-rank forms during training. At the same time, low-precision rounding errors are biased rather than random, so they accumulate in one direction. The two effects feed each other, corrupting weight updates until training derails. To test the diagnosis, the authors make a minimal change to Flash Attention that counteracts the rounding bias. That single change stabilized the previously failing training runs. A confirmed mechanism converts folklore about low-precision instability into an actionable fix.
arxiv-2510-04412:
Takayuki Hibi and Peter Schenzel wrote this 2025 paper in algebra on how modules break into free pieces. A free resolution lists the building blocks of a module and the maps between them. Some resolutions look linear for a stretch, then jump to a higher degree, then look linear again. The size of that jump is called the gap. The pair asked whether the gap could be as large as one wishes.

They built explicit chains of free modules for four elements of a ring, with tests for when the chains are exact. Using those chains, they described the key module of a monomial curve that lies on a smooth quadric surface. The description shows the module is generated in a linear way. Yet its higher relations can have arbitrarily high degree. That example answers the opening question in the affirmative.
arxiv-2510-04512:
Fumio Nemoto and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on bike sharing systems in busy cities. Riders often find empty docks where they need a bike and full docks where they want to return one. The team modeled the system with a quantum generative model, a circuit whose time evolution mimics the data. The model learns how bike counts at each port rise and fall through the day. It also learns how ports move together.

Bike counts are naturally discrete, which suits the quantum circuit encoding well. Once trained, the model can run what if simulations of the whole network. One test added bikes early to ports with heavy demand and tracked the effect. Total rentals across the system rose in the simulation. That kind of forecast helps operators rebalance fleets before shortages bite. The core engine is a Monte Carlo simulation, so the authors see uses far beyond bikes.
arxiv-2510-04612:
Simon Boche and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a mapping system for mobile robots. A robot that moves through the world must track its own pose and build a map at the same time. Their system, OKVIS2 X, fuses camera views with motion sensors as its base senses. It can also take depth from sensors or learned estimates, laser range data, and satellite positions. One framework accepts all feeds without separate pipelines.

The map is a volume of occupied space, built from submaps that tile large areas. That design scales to runs up to nine kilometers in their tests. Alignment terms tie the estimator tightly to the submaps, which lifts both accuracy and robustness. The system can calibrate camera positions online while it runs. On a drone benchmark it took top trajectory accuracy against rival systems. The code is public, so robot teams can adopt the stack.
arxiv-2510-04812:
Grzegorz Kudra and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on disks that stick and slip while spinning on moving belts. Friction drives the motion: a disk slides and rotates on a belt, held by springs to a support. A direct current motor powers the belts, so the energy source is limited. Contact spreads over a patch, coupling the friction force and torque together. The team built a model with friction laws that avoid jumps when sliding stops.

Simulations mapped how the disks behave as settings change. The system shows stick slip motion, mixing slide and spin. Most behavior is periodic, though some cycles run long. The two disks can lock together and move in phase, or settle into counterphase motion. Maps and bifurcation diagrams chart where each regime lives. Dynamics appear in brakes, clutches, and belt drives that squeal or judder. Predicting synchronization helps engineers design chatter out, or harness it.
arxiv-2510-04912:
Ngeyen Yinkfu, Sunday Nwovu, Jonathan Kayizzi, and Angelique Uwamahoro study self-driving challenges in Rwanda in this 2025 arXiv paper. Motorcycle taxis dominate traffic in Kigali, the capital. They weave through traffic and often ignore the rules. A self-driving car there must spot motorbikes quickly and reliably to stay safe.

The team trained four well-known detection models on a custom set of 198 Kigali street images. YOLOv5 gave the best balance of accuracy and speed for live navigation. RetinaNet located bikes most precisely, but it ran too slowly for real-time use. SSD was fastest yet least accurate, while Faster R-CNN was precise but slow. The authors urge larger datasets and simpler models for poorer settings.
arxiv-2510-05112:
Lijuan Jiang and six co-authors make parallel training of giant neural networks easier to tune in this 2025 arXiv paper. Training splits a model across machines in pipeline stages. Each architecture needs its own carefully crafted schedule of micro-batches. Hand-writing those schedules is slow, and fixed presets cannot adapt to new models.

Their framework, FlexPipe, pairs a small domain-specific language with an automated scheduler. Users describe custom schedules compactly, and the scheduler explores alternatives at low search cost. The language also lets new operations enter schedules as needs change. In evaluations, FlexPipe ran up to 2.28 times faster than the popular Megatron-LM framework. It also beat a leading automated pipeline system by up to 1.49 times.
arxiv-2510-05312:
Micheli T. Moura and four co-authors test whether simulations reproduce the universe's most extreme galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. Massive compact galaxies, nicknamed red nuggets, formed early and barely grew afterward. Relic galaxies are their untouched survivors today. The team selected compact massive galaxies in the TNG50 simulation with criteria matching real surveys.

Simulated compacts followed the observed mass-size relation at three redshifts. Their numbers also rose toward earlier times, as observations show.
