Differences appeared in chemistry and motion, though. Observed relics look like outliers in velocity dispersion, while simulated ones stayed uniform across histories. Simulated compacts were all more metal-rich than typical quiet galaxies. Real relics stand out more sharply than their simulated counterparts.
arxiv-2510-05412:
Matthew Elpers shows that surgery slopes fail to identify knots far beyond the three-sphere in this 2025 arXiv paper. A characterizing slope pins down a knot: matching surgeries force the knots to be the same. Some knots, though, admit infinitely many non-characterizing slopes. Elpers generalizes that failure to arbitrary compact orientable 3-manifolds with torus boundary.

For any homotopy class in such a manifold, he produces infinitely many pairs of distinct knots representing it. The paired knots have orientation-preserving homeomorphic zero-surgeries, so surgery cannot tell them apart. Volume arguments show the knot exteriors themselves are genuinely different. The construction extends earlier counterexamples from special manifolds like the product of a sphere and a circle. Characterizing-slope hope therefore fails in full generality.
arxiv-2510-05612:
Pathak and Mankodi teach databases to predict their own query runtimes. Query optimizers pick execution plans using cost models built on static heuristics. Those guesses often miss real performance under complex, shifting workloads. Their 2025 framework replaces the guesses with machine learning on execution plan features.

The pipeline generates parameterized TPC-H queries and runs them in PostgreSQL. Over a thousand queries supply execution traces for training. Scalar, structural, and semantic features describe each plan and query. The team compares baseline regressors, a tuned XGBoost model, and an LSTM. XGBoost wins clearly, landing within ten percent of true runtime in over sixty-five percent of cases. The framework is reproducible and extensible for other database systems. Better runtime estimates mean better plans, lower latency, and steadier service levels. Tree learning on real plan features looks ready for real optimizers.
arxiv-2510-05712:
Jiang and colleagues read the ashes of the first stars in ancient survivors. Extremely metal-poor stars carry the chemical fingerprints of the universe's first supernovae. Those explosions came from Population III stars, the first generation ever formed. Their 2025 study fits the fingerprints with Bayesian inference to recover the culprits.

The team first applied NLTE corrections to the measured abundances. Those corrections shrank mismatches for odd elements like sodium and aluminum. Their framework also handles explodability and uneven model grids without bias. Three homogeneous samples from high-resolution spectroscopy fed the analysis. Fits confirm a top-heavy initial mass function for the massive first stars. They also derive a mass-energy relation for the first supernovae. Energy grows with the square of the progenitor's mass. A new sensitivity metric shows which elements steer the progenitor inference most. Abundance work thus probes early supernova physics independently.
arxiv-2510-06012:
Tschofenig and Guilbeault study how behaviors, ideas, and products spread through social networks in a 2025 paper. They focus on complex contagions, which people adopt only after several contacts have adopted them first. Simple contagions, such as easy information, need just one contact.

The authors build a causal framework that simulates the possible paths a contagion could take and ranks the links and people that matter most. Their central discovery is that complex contagion paths often work in only one direction, even on networks drawn as fully symmetric. The more social proof adoption requires, the stronger this one-way pattern becomes. Spread also tends to run from the edge of a network toward its core, which reverses standard centrality thinking. The framework explains odd patterns in a LinkedIn study of how jobs spread.
arxiv-2510-06112:
Chandrasekaran and three co-authors explain when a hard optimization problem secretly has a convex twin in a 2025 mathematics paper. Some nonconvex problems become solvable after the right transformation, a phenomenon called hidden convexity. Knowing in advance which problems enjoy the trick has been difficult.

The team introduces the Lagrangian dual section, a continuous choice of Lagrange multipliers maximizing the Lagrangian. When such a section exists, the nonconvex problem admits a natural convex reformulation. The proofs lean only on continuity and connectedness, so topology does the heavy lifting. The framework unifies results for inverse spectral problems, including quadratic programs with quadratic constraints and Stiefel manifold optimization. It also covers unbalanced Procrustes problems, a staple of shape alignment. A Lie theory angle ties the spectral cases to the Kostant convexity theorem. New algorithms find globally optimal solutions on curved spaces.
arxiv-2510-06512:
Khare and four co-authors lift per-frame detector scores into temporal property scores in a 2025 computer vision paper. Detectors like YOLO and HuBERT score local properties, like a car in a frame or anger in speech. Users ask temporal questions: did the speaker eventually sound happy, or where does a car appear until a pedestrian shows up?

The authors formalize temporal property scoring over noisy prediction sequences. Their LogSTOP function computes such scores efficiently for Linear Temporal Logic properties. Query matching pairs LogSTOP with YOLO for video objects and HuBERT for speech emotions. It beat large vision/audio language models and other temporal-logic baselines by at least sixteen percent. Ranked retrieval over video objects and actions showed similar dominance. Mean average precision rose at least nineteen percent over zero-shot baselines. Formal temporal logic still outperforms giant multimodal models at structured temporal questions.
arxiv-2510-06612:
Zibo Su, Kun Wei, Jiahua Li, Xu Yang, and Cheng Deng build talking faces that speak many languages. Their 2025 paper addresses speech-driven face animation from audio. Current systems work well in English but falter in other languages. They produce wrong mouth shapes and stiff expressions. English-heavy training data and weak cross-language transfer cause the gap.

Their framework, MuEx, uses speech sounds and mouth shapes as a shared bridge. Sounds are broken into phonemes, and mouth positions into visemes, which both act as universal units. An alignment mechanism links the two sets across languages. A mixture-of-experts design then routes each case to suitable specialist parts. The team also built a test set covering twelve languages. MuEx led on multilingual lip sync while keeping its English quality. It even generalized to languages it had never seen in training.
arxiv-2510-06712:
Fabian Rennecke and Shi Yin study an odd regime predicted inside extremely dense matter. Their 2025 paper concerns the moat regime in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. In this regime, a meson's lowest energy sits at nonzero momentum, which is unusual. Low-energy models can describe the regime, but model artifacts can mislead.

The authors use a two-flavor quark-meson model at finite temperature and density. They propose a clean renormalization scheme that handles the momentum dependence of meson energies. Renormalization conditions matter greatly for consistent results here. Small changes in those conditions can shift conclusions about the moat. The regime's size in the phase diagram also depends critically on how quarks and mesons interact. Their message is cautionary for the field. Claims about the moat regime at zero density can be model artifacts. Careful renormalization is required before trusting effective-model predictions about dense matter.
arxiv-2510-06912:
Alexandros Vassiliades leads a team testing whether language models can build explainable machine learning pipelines on their own. Their 2025 paper prompts three leading systems, from OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek, to design training workflows. Two tasks anchor the study. One predicts driver alertness from behavior features, and the other is a multilabel problem on yeast data.

Each model wrote pipelines for four standard classifiers, from random forests to recurrent networks. The team scored the outputs on predictive quality and on explainability. Explainability was measured with SHAP, which credits each feature for its influence. Two SHAP measures mattered most, namely how faithfully the credits track the model and how few features dominate. The language models produced pipelines that matched hand-built baselines. Their explanations stayed faithful and sparse, like the human versions. The study marks a check on autonomous data science. It also flags limits that follow-up work should probe.
arxiv-2510-07312:
Motwani and co-authors present h1, a method that teaches language models to reason over much longer chains. Their 2025 paper starts from a clear weakness. Models handle short problems well but fade as steps multiply. Step-by-step supervision is costly, and prompting tricks scale poorly. The team instead builds long problems by composing short ones into dependency chains. Abundant easy data thereby becomes hard training material of any length.

Training uses reinforcement learning with rewards only for final answers. A curriculum raises the chain length automatically as the model improves. Models trained on composed grade-school math problems gained up to about double accuracy on harder contest benchmarks. Skills also transferred to unrelated reasoning gyms and long-context tests. Gains held even when many attempts were allowed, showing genuinely new solution paths. The approach offers a cheap route to long-horizon reasoning without new human-labeled data.
arxiv-2510-07512:
Nelson, Rajakumar, and Gullans find a sharp depth limit beyond which noisy quantum circuits forget everything fed into them. Their 2025 paper studies encoding information with random noisy circuits. It was known that very deep noisy circuits without resets output near-total noise, erasing all input. The open question was whether shallow circuits can preserve information by encoding it into an error-correcting codespace as they go. Simulations reveal a clean phase transition. Below a critical depth that scales inversely with the noise rate, quantum information survives the encoding.

The authors then prove this trade-off is the best any noisy circuit can achieve when encoding a constant rate of information. Random circuits, often treated as toy chaos generators, are therefore optimal noisy encoders in this precise sense. The result ties the breakdown of long-range entanglement to the encoding failure at the same threshold.
arxiv-2510-08612:
Devang Dhanuka reviews how large language models are changing teamwork in software development in a 2025 arXiv paper. The study reframes and updates earlier work with literature and case studies current as of 2025. It follows collaboration across the full software development life cycle, from planning to release. Tools examined include AI project management agents and assistants that generate code.

Evidence comes from two case studies, a team survey, industry examples, and a literature review. Dhanuka finds language models raise efficiency by automating documentation and other repetitive tasks. Communication clarity and cross-functional collaboration also benefit, according to the gathered evidence. New challenges arrive alongside: model limitations and privacy concerns head the list. The paper sets out research questions, evaluates threats to validity, and suggests future directions. Domain-specific customization, deeper tool integration, and trust and security strategies are proposed.
arxiv-2510-08712:
Zheheng Liu, Nicola Vigano, Henry Proudhon, and Wolfgang Ludwig set out the math behind topo-tomography in a 2025 arXiv paper. This X-ray method maps grain shape and crystal tilt inside materials made of many small crystals. It uses diffraction, the bending of X-rays by crystal planes, at a synchrotron light source. Turning its raw data into 3D maps of grain tilt lacked a firm theory until now.

The team derives formulas for the imaging geometry under a simple diffraction model. Grain shape, small lattice turns inside each grain, and elastic strain all enter the formulas. Small-strain and small-grain shortcuts then simplify the math a great deal. The worked images match views of a slightly warped grain volume, they show. Fourier tools on that volume reveal when tilt field recovery can work. They also give a lower bound for sampling fineness, checked in simulations.
arxiv-2510-08812:
Kim and colleagues design a planner that lets a distant spacecraft run its own science, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Deep space probes face radio delays of an hour or more, so ground teams cannot steer them live. Samples gathered in a search for life can also spoil within days. The planner must therefore decide on board which instrument to run next, under deep uncertainty about what the samples hold.

Their framework treats the problem as decision making with partial information, a standard formalism for acting under uncertainty. A Bayesian network, a compact web of linked probabilities, organizes the messy measurements inside it. Policies are computed on Earth before launch, so they can be checked thoroughly. Tested on the proposed Enceladus Orbilander life-detection suite, the planner cut sample identification errors by nearly forty percent against the mission's baseline plan, and it held up when samples arrived off schedule.
arxiv-2510-09012:
Ma and a large team improve image generators by listening to the information content of each token, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autoregressive image models emit a picture token by token, borrowing machinery built for text. The authors observe that image tokens differ from words: each carries less information, and that information is spread unevenly across the picture. Treating all positions alike wastes effort on empty sky and starves busy detail.

Their decoding strategy adjusts the randomness of sampling, called temperature, according to the spatial entropy of the token distribution at each step. Busy regions get careful, conservative choices, while dull regions move fast. A second rule uses the same entropy signal to accept or reject drafted tokens in speculative decoding, a shortcut that guesses ahead. The combination raised quality and speed together across many models, reaching near-lossless output at a fraction of the usual acceleration cost.
arxiv-2510-09212:
Li and co-authors teach a video generator to learn from its own mistakes so it can produce endless, steady footage, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Long video generators drift because each new frame is built on their own imperfect earlier frames, while training only ever showed them clean footage. Errors compound until scenes repeat or dissolve. Most fixes patch symptoms with handcrafted tricks. This team closes the gap between training and use.

Their method, error-recycling fine-tuning, deliberately injects the model's past errors into training inputs, simulating the messy trajectories it will face when generating. The errors are collected cheaply and stored in a replay bank, then resampled to supervise new corrections. The model learns to notice and fix its own drift. The system scales clips from seconds to effectively infinite length at no extra generation cost. It accepts text, audio, and skeleton guidance, and led on three benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-09512:
Mark Jones and Jannik Schestag study conservation planning with evolutionary trees in a 2025 arXiv paper. The phylogenetic diversity of a set of species is the total branch length connecting them on their family tree. Choosing small sets with maximal diversity tells planners where scarce conservation money does the most good. Real cases add two complications: relationships may form a network rather than a tree, and a food web constrains which species can survive together.

The authors define decision problems that combine a phylogenetic network, a food web, and targets for set size and diversity. A chosen set must also stay viable, meaning enough prey species survive to support the predators. They map the parameterised complexity of these problems, asking which combinations of parameters make them efficiently solvable. For several favourable combinations they give fixed-parameter tractable algorithms, completing a dichotomy that separates the tractable cases from the rest.
arxiv-2510-09612:
Vikash Sahu, Waseem Lone, and Amit Verma develop wavelet tools tied to a special transform in a 2025 arXiv paper. The special affine Fourier transform generalises the classic frequency analysis of signals with extra parameters. Its multiresolution analysis gives a structured way to build orthonormal bases, sets of perfectly independent building blocks, for the space of finite-energy signals.

Motivated by the need to sample band-limited signals in this transform domain, the authors establish a sampling theory for it. Sampling theory states when a continuous signal can be rebuilt exactly from discrete snapshots. They construct multiresolution structures inside the transform domain that support the formation of orthonormal wavelet bases. A method for building such bases in the signal space is proposed, and the theory is demonstrated through worked examples. The authors present the framework as a foundation for advanced signal analysis in this generalised frequency setting.
arxiv-2510-10212:
Yu. Kulinich and co-authors compute the global signals of the first molecules in this 2025 arXiv paper in cosmology. In the dark ages, before the first stars, the first molecules formed: hydrogen, hydrogen deuteride, and helium hydride. Their spin and vibration lines can create faint global signals that telescopes may one day pick up.

The authors ask how primordial magnetic fields, weak fields that may date from the early universe, change that chemistry. They model how the molecules form and how their energy levels fill up when such fields are present. If the fields heat or cool the gas, the predicted signals shift. The size of the shift tells observers whether a future detection could also reveal the fields.
arxiv-2510-10312:
Ablowitz, Ramesh Gupta, Ziad H. Musslimani, and Nicholas J. Ossi derive a six-wave interaction system in this 2025 arXiv paper in nonlinear optics. Multi-wave interactions describe how light beams exchange energy in a nonlinear medium. The authors start from Maxwell's equations for the electric and polarization fields.

A space-time multi-scale asymptotic expansion then produces a hierarchy of coupled equations for the evolving fields. From that hierarchy they obtain the six-wave interaction system in several dimensions. They also study a space-time shifted reduction of the system, a simpler special case with its own dynamics. Exact reduced models of light-matter interaction feed both theory and the design of photonic devices.
arxiv-2510-10812:
William Acero, Isabel Molina, and J Miguel Marín estimate statistics for small regions in years when no census is taken, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Official statistics often lean on census microdata, which ages badly between censuses. Their procedure replaces the outdated census file with a bigger unit level survey covering the areas of interest and records useful auxiliary variables.

They also develop a mean squared error estimator that accounts for the uncertainty introduced by using the large survey in place of the census. In empirical results, their predictors clearly beat alternatives when census data are outdated. When census data are correct, the predictors stay very close to optimal. The new error estimator also corrects the bias of purely model based error estimators that ignore the survey's own uncertainty. The method targets statistics producers who must publish regional figures every year.
arxiv-2510-10912:
Xinyu Shao and eight co-authors replace the single target point in robot grounding with a heatmap, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language guided robots usually collapse spatial reasoning into discrete points, which makes them brittle to noisy perception and ambiguous wording. Their framework, RoboMAP, turns spatial targets into continuous affordance heatmaps that adapt. The dense representation carries uncertainty about where the target is, and gives downstream control policies richer information to act on.

RoboMAP surpassed the previous state of the art on a majority of grounding benchmarks, with up to a fiftyfold speed improvement. In real world manipulation it achieved an 82 percent success rate in the reported experiments. Across extensive simulated and physical tests, it stayed robust and showed strong zero shot generalization to navigation. The authors argue that carrying uncertainty explicitly, instead of committing to one point early, improves both task success and interpretability.
arxiv-2510-11012:
Sanchit Sinha, Guangzhi Xiong, and Aidong Zhang hand vision language models a reasoning scaffold built from concept trees, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models falter at compositional reasoning: tasks that hinge on how several objects, attributes, and relations interact in an image. Prompt tricks help inconsistently, and borrowing a big language model's reasoning is costly or opaque. Their COCO-Tree method augments model outputs with neurosymbolic concept trees learned from language models, then reasons over them with a beam search like process.

The trees make the reasoning interpretable: readers can see the rationale behind a prediction. The team tested four compositionality benchmarks: Winoground, EqBench, ColorSwap, and SugarCrepe. Across seven open source vision language models of varying sizes, COCO-Tree improved compositional generalization by 5 to 10 percent over baselines in the reported experiments. Structured concepts, the authors argue, supply the linguistic discipline that raw vision models lack.
arxiv-2510-11212:
Gröbner bases are the workhorse of computational algebra, but standard theory lives in polynomial rings, while many algebras prefer their own monomial bases. Joshua A. Grochow and Abhiram Natarajan build the theory natively inside such algebras in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Their setting is any commutative algebra over a field equipped with a notion of monomial and a suitable term order, including Hodge algebras.

Rather than lifting ideals into a polynomial ring quotient, their theory works entirely within the algebra and its monomial structure. Applied to bideterminants, the framework packages standard results cleanly and enables new ones. Once set up, the machinery gives an almost trivial proof of a universal Gröbner basis for the ideal of t-minors, for any t. The nativeness is essential: in the bideterminant basis each minor is a single variable, not a sum of many terms.
arxiv-2510-11512:
Video generators can produce footage of impossible physics, and judging whether a model truly understands physics is hard because wrong motion can still look pretty. Jianhao Yuan and co-authors introduce LikePhys, a training-free evaluation method, in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Their method uses the model's denoising objective as a likelihood: a model that understands physics should find physically valid videos more probable than impossible ones.

The team built a benchmark of paired valid and impossible videos across twelve scenarios in four physics domains. Their metric, the Plausibility Preference Error, is the rate at which a model prefers the impossible clip. That metric aligned strongly with human preference and beat state-of-the-art evaluator baselines. Benchmarking current models, they found they still struggle with complex, chaotic dynamics, though physics understanding improves as capacity and inference settings scale. They released their data and code.
arxiv-2510-11812:
Souradeep Mukhopadhyay and seven colleagues test whether large language models truly reason or merely remember. Models ace classic logic puzzles, but those puzzles fill their training data. The team's 2025 arXiv paper introduces PHANTOM RECALL, a benchmark of twenty-five famous puzzles plus one hundred forty-nine careful edits. Each edit keeps the reasoning structure but changes surface details and the correct answer.

The researchers evaluated eleven leading models, including the GPT, Gemini, and Claude families. On untouched puzzles the models scored near perfectly. On edited ones they fell well below human performance. The failure mode is telling: models confidently recited the memorized solution even when it no longer fit, a habit the authors name phantom recall. They also over-explained simple problems. The team contributes three tools: an automated judge of logical equivalence, a taxonomy of reasoning errors, and a prompting framework built from that taxonomy to reduce the mistakes.
arxiv-2510-12312:
Delgrange, Avalos, and Röpke bring the safety guarantees of safe policy improvement into online reinforcement learning with learned world models, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Safe policy improvement aims to update a decision making policy without risking a drop in performance. Existing guarantees mostly cover offline, tabular settings, far from the deep learning agents used in practice.

The authors develop theory showing that restricting updates to a clearly defined neighborhood of the current policy ensures monotone improvement and convergence in general online settings. Their analysis ties transition and reward prediction losses to the quality of the learned representation. Building on this, they introduce DeepSPI, an on policy algorithm pairing local model losses with regularized policy updates. On the ALE-57 benchmark of Atari games, DeepSPI matched or beat strong baselines including PPO and DeepMDPs. Unusually for a deep method, it does so while keeping the theoretical guarantees that motivated the design.
arxiv-2510-12912:
Arous, Haif, and Arslan tackle self-interference in combined sensing and communication systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting merges radar sensing and data communication in one device that transmits and receives at once on the same band, so its own outgoing signal floods the radar receiver. Canceling that interference without wasting spectrum is the central challenge.

Their design splits the frame between two signal types, one for communication and one for radar, both produced by a single modulator block. They prove that in the radar's affine domain the interfering signal behaves like ordinary white noise, so it can be subtracted with little residue. An iterative windowing step and a later spreading step shrink what remains. Simulations showed better detection probability and more accurate range and velocity estimates than alternatives, at low complexity.
arxiv-2510-13212:
Zhang and co-authors ask which preference data actually help align a language model in this 2025 arXiv paper. Alignment training learns from human preference comparisons, so data quality is critical. Yet teams usually filter datasets with external reward models. They rarely check whether an individual selected pair truly benefits the model being trained.

The authors measure each pair's influence on validation data with a new truncated influence function that corrects the over-scoring of classical influence measures. Their key discovery is that preference data quality is inherently model-dependent: a pair helping one model may harm another. They then propose two simpler model-dependent scoring functions correlated with the influence measure, and combine them to cancel their differing error sources, yielding a practical selection rule. Across alignment benchmarks and model families, training on less but better chosen data improved alignment performance.
arxiv-2510-13312:
Lupart, Aliannejadi, and Kanoulas train conversational question answering with reinforcement learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. In dialogue, user intent evolves across turns and questions are underspecified. A system must interpret context, reformulate queries, and run retrieval with generation. Static rewrite-retrieve-generate pipelines cannot explore or adapt that way.

Their framework, ChatR1, interleaves search and reasoning across turns, learning this through reinforcement learning. Sparse, delayed rewards are the obstacle. They propose an intent-aware reward giving turn-level feedback by matching retrieval and reasoning with the user's evolving goals. ChatR1, on two model sizes, outperformed rival systems across five datasets. These cover topic shifts, evolving intents, mixed-initiative dialogue, and multi-document grounding, scored by several metrics. Ablations confirmed the intent-aware reward's value. Analysis showed diverse reasoning trajectories with skilled search tool use.
arxiv-2510-13512:
Wu, Thareja, Vepakomma, and Orabona study private reinforcement learning from human feedback for language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper adds local differential privacy to preference labels, which can carry personal information. The objective keeps the tuned model close to a base model through a KL penalty. Privacy noise on each label makes learning harder in both offline and online modes.

In the offline mode, their pessimism-based algorithm reaches a suboptimality gap the authors prove is best possible. A matching lower bound confirms no algorithm can do better under their assumptions. For the online mode, they give the first theoretical treatment of this private problem. Their optimism-based algorithm earns a logarithmic regret bound over time. The analysis also yields the first results for the online problem without privacy. Code for the offline method is released openly.
arxiv-2510-13612:
Farrán, Rosales, Tapia-Ramos, and Vigneron-Tenorio introduce P-semigroups, a new family of affine semigroups. Their 2025 arXiv paper works inside the theory of C-semigroups, sets of integer vectors closed under addition. Such semigroups generalize the classic numerical semigroups of one dimension. The authors tie membership in the new family to a finite-state automaton.

Each C-semigroup carries an associated automaton, a simple machine that reads symbols in finite states. Whether the semigroup is a P-semigroup depends on the language that machine accepts. This builds an unexpected bridge between semigroup theory and discrete mathematics. The team also gives algorithms that list all P-semigroups with a fixed key invariant. The invariants used are the Frobenius element, the genus, and the multiplicity. Rooted trees enter the picture as the automaton's state structure.
arxiv-2510-13912:
Carro and a large team find that AI debaters persuade better when arguing for what they already lean toward believing. Their 2025 arXiv paper probes debate as a scalable oversight technique for judging AI claims. Prior debate tests used factual questions, reducing lying to defending a known falsehood. Subjective questions add the missing dimension of the debater's own prior stance.

The team measured each model's prior beliefs before staging any debates. Debaters chose their preferred side, then faced a judge persona built to conflict with those priors. Models mostly picked the judge-pleasing side over their own beliefs, a sycophantic tilt. Yet when arguing aligned with their priors, they persuaded more effectively. Paradoxically, belief-misaligned arguments scored higher quality in pairwise ratings. Sequential debate also biased outcomes toward the second speaker. The findings shape how human judges should read AI debates for training signals.
arxiv-2510-14312:
Mason Nakamura and co-authors present Terrarium, a testbed for studying safety, privacy, and security failures in systems of cooperating language-model agents, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such multi-agent systems can automate tedious work like scheduling meetings. Their nuanced protocols handle private data and user preferences. That creates risks from misalignment and from malicious parties who compromise agents or steal data.

Terrarium revives the blackboard design, an early multi-agent architecture where agents share a common workspace, to build a modular environment for experiments. The authors list key attack vectors, including misaligned agents, malicious agents, compromised communication, and data poisoning. They build three collaborative scenarios and show four attacks within them, showing the framework's flexibility. By letting researchers rapidly prototype and iterate on defenses and designs, Terrarium aims to accelerate progress toward trustworthy multi-agent systems before such systems are widely deployed with real user data.
arxiv-2510-14512:
Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, and Aaqib Saeed present Helmsman, a crew of language-model agents that designs and builds federated learning systems from a specification, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Federated learning trains models on decentralized data without centralizing it, but engineering a system means selecting and tuning strategies for varied data and device constraints, a bottleneck that produces brittle solutions.

Helmsman emulates a research-and-development workflow in three phases. The first is interactive planning with a human in the loop to form a sound research plan. Then comes modular code generation by supervised agent teams. Last is a closed loop of autonomous evaluation and refinement inside a sandboxed simulation. The authors introduce AgentFL-Bench, sixteen tasks for assessing system-level generation of federated learning solutions. In experiments, the generated systems proved competitive with, and often better than, baselines, a step toward engineering of decentralized AI.
arxiv-2510-14712:
Hosseini, Feinberg, and Karlin present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a lattice Boltzmann model for fast, compressible flows of real gases. Lattice Boltzmann methods simulate fluids by tracking particle distributions on a grid, and they are prized for simplicity. High-speed flows of non-ideal gases, though, usually force extended grids or ad hoc fixes that can break physical consistency, such as giving negative dissipation or frame-dependent errors.

The authors keep the simplest first-neighbor lattices. They add a consistent set of correction terms, built through quasi-equilibrium attractors, so the dissipation rates stay positive and the same in every frame of reference. The model remains stable and thermodynamically consistent across many regimes, and it reproduces both Euler-level and Navier-Stokes-level behavior. As a hard test, they simulate a drop struck by a shock at Mach numbers up to 1.47 with quantitative accuracy, a first for this framework.
arxiv-2510-14812:
Tyagi and co-authors close, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a quality gap between two ways of making neural networks sparse. Unstructured dynamic sparse training prunes individual weights wherever it likes and reaches high accuracy, but graphics processors prefer structured sparsity, where whole blocks vanish in regular patterns. The structured patterns, though, can express far fewer weight configurations, and accuracy suffers.

Their fix is to learn one permutation matrix per layer, trained jointly with the structured weights. Permuting a layer's neurons before applying the block pattern unlocks many more configurations at no extra hardware cost. Applied to block, N-to-M, and diagonal structures, the method matched strong unstructured baselines at ninety to ninety-five percent sparsity. Tests covered image classification with a vision transformer and language modeling with GPT-2. Training ran up to 1.21 times faster and inference up to 2.9 times faster in the reported results.
arxiv-2510-15012:
Chu and Kuo revisit, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the theorem that neural networks can approximate anything, and ask what it teaches about where to start training. The Universal Approximation Theorem builds a network as a finite sum of shifted, scaled sigmoids. Tropical geometry reveals that ReLU networks make decisions with a combinatorial structure, differences of tropical polynomials. The authors use the tropical viewpoint to design better starting weights for smooth networks.

Their construction concerns planar binary classification. They build sigmoidal multi-layer perceptrons in the theorem's finite-sum format, initialized so that the decision boundary matches a prescribed shape before any training. Standard training can refine the boundary. The result is a shape-driven initialization that borrows the tropical perspective's insight without adopting ReLU architectures. The paper offers the construction and two-dimensional demonstrations; theory and higher-dimensional versions are left for future work.
arxiv-2510-15212:
Sarah Houdaigoui and Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi improve a thirty-year-old bound in graph theory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A famous theorem by Robertson and Seymour says the graphs that fit on any fixed surface are exactly those avoiding a finite list of forbidden smaller graphs, called minimal excluded minors. Their proof never said how large those forbidden graphs could be, and the only bound since 1993 was double exponential in the surface's genus.

Houdaigoui and Kawarabayashi lower that bound to quasi-polynomial, a vastly smaller scale. The key step shows a minimal excluded minor cannot contain many nested contractible cycles; the old argument allowed a number growing with the genus, theirs only its logarithm. They also bound the graph's largest degree and face sizes for the first time. Side results improve the known limits on its treewidth and on the grid minors it can contain.
arxiv-2510-15712:
Local search can be surprisingly hard when each small improvement is cheap but the path is long. Dominik Scheder and Johannes Tantow study such problems with lexicographic costs in this 2025 arXiv paper. Lexicographic costs make earlier items dominate totals completely, like digits in a long number. For weighted Max-Cut style problems, finding a local optimum is complete for the class PLS. The pair ask which lexicographic problems share that worst-case hardness.

They prove finding a locally maximal assignment for 4-CNF formulas is PLS-complete under lexicographic weights. The result also holds for 3-CNF when two variables may switch at once. They further settle an open question about orbit minimization under commuting permutations.
arxiv-2510-15912:
Jack Cashman, as sole author, sizes program tiles by timing the machine's own memory rather than by slow auto-tuning. Tiling splits loop nests so data reuse fits inside fast cache levels. Auto-tuning finds good tiles but can take prohibitively long, while wrong guesses waste the memory hierarchy.

Latency Based Tiling runs triangular loops to chart how miss ratio scales with working set size, avoiding prefetcher distortion. Sharp latency jumps mark where the footprint outgrows each cache level, giving approximate level sizes that lean low, as expected when caches are shared among processes. Combined with the footprint per iteration, those sizes set the tiles for a subset of the polyhedral model. The implementation in Rust is hardware-agnostic, memory-safe, and adds negligible compile-time cost, Cashman reports.
arxiv-2510-16212:
N Kaiser, in lecture-style notes, works out the Born series for the s-wave scattering length, the single number summarizing how a particle wave scatters off a central potential at low energy. He carries the expansion to sixth order in a dimensionless coupling strength for a class of potentials.

Examples include exponentially decaying potentials and truncated potentials built around one length scale. In favorable cases the exact coupling-dependent scattering length comes out in closed form through special functions, and one scattering problem even solves in elementary functions. The poles of the exact answer mark the thresholds where bound states appear one after another as the coupling grows, tying the perturbative series to non-perturbative physics.
arxiv-2510-16712:
Shivam Ratnakar and Sanjay Raghavendra, working as a pair, measure how often search-enabled language models change their stance during multi-turn conversations. They call this shifting chameleon behavior. A model that agrees with each new leading question cannot be trusted as a steady source of answers.

The pair built a benchmark of about seventeen thousand question and answer pairs across roughly twelve hundred conversations in twelve controversial domains. They score stance instability and how much sources get reused. Tests of Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini-2.5-Flash showed strong stance shifting in all three models. Results barely changed across temperature settings, which suggests the problem lies deeper than random sampling.
arxiv-2510-17812:
Anis Allagui, Enrique H. Balaguera, and Ahmed Elwakil give physical meaning to a puzzling fitting number. The number is the dispersion coefficient of the constant phase element. That element models imperfect capacitors in impedance spectroscopy data. Analysts usually treat its coefficient as a bare fitting parameter.

The team links the coefficient to energy stored or lost in the element. They split input energy into capacitive storage and resistive loss parts. Three test inputs were checked: constant, ramp, and quadratic voltages. In every case, energy ratios reduced to functions of that coefficient alone. The result grounds the coefficient in energy terms for device analysis.
arxiv-2510-17912:
Kunal Ghosh and three co-authors revisit how sprays of charged particles lose their charge in a neutralizer. The standard yardstick assumes the air stays nearly neutral and ignores fields from small charge imbalances. At high particle counts, the authors show, those ignored fields start to matter a great deal.

Their two-way model follows ions as they form, drift, spread, recombine, stick to particles, and hit walls. Even small net charges built fields that sped up ion drift and faster charge loss. Makers of aerosol tools get a warning: the old product rule can misread dense sprays.
arxiv-2510-18012:
Aida Abiad, with five co-authors, bounds how many region crossings any path needs in a plane covered by overlapping disks. The disks are topological, so their shapes can be wild, and two disks may meet in many separate pieces. The dual graph of the arrangement turns the geometry into a network whose diameter is the target.

For two disks the bound is exact and tight. For many disks the diameter grows with the disk count and the overlap count in a stated form. A key step counts faces with the deepest stacking. Geometry readers get a clean link between overlap mess and travel cost.
arxiv-2510-18112:
Patricia Delafuente, Arya Honraopatil, and Lara J Martin test whether reasoning models play Dungeons and Dragons better than plain instruct models. The task is to predict what a player does next and write it as a bot command for the Avrae system on Discord. Two mid-size open models face each other on a public game data set.

Clear, specific instructions mattered more than model type, and one changed sentence could swing the output a lot. The instruct model proved sufficient for the job against the reasoning model. Game tool builders get a useful lesson: prompt wording can beat a fancier model.
arxiv-2510-18212:
Dan Hendrycks, with thirty-two co-authors, defines general intelligence in a way that can be scored. A vague target hides the gap between narrow AI and human-level thought, so the authors set the bar at matching a well-educated adult's versatility and skill. Their frame rests on a leading theory of human cognition with strong empirical support.

Ten core domains, from reasoning to memory to perception, are tested with adapted human exam batteries. Today's models show a jagged profile: strong on knowledge-heavy areas, weak on basic machinery like long-term memory storage. Policymakers and labs get a yardstick with numbers attached.
arxiv-2510-18612:
Muhammad Hassan and his three co-authors build a detector for subtle attacks on RISC-V processors, an open chip design spreading into critical systems. The attacks in question leak information through the processor's microarchitecture, exploiting faults and cache behavior, and far less detection work exists for RISC-V than for older chip families. Earlier machine learning detectors left practical questions open.

The new method combines statistical preprocessing of processor signals with association rule mining, a technique whose rules people can read and understand. Because it rests on rules rather than one fixed model, it can be reconfigured for new attack variants. Tested in a chip simulator under cryptographic, computing, and memory-heavy workloads, it improved accuracy by up to about five percent over leading methods, with smaller gains in precision and recall. It also caught a new variant of the flush-and-fault attack family.
arxiv-2510-18812:
Jesús García Fernández, Nasir Ahmad, and Marcel van Gerven review one shared language. It is optimization, spoken by machine learning and neuroscience alike. Training networks proceeds by small improving steps. Biological learning does the same. The authors sort methods by derivative use. Full gradient methods sit at one end. Zeroth-order methods sit at the other. Those need only function values and randomness.

Backpropagation powers the gradient methods. It dominates machine learning. Yet it is biologically implausible and costly at scale. Zeroth-order methods are lighter and less sample efficient. Recent versions approximate gradients well. They can rival backpropagation in neural network models. Their core ideas echo the brain, too. Random probing and feedback-driven reinforcement are key mechanisms there. One math framework thus illuminates both fields.
arxiv-2510-19212:
Ernest Fokoué argues that statistics is the hidden base of artificial intelligence. The common story credits computer science and engineering. He says that story misses the core. The theory and methods of these systems are statistical. They have been so from the start.

His case runs pillar by pillar. The pillars span inference, density estimation, and sequential learning. They also span generalization, representation learning, and interpretability. Causality, optimization, and unification close the list. Each pillar rests on statistical ideas from the past century. The essay asks teachers to give statistics its central place.
arxiv-2510-19312:
Piotr Dyszewski and Tamara Mika study how heavy-tailed behavior, called regular variation, passes through Markov chains and random coefficient models. Such models drive time series in economics and risk, and their extreme values depend on whether the stationary distribution inherits the tail behavior of the random inputs.

Under a monotonicity condition tied to a gauge function, the stationary law does inherit regular variation from the innovations. For random linear models built by an explicit iteration, the exact structure of the chain shapes the spectral measure that describes tail directions. The results sharpen tools for modeling rare, large shocks.
arxiv-2510-19512:
Cedric Faas and four co-authors examine how to design the job of supervising artificial intelligence systems. As AI takes over routine work, experts increasingly check its output instead, and missed errors can be costly. Good oversight tools must also keep the human reviewers motivated and able to contribute meaningfully.

The team ran four co-design workshops with experts from psychology and computer science, who first graded with an AI system, then discussed their experience and sketched better interfaces. Four needs stood out, from clear responsibilities to real insight into the AI's decisions. Combined with the SMART model of work design, these became twelve design considerations meant to apply across fields.
arxiv-2510-19612:
Nathanaël Cuvelle-Magar and Stéphane Mallat build a denoising method for images that goes beyond the usual sparse-representation playbook. Classic estimators clean noisy signals by thresholding frame coefficients, but those representations miss some geometric regularities. For cartoon-like images with smooth edges, wavelet and curvelet frames fall short when the edge smoothness is unknown.

Their estimator works with wavelet scattering coefficients, quantities borrowed from simplified neural network models. By jointly shrinking and boosting different subsets of these coefficients, it separates noise from several kinds of geometric structure. Experiments reach the best possible asymptotic error for all edge smoothness levels tested. The authors state the result as a conjecture and frame the method as a bridge between harmonic analysis and deep network denoising.
arxiv-2510-19812:
Ibrahima Bah and three co-authors work out how continuous non-Abelian symmetry operators arise holographically in string theory. The setting is type IIB string theory on a space combining five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space with a five-sphere, dual to four-dimensional super Yang-Mills theory with an SO(6) R-symmetry. Topological operators for such symmetries need a concrete bulk realization.

The authors argue these operators are bound states of D5-branes and Kaluza-Klein monopoles hanging from the conformal boundary. Each component accounts for one contribution to the Gauss law constraints, one from the self-dual five-form flux and one from the gravitational term. They also show how the bound state measures the representation carried by the endpoint of a Wilson line built from D3-branes.
arxiv-2510-19912:
Thomas Cornish and three co-authors extend a young statistical method that computes angular power spectra directly from catalogues of objects on the sky, skipping the usual step of pixelating maps. Their addition is template deprojection, a way to strip out systematic contamination, worked into the catalogue-based formalism. Deprojection removes some real signal too, a bias they correct with a transfer function estimated from simple simulations.

They also derive exact expressions for the bias deprojection introduces into the shot-noise part of the spectrum. On simulated data, including galaxy clustering with realistic survey selection, the corrected method returns unbiased spectra in every scenario tested. Applied to real data it matches the standard map-based results, and the implementation ships in the public NaMaster code.
arxiv-2510-20012:
Adam Diamant builds an artificial intelligence pipeline that measures body movement during resistance training from video. He uses recordings of twenty-six people doing eight upper-body exercises in two styles, full range of motion and lengthened partial range. Five pose estimation models track joint angles frame by frame under one shared processing method.

Diamant finds that the partial style cuts range of motion but does not clearly change how long each repetition takes. It also makes movement less steady across people and across exercises. On average the partial style reaches about fifty-six percent of the full range, though the share varies a lot by exercise, which helps guide fair training advice.
arxiv-2510-20112:
Borui Du and three co-authors design signals for a system that combines radar sensing and wireless communication in one waveform using orthogonal time frequency space modulation. That modulation handles mobility well for both jobs, yet the best signal design for the combined task has been little studied. Their formulation covers both pilot symbols for channel estimation and power allocation for data.

For sensing they use the integrated sidelobe level of the ambiguity function, counting both random data symbols and fixed pilots. For communication they derive a capacity lower bound that includes channel estimation errors. An alternating optimization maximizes a weighted sum of the two goals, and simulations show clear gains over conventional schemes on both sides.
arxiv-2510-20212:
Yanghao Wang, Zhen Wang, and Long Chen propose FlowCycle, a target-aware method for editing images with text prompts using pre-trained flow models. Most editing methods first corrupt a source image into an intermediate state and then restore it toward the target, but that state is usually built without regard to the specific edit requested. Large requested changes then edit poorly or break consistency with the source.

FlowCycle instead corrupts selectively, damaging only content relevant to the edit while preserving the rest. Learnable noises are tuned through a cycle that edits the source to the target and back again under dual consistency constraints. Dynamic adjustment of sampling steps speeds the process, and ablation studies show superior editing performance.
arxiv-2510-20412:
Benjamin Girard and Alain Plagne study the Davenport constant for subsets of abelian groups, focusing on discrete Euclidean balls in two and three dimensions. For a set of group elements, the constant is the largest length of a sequence whose total sum is zero while no proper non-empty sub-sum vanishes. Such zero-sum questions sit at the heart of additive combinatorics and number theory.

The authors investigate that constant when the underlying group is the integer lattice in two or three dimensions and the set is a discrete ball. Their ball results then feed an application to the classical problem of estimating the Davenport constant of a box, meaning a product of integer intervals. That box problem has a long history in zero-sum theory.
arxiv-2510-20712:
Murod Mirzhalilov, Nandini Trivedi, and Mohit Randeria explain why placing a thin magnetic insulator against a topological insulator can raise the heat level at which the magnet keeps its order. Recent lab work saw a clear rise in that Curie point, and the mechanism needed a firm account.

The authors find that a short range effect from virtual jumps between filled and empty bands beats the longer oscillating effect often cited for dilute magnets. The boost scales with a known magnetic response measure, and the locked spin and motion of surface states favor order pointing out of the plane. Thin film mixing between top and bottom surfaces is also traced, helping read new results on layered chromium telluride stacks.
arxiv-2510-20812:
Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, and Shengjie Wang help vision language models reason over dense images where text notes and fine graphics are packed together, as in infographics and charts. Models often miss the key cue in a crowded layout or fail to chain facts spread across the page.

Their Speculative Verdict method sends several small models ahead as draft experts, each charting a reasoning path with its own guesses at key locations. A large model then acts as judge, merging the drafts into a final answer, while an agreement filter forwards only paths the drafts broadly share. Gains hold across four hard benchmarks for dense and high resolution question answering, at modest extra cost.
arxiv-2510-21112:
Hezam Albaqami leads seven co-authors on city scale three dimensional change detection from LiDAR scans, for planning, compliance, and map upkeep covering buildings and urban greenery alike. Standard surface differencing suffers vertical bias and viewpoint mismatch, while raw point cloud methods demand huge memory and perfect alignment.

Their uncertainty aware, object centric method aligns scans from different times with a multi resolution distribution transform and reasons about changed objects rather than raw points. Thin structures that voxel methods degrade are better preserved. Cities gain a route to fresh high definition maps without resurveying everything by hand.
arxiv-2510-21212:
Nilanjana Dey Choudhury and three co-authors model the faint far-ultraviolet halos seen around two bright stars, Spica and Achernar. Such halos are thought to arise when starlight scatters forward off dust grains in thin clouds lying in front of the stars, along our line of sight.

Earlier fits used a simple stand-in formula for how grains scatter light. Here the team uses full theoretical scattering functions for clumpy, porous grains of varied size and makeup, placed in a two-layer sheet whose distance and thickness are adjusted for the best fit. Tiny porous grains fit both halos, silicate-rich for Spica and carbon-rich for Achernar, and the cloud before Achernar proves thinner than the one before Spica.
arxiv-2510-21312:
Dhruv Sarkar, Nishant Pandey, and Sayak Ray Chowdhury revisit how success is measured in multi-armed bandit problems. In these problems, rewards may be shared across a population, such as patients in a medical trial. Standard measures care about the total or average reward. They can hide unfair splits between people.

A newer measure, Nash regret, uses the geometric mean of rewards. That rewards fairness as well as total size. Earlier methods for it needed special designs and strong assumptions. Those assumptions rule out even bell-shaped reward noise. The authors show that a simple recipe reaches near-best Nash regret under mild assumptions. The recipe is a short spell of uniform exploration, followed by the classic UCB rule. They extend the result to a whole family of fairness measures.
arxiv-2510-21412:
Whie Jung, Semin Kim, Junee Kim, and Seunghoon Hong ground visual concepts in words on real photographs, beyond toy scenes. Older methods pick a few axes in advance, such as color or shape, and test on synthetic data, which leaves most of the concepts people actually use untouched.

Their framework lets a pretrained vision-language model propose the relevant axes for each image, with a prompting scheme that needs no prior knowledge of the scene. A shared encoder then ties picture features to those axes without adding new parameters per concept, and a training goal keeps each axis adjustable on its own. On subsets of three real collections covering objects, faces. Animals, the method edits scenes more cleanly than earlier concept learning and text-based editing tools, and it recombines concepts in new ways.
arxiv-2510-21712:
Hao Sun and eight co-authors reorganize how AI agents search the web, by divorcing the planning from the searching. In agentic retrieval systems, one model must both chart a multi-step reasoning path and ground each step in fetched evidence. The two skills rise or fall together while nothing supervises the middle steps.

DecoupleSearch gives each job its own value model, so plan quality and search quality can be optimized separately. Candidate reasoning grows as a tree whose nodes pair a plan step with a search step, scored by Monte Carlo tree search to manufacture the missing supervision. At answer time, a hierarchical beam search refines plans and searches together under both value models. Experiments across language models of several sizes show the decoupled design consistently outperforming coupled rivals.
arxiv-2510-21912:
Marcus Högås and Edvard Mörtsell solve a bookkeeping problem that quietly haunts data analysis. Every measurement may carry a yes-or-no correction, such as belonging to one group or another, or being contaminated or clean. Ignoring the labels can bias results, but tracking every combination explodes beyond reach as datasets grow.

The pair shows that, under broad conditions, handling those binary choices exactly produces the same mathematics as the Ising model, a classic tool from statistical physics. That bridge unlocks fast, accurate ways to compute likelihoods, along with cheap approximation schemes. In a test on supernova calibration, uncertainty about which galaxies host the explosions turned out to barely move the inferred Hubble constant, a reassuring result for cosmology.
arxiv-2510-22012:
Ana-Maria Boldeanu and Mircea Neagu recast COVID-19 spread in the language of geometry. They start from a dynamical system for how the disease moves through a population. A least squares method then builds the linked Lagrange and Hamilton geometries.

Those constructions carry tools from modern differential geometry. They include nonlinear connections and torsion-like quantities. They also include an energy term modeled on the Yang-Mills energy of force fields. Here it is read for the epidemic system. The authors also test the Jacobi stability of the system. That test shows whether nearby solution paths converge or peel apart. It speaks to how predictable the modeled outbreak remains. The paper is a formal exercise. It translates an epidemic model into a geometric frame where stability tools apply.
arxiv-2510-22212:
Maria Korobeynikova, Alessia Battisti, Lukas Fischer, and Yingqiang Gao build a judge for German text simplification, a field that has graded its tools with borrowed rulers. Generic scores borrowed from translation measure overlap and fluency in a general sense. Simplification lives or dies on three things at once: is it simpler, does it keep the meaning, and does it read well.

Their metric, DETECT, adapts an English framework to German and grades all three dimensions, trained entirely on synthetic scores produced by large language models, so no scarce human-annotated corpus was needed. A refinement pass aligns the grading criteria with what simplification actually requires. The authors present DETECT as the first German-specific holistic measure of its kind, giving developers of accessible German text a yardstick shaped to the task.
arxiv-2510-22412:
Arpan Aryam John and three co-authors build deep learning classifiers for gamma ray transients spotted by the Fermi space telescope. Older sorting methods lean on fixed cut offs and hand picked light curve traits, which can be slow when fast follow up matters. Their models mix convolutional and recurrent networks and read several time series at once from Fermi data.

The classifiers sort events into gamma ray bursts, terrestrial flashes, solar flares, and soft gamma repeaters. They also flag events that fit none of those classes, which could point to rare new types. Trained on trusted events, the models reach high overall accuracy.
arxiv-2510-22912:
Battery performance hinges on a thin layer called the SEI. SEI means solid electrolyte interphase. Peichen Zhong and Kristin A Persson study its conductivity in 2025. The key ion conducting phase inside it is still unresolved. Crystal phases in it conduct poorly.

They focus on lithium difluorophosphate, a mixed anion compound. Machine learning potentials and generative structure search guide the work. A stable crystal form is identified. Its amorphous form conducts much better. Disorder flattens the lithium site energy landscape. Easy interstitial defects supply more mobile carriers. Interstitial means sitting between regular sites. The authors propose amorphous mixed anion phases as the conducting medium.
arxiv-2510-23012:
Pravin Nair proves a sharper bound on how much the softmax function can stretch its inputs. Softmax appears in classification, attention, reinforcement learning, and game theory. Most guarantees treated its Lipschitz constant as one in the Euclidean norm, which may overstate how unstable models can be.

Nair shows the constant is one half, and that this holds for every Lp norm with p at least one. He also studies the local constant at each point. A tighter bound can improve robustness proofs and convergence checks for the many algorithms that rely on softmax, at no extra cost in practice.
arxiv-2510-23212:
Quan Gu, Han Ye, Junjie Chen, and Xiongfeng Ma count the quantum resources needed to break elliptic curve cryptography with Shor algorithm on a two-dimensional lattice layout. Factoring estimates are well known, but elliptic curve attacks under realistic layouts were less studied. The cost hinges on the quantum adder at the heart of the circuit.

The team designs a carry-lookahead adder with low depth and only linear extra qubits, matching the best depth while avoiding heavy overhead. Their full analysis gives concrete qubit and gate counts. Such estimates tell cryptographers how large a quantum machine must be before elliptic curve keys fall.
arxiv-2510-23512:
Martin Huber and seventeen co-authors address a blind spot in surgical robotics: the robots cannot sense where they are in the room. That weakness causes collisions and workflow breaks, and bulky camera-and-marker tracking gear crowds the operating room. The problem grows as hospitals adopt systems with several independent robot arms working side by side.

The team tracks fully draped robots using only light stereo color cameras and transformer-based deep learning models. They trained on the largest dataset of its kind, 1.4 million self-labeled images from cadaver and live preclinical studies across several centers. Because the method watches the whole scene rather than single markers, it keeps working when views are blocked. Tests include live breathing compensation and multi-robot setups, and tracking visibility improved by a quarter over older systems.
arxiv-2510-23712:
Rishav Roshan and a co-author revisit the minimal type-I seesaw, the standard story for why neutrinos have tiny masses. Most studies drop the heaviest right-handed neutrino from the model, assuming it decouples and adds nothing to masses or to leptogenesis, the early-universe process that may explain the matter surplus. The authors show that assumption can mislead when the particle lives long.

A long-lived heavy neutrino changes the temperature at which charged lepton Yukawa interactions come into balance in the hot early universe. That shift forces a fresh look at flavor effects in thermal leptogenesis and can move the borders between flavor regimes. The paper also points to probes: neutrino oscillation data and gravitational wave observations could test the scenario. Beyond leptogenesis, the altered expansion history touches dark matter production and the primordial gravitational wave spectrum.
arxiv-2510-23812:
Jonathan Clivio constructs a lift of the Goresky-Hingston coproduct, an operation on the based loop space of a manifold. That space holds all loops that start and end at one fixed point. Coproducts in this setting split loop-space homology classes into pairs, and they interact delicately with the geometry of the underlying manifold. A lift sharpens the operation so that finer information survives.

Using the lift, Clivio derives formulas for how the coproduct interacts with the action of the fundamental group on the loop space. He also works out how it behaves under maps between manifolds. Those two compatibilities are enough to compute the coproduct explicitly for a family of examples: manifolds built as a sphere divided by a group action. The results extend the reach of string topology, the field that studies exactly such operations on loop spaces.
arxiv-2510-23912:
Marko Karbevski and a co-author ask whether transformers really need all three of their attention weight matrices: Query, Key, and Value. Under mild assumptions, they prove one of the three is redundant. It can be swapped for the identity matrix, cutting attention parameters by a quarter. If the Query or Key matrix goes, training also gets simpler, since the attention scores then depend on one learned matrix instead of a product of two.

They test the claim by training small GPT-style decoder models from scratch with the Query weights removed. The slimmed models matched baseline performance with fewer parameters, and won outright when the saved parameters were spent elsewhere. A side result draws a sharp line in a tractable ReLU setting, where skip connections push networks into a separate function class. The authors urge testing the idea at scale and across modalities.
arxiv-2510-24012:
Byeonghu Na and eight co-authors add a safety steering wheel to text-to-image diffusion models that requires no retraining. Models trained on web-scale data can produce harmful images when prompted maliciously, and most fixes mean expensive fine-tuning or brittle filters. Their method, Safe Text embedding Guidance, adjusts the prompt embedding during sampling instead.

A safety function scores the expected final image, and the embedding is nudged so the output moves toward the safe side. The theory shows this aligns the model's output distribution with the safety constraints while barely disturbing generation quality. In tests covering nudity, violence, and artist-style removal, the method beat both trained and training-free baselines at removing unsafe content. Crucially, it preserved the core meaning of the prompt rather than mangling the request. Code is public, so the guardrail can be bolted onto existing diffusion pipelines at sampling time only.
arxiv-2510-24112:
Junchi Wu and seven co-authors present SLOTH, a tool to find slowdowns inside chips that run deep neural networks. Spatial accelerators are key for fast inference, but small fail slow faults are widespread and drag down performance. Finding them on the chip itself is hard because memory is tight and faults must be located within the chip layout.

SLOTH watches work at the level of single operations with little overhead and squeezes traces to fit in a few kilobytes. A ranking method that knows the chip topology then points to the likely root cause. Tests on many workloads show SLOTH cuts storage greatly while still detecting and locating the slowdowns well.
arxiv-2510-24512:
Magnus Heimpel, Irena Hajnsek, and Othmar Frey, three authors, study radar phase data. InSAR uses radar images over time to track ground motion. Phase linking merges a pixel's phase history into one clean record. Scattered pixels give messy phase data that may not support the merge. Users need a score that says how much to trust each pixel.

The team propose three quality scores inside one shared framework. One score grades fit, from best case down to a noise floor. One score reads closure phase from the data before any merge. One score compares the merge with its best rival option. All scores run from zero to one, with one most trusted. Tests on radar data over Visp in Switzerland looked plausible.
arxiv-2510-24812:
Junsoo Oh, Jerry Song, and Chulhee Yun give a formal take on a curious fact: a strong model taught by a weak one can beat its own teacher. Past work on this weak to strong effect stayed with plain line models or vague frames. Their case is sharp: a line based weak net teaches a two layer bent net.

The data hold signs of mixed ease plus plain noise that bears no label. Two zones show up, one with scarce data and one with plenty. In the scarce zone, the strong model may fit in a kind way or a harmful way, and the team maps the switch line. In the rich zone, a new route drives the gain.
arxiv-2510-24912:
Shahab Ramezanpour and Amr Helmy built a twin light part that can be set by code, for use in chip scale light work. New light systems need small size, low power, and fine grip on loss and tone at once. Their part pairs two stuffs: one whose index nears zero, to guide loss, and one that swaps phase, to tune tone.

By drive with a wire signal, the pair can be steered to a rare point where two modes merge. That point gives high sense to small shifts. The twin holds at least sixteen set states for its paired rings, the team reports. The work aims at light chips that can be reset in the field, not fixed at build.
arxiv-2510-25412:
In Gim and Lin Zhong propose serving programs, not prompts. Their 2025 paper rethinks large language model serving systems. Current systems were designed mainly for text completion. Complex language model applications need more flexibility. Inflexible designs make systems inefficient and hard to adapt. Programs could give users runtime customization instead.

They call these LLM Inference Programs, or LIPs. Users customize token prediction and cache management live. Application logic like tool execution can offload server-side. Their example system is named Symphony in the paper. It functions as an operating system for programs. Model computations are exposed via system calls. A dedicated file system virtualizes the KV cache. That cache stores prior token information for speed. A two-level scheduling scheme ensures GPU efficiency. Symphony could enable a more extensible serving ecosystem. Future language applications may benefit from that flexibility.
arxiv-2510-25612:
Amit Giloni led five co-authors introducing CAIR. Chiara Picardi, Roy Betser, and Shamik Bose helped. Aishvariya Priya Rathina Sabapathy and Roman Vainshtein followed. Their 2025 paper ranks agent influence in AI workflows. Agentic workflows assemble several language model agents collaboratively. They work autonomously toward a shared goal together. Understanding their operations matters for quality and security.

No existing methods assess each agent influence level. Static structural analysis is unsuitable for inference-time execution. Their ranker is the first such method. Counterfactual analysis compares output with agents removed. The analysis is task-agnostic in its design. It can run offline and at inference time. Evaluation used their own dataset of thirty use cases. CAIR produces consistent rankings across those cases. It outperforms baseline methods in their evaluation. Downstream task effectiveness can improve using its rankings. Security audits of multi-agent systems may also benefit.
arxiv-2510-25712:
Jack Storror Carter and Cesare Molinari wrote a 2025 statistics paper about estimating connections among many variables. Their focus is PCGLASSO, a method for Gaussian data, meaning data with a bell-shaped spread. It estimates partial correlations, the direct link between two variables after other variables are considered.

It builds on the graphical LASSO, an older tool, by adding a penalty that keeps only strong links. Its results stay the same when variables are measured on different scales. Its fitting problem lacks a single smooth valley, so finding the best answer is hard. Carter and Molinari prove an answer always exists, even with fewer observations than variables. They also provide a new step-by-step method in a free R package, the first released openly. Tests show it runs at speeds close to rival tools for medium-sized problems.
arxiv-2510-25912:
Farshid Reza, Beihan Chen, and Miaomiao Jin study how mixing aluminium into gallium nitride changes its structure and defects. The alloy, written AlGaN, is key for light based and high power devices, but modeling a disordered mix with first principles methods is slow and limited. They instead use a machine learning interatomic potential, a fitted model that predicts forces between atoms quickly.

Reza and the team first check the model against known values for the pure end materials and for defect energies. They then map stiffness across mixes and find a nonlinear trend. Nitrogen pair defects and moving nitrogen defects depend strongly on local chemistry, while metal vacancies move more steadily across compositions, which guides device design.
arxiv-2510-26012:
Siyi Wu leads nine co-authors in a system that automates the writing of literature surveys, the long papers that sum up a research field. Survey writing has grown harder as publication volume, especially on large language models, keeps rising. Their system, AutoSurvey2, works in stages, generating sections in parallel, refining drafts in rounds, and retrieving fresh papers in real time to keep coverage current and citations faithful.

Quality is judged by a panel of language models that score coverage, structure, and relevance against expert review standards. In experiments, the system beat retrieval based and automated baselines on structural coherence and topical relevance while keeping citations accurate. The authors release code and resources for reuse.
arxiv-2510-26212:
Yifeng Cai and Ziming Wang lead seven co-authors in a defense for AI agents that operate phones and software on a user behalf. Such agents, with graphical interface understanding and tool protocols, often hold broad, static permissions. That over privilege enables instruction injection, where malicious text hidden in benign content, such an email, hijacks the agent into unauthorized actions.

Their framework, AgentSentry, applies task centric access control at runtime. Instead of persistent broad rights, it generates minimal, temporary policies matched to the current task, such as registering for an app, and revokes them on completion. In a demonstration, it blocked an attack that tried to make the agent forward private emails, while the legitimate task completed normally.
arxiv-2510-26512:
Dipak Meher and Carlotta Domeniconi pull apart a system they studied before, to see which parts do the work. The system, CORE-KG, builds knowledge graphs from legal case files about human smuggling. Such files are dense, loose in form, and full of shifting references to the same people, which tends to yield noisy graphs with repeated nodes.

Meher and Domeniconi run an ablation study, removing one part at a time. Without the step that resolves shifting references, node duplication rose by about twenty-eight percent and noisy nodes by about four percent. Without the domain-guided structured prompts, duplication rose by about four percent, while noisy nodes jumped by about seventy-three percent. The results tell builders of such pipelines where the gains come from.
arxiv-2510-26612:
Vikash Mittal and Tomasz Sowiński study quantum walks, where a particle moves on a line or grid by rules set by a small internal state called a coin. Earlier studies let two walkers interact in fixed ways. The pair set out a broader frame: a two-parameter family of local interactions between walkers, shaped by the state of their coins.

Mittal and Sowiński show that several known models appear as special cases of their family. They then pick particular cases and trace how the interaction changes the motion of two walkers that start apart and unrelated. The frame is offered as a platform for building quantum correlations on purpose. Uses they name include quantum simulation, state preparation, and sensing, plus a route to many-walker systems.
arxiv-2510-26812:
Garima Jain, Anand Bodade, and Sanghamitra Pati set out a protocol for a systematic review of clinical decision support systems in poorer countries. These systems give clinicians advice at the point of care, and evidence from low- and middle-income countries is scattered. The protocol states, in advance, how the review and meta-analysis will be run.

Jain and her two co-authors will include comparative quantitative studies, from randomised trials to cohort studies, set in World Bank-defined low- and middle-income countries. Searches cover eleven named databases plus grey sources, up to the end of September 2024. Screening and extraction will be done in duplicate, and bias will be graded with standard tools for randomised and non-randomised studies. Where outcomes are comparable, a random-effects meta-analysis will pool them; otherwise a structured narrative synthesis will be used.
arxiv-2510-27012:
Yumou Fei proves a broad limit on fast property testing for constraint problems. In the bounded-degree query model, a tester probes only a small part of a huge graph to judge a property. Many properties, such as bipartiteness and colorability, can be written as constraint satisfaction problems, where values must meet a set of rules.

Fei shows that for every unbounded-width problem in this class, testing satisfiability needs a number of queries that grows with the whole input size. No sublinear shortcut exists for the full class.
