The result unifies several older lower bounds and covers all such problems known to be hard to solve exactly, including hypergraph coloring cases. The proof merges earlier testing techniques with results from universal algebra.
arxiv-2510-27112:
Klajdi Hoxha, in a 2025 study of online markets, takes up a design puzzle for shopping sites. Big platforms ask shops to pool what they know about buyers, then aim ads with the shared facts. Shops fear a catch: rivals may use the pool to steal their own buyers. Hoxha asks what rules would make shops share anyway.

He builds a math model and finds the best setup for the platform. At its core are three markets. In one, shops sell all their data at a set price. In the next, shops swap data for ads that draw more clicks. In the third, rich shops buy those strong ads at full price. He notes the same design may fit carbon credit trades and shared public funds.
arxiv-2510-27512:
Mahi Aliyu Aminu, Chisom Chibuike, and three other co-authors help AI cope when languages and domains shift, in a 2025 paper. Models trained on one text style often fail on another, and low-resource languages have little data to spare. Causal methods, which chase true drivers rather than surface links, promise steadier behavior. The team tests two such methods on African language tasks.

First, they use a chat model to write counterfactual paraphrases, reworded texts with flipped sentiment, for Yoruba and Igbo tweets. Training on these hardened the sentiment classifier. Second, they extend a debiasing framework to aspect-based sentiment, judging feelings toward specific targets. Their new Afri-SemEval set covers seventeen languages translated from a standard source. Both methods improved results on unseen domains.
arxiv-2511-00112:
Yanbing Mao, Yihao Cai, and Lui Sha introduce Real-DRL, a framework that lets a deep reinforcement learning agent learn safely at runtime on a real physical plant. Safety-critical systems cannot afford exploratory failures, yet offline training rarely matches reality. Three components interact: a learning student agent, a physics-model-based teacher, and a trigger that mediates between them.

The student uses dual self-learning and teaching-to-learn ideas with real-time safety-informed batch sampling, while the physics teacher guards safe behavior. Control readers get a design for learning in reality without surrendering safety. Runtime learning on real plants could adapt controllers to wear and drift that simulators never modeled.
arxiv-2511-00312: J-H Eschenburg, K K Santos, and R Tribuzy study equivariant embeddings, maps that place a symmetric Kählerian space inside another space while keeping its symmetries. Guided by a theorem of Cartan and Wallach on such embeddings, they describe the embeddings fully for one key case, the complex projective space. They also prove that an embedding with parallel plurimean curvature must be the standard symmetric one. The note is short and written for experts in geometry.
arxiv-2511-00812:
Shashank Nag and a large team present LL-ViT, a vision transformer redesigned to run on low power edge hardware such as FPGA chips. Transformers lead on vision tasks, but their size, memory use, and energy needs make small devices a poor fit.

The design swaps the transformer's channel mixer, where most weights and computation sit, for neurons built from lookup tables that are learned directly during training. A custom FPGA accelerator runs the result. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, accuracy stays close to the baseline transformer, while over sixty percent of the weights and half the multiplications disappear. The system also improves energy efficiency and latency over a quantized transformer accelerator at a modest power budget.
arxiv-2511-01112:
Luana Passos-Reis and colleagues model how cosmic rays are accelerated in the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. That the IceCube observatory has identified as a likely neutrino source despite no matching gamma ray signal. The missing gamma rays suggest strong absorption, plus a hadronic component and efficient particle acceleration near the central black hole.

Their one zone model places the action in the coronal accretion flow, where turbulence driven magnetic reconnection accelerates protons and electrons. Photon fields in the corona serve as targets for proton interactions, and pair production attenuates the gamma rays. Contrary to some recent studies, they find the extreme energies needed come mainly from first order Fermi acceleration inside the turbulent reconnection layers of a large scale current sheet.
arxiv-2511-01412:
Rui Hu and Ted Westling work on a weakness of medical observational studies. Patients who receive a treatment may differ from those who do not in ways nobody measured. Those hidden differences can fake or hide a real effect. Their setting is survival data, where the outcome is how long patients live.

Earlier sensitivity tools leaned on strict model assumptions and on hazard ratios, which are hard to interpret causally. Hu and Westling build a nonparametric framework instead. It derives bounds for the gap between observed and true survival curves, and for restricted mean survival time. Its estimators are grounded in semiparametric efficiency theory. They test the method in simulations and on the effect of elective neck dissection in patients with high-grade parotid gland cancer.
arxiv-2511-01712:
Ernst-Ulrich Gekeler studies modular forms in the function field world, where polynomials over a finite field replace the integers. His objects are modular forms for the group GL(r) over the polynomial ring Fq[T]. The ring they form is generated by a specific list of coefficient forms. The list ends with the analogue of the discriminant function, plus one more form.

Gekeler determines exactly how the Hecke operators at a prime ideal act on every generator: all are eigenforms, with eigenvalues given by powers of the prime's monic generator. He also describes the growth of the discriminant's expansion coefficients. Its product expansion converges on the natural fundamental domain for the group. So does the expansion of every modular form in the ring.
arxiv-2511-01812:
D. Aristizabal Sierra, L. Duque, O. Miranda, and H. Nunokawa turn reactor neutrino detectors into hunting grounds for axionlike particles. These are light, hypothetical particles beyond the Standard Model. Big liquid scintillator detectors near reactors find neutrinos through inverse beta decay. Its prompt-then-delayed light pattern rejects background sharply. Other searches can borrow that edge.

The particles could be made by Primakoff-like or Compton-like processes. They could then be caught through the inverse routes: axio-electric absorption, or decay into photon or electron pairs. One signature stands out. A scattering event would flash a prompt photon, then a second one about five nanoseconds later. Radioactive background rarely mimics that. The authors estimate the reach of setups like JUNO-TAO and CLOUD, in both nuclear and electron channels.
arxiv-2511-01912:
Wenzhe Fan, Ning Yan, and Masood Mortazavi give planning agents a memory that learns in two directions at once. Language-model multi-agent systems can plan trips and schedules, but how memory should coordinate the agents is underexplored, even though constraint tracking and error correction decide success. Their framework, EvoMem, borrows its design from the working memory model of cognitive psychology.

Three agents, a constraint extractor, a verifier, and an actor, share two memory modules. Constraint memory stores task rules and constraints, fixed within one query but evolving across queries. Query-feedback memory accumulates feedback across iterations within a query, refining the solution as it goes; both reset when a session ends. On trip planning, meeting planning, and calendar scheduling benchmarks, the dual-evolving memory delivered consistent improvements.
arxiv-2511-02012:
Zhexing Zhang proves bounds in harmonic analysis for waves and vibrations restricted to surfaces inside curved spaces. The setting is a complete Riemannian manifold with nonpositive curvature and well-behaved geometry. The objects are spectral projections, which isolate waves near a chosen frequency. These apply when those waves are viewed only along uniformly embedded submanifolds.

On surfaces with pinched negative curvature, Zhang also proves restriction bounds for the Schrödinger equation along geodesic segments, with bounds that do not depend on it. For surfaces that are hyperbolic at large scales, the bounds improve further along complete geodesics that never trap waves. A threshold condition extends one all-time bound to the continuous part of the spectrum.
arxiv-2511-02112:
Saad Raza and six co-authors study when a layer of fluid seeded with tiny particles will start to convect. The setup mirrors a classic heated-from-below layer, except thermal particles are continuously injected at one wall and removed at the other. Stability analysis asks how the thermal coupling between particles and fluid, measured by a specific heat ratio, changes the onset of motion.

Raising that ratio consistently stabilised the layer, for heavy and light particles alike and across changes in flux, injection speed and direction, and temperature. The effect levels off once the particles' heat capacity per volume approaches the fluid's. The team attributes the delay to heat exchange reshaping the base temperature profile, flattening gradients near the injection wall and weakening buoyancy.
arxiv-2511-02512:
A. Backis and seven co-authors measure how candidate shielding materials interact with neutrons, for a spectrometer being built at the European Spallation Source. The T-REX instrument will detect scattered thermal neutrons with Multi-Grid detectors, thin boron carbide coatings on aluminium blades. Internal shielding is needed to stop neutrons scattering more than once inside the detector and blurring the data. A Monte Carlo study had shortlisted materials; this work tests twelve of them at the ISIS neutron source.

Transmission was measured across a range of wavelengths with a position-sensitive detector, and scattering was measured for six samples on a second instrument. The tests identify a boron carbide and aluminium composite, plated with nickel to suppress its own alpha-particle background, as an effective neutron absorber. The authors conclude it is suitable for building into the Multi-Grid structures of inelastic neutron spectrometers.
arxiv-2511-02612:
Aidi Yang, Chikako Idegawa, and Fa Peng Huang ask how precisely two space gravitational-wave detectors could read the fingerprints of the early universe's electroweak phase transition. If new physics made that transition strongly first-order, it would have filled space with a stochastic background of gravitational waves. As their model the authors extend the Standard Model with a dimension-six Higgs operator, controlled by a new-physics scale.

They simulate the measurement for the TianQin and LISA detectors, including instrument noise shaped by time-delay interferometry, astrophysical foregrounds, and the model's signal. They then reconstruct parameters with Fisher analysis, Bayesian nested sampling, and machine learning. For strong benchmark signals, the amplitude came back with uncertainties of roughly twenty to thirty percent, while the underlying model scale was pinned to sub-percent precision. That statistical figure, the authors carefully note, excludes theoretical uncertainties and holds the bubble wall speed fixed.
arxiv-2511-03312:
Jiali Xu, Valeria Loscri, and Romain Rouvoy warn that a rogue base station could twist how 5G networks hand out service slices. Slicing lets one physical network act as many tailored networks, yet weak settings can leave that handout open to forgery. Acting as a middleman, the rogue station can fake slice requests and seize a phone's connection.

On a live 5G test bed, the team shows harms that range from a near-total drop in bandwidth to quiet theft of resources meant for others. Some effects stay loud and obvious, while others hide in normal traffic. The study maps the threat from a risk review tied to allowed but unsafe configurations. Its message is that slice integrity needs guarding as strongly as privacy already is.
arxiv-2511-03412:
Yiquan Yang and colleagues use entangled light to tell left-handed from right-handed biological molecules more sharply than classic optics allow. Handedness matters in chemistry and medicine, yet standard probes give weak signals and can harm samples with strong light. Classic probes also hit a hard noise floor set by photon counting itself.

Squeezed, entangled polarization states push past that floor while keeping light levels moderate. The team reports a clear gain beyond the standard limit when sorting two mirror forms of amino acids in liquid. The method leaves samples intact and suits delicate biological material. Sharper handedness checks could speed drug work and biochemical screening.
arxiv-2511-03512:
Alexis Marin and Dorothea Vienne-Pollak give a lean proof of the uniformization theorem for Riemann surfaces. That theorem says every such surface can be reshaped by a angle-preserving map into one of a few standard forms. Standard proofs lean on heavy tools, including a topological property called paracompactness.

Their route uses only basic facts about holomorphic functions. Key steps borrow a sphere test from topology, a doubled-surface construction for surfaces with edges, and old arithmetic about separation in surfaces. A self-contained proof lowers the entry cost for students meeting the theorem. It also shows how much mileage careful elementary methods can still give in complex geometry.
arxiv-2511-03712:
Turgut Yilmaz and colleagues watch potassium doping peel one layer of a layered crystal into near independence. Titanium diselenide stacks weakly bound sheets, and potassium atoms slip into the gaps between them. Photoemission maps of the electron bands before and after dosing show the conduction band split into two branches.

Cooling widens that split to a clear value. One branch behaves as a flat, two-dimensional layer while the other keeps bulk-like spread, marking a quasi-freestanding sheet. Core-level signals confirm the potassium sits mainly in the gaps. Dosing also erases a periodic lattice distortion near the surface. A self-isolated sheet inside a bulk crystal offers a clean stage for two-dimensional physics.
arxiv-2511-03812:
Sneha Banerjee, Shital Lawande, Subhadeep Rana, and Kuldeep Saha prove a result about spun embeddings, a way of building an embedding of one manifold inside another from an open book decomposition. Open books describe a manifold through a binding and pages that sweep around it.

Suppose a closed manifold appears as part of the binding of an open book for a larger manifold. Then, the authors show, every open book decomposition of that smaller manifold spun embeds in the larger one. Consequences follow: open books of simply connected spin five-manifolds spun embed in the seven-sphere, and three-dimensional open books spun embed in the five-sphere. A version for Morse open books is also defined.
arxiv-2511-04112:
Biao Liu and Yuanzhi Liang present SpatialLock, a framework for placing objects exactly where a text prompt wants them in generated images. Text-to-image systems now produce strong pictures and useful synthetic datasets, yet exact object location remains shaky because position data in prompts is underused.

One component injects spatial information directly through an attention layer so grounding is learned well. A second uses perception-based guidance to refine placement further. Together they generate objects in precise spatial layouts while improving overall visual quality. Experiments set a new state of the art for precise positioning, with overlap scores above nine tenths across several datasets in its tests.
arxiv-2511-04212:
Michael Thies, writing alone, gives an explicit example of a multiple Peierls instability in the chiral Gross-Neveu model at finite density. With one density, the model is solved semiclassically by a chiral spiral mean field, and its fermion spectrum shows a single gap at the Fermi energy, the classic Peierls signature.

Splitting the fermion flavours into two groups with two different densities changes the picture. The Hartree-Fock ground state is again analytic, using the twisted kink crystal mean field of Basar and Dunne. Its spectrum shows two gaps whose lower edges meet the two Fermi energies. That state beats the homogeneous one, confirming a genuine double instability.
arxiv-2511-04412:
Mark-Oliver Wolf, writing alone, compares ways to value a life insurer's own funds. The Solvency Capital Requirement under Solvency II depends on that value, and computing it is costly. Rules favor the direct method, though theory says direct and indirect methods agree.

Wolf gives a simpler proof that both estimators reach the same value. He then builds a large family of mixed estimators that contains both as edge cases. Set inside a control variate framework, the mixes cut variance sharply. Tests on three life insurance portfolios, with market frictions added, show which estimator works best in practice.
arxiv-2511-04512:
Victorita Dolean leads four authors on speeding up GMRES for Helmholtz problems with quasimodes. Finite elements handle complex shapes and mixed media well for these wave problems. The linear systems, though, are large and indefinite, and they strain iterative solvers near resonance.

The team derives a convergence bound that tracks the nonlinear path of the residual. It links slow convergence to small eigenvalues tied to quasimodes, and shows when they stop mattering. Domain decomposition tests display the effect in action. Adding deflation with tailored eigenvectors then targets the resonant cases that stall solvers most.
arxiv-2511-04612:
Victor-Emmanuel Brunel, writing alone, develops asymptotics for constrained M-estimation with convex loss. M-estimation, also called empirical risk minimization, underlies classification, regression, and location problems. Classic theory needs smoothness that many real losses do not have.

Brunel allows convex losses that may not even be differentiable. Convex constraints on the estimates are part of the setup as well. The limiting distribution turns out to depend on how the loss meets the constraint boundary. He extends earlier results into this rougher setting, which covers tools like quantile and hinge losses used daily in machine learning.
arxiv-2511-04712:
Longlong Lin leads eight authors with NCSAC, a neural method for community search in networks. The task is to find a dense local community tied to a user's query node. Older tools lean only on fixed rules or only on deep learning.

NCSAC blends both by defining attribute-augmented conductance as its quality target. That measure joins structural closeness inside and outside the group with attribute similarity. A neural search then optimizes communities against the blended score. The hybrid design aims at communities that are tight as graphs and coherent in their labels, useful from social networks to knowledge bases.
arxiv-2511-06212:
Seif Ikbarieh, Kshitiz Aryal, and Maanak Gupta attack a security system to test how robust it really is. Their target is a framework that uses a large language model to analyze attacks on Internet of Things networks and suggest fixes. Such systems lean on a retrieval knowledge base, which itself can be poisoned.

The team built an attack description dataset and slipped small, meaning-preserving word changes into the knowledge base. They then compared the model's mitigation advice before and after poisoning, using a rubric for human experts and judge models. Even small changes weakened the link between traffic signs and attack behavior and made the suggested fixes vaguer and less practical.
arxiv-2511-06912:
Abdullah Aloufi and four co-authors develop Bayesian methods for designing cluster randomised trials, where whole groups rather than individuals receive a treatment. They handle both continuous and binary outcomes using mixed-effects models, and summarize treatment effects through posterior distributions. Sample sizes are chosen by assurance, a Bayesian measure of the chance a trial succeeds.

Two computational engines for the inference, Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations, are compared for speed and accuracy across many cases. The test case is the SPEEDY trial, which studies pre-hospital redirection of stroke patients for thrombectomy, using priors elicited from two clinical experts. The paper ends with concrete recommendations for when each computational method should be preferred.
arxiv-2511-07112:
Khashayar Alavi, Zhastay Yeltay, Lucie Flek, and Akbar Karimi test whether teams of language model agents stay reliable when math questions are corrupted. Voting among many sampled agents, their Agent Forest system, reliably raises accuracy on clean problems. The authors perturbed questions with punctuation noise at three intensities and with realistic human typos from the WikiTypo and R2ATA collections. They then tested six open-source models on four benchmarks with up to twenty-five agents.

Collaboration helped: accuracy rose with agent count, with the largest gains between one and five agents and diminishing returns past about ten. But the adversarial gap never closed. Punctuation damage scaled with severity, and human-like typos remained the dominant bottleneck, producing the largest accuracy gaps and highest attack success rates even for big agent teams.
arxiv-2511-07212:
Imogen Camp and Nick G Jones map exact structures inside interacting quantum spin chains. A matrix-product state skeleton is a connected network of Hamiltonians whose exact ground states are matrix-product states, underlying a whole phase diagram. Skeletons were known for free-fermion models, where they are dense. The authors partially expose the skeleton in the interacting, Onsager-integrable chiral clock classes, which generalize clock models with a tunable number of states.

They construct matrix-product states forming a dense skeleton in the gapped regions around a sequence of fixed-point Hamiltonians generating the Onsager algebra. Outside those regions the same states remain eigenstates but drop to certain excited sectors, and the methods uncover further low-lying excited states. As an application, they obtain a closed form for the disorder parameter in a family of interacting models.
arxiv-2511-07312:
Samuel Sokota and five co-authors present Ataraxos, an AI that plays Stratego at superhuman level. Hidden information defeats standard reinforcement learning and search, and despite multimillion-dollar industrial efforts, top human Stratego play had resisted AI. Ataraxos combines general tools the team developed for self-play reinforcement learning and for test-time search under hidden information, rather than game-certain engineering.

It defeated the most decorated human Stratego player of all time by a large margin, the first superhuman result in the game's history. Using orders of magnitude less compute and data than earlier efforts. The same tools produced a superhuman Barrage Stratego player and state-of-the-art systems for Hanabi and dou dizhu. The authors argue this establishes a reusable design pattern for adversarial, cooperative, and team games saturated with hidden information.
arxiv-2511-07412:
Training surgical robots inside real operating rooms is risky and tightly restricted. Han Zhang and a large team propose TwinOR, a system that builds lifelike digital copies of operating rooms instead. Such copies let embodied agents practice and be tested without endangering patients or staff.

TwinOR rebuilds the fixed layout of a room, then tracks people and equipment as they move. Static and moving parts merge into one immersive three-dimensional scene that researchers can control and rerun. The design aims to capture spatial, visual, and behavioral detail faithfully. It offers a safer testbed for learning and judging intelligent surgical systems.
arxiv-2511-07812:
Zhenchen Tang, Songlin Yang, and Bo Peng fix a mismatch when multimodal models grade image quality. Quality scores are continuous, but language models answer in discrete tokens. Converting word levels like good into numbers introduces errors, and level words blur meaning, dragging down related abilities.

An error analysis names the failure modes, then a remedy reworks how scores are produced. Keeping the model strengths while extracting smooth scores is the goal. Automated quality assessment feeds photo tools, compression, and medical imaging triage. A judge that confuses its own scale helps none of those, so aligning output form with task form matters.
arxiv-2511-07912:
Jun-Young Kim, Young-Seok Kweon, and Gi-Hwan Shin record brain activity while people switch strategies in a flexible way. Adaptive reasoning means changing inference rules when contexts shift, and its neural pattern is unclear. A card-sorting task with brain recording captures rule hunting and rule locking in real time, with a multimodal model compared alongside.

Early slow brain rhythms track exploration and rule inference. After a rule clicks, occipital alpha activity marks settled attention. Human dynamics thus split into searching and confirming phases. Comparing machine behavior against those phases offers a yardstick for machine reasoning that adapts rather than merely answers.
arxiv-2511-08012:
Haowen Li and co-authors revisit direction of arrival estimation, the task of finding where a sound came from. Most models learn from synthetic scenes made by mixing clean speech with room responses, which limits acoustic variety. A newer data set built with help from large language models offers richer, more realistic spatial audio scenes.

The authors benchmark several neural methods on that data and propose LightDOA, a light model using depthwise separable convolutions. It accepts multi-channel input and aims at varied rooms without heavy computation. Results show sound accuracy and robustness across scenes, making the approach suitable for devices with limited resources.
arxiv-2511-08212:
The CMS Collaboration reports a search for long lived particles in proton proton collisions at thirteen teraelectronvolts at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. Data from 2017 and 2018, totaling one hundred inverse femtobarns, are scanned for displaced vertices with low momentum tracks, large missing transverse momentum, and a jet from initial state radiation. Supersymmetric coannihilation scenarios supply the benchmark signals.

In those models a heavier partner sits close in mass to the lightest supersymmetric particle, a bino like neutralino. No excess signal is reported, so the search sets the strongest limits yet for the top squark and bino wino benchmark models. Excluded masses depend on lifetime and mass splitting.
arxiv-2511-08312:
Franziska Stamer and Thomas Titz Mite construct the first chamber regular lattices acting on buildings of type C2 tilde, a class of highly symmetric geometric structures from Lie theory. A lattice here is a discrete group of symmetries, and chamber regularity means the group moves any chamber to any other in a tightly controlled way. Assuming a conjecture of Kantor, their list of examples becomes a complete classification for type preserving cases on locally finite buildings.

Special vertex links in their buildings are all the unique generalized quadrangle of order three, five. The constructions need chamber regular actions on that quadrangle, which are new and possibly the only ones. None of the examples are Bruhat Tits buildings, so every lattice produced is exotic.
arxiv-2511-09012:
Francesco Alemanno accelerates fixed-point iterations, the workhorse solvers of nonlinear equations, at the exact point where they usually stall. When the Jacobian at the solution has an eigenvalue creeping toward one, progress per step nearly vanishes. His booster needs no stored history and no dense least-squares solves.

Under two assumptions, a quadratic blend of three iterates is built whose error polynomial has a double root at that stubborn multiplier. The assumptions are that one multiplier dominates the linearized error and that residuals shrink monotonically. The mode is cancelled to leading order. The scheme reduces to Aitken's classic process in one dimension. It matches a doubly blended Anderson step while keeping Picard's tiny memory footprint. Tests on clustered linear systems, a large nonlinear fixed point, and a Poisson grid reach tight targets in far fewer steps than rival methods.
arxiv-2511-09312:
S. Bellotti and ten co-authors map the magnetic fields of two fast-rotating, radio-bright M dwarf stars, StKM 1-1262 and V374 Peg. Low-frequency radio emission reveals stellar magnetism and the surrounding plasma, but reading it requires knowing the field itself. Both stars were detected with the LOFAR radio array, and one had shown a Type II burst.

Using infrared spectropolarimetry from SPIRou, the team refined each star's temperature, gravity, and metallicity, then imaged the large-scale fields. StKM 1-1262 carries an average total field near 3.5 kilogauss with a dipolar large-scale pattern around 300 gauss. V374 Peg is stronger still, near 5.5 kilogauss overall and about 800 gauss large-scale. The maps help interpret each star's radio behavior.
arxiv-2511-09512:
Jingquan Yan and six co-authors predict which abnormalities appear when a gene is knocked out, reading only the gene's sequence. Earlier methods leaned on curated genetic knowledge, limiting their reach, or studied narrow variant effects. GenePheno instead tackles broad, multi-label prediction of knockout effects directly from gene sequences.

A contrastive multi-label objective captures links among phenotypes, while an exclusive penalty enforces biological consistency. A gene function bottleneck layer expresses predictions through human-readable functional concepts. The authors curated four data sets pairing sequences with knockout labels. GenePheno reports state-of-the-art scores on gene-centric and phenotype-centric measures, and case studies show plausible functional mechanisms behind its predictions.
arxiv-2511-09612:
Joshua Holstein and three co-authors show that incentives change how people use AI advice. Paying people to think for themselves curbs overreliance on the machine. Human-AI teams should beat either party alone, yet people defer to the machine even when their own judgment is better. The authors trace that failure partly to how incentives are usually structured.

They design an alternative incentive mechanism meant to reward independent thinking where it pays. In a behavioral test with 180 participants, the mechanism significantly reduced overreliance and improved decision quality. Poorly designed incentives, by contrast, distorted behavior and degraded performance in their tests. The lesson is that collaboration incentives must fit the task context and the actual complementarities between human and machine.
arxiv-2511-10012:
Yujun Shi and Xiaoting Fen revisit Koehler's test, a 1950 design that finds the ratio of specific heats of air from self-sustained swings of a piston. The design is a clever twist on Ruchardt's classic test, but Koehler's own write-up is long and dense with sums, which puts off readers and teachers. The pair keep his shortcut for pressure change and restate the model in a cleaner form.

In their hands the model splits into straight-line pieces, and the swing cycles can be read off from shapes and plots, not from heavy algebra. That view answers the core riddle of the test: why the swing rate lands so close to the Ruchardt rate. Since the proof skips hard sums, the authors say lab teachers can bring Koehler's test back into class.
arxiv-2511-10512:
Chian Yeh Goh, Daniel Brito Matehuala, and Guillaume Blanquart investigate Rayleigh-Taylor turbulence, the churning mixing that occurs when a heavy fluid sits above a lighter one. They use a statistically stationary simulation setup that sustains self-similar mixing layers at lower cost than conventional growing-layer simulations.

Across a wide range of Atwood and Reynolds numbers, the team develops normalizations for the main terms in the mass and energy budgets, and most normalized quantities collapse onto common curves. Where profiles shift with density ratio, they trace the cause to division by density. Their analysis ends with a revised growth law. Replacing the standard Atwood number with an effective one based on the logarithm of the density ratio keeps the growth parameter nearly constant, unifying the scaling.
arxiv-2511-10812: John Machacek and George D. Nasr work in matroid theory, classifying which positroids are also sparse paving matroids. Their tools are Postnikov's Le-diagrams, decorated permutations, and Grassmann necklaces, combinatorial objects that encode positroids concretely enough to test the sparse paving property. The classification also yields an enumeration of the sparse paving positroids, which turns out to connect with a known integer sequence involving the golden ratio and with the Lucas numbers.
arxiv-2511-10912:
Arsh Gupta, Ajay Narayanan Sridhar, Bonam Mingole, and Amulya Yadav test whether language models can diagnose rare diseases from story-like case presentations, using an unlikely source: the television series House M.D. The show is validated for teaching rare disease recognition in medical education, and the team extracted 176 symptom-diagnosis pairs from it.

Four state-of-the-art models, from OpenAI and Google, attempted the diagnoses. Accuracy ranged widely, from about 16 percent to about 39 percent, with newer model generations performing roughly 2.3 times better than older ones. Every model still struggled badly with rare disease diagnosis from narrative cases. The authors release the benchmark publicly as a baseline for narrative medical reasoning and a yardstick for future AI-assisted diagnosis research.
arxiv-2511-11212:
Mohammad Areeb Qazi, Munachiso Nwadike, and their colleagues present a framework that lets one medical foundation model grow into many tasks through small add-on modules. Medical imaging data are scarce, so training a fresh foundation model for each scan type or task is rarely feasible. The modules act as skill sets that switch on at use time to fit the input and clinical goal.

The team adapted a chest CT foundation model first trained for classification into prognosis and segmentation modules. Results improved on both tasks. Adding PET scans lifted a key overlap score by about five percent over baselines, which supports the unified, expandable design.
arxiv-2511-11412:
Antoine Mazières and Thierry Poibeau introduce MajinBook, an open catalogue of digitally mediated world literature built for social science and cultural studies. The catalogue links metadata from large crowd-sourced shadow libraries with structured library data from Goodreads. The aim is a precise corpus of books as they actually circulate in digital form, a view that older print-based corpora miss.

The corpus holds over five hundred thirty-nine thousand references to English-language books across three centuries, enriched with first publication dates, genres, and popularity metrics. EPUB files born digital are favored, since their text is clean for machines, with companion sets for French, German, and Spanish. Linkage accuracy is evaluated, all data are released openly, and legal grounds are discussed.
arxiv-2511-11612:
Aasish Kumar Sharma and Julian Kunkel test language models on a scheduling task stated in words alone. Twenty-one public models got the same task. Each had to assign jobs to nodes in a mixed high-performance computing system. Each also had to compute the total finish time and explain its steps. The task came with clear limits and constraints.

A hand-derived best time set the standard. It was nine hours and twenty seconds. Just three models matched it while obeying all the rules. Many others broke rules or did the math wrong. Fluent explanation and correct constrained reasoning are not the same thing. The gap warns against trusting such models with real scheduling, unchecked.
arxiv-2511-11812:
Thomas Gehrmann and Peter Meinzinger study jets produced by photons at future lepton colliders, where most hadronic final states begin with a quasi-real photon radiated from an incoming electron. The photon may strike directly or resolve into its own parton content, a structure still loosely pinned down by data.

A detailed phenomenological analysis of photon-induced jet production in high-energy electron-positron collisions weighs how well such measurements could separate the direct and resolved contributions. Sharper knowledge of the photon's internal structure feeds into precision predictions across collider physics. Planned lepton machines would gain a concrete physics case from these channels, beyond their headline Higgs and electroweak programs.
arxiv-2511-12012:
Jiuhua Hu, Daniel Appelö and Yingda Cheng develop a framework for solving the Lindblad equation, a key model for open quantum systems whose energy can change over time. Their goal is schemes of any chosen high order that still keep the physics valid. The schemes stay completely positive and trace preserving, two basic checks for a sound quantum evolution.

Their approach builds on nested Picard iterative integrators, which repeat a step to raise accuracy in stages. The resulting schemes take Kraus form and can use low rank structure, so they cost less when the density matrix is simple in that sense. That makes the method suited to large problems where a full dense calculation would be too heavy.
arxiv-2511-12112:
Neda Bagheri Renani, Maryam Jaefarzadeh and Daniel Sevcovic compare two methods for large-scale nonlinear optimization, a core task in engineering and data work. One is the Improved Inexact-Newton-Smart method, and the other is a primal-dual interior-point framework. They test both head to head on broad synthetic benchmarks.

The interior-point method reaches the target in about a third fewer steps and about half the time, with slightly higher accuracy. The Newton-Smart method solves fewer cases by default, but tuning its regularization and step length helps a lot, though it does not close the gap. The study also shows interior-point results stay steadier when settings change.
arxiv-2511-12312:
Bhawna Mukhija and Amit Kashi model giant eruptions in massive stars in the years before a supernova explosion. Such stars can shed large amounts of mass in repeated outbursts, and the combined effect may change the state of the star in ways that favor the final explosion.

They evolve a star of one hundred solar masses and impose three one-year eruptions, varying the mass loss rate and the metal content. After each eruption the star recovers toward equilibrium, with luminosity first dropping and later rising again. Recovery is faster at lower metal content, and at higher mass loss the outer layers oscillate and compress during recovery, especially at higher metal content.
arxiv-2511-12712:
Christopher Cruz presents Adaptive Focus Memory, a system for keeping long chats with a language model on track. Replaying the whole history is costly, while cutting old messages lets early but crucial user constraints fade. AFM instead grades each past message and stores it at one of three fidelity levels: full text, compressed, or a placeholder, chosen by relevance, age, and importance.

Messages are packed in time order under a fixed token budget, so vital constraints stay sharp while trivia degrades gently. Cruz tested it on two hard scenarios: travel planning for a user with a severe peanut allergy, and a tax case built around an illegal evasion request. AFM preserved the allergy constraint in most runs where all baseline strategies failed, and it kept correct refusal behavior on the tax case. The system changes no model weights and is released as open source.
arxiv-2511-12812:
Sajad Salami and Tanush Shaska sort out three counts that are easy to confuse for weighted projective spaces over finite fields. The ordinary point count and the stacky mass do not depend on the chosen weights, but the number of orbits of nonzero representatives under the weighted scaling action does. They prove a closed formula for that orbit count and show it equals the number of isomorphism classes of the weighted projective stack. The twists lying over the ordinary points, with the gap explained by Kummer groups.

Their twist zeta function is rational, with a pattern independent of field size. For certain hypersurfaces they compute the function explicitly, with roots given by Gauss sums and curve eigenvalues. The paper is pure arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2511-13012:
Zhen-Qing Chen and Xicheng Zhang prove Harnack inequalities for a nonlocal equation whose drift is rougher than older theory allows. These bounds limit how much a solution can vary, and much of what analysts can prove rests on them. Their equation pairs the fractional Laplacian, which spreads influence over long range, with a drift field that has no divergence and a rough forcing term. The field sits in a critical or supercritical regime. Proving the bounds anyway pushes into ground where the drift could swamp the diffusion.

The bounds then do work. They yield well-posedness for critical stochastic quasi-geostrophic equations with additive noise, and weak solutions for two-dimensional fractional Navier-Stokes equations that start from measure-valued vorticity. They also yield well-posedness for generalized martingale problems tied to critical stochastic differential equations. One estimate settling several hard equations is why Harnack inequalities are prized.
arxiv-2511-13112:
Wenya Wei and fourteen co-authors let players talk to their AI teammates. In cooperative shooters, companions are usually steered by hotkeys or command wheels offering a few canned orders, with no way to name a target or a place. F.A.C.U.L. is, its authors say, the first real-time system where a player instructs an FPS companion in natural language. It decomposes complex commands, gauges its confidence in the interpretation, and retrieves the relevant entities from the environment so spoken orders can be carried out.

The companion answers with behavior and voice feedback, keeping the collaboration flowing. Using the commercial game Arena Breakout: Infinite as the testbed, the team compares the system against conventional control and reports user feedback on its strengths and limits. It targets immersion: a teammate you can brief like a person.
arxiv-2511-13212:
Bao-Duy Le and Dinh-Thi Nguyen map the vortex patterns of a spinning two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate pushed near its centrifugal limit. How the ground state organizes depends on the sign of the contact coupling. The authors use the method each case demands: for repulsion, GPU-accelerated variational minimization projected exactly onto the lowest Landau level; for attraction, imaginary-time evolution of the full Gross-Pitaevskii equation. With repulsion, they reproduce the triangular Abrikosov vortex lattices familiar from superconductors, closely matching Thomas-Fermi theory.

Attraction tells another story: no vortex lattice forms at any rotation speed. Instead the cloud contracts and collapses as the interaction nears a critical value, at nearly any rotation. The only stationary vortex states are giant vortices, trapped Townes solitons whose charge sectors collapse at thresholds the authors compute from an inequality and confirm in runs. The study benchmarks vortex formation and collapse.
arxiv-2511-13712:
Kiana Vu and 5 co-authors study how explainable AI can make extreme event forecasts usable for real decisions, with wildfire prediction as the test case. Climate change is raising the frequency and severity of such events, yet forecast models stay black boxes that responders hesitate to trust. Accuracy alone does not tell a response team why a warning fired.

Several AI models are graded, and SHAP explanations uncover the features, decision paths, and biases behind their wildfire calls. Added visuals place feature importance beside seasonal and geographic patterns so practitioners can read the output in context. The authors argue preparedness systems must be accurate, interpretable, and trustworthy at once to serve disaster planning.
arxiv-2511-13812:
Yonatan Kahn, Michael Wentzel, and Nicolás Yunes compute how a lighter-than-QCD axion would deform a neutron star and change its tidal response. At high density the axion's effective potential can flip, growing a real field inside the star. Their study is the first full numerical treatment of that dynamics in one-plus-one-dimensional general relativity, extended to light axions with kilometer-scale wavelengths.

Across a broad range of masses and decay constants, the star's mass, radius, and compactness shifted at order-one level. That shift breaks the usual near-universal link between tidal deformability and compactness, turning it into a probe of such axions that does not depend on the unknown nuclear equation of state. Future gravitational wave data could exploit the effect.
arxiv-2511-14012:
Pranendu Darbar studies the values of a quadratic Dirichlet L-function at the point one, averaged over hyperelliptic curves of growing genus over a fixed finite field. Earlier work by Lumley showed the distribution of these values has a tail that decays doubly exponentially. Darbar sharpens how far that decay range extends uniformly.

Using a long resonator method, he also proves a matching lower bound for the distribution function. That lower bound suggests the improved range may hold all the way up to its conjectured limit. The paper is a technical contribution to the statistics of L-functions over function fields, where extreme values are rare but structured.
arxiv-2511-14112:
Truong Vo, Weiyi Wu, and Kaize Ding generate synthetic hospital discharge notes to fix a long-tail problem in medical coding. Automatic ICD coding from clinical text fails on rare diagnosis codes because data sets like MIMIC-III contain few or no examples of thousands of them. Their framework builds realistic multi-label code sets anchored on rare codes.

Prompts draw on real co-occurrence patterns, code descriptions, synonyms, taxonomy, and similar real notes. The team generated ninety thousand synthetic notes spanning nearly eight thousand codes and fine-tuned two leading transformer coders on the enlarged data. Macro-level scores improved while overall accuracy held strong, suggesting crafted synthetic data can make rare-code prediction fairer.
arxiv-2511-14312:
Chenyang Xu, Siming Li, and Hao Wang make fake heart sound tapes to ease a data gap in heart care. Heart sound tapes, called phonocardiograms, help spot heart disease, but tapes with labels for rare ills are scarce. Their model, H-LDM, is a layered diffusion model. It makes true-to-life heart sounds from plain clinic data, with fine control over which ill it shows.

A multi-scale coder splits rhythm, heart sounds, and murmurs in its inner space. A medical focus block guides the build and keeps it clear to read. On the PhysioNet CirCor set the scores were strong, and heart doctors judged most tapes sound. Adding the fake tapes raised rare-ill scores by a clear margin.
arxiv-2511-14812:
Charles D. Coleman compares two families of loss functions used to grade forecasts and estimates. One family scores the level of a miss, the other scores the share or ratio of the miss. Both take a target value and its realized value, and both are widely used to rank accuracy across many units.

Coleman proves the two families agree in the long run whenever their averages settle to a fixed ratio. The proof covers a broad class of weighted power-style losses with a product form for the weights. A practical payoff follows: with many units and small average error, rankings by level and by share nearly coincide, so the choice between them matters less than users may fear.
arxiv-2511-14912:
Frank C. van den Bosch and Shashank Dattathri test two odd effects inside dark matter halos whose particles can collide with each other. In standard collisionless halos, heavy objects sinking toward the center stall once they reach the flat core, and the core itself can push objects back out. Both effects have only ever been shown in systems with no collisions at all.

Using idealized simulations, the authors ask whether the effects survive when dark matter interacts with itself. With strong enough interactions, neither stalling nor the outward push appears, and sinking objects keep falling. The finding changes how self-interacting dark matter models should predict the motion of black holes and star clusters inside galaxies.
arxiv-2511-15012:
Gi-Hwan Shin develops a quantitative framework for scoring sleep quality from brain wave recordings. Poor sleep is widespread in modern life and is known to erode thinking and weaken immune defenses. Yet sleep quality is shaped by many brain and environmental factors at once, which makes a single trustworthy number hard to define.

Shin's approach studies how slow and fast brain rhythms couple during sleep, wakeful rest, and a working memory task. Distinct patterns appear in beta power and delta connectivity across those states, and the coupling between delta and beta rhythms stands out as a strong marker. Reaction times on the memory task add a behavioral check. The framework points toward objective sleep scoring from EEG alone.
arxiv-2511-15212:
Jens Harlander and Stephan Rosebrock prove that a key group property survives inside well-behaved two-dimensional complexes. The property is local indicability of the fundamental group. Roughly, it means each finitely generated piece of the group can map onto the integers. The setting is diagrammatic reducibility, a condition on how disks can fill loops in a complex.

Using a Corson-Trace style test for reducibility away from a chosen subcomplex, the authors prove a much stronger result than before. They apply it to Whitehead's asphericity question, a famous open problem. A class of labeled oriented trees, and all their quotients, come out locally indicable under the stated conditions. Group theorists gain a new tool for a stubborn problem.
arxiv-2511-15412:
Evgenii Vinogradov and four co-authors model air to ground radio channels with spatial consistency using three dimensional shadow projections. Drone assisted networks need channel maps that respect building blockage as users move. Their method projects building shadows efficiently to map line of sight regions. Fast line of sight maps replace costly ray tracing in many uses.

Deterministic path loss tied to line of sight is blended with stochastic shadow fading. The result is a spatially consistent radio map for performance prediction. Tests in standard Manhattan grid layouts reproduce blockage and outage patterns well. The approach serves mobility aware planning for sixth generation non terrestrial networks. It balances physical realism with the speed planners need.
arxiv-2511-15612:
Sunder Ram Krishnan develops a geometric form of classic limits on how well a statistical parameter can be estimated. The Cramér-Rao bound sets a floor on estimator variance from the information in the data. Later bounds add correction terms. Krishnan recasts those curvature corrections using Cartan geometry and jet bundles, which package a function together with its derivatives.

For a one-parameter family, the square root of the density is seen as a curve in a function space. It is then extended to its tower of derivatives. A classic efficiency condition then matches the existence of a differential equation of fixed order for that curve. The block to such an equation is shown to be a curvature term, unifying two views.
arxiv-2511-15712:
Vivek Acharya presents a blockchain approach for verifying authenticity and intent in payments made by autonomous AI agents. Agents increasingly initiate financial transactions for users or other agents. Classic payments assume a human authorizes each transfer, a safeguard agent payments remove. In a decentralized, trustless setting, both agent identity and true user intent must be proved.

Decentralized identity standards and verifiable credentials establish who an agent is. On chain intent proofs record user authorization for later audit. Zero knowledge proofs preserve privacy while proving policy compliance. Secure execution attestations guarantee the agent code ran untampered. Together these layers aim to make agent led payments accountable without a central trusted intermediary.
arxiv-2511-16312:
Xiao-Min Zhang and five co-authors compute primordial non-Gaussianity in a warm inflation model where the inflaton is driven by pure kinetic energy and coupled through a nonminimal derivative term. Non-Gaussianity measures how the early universe's fluctuations depart from a simple random pattern, and it is a sharp test between inflation models.

Two parts of the signal are worked out separately: an intrinsic part from the inflaton's three-point correlation, and a delta-N part tied to the four-point correlation. The authors compare the two contributions with each other and with observational limits. That comparison pins down which model parameters remain allowed, showing what future measurements of the three- and four-point signals could rule in or out.
arxiv-2511-16512:
Nicholas Pellegrino, David Szczecina, and Paul Fieguth propose two loss functions that make supervised learning robust to wrong training labels. Mislabeled examples are usually harder to classify, so the idea is to let hard examples count less, or not at all, before they can poison the model.

Blurry Loss and Piecewise-zero Loss de-weight or disregard the most difficult samples during training. On a range of artificially corrupted datasets, the new losses beat the leading robust losses in nearly all cases, reaching better F1 scores for detecting the bad labels. Ablation studies show the gains hold for uniform and non-uniform corruption and across different error detection frameworks. Practitioners can use the losses to find, prune, or correct label errors more reliably.
arxiv-2511-16812:
Steven van den Broek, Marc van Kreveld, Wouter Meulemans, and Arjen Simons study a layout problem in linked bar charts. In such a chart, each bar is split into blocks, and matching blocks in unlike bars are joined by lines that pass over the bars between them. The order of blocks inside a bar changes how long those joining lines must run up and down.

The team asks how to order the blocks so the total up-and-down length is as small as can be, for a fixed order of bars. They give fast methods for cases where the hard shared links form a tree-like shape, and a slower method for a wider case. For the fully general case, they show the problem can still be solved when each bar carries few links.
arxiv-2511-16912:
Trieu Nguyen, Hao-Wei Pang, and Shasha Feng present PepEVOLVE, a method for improving ring-shaped peptides, a drug form that mixes traits of large and small medicines. The search space is huge, and chemists often must guess in advance which spots in the ring may be changed. Prior tools also lean on fixed training, which can limit how well they adapt during the search.

PepEVOLVE learns both where to edit and how to edit. It trains with shifting masks, uses a simple router to find spots that tend to give high rewards, and pairs a changing search method with a group-based scoring rule for steadiness. The aim is faster lead improvement across several goals at once, without a chemist fixing the editable spots first.
arxiv-2511-17412:
Faruk Abdulla, Anna Keselman, and Daniel Podolsky study what an orbital magnetic field does to a Weyl semimetal, a material whose electrons behave as massless particles near special momentum points. A field applied across the separation between a pair of Weyl points can couple them and open a gap in the spectrum, breaking the celebrated chiral anomaly. The authors examine how this gap opens when the material's lattice is treated honestly, rather than in a continuum approximation.

The lattice picture reveals layered Chern insulating states that the continuum misses. The anisotropy of the Weyl cones shapes the sequence of phase transitions between regimes, and the authors trace the connections back to the continuum limit. They also follow the surface Fermi-arc states, the material's hallmark surface excitations, and show how differently they behave across the gap-opening transitions. The work refines the theory of magnetic responses in topological semimetals.
arxiv-2511-17612:
Siddiqua Namrah's master's thesis work tackles a perception problem for self-driving and traffic monitoring systems: cameras see poorly at night. Low-light traffic scenes suffer from dim illumination, noise, motion blur, uneven lighting, and glare, all of which degrade object detection and scene understanding. The proposed framework enhances such images in multiple stages, without any paired ground-truth training images, by splitting each image into an illumination layer and a reflectance layer and refining both progressively.

Three specialized modules correct brightness globally and locally, restore structure while suppressing noise with spatial-channel attention, and rebuild overexposed regions blown out by headlights. Self-supervised losses, covering reconstruction, smoothness, perceptual consistency, and domain awareness, drive the training. On general and traffic-specific datasets, the method beat leading approaches on standard quality metrics and in visual quality, promising more reliable downstream perception at night.
arxiv-2511-17812:
Xinshuang Liu, Runfa Li, Shaoxiu Wei, and Truong Nguyen improve how samples are drawn from flow matching models, a family of generative models that turn noise into data. When only a few samples are affordable, independent draws can miss rare outcomes that strongly affect an average.

Their method draws samples jointly so they spread across important regions, using the model's score to keep them apart without drifting off the data. They also learn weights that correct the bias from joint drawing. Tests show diverse, high quality samples and accurate weighted averages, helping users judge what a flow model really produces.
arxiv-2511-18012:
Jiaying Zhou and Qingchao Chen improve weakly supervised open vocabulary object detection. The model must find objects from new categories using only box labels for some classes and image level labels for others. Fixed text prototypes miss how an object's look changes with its state, and proposed boxes carry scene context that text labels lack.

Their method enriches prototypes with state aware descriptions, such as a sleeping cat, and with scene aware descriptions, such as a cat on a sofa. A soft alignment step then matches regions and text more consistently. Together the two prototype upgrades sharpen discrimination and improve detection results.
arxiv-2511-18812:
Yu Jia, Chengyu Wu, Hao Wu, and Jiaqing Yang recover a jumpy viscosity from flow measures at a boundary alone. In a Stokes flow, viscosity sets the drag. If it jumps across an inner surface, can wall reads of velocity and force pin it down in a three dimensional body? Inverse problems of this kind test if hidden traits are knowable at all.

The team study how the Dirichlet Green's function blows up in a slope based norm. They then build a coupled Stokes-Brinkman system on a small local zone that probes the jump. The two tools yield a global uniqueness theorem: boundary data fix the viscosity in full. Unique recovery backs imaging of fluids whose makeup hides inside.
arxiv-2511-18912:
Orphée Collin studies the free energy of the random field Ising chain when its coupling grows without bound. The model is a line of spins in a random field, with centered independent disorder and one uniform coupling. The limiting free energy per site admits an expansion in the strong coupling limit, whose terms Collin refines.

A past first order result by Collin held under tighter claims on the disorder. The new work extends it to the general case where the disorder has a finite second moment. Collin also pins down an unknown constant from a joint past theorem, the first non universal constant in the expansion. Sharp terms ground the model's low temperature story.
arxiv-2511-19212:
Michał Pilipczuk, Sylvain Schmitz, and Henry Sinclair-Banks study the coverability problem for vector addition systems, a model of processes that add integer steps while never dropping below zero. The question asks whether a target configuration can be reached or exceeded from a start state. They examine how hard the problem is when measured by two natural parameters.

Those parameters are the system dimension and the total encoding size of its vector set. Among several results, coverability with dimension as the parameter and numbers written in unary is complete for the complexity class XNL under log-space reductions. The authors also flag open questions, including whether the encoding-size parameter allows a fixed-parameter algorithm.
arxiv-2511-19512:
Huanning Dong, Yinuo Huang, Fan Li, and Ping Kuang present LatentDreamer, a framework that turns a single image into a high-quality three-dimensional object. Image-to-3D generation has advanced fast, yet speed, detail, and fidelity rarely arrive together. The key step is a pre-trained autoencoder that maps 3D shapes into latent features, a compact code that makes the generation problem far easier than working with raw geometry from the start.

From those features the pipeline builds a coarse shape, refines it, and then adds realistic textures in sequence. The resulting objects stay faithful to the input image, and the whole process typically finishes in about seventy seconds. With only a small amount of training, the authors report, the system competes with heavier rivals, a useful trait for content creators who need assets quickly.
arxiv-2511-19612:
Ruihua Fan, Yantao Wu, Yimu Bao, and Zhehao Dai prove limits on building two-dimensional chiral states with step-by-step quantum circuits. Such circuits prepare states layer by layer, and a correspondence links them to tensor network states and one-dimensional channel dynamics. Chiral states, which break mirror symmetry, are a prized target.

Two no-go theorems result, one for free fermion systems and one for interacting ones. In the free case, the needed long-range correlations cannot arise from local, uniform channel dynamics. In the interacting case, causality constraints block the three-way entanglement a chiral state requires. Sequential preparation thus has a firm ceiling here.
arxiv-2511-19712:
Jonathan Jenvrin proves a lower bound for a height function on elliptic curves, giving a new proof of a theorem first due to Baker. The Néron-Tate height measures how arithmetically complex a point on a curve is, and small heights are hard to rule out. The setting is points over the largest abelian extension of a number field, for curves with complex multiplication.

Following a strategy of Amoroso, David, and Zannier, the proof produces a bound that is fully explicit. Notably, the bound does not depend on the discriminant of the base field, a quantity that usually creeps into such estimates. Only non-torsion points are covered.
arxiv-2511-19912:
Reasoning-VLA, from Dapeng Zhang and seven co-authors, aims to make driving decisions faster and more portable. Vision-language-action models decide well, but they often run slowly and fail to adapt to new vehicle setups or new scenes. The authors set out to fix both weaknesses in one framework.

The model uses learnable action queries, seeded from real recorded paths, that interact with reasoning-rich image and language features to produce smooth action paths in parallel. Training rests on eight public driving datasets remade into one standard chain-of-thought format. With supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning, the system reports top scores, strong generalization, and the best inference speed to date.
arxiv-2511-20112:
Amano, Ohshiro, Suzuki, Fukushima, and Yamaguchi map plasma conditions across a supernova remnant. Their 2025 paper uses the Reflection Grating Spectrometer aboard XMM-Newton. The target, DEM L71, is a fairly wide remnant. High-resolution X-ray spectra reveal individual emission lines. Line ratios diagnose temperature and plasma processes region by region.

The grating's wide dispersion spread lines across the detector. That spread let the team reconstruct spatial line maps. Oxygen lines came mostly from surrounding interstellar gas. Iron emission traced the star's ejected debris instead. Images blurred along that spread direction visibly. Expansion of gas and ejecta explains that blur. Some regions showed oddly lopsided oxygen line ratios. Plain shock-heated plasma models cannot explain those ratios. Resonance scattering can account for the enhancement. Charge exchange offers another plausible contributor there. The ratios grew alongside forbidden line brightness.
arxiv-2511-20212:
Wang, Chen, Sun, and Zhang settle when scoring a quantum optimizer is itself hard. Their 2025 paper analyzes QAOA expectation computation at fixed rounds. QAOA is a leading quantum method for hard puzzles. Judging its expected score guides its use. For general problems that judgment was murky.

For Max-Cut on general graphs, exact scoring is NP-hard. That holds for any fixed round count of two or more. Even rough additive approximations stay NP-hard too. The error tolerance shrinks exponentially yet hardness persists. A dynamic programming algorithm offers the other side. It exploits tree decompositions of the input graph. When local treewidth grows only logarithmically, scoring becomes fast. Polynomial-time exact evaluation follows in that regime. The framework extends beyond Max-Cut to binary problems generally. Tests ran up to three rounds on structured graphs. Locality-matched classical baselines framed the cut ratios.
arxiv-2511-20312:
Beiser, Martinelli, Gerstner, and Brea steal a neural network's weights using only its answers. Their 2025 paper reverse-engineers networks from input-output queries. A student network trains to mimic a hidden teacher. Enough probing should reveal the teacher's parameters. Standard training data often fails as query sets though.

Big teachers have more weights than available data points. Students then overfit queries instead of matching weights. Classic image tricks like rotation and noise help little. The team designed augmentations aimed at hidden layers. Their queries excite richer internal representations deliberately. Biased-noise augmentation aligned student and teacher weights excellently. Previously unrecoverable teachers on MNIST became identifiable. The method scales far beyond earlier limits. Networks with one hundred times more parameters than data were recovered. The augmented set grew to thirty-five times the original size. Scaling tests stopped at 512 hidden neurons.
arxiv-2511-20412:
Wang, Slud, and Ma trace how genes might cause brain disorders through brain wiring. Their 2025 paper builds a new mediation model for imaging genetics. Disorders like nicotine dependence run in families and involve many genes. Genes likely act by changing brain structure and function first. Mediation analysis makes that chain of influence precise. Thousands of genes and brain features overwhelm older versions.

Their model handles many exposures and many mediators jointly. Both sides compress into low-dimensional summary scores. Those summaries are chosen to maximize the mediation effect. Sparsity in the loadings keeps the summaries easy to read. An alternating algorithm with block updates solves the fitting problem. Simulations beat rival methods across signal and noise settings. Applied to UK Biobank data, the method linked genes to smoking. Specific genes affected nicotine dependence via wiring changes in the brain. Particular brain regions carried those indirect effects.
arxiv-2511-20612:
Kim and Dean rebuild whole flow fields from a sparse scatter of sensors. Their 2025 paper introduces Stochastic NODE-DMD for system identification. Wind fields and ocean currents evolve continuously and resist modeling. Classic dynamic mode decomposition assumes dense, clean data. Noise, sparsity, and nonlinearity break it in practice.

Their method recasts decomposition as a generative model. A neural implicit field allows reconstruction at any coordinate. A stochastic neural ODE adds the nonlinear leftovers to linear modes. Uncertainty travels with the predictions, properly quantified. Four benchmarks tested the approach against baselines. Only ten percent observation density was allowed in training. Reconstruction accuracy beat the baseline under that sparsity. Learned modes and eigenvalues matched ground truth structure. Long rollouts kept coherent geometry and phase. Training on many runs learned a spread of dynamics, not one average. Balloon and drone navigation in wind are target uses.
arxiv-2511-20812:
Chiara Fusar Bassini and colleagues test in 2025 whether automated price caps in US electricity markets deter market power, or merely look strict. Automated mitigation procedures screen bids in real time and penalise abusive prices, but only switch on when a structural index like congestion crosses a cutoff. The authors exploit that quirk with a regression discontinuity design on 2019 bid data from the New England and New York markets.

The deterrence is real but narrow. Around 30 to 40 percent of bidders cut their bids when screening activates. The median cut is 4 to 5 dollars per megawatt-hour in New England and 9 to 10 in New York. Yet the market-wide effect, a dip of 1 to 2 dollars, is not detectable, suggesting thresholds set in the early 2000s, never recalibrated, are too lax. Their merit-order simulation prices tighter thresholds at 350,000 to 980,000 dollars of buyer surplus per mitigated hour. Such hours number fewer than 33 a year.
arxiv-2511-20912:
Dongxing He, Arianna Formenti, Spencer Gessner, and Michael Peskin simplify in 2025 the physics of beamstrahlung, the hard radiation electrons and positrons emit when dense bunches collide. At future 10 TeV colliders, bunches of a billion to ten billion particles will pass through each other's intense fields. Beamstrahlung sets the energy spectrum of the most energetic particles and seeds every other quantum process, so collider designers need it in fast, usable form.

The simplification appears when the quantum parameter Upsilon grows large. It is of order 1 for colliders below 1 TeV, but reaches roughly a thousand at 10 TeV. In that limit, the electron and photon spectra collapse onto universal functions, independent of machine details. The authors supply analytical approximations to those functions, ready for general beam-beam studies. The work backs wakefield collider designs now being drawn up for the next energy frontier.
arxiv-2511-21012:
Hyunwook Jheonn and colleagues sharpen in 2025 the sorting of two easily confused star types: young stellar objects, stars still forming, and asymptotic giant branch stars, dying suns swollen and dusty. Both glow similarly in infrared light, thanks to comparable temperatures and dust shells, so catalogues contaminate each other. Their Double Filter Model adds a second sieve beyond colours and magnitudes: light curves, since the two classes vary by different mechanisms.

The model was validated on Taurus young stars and spectroscopically confirmed giant branch stars, and it caught objects that infrared-only classification had mislabelled. The team then applied it to the SPICY catalogue, the largest young-star candidate list, with nearly 120,000 sources in the inner galactic plane, to flag hidden giant-branch contaminants for follow-up spectroscopy. Earlier machine-learning efforts topped out near 90 percent accuracy in the overlap regions; the time-domain filter aims to clean what photometry cannot.
arxiv-2511-21112:
Swathi Shetty, Sayinath Udupa N. V., and B. R. Rakshith study in 2025 coalitions in graphs, in domination theory. A dominating set is a set of vertices so placed that every outside vertex touches one of them. A coalition is a pair of disjoint sets that each fail to dominate alone but dominate together when united. A coalition partition splits the vertices into such partnering sets; the coalition graph records the partnerships.

Earlier work proved every graph can appear as the coalition graph of some larger graph, but asked whether a smaller host would do. The authors answer yes, constructing a small host whose coalition graph reproduces a given graph. They also take up the coalition count, the most distinct coalitions in a partition, defined recently by Haynes and colleagues. They characterise graphs whose coalition count equals one, and derive properties of the count under conditions on the coalition number.
arxiv-2511-21312:
Martin Jacquet, Marvin Harms, and Kostas Alexis give flying robots a learned sense of nearby space in a 2025 robotics paper. Their drones navigate unknown, cluttered places without a prebuilt map, using only onboard range sensing. Two cascaded neural networks compress a single depth image into a compact code. They then expand it into a signed distance function, a field stating how far each point is from the nearest surface.

Jacquet and his coauthors embed that distance field as an explicit safety constraint inside a nonlinear model predictive controller, which plans thrust and attitude commands while tracking a target velocity. They verify the controller's recursive feasibility and stability under fixed observations. Closed-loop tests beat two leading local navigation methods, tolerated drifting odometry, and real flights in forests showed the system dodging trees and clutter against an adversarial reference velocity pushing it toward trouble.
arxiv-2511-21512:
Sara Ellison and Leonardo Ferreira weigh the stars that galaxy mergers actually build, in the fourth paper of a series, in 2025. Mergers are known to ignite central bursts of star formation, which should pile new stellar mass into galactic cores, but direct measurements of that burst mass fraction are rare. The authors assemble about 14,000 post-coalescence galaxies, systems whose merger starbursts have just finished, and compare their central masses against carefully matched non-merging controls.

Ellison and Ferreira find burst mass fractions of 10 to 20 percent, measured both in a fixed central aperture and in the galactic bulge. For 61 nearby systems with MaNGA integral-field data, the central excess runs 15 to 20 percent. Surprisingly, a 15 percent excess persists out to about 7 kiloparsecs, far wider than the compact growth earlier studies inferred. Theirs is the first such measurement made directly from stellar mass, independent of population modeling or light-profile fitting.
arxiv-2511-21612:
Shahir Abdullah and Syed Rohit Zaman argue that cloud databases scale in the wrong direction, in 2025. Providers offer a binary choice: scale out by adding nodes, or scale up by fattening each node. Reality is joint: performance and cost emerge from node count interacting with per-node CPU, memory, bandwidth, and storage speed. One-dimensional reactions overshoot load spikes or oscillate between poor states.

Their Scaling Plane maps every configuration as a point: node count on one axis, per-node resources on the other, with surfaces for latency, throughput, overhead, and cost. Analysis and experiments show optimal scaling paths often run diagonally, adjusting both dimensions at once. Their DiagonalScale algorithm searches horizontal, vertical, and diagonal moves for the best configuration under service-level constraints. Tests on synthetic surfaces and distributed SQL and key-value systems show lower tail latency, lower cost, and far better stability, with monotone convergence guaranteed.
arxiv-2511-21812:
Vandersnickt and colleagues report evidence for a magnetic field buried inside HD 192575, a hot star about twelve times the Sun's mass that pulses in brightness. They studied 1,951 days of light-curve data from the TESS space telescope, focusing on one pulsing pattern split into nine closely spaced frequencies. Explaining all nine at once is the key test.

Rotation alone, including the Coriolis effect from the star's roughly 5.3 day spin period near its core, could not reproduce the nine frequencies and their relative strengths. Adding a tilted internal magnetic field did work, with a peak strength near 24 kilogauss in the successful model. The authors present this as the first such modelled detection inside an evolved star of this type, a future supernova. It matters because hidden fields can move angular momentum and mix material inside stars.
arxiv-2511-22012:
Parekh, Gao, and Jaiman, engineers, build a stand-in for fluid-structure simulations of inverted elastic foils, flexible panels clamped at the trailing edge that flap in a flowing fluid like fluttering leaves. Such self-sustained flapping can harvest energy from currents, but high-fidelity simulations are too slow to search wide design spaces, so a trustworthy surrogate has real practical value for energy-harvesting devices.

The network treats mesh nodes and elements together as a hypergraph. Their rotation-equivariant hypergraph neural network compresses the foil's mesh motion with proper orthogonal decomposition and evolves the flow field on the mesh itself. It is trained on finite-element simulation data across a range of mass ratios. Over thousands of time steps the surrogate predicts tip displacement and force coefficients with errors below 1.5 percent, reproduces the vortex-shedding frequencies, and matches energy-transfer metrics within 3 percent of the simulations.
arxiv-2511-22312:
Praharaj and Kasundra tackle a trust problem with generative AI classifiers used for content safety. Models like LLaMA Guard label unsafe content and its categories, but they output words, not probabilities. Without class probabilities, moderators cannot judge confidence, set flexible thresholds, or study errors closely. That gap limits fine-grained error analysis for the teams who run these systems.

The team proposes three ways to recover probabilities from the model's token scores, called logits. The three are conditional, joint, and marginal probability estimates over the label tokens. They test the methods on a synthetic, carefully annotated dataset across several instruction-tuned models. Using logits clearly improves how readable and trustworthy the classifiers are. The marginal method, which adds up probability across many token paths, gives the most robust and accurate confidence scores. It also delivers the best overall classification scores of the methods tried.
arxiv-2511-22412:
Nam studies how chiral symmetry, a symmetry between left- and right-handed quarks, is restored in hot, dense quark matter. Inside the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, an effective theory of quarks, heating or compressing matter melts the quark condensate and shrinks the dynamical quark mass toward zero. Nam proposes a diagnostic built from quantum information: a chirality entanglement entropy measuring how mixed the two sectors are.
