Their review covers more than two hundred safety benchmarks and maps the common failures. They draw on engineering science and long-standing theories of risk and safety for guidance. If the measuring tools are flawed, safety claims built on them cannot be trusted. Engineering sciences and established risk theory supply the standards the review uses to judge the benchmark field. Shortcomings are grouped as technical, epistemic, and sociotechnical, a map meant to guide repairs.
arxiv-2601-23212:
Joshua Southern and six co-authors predict how multispecific antibodies will behave using graph neural networks. These engineered antibodies grab several targets at once, offering powerful new therapies. Their effect emerges from complex molecular architecture, so small design changes can flip the outcome.

Experimental data are scarce, which makes prediction even harder. Treating the antibody as a graph lets the network reason over its domain layout. Good predictions could shorten the costly trial-and-error of therapeutic design. Domain topology is the variable under study: how the antibody's parts are arranged governs what the assembled molecule can do.
arxiv-2602-00112: Beldjilali Gherici and coauthors study torse-forming vector fields, which generalize several important vector fields in geometry. The paper gives techniques for turning a proper torse-forming field into its special cases, showing how the general form narrows to the familiar sub types. Concrete examples illustrate each transformation, so readers can see the abstract method at work on specific fields. Though brief, the paper offers a handy toolkit for geometers who meet torse-forming fields and need to recognize or reduce them in practice.
arxiv-2602-00412: Marcos L. P. Bueno and Joaquin Vanschoren study how AutoML holds up on dirty categorical data. Dirty sets often have several categorical fields with many values, from lack of curation and auto collection. Recent research today shows models gain from morphological encoders for dirty categorical data, with much better results. The authors propose a pipeline turning categorical data into numerical data for AutoML use with advanced encoding schemes, testing current robustness.
arxiv-2602-00712: Peter J. Cameron studies graphs defined on algebras, building on recent work on group-element graphs. The commuting graph, joining elements that commute, is the oldest and most famous case. The author argues its definition is unlikely to extend to general algebras, as with nilpotency and Engel graphs. For graphs defined through generated subgroups or subalgebras, the existing definitions carry over unchanged. These include the power graph, enhanced power graph, generating graph, independence graph, and rank graph. The paper also extends definitions to directed graphs and simplicial complexes.
arxiv-2602-01212: Marco Chen and co-authors lift GPT training with SimpleNorm, a plain scale rule from second-order geometry. They link net design, act scale, the Hessian map, and top safe learn rate. SimpleNorm steadies mid act scales by build, and Hessian math shows it shrinks the Hessian's top singular value a lot, so bigger safe learn rates hold. Tests on GPT nets from 1B to 8B weights show far bigger tolerated learn rates, firm trains, and better scores than baselines, with lower train loss at 7B scale.
arxiv-2602-01312: Han Tong and co-authors give TRAK, a popular data-credit tool, its first theory. TRAK first swaps the model for a kernel machine, then borrows leave-one-out tricks to guess each training case's pull on a prediction. Though it scores well in practice, the rules for when its guesses hold and where they break stayed dim. The team maps its errors and shows that, even with big errors, credit guesses stay tightly linked to true credit, so case rankings largely survive. Sims and real tests back the theory.
arxiv-2602-01412: Kamélia Daudel and co-authors dissect score-function estimators for importance-weighted variational inference, which approximates intractable densities via Monte Carlo objectives. Without reparameterization, optimization leans on REINFORCE estimators. Standard VIMCO estimators lose signal-to-noise as counts rise. The team builds a VIMCO mechanism dodging that collapse, including a High-Effective Sample Size estimator with square-root-of-N scaling. That estimator lacks zero variance at optimality, so the team adds VIMCO estimators reaching zero variance with tempering. Discrete latent-variable and state-space tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2602-01812: Cheng Wang and colleagues register chest CT images, where large deformation, background and overlap make the task harder than brain registration. Their fast unsupervised deep method, LDRNet, first predicts a coarse registration field and then refines it from coarse to fine. Two components drive it: a refine block improving the field at resolutions, and a rigid block learning a transformation matrix from deep features. Tested on private and SegTHOR sets against traditional methods and VoxelMorph, RCN and LapIRN, it leads large deformation registration. It also runs much faster.
arxiv-2602-02112: Chunsan Hong and colleagues present order-expressive masked diffusion model (OeMDM) for varied orders. OeMDM unifies MDM, ARM, and block diffusion. Masked diffusion models rival autoregressive models, but quality hinges on sequence. Prior work either hard-codes an ordering or learns one. That path costs extra and can yield weak solutions. Building on OeMDM, they introduce learnable-order masked diffusion model (LoMDM), learning ordering and backbone. LoMDM thus generates text in context order. LoMDM outperforms discrete diffusion models across language modeling benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-02212: Zheyuan Zhou and others propose MAIN-VLA, grounding vision-language-action decisions in deep meaning match rather than surface pattern matching. Complex dynamic worlds overwhelm current models with redundant sensor streams, hiding action-critical signals. The intention module compresses verbose instructions and thought into compact meaning primitives. The environment module turns visual streams into structured topological affordance maps. Aligning both abstractions concentrates focus, enabling token pruning without settings, and tests in Minecraft and large player-versus-player games set a new state of the art.
arxiv-2602-02512:
Changan Liu and 3 co-authors rewire social network edges to give disadvantaged groups a fairer share of visibility, in a 2026 arXiv paper. PageRank fairness means allocating PageRank weight, a measure of a node's importance, fairly among distinct groups. A group stuck at the network's edge, such as women in a male-dominated industry, sees fewer job posts and opportunities.

The problem is to maximize fairness for a disadvantaged group by rewiring a fixed number of edges. Building on a greedy approach, the authors use fast sampling of rooted spanning forests to reach an effective linear-time algorithm. Experiments on varied real-world networks show the algorithm significantly outperforming existing methods. It produced accurate solutions for networks with a million nodes in just a few minutes. The work turns fairness from a measurement into an actionable network edit.
arxiv-2602-02712:
How hard should you push when steering a language model's internal representations? Magamed Taimeskhanov and 2 co-authors give the first theoretical analysis of steering strength, posted to arXiv in 2026. Steering nudges activations along a chosen direction at inference time to evoke a behavior. Too small a push and nothing changes; too large and the model degrades beyond repair.

The analysis characterizes steering's effect on next-token probability, on the presence of a concept, and on cross-entropy loss, deriving precise qualitative laws for each. Surprising non-monotonic behavior appears: more push does not always mean more of the intended effect. Eleven language models, from a small GPT-style system to modern architectures, validated the predictions empirically. Practitioners who steer models gain principled guidance where they previously tuned by feel.
arxiv-2602-02812:
Randall Clark and 6 co-authors classify a fusion plasma's confinement state from the few diagnostics that could survive inside a future power plant, in a 2026 paper. Fusion pilot plants restrict diagnostics severely: port space is scarce and instruments must endure a reactor environment. Control still needs reliable plasma state information from that limited set.

The team previously built a confinement mode classifier on electron cyclotron emission data. A new classifier based on a profile reflectometer reaches ninety-seven percent test accuracy. An ensemble combining both diagnostics pushes accuracy to ninety-nine percent. The progression matters because no single diagnostic is guaranteed in a plant design still under debate. Machine learning tools matched to several viable diagnostics give operators redundancy. The work belongs to a larger project extracting control-grade state information from deliberately sparse instrumentation.
arxiv-2602-03012:
Turning sparse vulnerability records into runnable security tasks is automated by Xianzhen Luo and 10 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Evaluating code agents on security needs executable tasks, but manual reproduction is costly and old datasets miss emerging threats. Their multi-agent system, CVE-Factory, performs that transformation automatically at expert-level quality.

Cross-checks against human expert work showed high answer correctness and environment fidelity. The team built LiveCVEBench, a continuously updated benchmark spanning many languages and repositories, including AI-tooling flaws. They also synthesized over a thousand training environments. A fine-tuned model improved sharply on the benchmark and transferred to a terminal benchmark. All resources, including code and leaderboard, are openly released.
arxiv-2602-03112:
Candidate trajectories for self-driving are redesigned by Zhengfei Wu and 4 co-authors in a 2026 paper. End-to-end driving systems increasingly make several trajectory options and select one. A fixed vocabulary of trajectories covers routine driving stably but misses the best option in complex interactions. Scene-changing refinement, meanwhile, can over-correct simple cases by disturbing already strong options unnecessarily.

Their system, CdDrive, keeps the original vocabulary options untouched. It augments them with scene-changing options produced by vocabulary-conditioned diffusion denoising. A shared module scores both types jointly. An adapter improves the smoothness and continuity of diffusion options through time smoothing and horizon-aware noise. Tests on two NAVSIM benchmarks led the field, with ablations verifying each part.
arxiv-2602-03412:
Training a language model agent on long tasks is hard because a single final reward cannot say which step mattered. Mukai Li and 7 co-authors propose Critical Step Optimization in a 2026 paper. The method hunts for critical steps, decision points where a different action demonstrably flips the task from failure to success.

Starting from the agent's own failed runs, a process reward model flags candidate steps, and an expert model suggests better actions. Only alternatives that the agent itself can carry through to a correct finish are kept as training data. On two agent benchmarks, the method improves over supervised fine-tuning by wide margins while using verified supervision at only a small share of steps.
arxiv-2602-03612:
Generating realistic new graphs matters for chemistry, biology, and social network research alike. Anthony Stephenson and 2 co-authors propose a graph generation method in a 2026 paper based on heat diffusion. They adapt the Generator Matching approach to graph-structured data, using the graph Laplacian as the engine of the process.

The Laplacian generates a continuous-time diffusion on each graph, and its heat kernel supplies a family of small changes to the starting graph. A neural network learns to match that generator by shrinking a Bregman divergence against a trainable stand-in. Sampling then runs a time-reversed diffusion from the learned generator. The authors report that the method reproduces the structural character of real and synthetic graphs well.
arxiv-2602-03712:
Refactoring code means improving its structure without changing its behavior, a stricter test for language models than writing fresh code. Yisen Xu and 2 co-authors release SWE-Refactor in a 2026 paper, a benchmark of real-world refactoring by human developers. Earlier benchmarks mixed refactorings with unrelated changes and starved models of repository context.

The benchmark mines 1,099 behavior-preserving refactorings from 18 Java projects, most atomic and the rest compound. Every instance is validated by compiling, running tests, and checking with automated refactoring detectors. Nine widely used models are evaluated as reference points. Compound refactorings cause most failures: even a strong coding agent succeeds on under forty percent of them, marking clear headroom for improvement.
arxiv-2602-04012:
Birds telegraph turns before they make them, and Hossein B. Jond and 1 co-author borrow that trick for robot swarms. Their 2026 paper adds anticipation to flocking algorithms, which usually react only to neighbors' current motion. Multirotor drones likewise tilt before changing direction, giving early cues.

In future direction-aware flocking, each agent blends reactive alignment with predicted neighbor velocities a short moment ahead. A single tuning knob sets the mix. Simulations show faster, stronger alignment and steadier cohesion than reactive baselines. The predictive term also resists sensing delays and measurement noise that normally destabilize swarms.
arxiv-2602-04212:
Learning a new concept in context is not the same as using it. Michael A. Lepori and 3 co-authors test that gap in a 2026 paper. Earlier work showed language models can form rich internal representations of novel information presented in the prompt. Whether they can deploy those representations remained open.

The team probed open-weight models on next-token prediction with new semantics and on an adaptive world modeling task. In both, models struggled to use what they had apparently learned. The result tempers hopes that in-context learning alone yields flexible adaptation to radically new situations at deployment time.
arxiv-2602-04312:
The chiral effective potential of maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory turns out quite tame. I. L. Buchbinder and 4 co-authors compute it in a 2026 paper, writing the four-dimensional theory in terms of simpler superfields. The potential captures the leading low-energy behavior of the effective action.

At one loop and beyond, every quantum correction is finite and scales with the classical potential. The authors find all corrections in closed form, folded into a single coefficient. Such tidiness is rare in quantum field theory and reflects the theory's rare symmetry. Exact structures like this serve as benchmarks for approximate methods used on messier, real-world theories.
arxiv-2602-04612:
Leonardo Pisani studies how a moving impurity stirs an ultracold Fermi gas in a 2026 paper on zero sound, a collective vibration that travels through the gas as a whole. The work sits at zero temperature and assumes strong interactions among the atoms.

As the impurity moves uniformly, it creates a density modulation, a ripple in how crowded the atoms are. Above a threshold speed, that ripple is carried by the zero sound mode. Pisani evaluates how much of the oscillation comes from zero sound versus ordinary particle-hole excitations. The answer depends strongly on the interaction between atoms. He therefore varies its strength, range, and shape to map how the effect changes.
arxiv-2602-04812:
Lorenz Wendlinger and 3 co-authors improve link prediction on legal citation networks in a 2026 study. These networks mix statutes, cases, and rich metadata, and predicting missing links can surface relevant law. Recent results, the authors find, leave room for stronger and more portable models.

Two changes drive their gains. Edge dropout in training and joining features yield more robust representations, cutting error rates by a lot. A second approach uses multilingual node features with an improved asymmetric decoder built for fit between varied node types. That version extends prediction to data from New Zealand, far apart in place and language from the sources. The changes also improved transfer between disjoint legal systems.
arxiv-2602-04912:
Explaining a retrieval-augmented generation system's answer means tracing which tool contributed what, and most systems cannot do it. It is the work of James Gao and 4 co-authors. In tool-based RAG, a language model calls outside tools and blends their outputs into one answer. When the answer is wrong or odd, it is hard to tell which tool contributed what.

Their system, Atomic Information Flow, breaks tool outputs and model calls into atoms, the smallest self-contained pieces of information. The flow of atoms is drawn as a network ending at the final answer, which makes each tool's share measurable. The authors then train a small Gemma model to spot the critical pieces, guided by the flow analysis. Its accuracy on a question-answering test jumped from about 55 to about 83 percent, close to a model nearly seven times larger.
arxiv-2602-05012:
In-context learning lets a language model pick up a new task from a few examples in the prompt, but those examples may hold private information. Rob Romijnders and 5 co-authors address that privacy risk in this 2026 machine learning paper. Earlier private versions were either expensive to run or leaned on heuristics with weak guarantees.

Their method, called Private PoEtry, reframes the problem as a product of experts, which gives the privacy protection a firm theoretical footing. The algorithm also parallelizes easily. Across five datasets covering text classification, math, and vision-language tasks, it beat earlier private in-context methods by more than 30 points of accuracy on average. The gains came while keeping strong differential privacy guarantees in place.
arxiv-2602-05112:
A bioeconomy swaps fossil inputs for biomass, and getting there is meant to take teamwork between old processing firms and new partners. Philipp Jonas Kreutzer and Josef Taalbi mapped that teamwork in this 2026 economics paper. Their data covers technology ties among innovating firms in Sweden over five decades, from 1970 to 2021.

Each extra direct partner was linked to clearly higher innovation output, and indirect ties helped too. Holding a brokerage spot between groups, by contrast, showed no clear link to output, and likeness of knowledge bases mattered less than theory might suggest. Firms deep in the bioeconomy acted much like innovators elsewhere, suggesting the same teamwork mechanics apply. The policy lesson is broad: spurring more teamwork outright may beat trying to fine-tune who teams up with whom.
arxiv-2602-05312:
Fuzzing, feeding programs malformed inputs to find bugs, now runs continuously in many projects, but nobody had asked whether the programming language changes how well it works. Tatsuya Shirai and 4 co-authors answer at scale in this 2026 software engineering study, accepted at MSR 2026. Their data covers more than 61,000 fuzzing bugs and nearly a million builds from 559 projects in Google's OSS-Fuzz service.

Patterns split clearly by language. C++ and Rust projects surfaced bugs most frequently. Rust and Python had low shares of true vulnerabilities, yet the ones found tended to be more critical. Crash types differed across languages, unreproducible bugs were common in Go and rare in Rust, and Python projects patched a higher share of findings but took longer to detect them. The authors argue language design shapes fuzzing outcomes enough that tools and strategies should be language-aware.
arxiv-2602-05512:
Knowledge graphs answer precise questions well, but only for users who can write graph query languages, while language models often invent facts. Larissa Pusch, Alexandre Courtiol, and Tim Conrad combine the two: their framework has a language model draft Cypher queries and explain them in plain words. Users then refine the queries through natural language, keeping a human in the loop at each step.

The team tests the setup on real-world graphs and on a benchmark of ninety queries over a synthetic movie graph. That benchmark grades how well models explain queries and spot faults, and smaller trials run on a hyena research graph and a mathematics research data graph. Results show how model performance shifts across domains. The authors argue the design widens access to complex data sets while keeping the factual rigor of graph queries.
arxiv-2602-05712:
Coding assistants powered by large language models save developer time but burn energy at data center scale. Lola Solovyeva and Fernando Castor measure where that energy goes during inference. They split it into a prefill phase, which reads the input, and a decoding phase, which writes output token by token. They test ten transformer models across two size groups on code generation and code understanding benchmarks.

Within each group, models showed distinct energy patterns across the phases. Higher prefill cost also amplified the energy cost of each decoded token, by amounts that varied widely by model. Three of the ten models babbled, adding needless content that inflated energy use. A babbling suppression step for code generation cut energy sharply without hurting accuracy. The authors conclude that phase level accounting reveals savings that total energy figures hide. The study speaks to teams pursuing greener AI in software development.
arxiv-2602-05912:
Sampling warm states of many body quantum systems is key for studying chaos and warm phases of matter, yet making large labeled sets is costly. Jiyu Jiang, Mingrui Jing, and 3 co-authors present the quantum thermal drift channel, a step that powers a measurement steered sampling rule. The sampler on its own makes warm states along with the Hamiltonians they belong to, as labels.

The authors prove the rule is quick, with gate counts that grow like powers in system size. They also sketch the sampled Hamiltonians as a normal spread reweighted by partition functions, weighing a tradeoff between sampling truth and label range. Level spacing stats from an Ising model show the expected shift to chaotic universality. A tuned sorter trained on the made data guessed traits of unseen Hamiltonians near best. The long paper frames the method as a quantum native route to training data.
arxiv-2602-06112:
Very light scalar fields may form large clouds around stars, held there by the star's own matter. Arturo de Giorgi and 2 co-authors ask what happens when that star suddenly collapses into a black hole. The source disappears, and the field escapes as an outgoing wave, like a scalar tsunami.

Earlier estimates treated space as flat. The new work adds general relativity and a better model of the starting cloud. The total energy released stays close to the simple estimates. The mix of frequencies in the wave, though, changes in clear ways. Such bursts could one day be a target for detectors hunting light new particles.
arxiv-2602-06412:
Masked diffusion language models write by revealing tokens step by step, but they recompute every position at every step, even settled ones. Daisuke Oba and 3 co-authors propose SureLock to stop that waste. When a revealed token's probability distribution stops changing across steps, the position is locked.

Locked positions skip their query and feed-forward work, while their stored attention keys and values stay available for others to read. As more positions lock, each step gets cheaper. On a large masked diffusion model, compute fell by roughly a third to a half at comparable output quality. A theory analysis shows watching the local change at lock time suffices to bound the final effect.
arxiv-2602-06512:
Generalist robot policies learn manipulation from demonstrations, but those demonstrations cluster: a few tasks have plenty of examples, most have few. Junhong Zhu and 4 co-authors analyze that long-tail problem in depth. Standard fixes like re-sampling the rare tasks, they show, do not rescue tail performance.

Digging deeper, they trace the failure to spatial reasoning: data scarcity on tail tasks directly weakens the policy's sense of space. Their remedy, Approaching-Phase Augmentation, transfers spatial knowledge from data-rich head tasks to scarce tail tasks without needing outside demonstrations. Experiments in simulation and on real robots showed the augmentation worked where re-sampling had failed.
arxiv-2602-06612:
Bintao Yuan and four co-authors look for weak points in low Earth orbit satellite networks, which are growing into huge constellations. Older safety checks focus on how the network is connected, but failures can spread through load shifts and tangled dependencies instead. The team builds a framework that models those links with a hypergraph, a map that lets one link join many nodes at once.

Their key measure rates each node by how much load it carries compared with its backup options. In tests using real Starlink orbit data, the measure found failure points that older scores missed. The riskiest nodes were not in the crowded satellite core but at the ground-space edges, where a single failure can cascade widely. The authors argue that backup planning should start at those edges.
arxiv-2602-06912:
Juan Gutiérrez and two co-authors segment objects in pictures without any training labels, and let a user steer the result. Self-taught vision transformers give patch clues, but scenes with many objects muddle those clues, and pictures with little meaning weaken them, so masks come out ragged. Their method, PANC, needs no training and stays steady.

PANC extends the normalized cut method by tying user-marked tokens to foreground and background anchors. That tie shapes a generalized eigenproblem whose low-frequency splits lean toward the wanted class while keeping the global spectral shape intact. Careful choice of eigenvector direction and cutoff then yields stable masks. Tests confirm the injected hints widen spectral gaps as theory predicts, with gains of about 2 to 3 percent on two standard sets and near 9 percent on a low-meaning crack set.
arxiv-2602-07212:
Traffic safety benchmarks usually spot crashes crudely, without tying judgments to official safety standards.  Xinyu Liu and six co-authors present RoadSafe365, a large vision-language benchmark built from real dashcam and surveillance video and organized by a hierarchy that refines crash, incident, and violation definitions.

The benchmark holds 36,196 annotated clips with rich attributes across event types, environments, and meeting scenarios, each paired with multiple annotations.  It lets teams test fine-grained safety understanding rather than coarse accident detection.  For teams building driving assistance and traffic monitoring, RoadSafe365 offers testing that speaks the language of regulators as well as models.
arxiv-2602-07312:
Drivers of semi-autonomous vehicles must cooperate with systems whose thinking they cannot see, so they invent explanations to fill the gap.  Yehuda Perry and one co-author interview sixteen drivers in the United States about those folk theories and the strategies drivers use when the system surprises them.

Drivers build sophisticated accounts, often describing systems that see, hesitate, or become overwhelmed, yet they lack information to check those accounts or to take part in governing the methods.  Opacity bites hardest in complex situations and during control handoffs.  Designers and regulators get a human-centered map of where transparency and feedback matter most in semi-autonomous driving.
arxiv-2602-07412:
Generative AI is changing how programmers work inside development environments, from code generation to review and repair, but the research agenda for that shift was scattered.  A large team led by Raula Gaikovina Kula reports on a four-day intensive meeting where 33 experts from software engineering, AI. Human-computer contact discussed the impact of generative AI on integrated development environments.

Four themes emerged as the areas teams and users should pursue, spanning the challenges and opportunities of raising the level of abstraction away from writing code by hand.  The paper is a research perspective, not a tool release: a map of questions for a field reorganizing around AI-assisted development environments.
arxiv-2602-07612:
Choosing a NoSQL database for knowledge graph processing is usually ad hoc, because static benchmarks miss the complexity of real graph workloads.  Rosario Napoli and three co-authors present a benchmarking method tailored to knowledge graphs, using connectivity density, scale, and a new graph-centric metric called Semantic Richness.

A four-tier query methodology reveals results crossover points across document-oriented, graph. Multi-model systems, tested empirically on the FAERS adverse event knowledge graph at three scales, from simple filtering to deep traversals.  Users get thorough guidance for matching storage paradigms to graph characteristics and query needs, replacing guesswork with measured trade-offs.
arxiv-2602-07812:
Language models stumble when comparing numbers written in different notations, like scientific notation against plain decimals. Fengting Yuchi and two co-authors ask whether the models secretly know the magnitudes even when their spoken answers go wrong.

Probing the hidden states of smaller open models, they find a single linear projection recovers log-magnitudes with about 2.3 percent relative error on synthetic text and 19 percent on scientific papers, and a linear classifier ranks paired numerals with over 90 percent accuracy. Yet the models' explicit answers score only 50 to 70 percent. Adding the probe's loss during fine-tuning lifts verbal accuracy by 3.22 percent, showing internal knowledge can be coaxed into speech.
arxiv-2602-08012:
Flow and diffusion models face two separate challenges: steering a pretrained model with rewards, and merging several models into one. Riccardo De Santi and three co-authors unify both problems in a single probability-space framework built from operators over model densities.

Within it, intersection can enforce safety, union can compose diverse models, interpolation can aid discovery, and all of these gain reward-guided versions, combinable into logical expressions via generative circuits. Their reward-guided flow merging method reduces the task to a sequence of standard fine-tuning problems solved by mirror descent. Generative-model researchers gain a principled language for combining and controlling models instead of ad hoc tricks.
arxiv-2602-08112:
Landslides on Mars matter for grasp the planet's surface, but labeled data for detecting them is scarce. Sidike Paheding and seven co-authors present MMLSv2, a multimodal dataset for Martian landslide segmentation combining RGB imagery, elevation, slope, thermal inertia, and grayscale bands.

The dataset holds 664 images across training, validation, and test splits, plus a separate test set of 276 images from a region far from the training area, to measure spatial generalization. Segmentation models train stably and perform competitively, yet struggle with fragmented, elongated, and small landslides, and results drops noticeably on the isolated set. Remote-sensing teams gain both a resource and a sobering benchmark for generalization beyond familiar terrain.
arxiv-2602-08312:
Two patches of sky get a close look in this first paper from a deep imaging survey run on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. Binyang Liu and sixteen co-authors describe the Two Deep Fields Imaging Survey, which aimed one field at a repeating fast radio burst and the other at a possible spinning galaxy cluster. The survey reaches faint magnitudes near 26 in the red band.

Most of the paper is a practical record: how the team planned the observations, cleaned the raw frames, and turned them into usable science products. Those products include calibrated single images, combined multi-color mosaics, and large catalogs of objects. They lay the ground for later work on the burst's home galaxy, the cluster's mass, and wider questions about the universe's structure.
arxiv-2602-08512:
The Higgs boson's couplings to third-generation fermions are now measured, but its far weaker couplings to lighter quarks remain elusive. Alberto Zucchetta presents the latest CMS results on light Yukawa couplings, with emphasis on the Higgs-charm coupling. This arXiv entry records a talk rather than a standard research paper, summarizing direct and indirect measurements.

Recent tagging advances have driven much of the progress in constraining these tiny couplings. The talk also sketches prospects for future improvement as data and methods advance. Readers get a concise status report on one of the Higgs program's hardest measurements, and a sense of how close the field is getting.
arxiv-2602-08712:
A population living on a finite interval faces a simple question: how far from the edge must it be to survive? Rinaldo B. Schinazi models individuals that give birth to neighboring sites at rate lambda and die at rate one, with no births crossing the boundary. His arXiv paper compares finite intervals with the infinite line.

On the whole line, survival with positive probability requires lambda above one half. For lambda between one half and about 0.707, a critical interval size exists: populations survive on larger intervals and die out on smaller ones. Crowding at the center does not save a too-small population. Readers get a crisp threshold result linking habitat size to survival odds.
arxiv-2602-08912:
Kushal Bhowmick and one co-author study a classic number puzzle: which whole numbers are congruent numbers for a triangle with a 60-degree angle? The question turns on the rank of 2-Selmer groups of an associated elliptic curve. Following Heath-Brown's strategy, they derive an asymptotic formula for the size of relaxed 2-Selmer groups.

The formula yields unconditional positive-density results. Among square-free numbers congruent to 13 mod 24 with all prime factors 1 mod 4, a positive share have 2-Selmer rank 1 or 3. Among those congruent to 5 mod 24 under the same prime condition, a positive share have rank 0 or 2. It is a firm step on a hard arithmetic problem.
arxiv-2602-09012:
AI agents now breeze through old CAPTCHAs, with top models passing logic puzzles like Bingo up to ninety percent of the time. Jiacheng Liu and five co-authors answer with Next-Gen CAPTCHAs, a defense built on a data-generation pipeline rather than a fixed test set. For backend-supported types, it can generate effectively unlimited fresh challenges.

The design exploits a persistent cognitive gap between people and agents in interactive perception, memory, decision-making, and action. Tasks demand adaptive intuition instead of step-by-step planning, redrawing a line that reasoning-heavy models had erased. The result is a scalable, diverse shield for the agentic web.
arxiv-2602-09212:
Mamadou Niang and three co-authors study exact controllability for semilinear measure-driven integrodifferential systems with nonlocal conditions. Such systems, where the evolution depends on history through integrals and on nonlocal constraints, arise in models with memory and distributed effects. The paper gives sufficient conditions for steering the system exactly to a desired state.

The argument uses the measure of noncompactness together with the Mönch fixed-point theorem, notably without assuming compactness of the evolution system relative to the linear part. That relaxation lets the results both generalize and improve many earlier findings, widening the class of nonlocal measure-driven systems known to be exactly controllable.
arxiv-2602-09412:
Minh Hoang Trinh and Hieu Minh Nguyen offer a book on controlling multi-agent systems, a field that has grown fast since the early 2000s yet lacks systematic textbooks even in English. The material grew from teaching since 2021, first as a concise Vietnamese-language reference for two courses at Hanoi University of Science and Technology: networked control systems and control of multi-agent systems. It selects fundamental topics of broad and lasting interest.

Part one introduces multi-agent systems and basic graph concepts. Part two designs and analyzes linear consensus algorithms. Part three turns to applications and research directions, including formation control, network localization, distributed optimization, opinion dynamics, and matrix-weighted networks. Though several topics reach research-level complexity, the analysis proceeds step by step toward standard methods and tools. Each chapter closes with notes on notable researchers, further reading, and exercises.
arxiv-2602-09512:
Extreme weather at several places at once threatens lives and homes, and modeling joint peaks matters for climate science. Lorenzo Dell'Oro and two co-authors review and extend Gaussian place-scale mixes for spatial peaks in their 2026 paper. A spatial base process scaled or shifted by a random variable gains flex: Gaussian mixes keep base gains while dodging balance, light tails, and weak tail links.

The paper develops new builds with good traits plus a general algorithm for given-data runs from these models. Its wider models fit both tails and bulk of the data, avoiding a stated choice of which events count as extreme. New fit methods dodge the number jam from latent place and scale factors. Simulated cases confirm the methods, and a use for wildfire-related weather factors in Portugal shows the approach in practice.
arxiv-2602-09812:
Eliahu Friedman and Avraham Gal review recent work using density-dependent lambda-nuclear optical potentials to calculate lambda-hypernuclear binding energies in their 2026 paper. All known lambda binding energies in the mass range from sixteen to two hundred eight are well fitted with just two interaction parameters. One attractive term covers the spin-averaged lambda-nucleon interaction, and one repulsive term covers the lambda-nucleon-nucleon interaction.

The lambda-nucleon term by itself overbinds lambda hypernuclei, in quantitative agreement with recent findings from effective field theory and femtoscopy studies. The strength of the lambda-nucleon-nucleon term proves compatible with values required to resolve the hyperon puzzle. Two parameters thus capture the known binding energies while connecting hypernuclear physics to the dense-matter puzzle.
arxiv-2602-10212:
Low-rank tuning nearly matches full tuning accuracy on fine-tuning tasks even at rank one, yet theory for how accuracy depends on rank has lagged. A 2026 paper by Michael Rushka and Diego Klabjan weighs low-rank LoRA updates against full updates through the lens of dynamical systems. Gradient flow study in full-rank and low-rank settings yields direct rank-accuracy links for two loss functions.

The authors derive the gradient flow equations with care, showing the same form for simultaneous and sequential parameter updates. The resulting system equations then give closed-form rank-accuracy links for the trace-squared loss and the Frobenius-norm loss. The work supplies the missing theory base for a widely used workhorse method.
arxiv-2602-10312:
Flood damage nowcasting needs fast, clear predictions, but fine-tuning is costly. A 2026 paper led by Lipai Huang, with three co-authors, offers R2RAG-Flood, a training-free retrieval setup for flood damage nowcasting with reinforced thought. A thought-first knowledge base is built from labeled tabular records holding structured predictors, a compact text summary, and a model-made thought path.

During inference, the target prompt gains nearby neighbors and free-shots supporting case-based thought without fine-tuning. A two-stage routine first settles damage occurrence, then grades severity on a three-level damage-extent scale, with a careful downgrade check for shaky over-severe outputs. In a Harris County, Texas, test on Hurricane Harvey, the setup reaches about sixty-one to sixty-seven percent overall accuracy across seven backbones, with reasons for each prediction. Lighter versions beat the supervised baseline on severity per cost.
arxiv-2602-10512:
Sho Sonoda and two co-authors defend the detour in agentic theorem proving in a 2026 paper. Learned provers often present lemmas, sketches, or subgoal decompositions before returning to tactic-level search. That looks wasteful: if proving lemmas is itself hard, why spend effort there first?

The paper gives a number learning answer. Instead of worst-case hardness over all claims, it studies the spread a teacher prover produces: initial states paired with successful verified traces. Modeled as imitation learning over a finite-horizon process, success depends on teacher proof length, action predictability, and student scores. Intermediate lemmas help, the analysis shows, because they shorten and regularize what the student must learn.
arxiv-2602-10812:
Sotiris Armeniakos and Jacopo Ulivelli derive a new tiny form of a classic rule in a 2026 paper. Splitting a curve rule from the Prekopa-Leindler rule yields a statement that at once lifts the weighed edge Poincare rule and the Brascamp-Lieb spread rule.

The resulting rule carries a times-based structure, which the authors use as an other to the older square-summed method for shape and exact rules. Uses include a calm guess for the weighed Poincare rule and new rewrites plus part results on the size Brunn-Minkowski conjecture. The paper turns one splitting into a handy tool for rule theory.
arxiv-2602-11012:
How often do fractions land near points on a curved surface? Sam Chow and three co-authors settle the convergence theory for multiplicative Diophantine approximation on all non-degenerate smooth manifolds. They also settle it for affine subspaces under a broad, near-best Diophantine condition.

The results answer a question posed by Beresnevich and Velani in 2005. Along the way they sharpen earlier work by Kleinbock and Margulis on strong extremality of manifolds, and by Kleinbock on affine subspaces. The paper thus closes a long-standing gap while tightening the tools that number theorists use for approximation on curved sets.
arxiv-2602-11212:
Focus costs explode with context length, and recurrent memory often trades principle for scale. Yunchong Song and four co-authors propose Elastic Memory, a design grounded in the HiPPO frame for online function approximation. History is treated as samples from continuous signals, compressed into a fixed-size state.

A polynomial sampling step rebuilds history summaries from that state for recall. On long-context sets across three domains, Elastic Memory beat rivals, including a memorizing model by a wide memory margin. It stayed ahead as model size grew and ran faster than a rival at larger scale. Its decoupled design also allows test-time biases to boost scores further.
arxiv-2602-11312:
A deformed Schrödinger equation can still behave like quantum mechanics. M. A. Rego-Monteiro and E. M. F. Curado build a curved deformed structure from a derivative tool that depends on a setting q. When q approaches one, the tool returns to the ordinary Newton derivative.

Their deformed Lagrangian yields a curved equation with a curved kinetic term and a standard possible. For zero possible near q equal to one, they solve it analytically. Energy, momentum, and a continuity equation survive, the Planck relation holds, and coupling to electromagnetism works. Numerics for a free particle show solitonic patterns in one spatial dimension for particular q values.
arxiv-2602-11412:
Visibility on social platforms can masquerade as credibility. Hanjing Shi and Dominic DiFranzo study checks timing in online discussion of agentic AI across two Reddit communities with contrasting cultures. Engagement signals like upvotes may act as credibility proxies, discouraging key tests.

Their survival analysis of time-to-first-checks reveals a popularity paradox: high-visibility threads face delayed or absent checks cues compared with quieter threads. That lag creates a window for narrative lock-in, where early unverified claims harden into shared bias before evidence-seeking emerges. The authors propose knowledge friction as a design move to rebalance engagement-driven platforms toward checks.
arxiv-2602-11912:
Superconducting qubit parameters drift within a second, motivating calibration and testing at millisecond speed. Malthe Marciniak and fifteen co-authors demonstrate an on-FPGA workflow joining pulse generation, data capture, analysis, and feed-forward, cutting CPU round trips. Sparse-sampling and on-FPGA inference tools cover exponential and sine-like responses, plus Nelder-Mead optimization and golden-section search on-FPGA.

Those methods enable low-latency tools for readout tuning, spectroscopy, pulse tuning, coherence checks, and testing. The toolset estimates decay time in 10 ms, optimizes readout settings in 100 ms, optimizes pulse amplitudes in 1 ms, and performs Clifford random gate testing in 107 ms. The qubit is a flux-tunable transmon. Running closed-loop on-FPGA re-tuning for 6 hours enables more than 74000 re-tunings. Gate errors stay better than first tuning, while re-tuning suppresses coupling of gate error to control drift.
arxiv-2602-12012:
Sea watching by robot teams faces water-warped vision and thin communication links. Muhammad Farhan Ahmed and one co-author present a spread-out framework in which multiple drones team with a driverless surface vessel to detect and track floating containers. Each drone runs YOLOv8 boosted by stereo depth and maintains per-target tracks with uncertainty-aware data matching.

Robots exchange compact track summaries fused safely by Covariance Intersection, keeping estimates sound under unknown cross-links. A data-driven planner assigns targets and picks drone hover viewpoints by balancing doubt reduction against travel effort and safety gaps. Built in ROS and tested in simulation against standard tracking and fusion baselines, the system improves identity tracking and pinpoint accuracy with modest link load.
arxiv-2602-12212:
Equilibrium thermodynamics works because vast numbers of microstates blur into the same local picture, but states out of equilibrium need a wider frame. Maurizio Fagotti works alone here, building that frame from ensembles of pure states that minimise average energy variance. Varying the weights inside that best family organises state space into minimum-variance leaves, generalising the stationary states of equilibrium.

On those leaves, states with the same energy density can become indistinguishable, a pattern the paper calls leaf typicality. At equilibrium, it reduces to eigenstate thermalisation and its variants. Numerical tests support leaf typicality on some leaves while stronger forms break on others, hinting at a rich thermodynamic order beyond equilibrium, and a path toward one statistical mechanics for both regimes.
arxiv-2602-12412:
Knot polynomials from Chern-Simons theory have deep algebraic roots, and this paper traces them to a trace map in factorisation homology. Kevin Costello led this work with two co-authors, identifying the Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant of links as such a trace. To recover Chern-Simons knot invariants, they build a filtered E3-algebra by BV quantisation of Chern-Simons theory for a semi-simple Lie algebra with invariant pairing.

They prove that a finite-dimensional representation of the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum group defines a perfect module over that algebra. For any framed link in three-dimensional space, they then prove an equality between the factorisation homology trace for that representation and the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant it determines. The result gives a clean homological route to classical knot invariants.
arxiv-2602-12612:
Auto design for suggestion systems by neural design search is limited by a fixed search space set by human priors. Sein Kim led this work with eight co-authors, noting that LLM-driven code growth opens the search space to programs. Yet it relies on scalar metrics such as NDCG and Hit Ratio that give no quality insight into failures or steering guidance. Their framework, Self-EvolveRec, builds a steering feedback loop instead.

A User Simulator gives quality critiques, while a Model Diagnosis Tool gives quantitative internal verification. A Tool-Model joint growth plan ensures testing rules adapt on the fly as the suggestion design evolves. Tests show Self-EvolveRec clearly beating top neural design search and LLM-driven code growth rivals on both suggestion scores and user happiness, with code released online.
arxiv-2602-13112:
Gradient methods live or die by stepsize choice, and adaptive methods like AdaGrad ease that tuning burden. Matia Bojovic and two co-authors propose AdaGrad-Diff, an AdaGrad-style method where adaptation follows cumulative squared norms of successive gradient differences, not gradient norms themselves. The intuition is simple: when gradients barely change, the stepsize should not shrink needlessly, while large gradient swings, signalling curvature or instability, should damp the stepsize automatically.

Numerical experiments show the new method hardier than AdaGrad in several settings that matter in practice. For practitioners tired of stepsize grids, adaptation driven by gradient change rather than gradient size offers a principled alternative: stable phases keep their pace, and turbulent phases slow down on their own.
arxiv-2602-13212:
Multi-drone missions directed by natural language need both flexible task thinking and hard guarantees at the physical layer. Ziyi Zhang and three co-authors propose UAVgent, a three-layer design. A human operator issues language instructions. A language-model supervisor regularly interprets, verifies, and corrects the commanded task against latest state and target guesses. A distributed inner-loop controller tracks the reference using only local relative information.

The authors derive a theory guarantee for tracking scores given bounded disturbances and piecewise-smooth references that jump discretely from language-model updates. The combination shows how centralised language thinking and distributed feedback control can jointly deliver complex behaviours with provable toughness and calm, a template for language-in-the-loop control beyond drones.
arxiv-2602-13312:
Perovskite solar cells promise strong performance at low cost, but developing them means chaining literature search, data gathering, experiment design, and synthesis into one loop, with physical rules carried across each step. Single models handle isolated steps yet fail to pass constraints along the chain. PeroMAS wraps perovskite-specific tools in a standard protocol and lets agents plan and call them across the whole workflow, from papers and data to property prediction and mechanism analysis.

An expert-built benchmark shows the system beats single models and classic search at finding candidates that meet several goals at once. Most tellingly, the authors verified the approach in the physical world through real synthesis experiments. Yishu Wang leads the work with ten co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13412:
Magnetic systems on tree-like lattices reveal phase changes through the stability of their disordered states. This paper studies a mixed-spin Ising model on a Cayley tree of order three. For the representative spin value five, the recursion becomes an eleven-dimensional dynamical system. Phase-transition regions are mapped by checking whether the largest Jacobian eigenvalue at the symmetric fixed point reaches one in magnitude.

To test whether the disordered phase can be reconstructed from far-away data, the author recasts translation-invariant Gibbs measures as tree-indexed Markov chains. He computes Dobrushin coefficients, with a spectral test matching the Kesten-Stigum condition. A Markov entropy rate is introduced as a computable observable, with closed forms at the symmetric point for arbitrary spin. Hasan Akin is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-14212:
D. Fargion and four co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv origin for puzzling TeV signals near SS433. This binary, with a black hole fed by a large companion star, has shown twin precessing jets for half a century. Years ago, H.E.S.S., HAWC, and LHAASO found a surprising far twin gamma beam at tens of TeV, some hundred light years out.

The authors suggest a rare eruption a century ago launched twin neutron beams at tens of PeV. Those neutrons decay in flight into protons, neutrinos, and tens-of-TeV electrons. The electrons then emit hard gamma rays by inverse Compton scattering on interstellar infrared photons, feeding the distant TeV traces. The story links one past eruption to beams seen far from the source.
arxiv-2602-14312:
E. Kongkui Berinyuy and four co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv plan to boost quantum entanglement in molecular optomechanics. Links are a key good for quantum tech, but making multi-mode links is strongly damped by the dark mode effect. The paper breaks that effect with a tiny cavity design.

A light cavity holds two tiny groups tied through inter-group coupling, with a hop rate phase-tuned by a made gauge field. Tuning coupling strength and tune phase flips between dark-mode-whole and dark-mode-broken regimes. In the whole regime, two-part and three-part links stay low or damped, while breaking the dark mode lifts both, giving flexible control over link making.
arxiv-2602-14612:
Long audio holds events spread over hours, and questions about them need exact times. Kartik Hegde, with four co-authors, presents LA-RAG, a system that turns audio into timestamped event records. It stores those records in a database and answers questions by search plus language-model text.

Two modes are offered: pre-indexed files for fast queries, and on-the-fly grounding for short clips. Tests use 24-hour home and factory audio sets plus a real-world question set. The system answers with low delay once files are indexed. It also shows that timestamped grounding beats raw model guessing on time questions.
arxiv-2602-14812:
Jaione Bengoetxea, Itziar Gonzalez-Dios, and Rodrigo Agerri build the first non-question-answering physical commonsense dataset for Basque, a low-resource language, in both standard and dialectal forms. Physical commonsense lets people grasp surroundings, foresee events, and navigate space, yet large language models have rarely been tested on such reasoning outside question answering in languages like Basque.

Starting from the Italian GITA resource, the team creates BasPhyCo and evaluates model performance on it, opening a gap in multilingual reasoning research. Basque speakers gain a benchmark in their own tongue and its dialects. Commonsense, the paper suggests, should be tested where resources are thinnest.
arxiv-2602-14912:
A. K. Dond and others work out after-the-fact error gauges for a tweaked Morley mesh, first put forth by Wang, Xu, and Hu, for thin-plate fourth-order laws and for non-linear von Karman laws. The gauges are shown to be both safe and sharp: they miss no true error, and they do not cry wolf.

A mesh that refines where gauges point is tried in number runs. Thin plates and shells with touchy, thin-scale acts thus gain error gauges one can trust and heed. Plates of thin kind thus find gauges that miss nothing and cry wolf never.
arxiv-2602-15012:
Bose and colleagues tackle cold-start personalization, where a system must learn tastes through chat with no prior user history. Each task spans dozens of preference dimensions, yet a given user cares about only a few, and which few depends on who asks. Asking without structure wastes a tight question budget. Reinforcement learning fits the problem in form, but its terminal reward ignores the factored shape of preference data, and learned policies often collapse to fixed question lists.

Their system, Pep, learns a structured world model of preference links offline from full profiles. It then runs training-free Bayesian inference online to pick sharp questions and predict full profiles, even for dimensions never asked. Across medical, mathematical, social, and commonsense tasks, Pep aligns with stated tastes about 81 percent of the time, against about 69 percent for RL. It uses far fewer turns and roughly 10 thousand parameters against 8 billion.
arxiv-2602-15112:
Garikaparthi and colleagues introduce ResearchGym, a benchmark for AI agents on end-to-end research. They repurpose five oral and spotlight papers from ICML, ICLR, and ACL. From each repository they keep data sets, test harnesses, and baseline code, but withhold the proposed method. The result is five containerized setups holding 39 sub-tasks, where agents must propose hypotheses, run experiments, and beat strong human baselines.

A controlled test of a GPT-5 agent reveals a sharp gap between capability and reliability. It beats provided baselines in just 1 of 15 evaluations, by about 12 percent, and finishes about 27 percent of sub-tasks on average. Failures recur: impatience, poor time management, overconfidence in weak ideas, trouble coordinating parallel runs, and context limits. Yet one run beats an ICML 2025 Spotlight solution, showing frontier agents can sometimes reach the top, but unreliably. Other scaffolds such as Claude Code and Codex show a similar gap.
arxiv-2602-15412:
He and colleagues offer a method joining meaning vectors with opinion motion view, giving a measured setup for joint building. Stores log change by catching coder talks through code acts such as pull asks and edits.

Their method packs code bits into high-sized arrow codes using coding nets, keeping grammar and meaning traits. These vectors are handled using PCA for size cut, with data leveled. They model time change using the Expressed-Private Opinion tool to draw faith grids and follow paths across rounds. These opinion paths show accord, sway spread, and shifting accord or split within groups, showing teamwork shapes and knowledge-swapping gears else hard to see. By linking building and social study, their tool gives a way to measure change, giving ideas into coder sway, accord, and venture staying power. They test the method on data from three open-source GitHub stores, showing its power.
arxiv-2602-15512:
Lepri and colleagues review how heat moves in Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chains, a classic test bed for non-equilibrium physics. The story starts with the old puzzle of why these chains fail to thermalise as expected. It moves to the finding that heat flow is anomalous, with effective thermal conductivity growing with system size instead of settling. The review draws a sharp line between two cases, with distinct growth exponents tied to different physics.

The FPUT alpha-beta model, with exponent one third, links to Kardar-Parisi-Zhang physics, while the symmetric FPUT beta model points to two fifths. Finite-size effects from thermostats can mask the true scaling, and nearness to integrable limits breeds long-lived quasi-particles that yield diffusive behaviour over middle scales. Open problems close the review.
arxiv-2602-15712:
Bumberger works alone to flip the main frame in image-based science. Today structure is usually found semantics-first, by guessing or forcing domain labels. But that approach fails where image science matters most. It fails in open-ended finding, in cross-sensor and cross-site compare, and in long-term watching where label sets drift across cultures, institutions, and settings. He proposes the reverse order: criteria-first, semantics-later.

The unified frame splits rule-defined, meaning-free structure work from downstream mapping into domain word lists. The first layer yields stable partitions, fields, or trees defined by stated optimality rules rather than local word lists. Meaning is not dropped but moved downstream as an explicit mapping. That move allows plural readings and crosswalks without redoing upstream work, and it treats shape products as FAIR, AI-ready digital objects.
arxiv-2602-15812:
Blackadar and Farah show the basic theory of separable C-star algebras needs no Axiom of Choice to go through. Nor does that theory rest on the Continuum Hypothesis, on Martin Axiom, or on any other usual assumption from set theory. The paper proves that claim in two ways. First, standard proofs are shown not to require Choice. Second, set-theoretic absoluteness theorems are used.

For analysts, the authors lay out the basics of projective complexity and absoluteness. They also give limiting examples consistent with ZF. One example is a commutative C-star algebra with a concrete Hilbert-space representation that fails to match C(X) for every compact Hausdorff space X. Its state space lacks compactness and contains no extreme points. Analysts gain a Choice-free foundation plus sharp examples of where classical expectations break.
arxiv-2602-16112:
Rachael Zehrung and Yunan Chen study people who live in cars, a growing form of housing insecurity that research has largely overlooked. Prior work on vehicle dwelling leans on digital nomadism and vanlife, missing the tighter constraints of smaller vehicles and the precariousness of dwelling as a last resort. Drawing on qualitative analysis of posts and comments from an online community, the authors examine the daily infrastructuring work car dwellers do under social, spatial, and infrastructural constraints.

Their experiences sit between homelessness and nomadism, and the authors trace how motivations and identity negotiations play out in that middle ground. Building infrastructural competence, learning where to park, wash, charge, and stay safe, shapes how dwellers see themselves. The paper closes with implications for human-computer interaction research and design recommendations for technologies that respect car dwellers diverse needs, circumstances, and identities.
arxiv-2602-16512:
Felix Fricke leads two coauthors on Framework of Thoughts, a foundation framework for dynamic reasoning schemes. Prompting schemes such as Chain of Thought, Tree of Thoughts, and Graph of Thoughts boost language model reasoning. But most demand fixed, problem-specific structures that cannot adapt to new problem types, and they are often under-optimized.

Framework of Thoughts builds and optimizes dynamic schemes, with built-in hyperparameter tuning, prompt optimization, parallel execution, and intelligent caching. The authors implement Tree of Thoughts, Graph of Thoughts, and ProbTree inside it, showing faster execution, lower cost, and better task scores through optimization. They release the codebase to support future dynamic, efficient reasoning schemes.
arxiv-2602-17112:
Arjun Ashok led a six-author team studying what keeps open-source projects alive inside foundations. Projects join bodies like Apache, Eclipse, and OSGeo for governance advice, incubation help, and community building. But foundations differ in policies, funding, and support. Projects also arrive at varied stages with varied needs. Matching project to foundation, and plan to project, is genuinely hard.

The paper analyzes incubator projects across the three foundations plus GitHub projects outside any foundation. From sociotechnical trace profiles, the authors build foundation-specific sustainability models and a triage tool that forecasts outcomes within and across foundations, and even beyond them. Case studies of failed incubators pair the forecasts with recovery strategies, showing how social and technical signals together can guide sustainability decisions.
arxiv-2602-17212:
Sumitra Shit led a seven-author team showing that quantum dots in atomically thin semiconductors react to strain far more sharply than free excitons do. Strain tuning of monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides tunes light-matter coupling and can create quantum dots. The team probed thousands of individual dots in two materials across several heterostructures and a piezoelectric device, from cryogenic cold to room warmth.

Dots in both materials showed markedly stronger strain sensitivity in their emission energies than delocalized excitons. The boost was roughly fourfold in one material and twofold in the other, broadening the ensemble emission line. Follow-up tests tie the boost to stronger coupling with low-energy phonons under quantum confinement. The work offers a versatile strain-tuning route toward matching spectra across solid-state, atomic, and hybrid quantum photonic networks.
arxiv-2602-17512:
Leila Gharavi led a seven-author team on real-life automated collision avoidance, dodging the moose. A static obstacle popping up on the road, the moose test, is a classic driving emergency. Model Predictive Control has long served vehicle planning and control. Yet live collision avoidance in such emergencies stays unsolved, since evasive control demands heavy computation.

The paper tests Model Predictive Control live for planning after a static obstacle appears. Since state-of-the-art nonlinear control often fails to yield a live answer, the team adds a human-like feed-forward planner. It steps in when optimization proves infeasible or stalls on a poor guess. A maximum steering maneuver shapes the planner, mimicking human reaction after the obstacle is spotted. Live trials run at varied speeds and emergency levels in the FPEV2-Kanon. Its strength is shown against a state-of-the-art Model Predictive Control motion planner.
arxiv-2602-17712:
Abhishek Tiwari presents HBAT 2, an updated Python version of the Hydrogen Bond Analysis Tool first published in 2007. Hydrogen bonds and other weak bonds hold proteins and nucleic acids together. Accurate study of those bonds matters for molecular recognition, protein folding and drug design.

HBAT 2 automates analysis for structures in Protein Data Bank file format. It finds standard hydrogen bonds, weak hydrogen bonds, halogen bonds, stacking links and related types, using geometric criteria. It also detects chain patterns and renders them as two-dimensional views. A point-and-click screen, a web screen, a simple command-line tool and a coder API make it usable across skill levels.
arxiv-2602-18012:
Pragati Kumari and Novarun Deb examine the energy and carbon cost of small language models in automated software testing. Sustainability analyses have focused almost entirely on large language models, leaving the energy and carbon profile of small models during test generation largely unexplored. That gap matters as language models spread through testing workflows.

Their DeCEAT framework carefully weighs energy and performance trade-offs for small models, using HumanEval plus adaptive prompt variants built on the Anthropic template. CodeCarbon measures energy use and carbon emissions under controlled conditions, while unit test coverage gauges the quality of generated tests. Different small models show distinct strengths: some use less energy and run faster, while others hold steadier or stay more accurate under carbon constraints. The findings show sustainability here has many dimensions, and prompt structure and model choice jointly drive both energy and performance outcomes.
arxiv-2602-18212:
Rui Chen and three co-authors built a light, soft shoulder exosuit driven by air. Their 2026 paper tackles a hard trade: portable air systems for two-direction shoulder help must balance push against speed, while several actuators crowd the design. The team's angled actuator cuts volume by about thirty-six percent yet keeps about ninety-four percent of its push and answers about thirty-five percent faster.

Two actuators built on that shape, one curved for lifting the arm out and one pouch-based for pulling it across, join into a textile suit weighing under four hundred grams. In tests with ten healthy volunteers, the suit cut shoulder muscle activity, up to fifty-nine percent for lifting with one actuator and up to about sixty-four percent for bending forward. Adding the second actuator helped forward bending only in one chest muscle. The work guides future multi-direction soft suits.
arxiv-2602-18312:
Zhaoming Xie and two co-authors teach animated characters smooth, lifelike motion without fussy tuning. Their 2026 paper notes that reinforcement learning policies for simulated characters often exploit jerky high-frequency signals no human or robot could perform. Older fixes add a reward penalty on action changes over time, but that penalty needs heavy tuning.

The team instead penalizes the action Jacobian, how actions change with state, computed directly by automatic differentiation, which kills unrealistic high-frequency control without task-specific tuning. A new Linear Policy Net makes that penalty cheap to compute, needs no parameter tuning, learns faster, and answers faster at inference. The combination learns smooth policies for backflips and parkour skills, and drives a real four-legged robot with an arm.
arxiv-2602-18412:
Ariel A. Galindo Duque and three co-authors use a quantum measure to read classical stickiness. Their 2026 paper asks how quantum localization encodes hierarchical stickiness, the layered trapping that rules transport in mixed classical phase spaces. The testbed is the periodically driven kicked top, a standard driven quantum system.

The participation ratio for coherent states in the Floquet eigenbasis uncovers the same layered structure seen classically in finite-time Lyapunov exponents. A Gaussian coarse graining of those exponents, matched to the intrinsic resolution of coherent states, makes the comparison quantitative. Local and global comparisons agree best within a finite window of times, where sticky structures resolve most clearly. The work turns the participation ratio from a global chaos measure into a sharp probe of hierarchical transport.
arxiv-2602-18812:
Planning a path through a maze needs both local geometry and a global sense of the whole problem, and generative models may be able to supply both at once. Agnieszka Polowczyk, with two co-authors, presents GenPlanner in 2026, an approach that uses diffusion models and flow matching, in two variants called DiffPlanner and FlowPlanner, to generate correct paths.

Conditioning comes from a multi-channel description of the environment, with an obstacle map and the start and destination points. Unlike standard methods, the models begin from random noise and iteratively transform it into a valid trajectory. Experiments show the approach clearly beats a convolutional baseline, with FlowPlanner staying strong even with few generation steps, suggesting that generative models can reason as well as plan.
arxiv-2602-18912:
Can short-term market spikes be predicted and traded? Szymon Lis, with two co-authors, tests that question on Apple stock in 2026. Intraday data combines price-swing-normalised returns with emotion features from Twitter messages, extracted by AI models. Spikes are defined as extreme returns relative to volatility and transaction costs, modelled as a three-class problem.

Several nonlinear classifiers are evaluated across intraday rates. Model outputs become trading strategies, judged by risk-adjusted measures and formal tests. Machine learning beats benchmark spike rules at ultra-short horizons. Classical human momentum dominates at mid rates, notably around ten minutes. Explainability analysis shows volatility and negative emotions, above all fear and sadness, drive predicted spikes. Emotion-driven spikes thus carry predictable structure. The market has moods. Those moods leave a trace in prices.
arxiv-2602-19012:
Phase I dose-finding trials more and more face delayed harms, especially with immune drugs and aimed drugs. Robert Amevor, with two co-authors, improves safety in 2026 by replacing fixed weights in the time-to-event ongoing re-checking method with changing weights.

Standard TITE-CRM handles partial follow-up with fixed linear weights. That ad hoc approach may expose patients to extra risk during dose escalation. Changing weights are posterior predictive probabilities from the evolving toxicity delay distribution. Under a Weibull timing model, closed-form updates come from maximum likelihood estimation, making real-time use straightforward. Simulations across three dose-harm scenarios test the new method against standard designs. Changing weighting cuts patient overdosing substantially against TITE-CRM, while preserving dose selection accuracy, and beats algorithm-based methods on dose identification. Performance stays robust across sensitivity analyses.
arxiv-2602-19312:
Sixth-generation wireless aims for fast, low-power edge inference, yet ordinary digital hardware for machine learning burns power. Kyriakos Stylianopoulos and three co-authors introduce metasurface-integrated neural networks, a framework that moves part of the computation into the radio channel itself. Programmable multi-layer metasurfaces and multi-antenna channels act as computational layers in the wave propagation domain, rather than in a chip alone.

The design has three modules: an encoder at the transmitter, a channel module holding propagation effects and metasurfaces, and a decoder at the receiver. Metasurface responses are trained as weights alongside the other modules, letting work shift flexibly across the physical layer. Results match fully digital networks on indicative tasks while cutting power use. The paper closes with open challenges for future edge-inference systems.
arxiv-2602-19412:
U-Net models lead biomedical image segmentation, yet they often miss long-range information. Mingjie Li and three co-authors trace part of the problem to conventional down-sampling, which favors speed over retaining information. Their strategy, Stair Pooling, slows the pace of down-sampling with a sequence of small, narrow pooling operations in varied orientations, concatenated together.

Each two-dimensional pooling step cuts dimensionality by one half instead of one quarter, and the approach adapts to three-dimensional pooling to preserve still more. Better preservation helps the U-Net rebuild spatial detail during up-sampling, improving long-range capture and segmentation accuracy. Tests on three biomedical benchmarks show gains for both two- and three-dimensional U-Net performance.
arxiv-2602-19712:
Treating a deep tumour with radiation means hitting a small target precisely while sparing the tissue around it. A 2026 arXiv paper by Kyrre Ness Sjobak and seven co-authors describes SHARP, a compact focusing system for medical use built around a diverging plasma lens.

A sharply converging round beam needs a wide beam at the exit of the focusing system. That is hard to achieve over a short distance with quadrupole magnets alone. SHARP first widens the beam quickly and without damage using a plasma lens in defocusing mode, then focuses it with quadrupoles, scanning the spot in three dimensions by changing magnet settings. Used with very high energy electrons, the system could yield compact radiotherapy sites and open the way to precise conformal treatment and FLASH techniques.
arxiv-2602-20212:
Machine learning for gravity-wave data depends on format choice. It also depends on how that format's internal structure is used. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jericho Cain, working alone, builds on ongoing wavelet encoder representations for crowded LISA data. It asks whether local latent shape or global latent density better shows which sources stand out.

Data creation and prep stay fixed in a controlled benchmark. Geometry-based one-class scoring is compared with likelihood-based latent models, along with shape-boosted versions of each. Likelihood scoring beats methods based on local surface distance on every one of three separate seeds, on both hit-rate and precision measures. Global latent density thus carries more resolvability information than local shape for crowded LISA segments, guiding format choices for future gravity-wave studies.
arxiv-2602-20312:
Guodong Chen and two co-authors present N4MC, a neural method to shrink time-varying mesh sequences. Earlier neural mesh methods treated each frame on its own, missing the overlap between frames. N4MC borrows from inter-frame video methods instead, learning motion compensation across long sequences. Consecutive irregular mesh frames become regular four-dimensional tensors, giving a uniform and compact form.

An auto-decoder then shrinks those tensors, using spatial and time links to cut redundancy. A transformer model predicts middle frames from latent codes tied to tracked volume centers, clearing up motion errors. In tests, N4MC beats the state of the art on rate-distortion while playing back in real time. The method suits uses that must stream or store moving 3D shapes with little delay.
arxiv-2602-20412:
Fake-image detectors often overfit their training data and fail badly on hard test sets with strong distribution shifts. Aayush Dhakal and six co-authors argue for a tighter approach: learn a close boundary around real images and treat fakes as a catch-all sink class. Their method, SimLBR, uses latent blending regularization to enforce that boundary, and it trains far faster than existing approaches.

On the challenging Chameleon benchmark, SimLBR improves cross-generator generalization by nearly twenty-five percent in accuracy and about seventy percent in recall. The authors also press for reliability-oriented evaluation, adding risk-adjusted metrics and worst-case estimates to judge robustness better. Code and models will be released openly.
arxiv-2602-20612:
For measurement-based quantum computation, the universal resource is a cluster state, whose parts share unusually strong entanglement. Motohiko Ezawa builds general short-range cluster states by applying quantum gates to a product state. Replacing the controlled-Z gate with the controlled-controlled-Z gate yields hyper-cluster states with five-body terms, enabling the controlled-Z gate inside measurement-based computation.

The paper generalizes further to a C-to-the-N-Z gate family, producing hyper-cluster models with multi-body states whose body count grows with N. The model keeps an even-odd symmetry that falls outside the Clifford group for N at or above three. An open chain shows highly degenerate states protected by that symmetry, matching N free spins at each edge. Those spins can serve as N qubits for measurement-based computation, and the setup enables a related multi-qubit gate.
arxiv-2602-21112:
Unit fractions and the Riemann zeta function may be linked through a classical conjecture about Egyptian fractions. Philemon Urbain Mballa explores that link in this 2026 arXiv paper, extending a quadratic parametrization from earlier work. Replacing the integer parameter by a real power and allowing real parameters yields a decomposition of each fraction into three unit fractions.

Summing those decompositions over all integers brings the zeta function into view. If the decomposition quantities admit an analytic continuation to complex values, a new function would emerge that is a multiple of the zeta function. The connection is therefore conditional: it holds subject to that continuation, and it would tie the conjecture's structure to the zeta zeros.
arxiv-2602-21312:
Choice trees and set covers are core tuning problems, and order-first rules link them in new ways.
