Michal Szyfelbein and Dariusz Dereniowski study both under order-first rules in this 2026 arXiv paper: if one test comes first, it must sit above the other, or in a cover, with it. Worst-case and average spotting times, plus cover size and average cover time, are all covered.

Method-based links let a near form for one problem serve another as a black box, with a maximum-density order-closed subset problem catching the counting-based core. Poly-time methods achieve a square-root-type near form for all problems covered. Hardness links give matching no-near-form results for most, with polylog promises for out-trees and in-trees, showing most results are tight.
arxiv-2602-21812:
Chalcogenide perovskites promise much as light-catching materials for next-generation solar cells, yet lab uptake lags amid rival phases, varied crystal shapes, and making hurdles. Diego A. Garzón and four co-authors present a data-driven and lab-grounded screening and ranking design for toughness and lab promise, mixing clear markers, machine-learning models, and green metrics.

From a curated lab dataset of halide and chalcogenide compounds, they derive a new tolerance factor via the SISSO algorithm that tells perovskite-forming mixes apart more exactly than older tolerance-factor rules. Joined with new crystal structure guesses, mix-based bandgap guesses, and machine-learning promise checks, the design explores a wide element space of new chalcogenide perovskites. Picks are ranked on multiple goals for single-junction and tandem designs, and the work finds several strong, fresh perovskites while showing a shared screening plan weighing power, use, and green metrics.
arxiv-2602-21912:
Harrison Agrusa and Patrick Michel ask what happens to a small moon made of loose rubble as its orbit slowly shrinks toward its planet. Their 2026 arXiv study centers on Phobos, the larger moon of Mars, whose path is already decaying through tidal drag. Using rough estimates and computer models, they test how such a moon fails as it drifts inward, based on its shape and how strongly its rubble holds together.

The key finding is a weak-strength case in which tides strip the surface away without breaking the moon apart inside. On that basis, the authors argue that earlier work gave Phobos too much strength, and so placed its breakup too close to Mars. They also raise a second fate: stripped debris could grind itself away in collisions. The final answer, they note, waits on internal structure data promised by Japan's Martian Moons mission.
arxiv-2602-22012:
Stars of different chemical makeup age along different paths, and astronomers read those paths from charts called isochrones and stellar tracks. Aaron Dotter and six co-authors expand the MIST library to cover stars enriched in alpha-capture elements, spanning a wide range of metal content. The new models carry the chemistry through consistently, from stellar interiors all the way to the synthetic spectra used to compare with telescopes.

The paper describes physics updates in the models and checks them against earlier MIST versions and rival stellar models. All products, tracks, isochrones, and brightness correction tables, are public through the MIST project site, with reproduction files archived for reuse. For astronomers dating star clusters and galaxies, the update adds a missing chemical dimension to a widely used toolkit.
arxiv-2602-22212:
Rebuilding a moving 3D object's surface from point clouds over long sequences is plagued by drift: incremental methods wander, and learned models demand category-specific training. Julian Kaltheuner and four co-authors present Neu-PiG, a fast deformation method built on a preconditioned latent grid. It encodes whole deformations across all time steps and spatial scales into one multi-resolution grid tied to a keyframe surface.

Time modulation and a lightweight decoder turn that grid into per-frame six-degree-of-freedom deformations, yielding high-fidelity reconstructions without drift. The method needs no category training and handles very long sequences. For animators and roboticists, it offers stable dynamic surfaces from raw point clouds alone.
arxiv-2602-23212:
Prottay Kumar Adhikary asks how eye problems change what face-finding models see. Eye problems affect millions of people and alter how visual input is handled and seen. The BrokenEyes system mimics five common eye ills: age-related macular degeneration, cataract, glaucoma, refractive errors, and diabetic retinopathy. It tests their effects on neural-like feature maps in deep learning models.

Models trained under normal and illness-specific settings, on human and non-human data, show clear breaks in feature maps. Cataract and glaucoma cause the worst warping, matching known neural processing problems in those ills. Scores such as activation energy and cosine similarity gauge the damage, showing how weak visual input reshapes learned codes and where face finding is most at risk.
arxiv-2602-23312:
Rafael Baptista and five co-authors benchmark small language models for leader-follower communication in human-robot interaction. Assigning roles in real time is hard for resource-limited mobile and assistive robots. Large language models show promise for natural communication, but their size and latency block on-device use, while small models have lacked systematic evaluation for role classification.

The team builds a benchmark and a novel data set from a published database plus synthetic samples capturing interaction dynamics. Two adaptation strategies, prompt engineering and fine-tuning, are tested in zero-shot and one-shot modes against an untrained baseline. With Qwen2.5-0.5B, zero-shot fine-tuning reaches 86.66 percent accuracy at 22.2 milliseconds per sample, clearly beating baseline and prompt-engineered approaches. One-shot modes degrade, since longer context strains the model's capacity, showing fine-tuned small models work well on-device while dialogue complexity still trades against reliability.
arxiv-2602-23412:
The SND@LHC Collaboration reports muon flux at SND@LHC, which studies neutrinos in the forward pseudorapidity range seven point two to eight point four. The detector combines a veto, a scintillating fiber tracker interleaved with emulsion cloud chambers, and a muon system. Muons from ATLAS collisions form the main background for charged-current neutrino interactions and set emulsion replacement timing, so precise flux knowledge matters.

Fluxes come from the central 31 by 31 centimeter area, using data from 2023 through 2025. For proton collisions the values are 190, 376, and 248, times ten to the minus four nanobarns per square centimeter in 2023, 2024, and 2025. A 2024 reference run at five point three six TeV gives 421 in the same scaled units. Heavy-ion fluxes are far larger, at 311, 553, and 324, times ten to the second in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Systematic effects dominate errors, with stats adding at most zero point one percent, and results match Monte Carlo forecasts.
arxiv-2602-23512:
James W. Webber and one co-author analyze a new spherical Radon transform. It sums a function over spheres with free centers and radii that vary smoothly. Such transforms arise in imaging, where the task is to rebuild the function from its sums.

The authors state exact conditions on the radius function and on the support of f for the transform to meet the Bolker condition. They add further conditions for steady recovery of f. They apply the theory to Compton scatter imaging and ultrasound reflection imaging. For each use, they prove the function can be uniquely fixed and give explicit reverse formulas, some built on Palamodov's theory. Their microlocal theory plus uniqueness results then yield steady bounds, checked by simulated image rebuilds.
arxiv-2602-23712:
Christopher T. -K. Lew and five co-authors show real-time size and phase gauging of AC fields with diamond spins. NV centers in diamond detect AC magnet fields with high reach, sharpness in spectrum, and sharpness in space. Most studies so far focused on time-mean or time-linked reads, with little focus on the single-shot regime.

The team shows size and phase of an AC field can be got from a single pair of two back-to-back reads. They show the concept by sizing a 4 MHz AC field with per-shot size and phase reach of 78 nT and 63 mrad, at a time resolution of 320 micro-seconds. They also study size errors from probe rate shifts and from working in the strong field regime. The read plan can change probe rate on the fly, pushing NV centers for real-time AC magnet field reads.
arxiv-2602-23812:
Muhammad Asad Khan and four co-authors report a high-precision spectrometer for carbon dioxide, locked to an optical frequency comb. The 2026 paper describes a setup that links a two-micron diode laser to a comb stabilized against a GPS-guided rubidium clock, through an optical parametric oscillator.

The team recorded absorption spectra for a chosen vibration-rotation line of air-broadened carbon dioxide with high fidelity. A refined line-shape analysis then gave line center frequencies and coefficients for pressure broadening and pressure shift. The setup also measured carbon dioxide mole fractions with sub-per-mille statistical uncertainty. The work offers a traceable route to precise greenhouse-gas spectroscopy, useful for calibration and atmospheric monitoring.
arxiv-2602-23912:
Mihyun Kang and two co-authors study random connected graphs whose distribution weights each graph by its number of blocks, the two-connected pieces into which it splits. The 2026 paper covers block-stable classes, including planar graphs, through a new notion of a decorated block tree.

The authors find a phase transition in both the singular behavior of the counting generating function and the typical shape of the block tree. For certain block-stable classes, including planar graphs, they obtain precise enumeration results and pin down typical sizes of the largest blocks in subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes. Those results sharpen earlier knowledge of block sizes in uniform random planar graphs and extend the picture beyond the planar case.
arxiv-2603-00012: Tyburec's team designs minimum-weight undamped frames under subresonant single-frequency harmonic excitation, limiting compliance, peak input power and eigenfrequencies under ellipsoidal load uncertainty. They recast robust dynamic compliance as a semidefinite problem equal to robust peak input power. Both become a free-vibration eigenvalue rule with mass added regardless of design, joining static, dynamic and modal needs. Certified global bounds come from a moment-sum-of-squares hierarchy, and tests on ten- and thirty-five-segment frames back the theory, with a built design matching predictions in the lab.
arxiv-2603-00112: Javid and González-Prelcic present a physics-informed neural network for MIMO channel estimation in the upper mid-band under tight pilot limits. An enhanced U-Net with transformer blocks and cross-attention merges rough first estimates with RSS maps into refined estimates. Tests on ray-tracing data from city settings show over 5 dB gain in NMSE over the best prior methods. Results hold when pilots are scarce and across frequencies with little fine-tuning. The decoder also forecasts several future channel snapshots from one estimate, aiding proactive beamforming.
arxiv-2603-00212: Ahmad applies Similarity Network Fusion to 644 breast cancer patients with matched RNA, methylation and copy-number profiles, testing whether multi-omics integration beats single-omic baselines at subtype recovery and survival. Patient similarity networks fuse iteratively and split into two clusters by spectral clustering, with cluster count fixed in advance. Fusion reaches the highest subtype agreement against PAM50, ahead of RNA-only and well ahead of early concatenation, with receptor data confirming cluster biology independently. Survival prediction beats copy-number-only but not conclusively RNA-only.
arxiv-2603-00312: Xu and colleagues build a test others can repeat, judging whether multimodal language models truly reason about ECG signals, rather than merely making plausible traces. They split reasoning into perception, spotting patterns in the raw signal, and deduction, applying clinical knowledge to those patterns. The first check uses code to test the time patterns a trace shows. The second check uses a set of known clinical criteria. Both checks let us judge genuine thinking at scale, not mere quiz scores.
arxiv-2603-00412: Su and three colleagues improve three dimensional vision language models, which suffer because paired shape text data are scarce. Language only training wastes geometry held in middle layers. Their PointAlign method adds feature level supervision that keeps point cloud tokens aligned with visual tokens through a consistency loss, training only a small projector and adapter weights. On ModelNet40 and Objaverse tests it lifts classification and captioning scores, with the largest gain on hard open vocabulary Objaverse classification.
arxiv-2603-01012: Li and seven colleagues cut the cost of repository-scale code reasoning by splitting scouting from reading. FastCode first maps a light sketch of the code to trace links and pinpoint targets, then builds a high-value context in one tuned step instead of reading full text again and again. On four test sets it beats top rivals on task scores while using far fewer tokens, backing a scout-first plan.
arxiv-2603-01112: Dhar and three colleagues count t-hooks in partitions from the first Rogers-Ramanujan identity and the first little Göllitz rule, following recent work on Euler's rule. For t equal to 1 and 2, they obtain count formulas for the t-hook counts and prove t-hook bounds from asymptotic formulas. The work extends hook-counting from Euler's setting to two further old groups.
arxiv-2603-01212: Le and five colleagues make comparative opinion mining explainable with XCom, a transformer split into aspect-based rating prediction and semantic analysis. A Shapley explanations module shows why the model decides as it does, addressing the trust problem of opaque comparison tools. Tests show leading performance against baselines, making XCom a more reliable aid for comparing products across reviews.
arxiv-2603-01312: In a 2026 paper, Higgins gives a geometric account of the links-quivers correspondence for rational links. The correspondence predicts that a generating function for links, built from HOMFLY-PT polynomials with colors attached, can be rewritten in quiver form, using one quadratic form and two linear forms. Where an earlier proof covered rational links, Higgins describes those forms directly through the first and second configuration spaces of a plane with three points removed.
arxiv-2603-01912:
Yinghao Tang, Yupeng Xie, Yingchaojie Feng, and colleagues build interactive teaching documents with human and agent teamwork. Their 2026 system, ViviDoc, turns one topic input into an interactive educational document. Interactive articles engage readers well, but making them takes both subject expertise and web skills.

Naive agent generation gives outputs that teachers cannot control or verify with ease. ViviDoc splits work among planner, executor, and evaluator agents in one pipeline. A human-readable plan format, DocSpec, breaks each visualization into state, render, transition, and constraint parts. Educators review and refine that plan before any code is written, which bridges intent and output. Expert review and a user study find large gains over naive generation and an intuitive editing flow.
arxiv-2603-02312:
Marco Bonvini, Stefano Frixione, and Giovanni Stagnitto refine proton structure calculations in this 2026 paper. Splitting functions describe how quarks and gluons share a proton's momentum as scales change. At very small momentum fractions, large logarithms must be summed to all orders. The team revisits the steps needed for accuracy at the next level of that summing.

They derive fresh all-order results for several key quantities in the theory. Most notably, one anomalous dimension is now properly resummed for the first time. That unlocks a correctly resummed splitting kernel that mixes quarks and gluons. The new implementation behaves better numerically than earlier versions. All advances ship in the upcoming fourth release of their HELL code framework.
arxiv-2603-02512:
Szilárd Enyedi proposes human-certified module repositories for AI-built software in this 2026 paper. Language models now generate code and assemble multi-part systems. The safety of those systems depends on the trustworthiness of their building blocks. Today's components often have unclear origins, thin review, and unpredictable interactions.

His repositories would stock reusable modules that humans have certified. Each module carries rich provenance, security review, and an explicit interface contract. Human oversight blends with automated analysis in the certification workflow. A reference architecture and threat analysis ground the proposal. Lessons from recent supply-chain failures shape the design. Governed, auditable module stocks could make AI-assembled software far more reliable, Enyedi argues.
arxiv-2603-02612:
Ritu Dey, Ayushi Agarwal, Reetesh Kumar Gangwar, and colleagues compute electron impact data for tungsten in this 2026 paper. Tungsten walls in fusion devices shed neutral atoms that glow in visible and near-ultraviolet light. Reading that glow needs consistent atomic structure and collision data. Their relativistic distorted-wave method supplies excitation cross sections at fine-structure resolution.

Target states come from multi-configurational Dirac-Fock wavefunctions with extensive correlation. Level energies are benchmarked against other theory and a standard reference database. Cross sections cover excitations from the ground level and six metastable levels. Incident electron energies run from threshold up to a high range. Most reported cross sections appear here for the first time. Results depend strongly on the starting level, a fact modelers must respect.
arxiv-2603-02812:
Klaus Deckelnick, Philip Herbert, and Michael Hinze prove that a basic shape-tuning method always settles down. Their 2026 paper concerns shape optimization, where a domain's outline is adjusted to meet a goal governed by a partial differential equation. The equation here is semilinear and elliptic, a common class in physics and engineering design.

They study steepest descent carried out directly in function space, with shapes compared through the Lipschitz topology, which controls boundary roughness. The main result is global convergence: from any start, the method converges rather than wandering or stalling. A second result gives conditional convergence of the shapes themselves in two dimensions. Such guarantees matter because shape algorithms are often trusted long before they are proven.
arxiv-2603-04012: Thierry Coquand presents two remarks of Stefano Berardi on game semantics that had not been published. The remarks concern classical logic viewed through game semantics, a setting where logical interaction is modeled as play. Coquand explains each remark, making Berardi's ideas accessible to readers. The paper thus preserves and clarifies part of Berardi's thinking on games and classical logic.
arxiv-2603-04312: Song and Nguyen extend Lindahl equilibrium to voting with ordinal preferences. The core blocks coalitions from backing pricier alternatives than their electorate share allows. LEO builds randomized outcomes meeting approximate core constraints, with each voter likely represented. A deterministic guarantee with factor 6.24 beats the old bound of 32, and structured cases compute fast. The result grounds fair representation and voting algorithms.
arxiv-2603-04412: Usatenko and colleagues model language model dynamics with additive multi-step Markov chains. Such models live in huge state spaces where token and hidden links resist classical Markov reduction. Additive chains split next token odds across many historical depths, taming high order explosion. The main result ties an additive chain to a stepwise memory chain. That link extends information temperature from stepwise chains to additive N-order chains.
arxiv-2603-04512: Kontchakov and colleagues test keeping in fusions of one variable first order modal logics. Without equality, global and local results keep both Kripke completeness and decidability, under growing and constant domains. With equality and non-rigid constants, or counting up to one, both properties fail. Diophantine encodings prove the negative side. The finite model property survives only locally even without equality. One variable fusions also read as propositional fusions sharing an S5 modality, giving a general sufficient condition for transfer.
arxiv-2603-05412: Adelle J. Goodwin and Andrew Mummery fit emission to constrain sub-parsec density profiles of 11 hosts. Sub-parsec density profiles are key to black hole accretion. Resolving sub-parsec scales requires high resolution and bright environments, impossible except nearby. Transient accretion onto quiescent black holes offers a new avenue to understand black holes and environments. Radio-bright outflows probe ambient density at 10 to the minus 3 to 1 parsec scales, constraining quiescent-host density. Findings reveal hosts exhibit Bondi-consistent profiles. Under a Bondi profile, outflow mass and densities are jointly fit.
arxiv-2603-05712: Ughade and Chatzidakis show missing-fuel finding in micro-reactor shapes using muon bouncing scans under cosmic-ray conditions. Sealed, mixed cores limit standard safeguards, reducing keenness for missing fuel. They present μTRec, rebuilding paths via Gaussian many-Coulomb bounces with Bayesian updates, then mapping density through voxel-wise M-values. In a core with 61 fuel flakes, one missing flake is found at 50 mm voxel detail using 3×10^6 muons. Per-muon push raises finding for laser sources by up to 149.85%, and the approach stays robust under sensor limits.
arxiv-2603-05812: Khazem presents Margin and Consistency Supervision, a design-free rule-setting frame for tuned vision models. Deep vision sorters score highly while staying poorly tuned and fragile under shifts. The method adds to cross-entropy a hinge-squared margin penalty holding a gap, plus a same-ness regularizer for shaken views. Theory links larger margins and lower response to spread and a toughness radius scaling with the ratio. Across base nets spanning CNN, transformer, it improves tuning and toughness while keeping top score, with no extra data or design changes.
arxiv-2603-05912: Huang and team address fact checking for deep research reports. Old fact-checkers target factoid claims, with no benchmark testing transfer to deep research reports. Static benchmarks prove brittle: alone experts reach only 60.8 percent score on hidden claims. Audit-then-Score keeps labels and reasons open: clashing checkers submit proof, judges decide, and passed fixes update the benchmark before scoring. Across four rounds, score rises above 90 percent, showing judges more steady than one-shot taggers. The approach yields DeepFact-Bench, a versioned benchmark, and DeepFact-Eval, beating old checkers outside.
arxiv-2603-06012: Sung turns bounded self-check failure, since self-copying adds time cost, into a domain-theory frame. The author defines a rule moving a finite halting look from bound i to i plus 1. While no bounded machine hits a fixed point under this rule, looping forms a rising omega-chain. The Scott limit of this chain gives the least fixed point, standing for endless work holding halting ways. The build offers a novel halting-problem view, framing finite seeing to least fixed point as steady putting off of the slant.
arxiv-2603-06112: Ali, Gili, and Caldarelli map a drug-like library aimed around MYH9 in chem space with network theory to surface agreed-stable screening compounds. From 6004 ZINC bits, cleaning leaves 5000 tag-complete compounds, compared via Morgan-finger-print Tanimoto distance plus single-tag distances. For each view the authors build k-nearest-neighbor networks and find Louvain-Leiden groups with highly strong clumping against null models. Cross-tag co-grouping reveals a sparse high-agreed core, and between hub-ness on spanning-tree spines picks central, tag-balanced compounds.
arxiv-2603-06312: Banerjee and colleagues study second order corrections to pseudoscalar Higgs decay into three partons, working at higher orders in dimensional regularization. They compute one and two loop amplitudes for A to three gluons and A to quark antiquark gluon in the effective theory framework. After suitable crossings of external momenta, the results feed predictions for the differential distribution of the pseudoscalar Higgs boson with a jet at hadron colliders.
arxiv-2604-00012: Li and team ask why post-training degrades safety in reasoning models, proposing SafeReAct, a lightweight solution restoring suppressed safety behaviors. Large reasoning models gain skill from chain-of-thought post-training, yet lose safety, with fine-tuned models showing more harmful outputs than base models. Analysis reveals post-training can mask original safety mechanisms while over-amplifying representations tied to post-training ability. SafeReAct restores suppressed safety with LoRA adapters on a few layers. Tests on four models show it improves safety on harmful prompts without harming skill.
arxiv-2604-00312: Do and three colleagues propose physically-intuitive privacy and security (PIPS), a paradigm giving privacy and security controls simple, physics-based mental models. Sensors in smart speakers, webcams, and RFID tags embed computing into rooms, but users distrust them despite controls, since makers, developers, and attackers want their data. PIPS rests on three principles: intent-aligned activation and deactivation, direct physical manipulation of sensor state, and perceptible assurance. Trials of a smart webcam cover and powering-for-privacy improved trust, as did on-demand RFID, over existing systems.
arxiv-2604-00512: Kumar and colleagues prove a 2008 conjecture on the maximum spectral sum of graphs. For a graph of order n, the spectral sum adds its two largest adjacency eigenvalues. Ebrahimi, Mohar, Nikiforov, and Ahmady conjectured that this sum never exceeds eight-sevenths of n. The proof draws on graph-limit theory, convex geometry, exterior algebra, and convex optimisation, and the techniques developed stand on their own as tools.
arxiv-2604-00612: Suzuki and Sanada study how spherical bubbles rising in a chain spread sideways in two stages. Wake-induced lift drives the destabilisation of the chain, and Moore's wake model predicts a slender, confined wake with limited interfacial vorticity, implying wake effects fade as spacing grows. Yet tests with bubble size and generation rate varied independently show large lateral spread and strong frequency dependence, even past the wake length. A reduced model with pairwise wake interactions captures the onset of destabilisation but underpredicts the large-scale spread.
arxiv-2604-00712: Li and Zhu prove the Helmholtz equation is well posed for rough coefficients held in a bounded region, under sharp regularity rules. Using a product calculus in rescaled weighted spaces, they make sense of the product of solution and coefficient at the lowest regularity level with no renormalization. A rescaled Lippmann-Schwinger form matches the equation with the Sommerfeld radiation rule. Well posed here means a solution exists, is unique, and changes steadily with the inputs, and the work also gives explicit bounds on the resolvent.
arxiv-2604-01112: Umeh develops a covariant multi-scale framework for structure formation that goes beyond the point-particle picture. He argues the real obstacle is that families of geodesics can stop being geodesics. So he splits spacetime into nested regions divided by matter horizons. He matches their shared boundaries at the level of the action. The result yields a backreaction term. As an application, it produces flat galaxy rotation curves without adding dark matter.
arxiv-2604-01212: He and colleagues introduce YC-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can plan and act coherently over long horizons. An agent runs a simulated startup for one year across hundreds of turns, hiring staff, choosing contracts, and staying profitable while adversarial clients and growing payroll punish early mistakes. Of 12 models tested, only three consistently end above the starting capital, with Claude Opus 4.6 finishing highest at 1.27 million dollars. Scratchpad use best predicts success, while missed adversarial clients drive most bankruptcies.
arxiv-2604-01512: Morone, Kent and Sels study VIRAL, a classic kicked-top version of quantum optimization. VIRAL beats QAOA on the spin-glass benchmark at all depths, with energy density reaching the ground state value evenly in one over p. QAOA-like methods work through repeat turns, and a classic version beats its quantum twin. The gain is traced to shrinking motion to Landau-Lifshitz motion for a single spin in a noisy magnet field, where the field's spread is nearly rank-one.
arxiv-2604-02112: Mazza, Pearson, Caleffi and Cacciapuoti present Q2NS, an open tool for quantum networks built on ns-3, the standard classical network tool. Using ns-3 event driven runs lets it mix quantum dynamics with classical signals, while plug in backends cover state vector, density matrix and stabilizer views. A visual tool shows both physical links and entanglement links. Demos run from basic entanglement sharing to multi party graph states, with examples needing no coding background.
arxiv-2604-02412: O'Connor, Kremer and Rasio explain low binary fractions in globular clusters analytically. Starting from solar neighborhood binaries as the initial state, dynamical dissolution of soft primordial binaries fully accounts for present day binary fractions. Estimates check against a Cluster Monte Carlo N-body simulation. Reading observed fractions as a constraint on the hard soft boundary at birth implies surviving Milky Way clusters began with radii similar to young massive clusters nearby. Stellar black holes, through black hole burning, play a crucial sculpting role.
arxiv-2604-02512: Mühlenbernd asks whether large language models match human social meaning in numbers, not just in broad pattern, and whether prompts drawn from pragmatic theory can close the gap. He introduces two calibration metrics and tests three leading models on how numerical imprecision carries social signals. All models capture the qualitative pattern but distort magnitudes, and prompting about speaker knowledge and motives most reliably shrinks the distortion.
arxiv-2604-02612: Navrátil and four colleagues review halo nuclei, exotic light nuclei with loosely bound neutrons. Their tool is the no-core shell model with continuum, an ab initio method that treats bound and unbound states together. Using only chiral two- and three-nucleon forces as input, the method predicts structure and dynamics for nuclei including helium-6, boron-8, beryllium-11 and carbon-15. It also tests the quality of chiral forces against experiment.
arxiv-2604-03312: In a 2026 paper, Sankaralingam argues that human-led chip design cannot keep up now that transistor scaling has stalled. Human teams test perhaps 50 to 100 designs per generation, a tiny share of the vast design space, while each new chip must still double performance on the same budget. He proposes automated idea factories that test thousands of candidates weekly and predicts human-only research will soon be obsolete.
arxiv-2604-03612: Chong tests whether tasks humans evolved built-in neural wiring for can serve as CAPTCHAs now that multi-mode large language models defeat old ones. He offers two CAPTCHA classes: a vision CAPTCHA drawing letter-digit strings as ASCII art, and an audio CAPTCHA asking questions over layered or noisy audio. No tested large language model solves a single ASCII CAPTCHA. The best guesses at most one or two symbols, and audio models perform only slightly better than random.
arxiv-2604-03912: Dalal Alharthi and Ivan Roberto Kawaminami Garcia built a secure-by-design system joining cloud forensics with language-model defense. PromptShield guards models against hostile prompts by checking inputs against a fixed map of concepts. The Cloud Investigation Automation Framework then works through all six forensic phases with the same concept-based logic. On AWS and Azure data, PromptShield scored above 93 percent on precision, recall, and F1 under attack, while the forensic side lifted ransomware detection.
arxiv-2604-04012: Kay Gijzen and colleagues built OASIC, a classifier for heavily occluded objects that first masks the occluder, then picks a model tuned to the occlusion level. Occlusion hurts in two ways: visible detail is lost, and occluder patterns distract. Masking occluders as visual anomalies at test time removes the distraction, while training with random masks at varied levels covers the detail loss. The team also showed occlusion severity can be estimated at test time. Combining gray masking with adaptive model choice beat standard training by wide margins.
arxiv-2604-04112: Boshuai Ye and team wrote the Replicated Computational Results report for C2|Q>, a framework bridging classical and quantum software building. It turns old-style specs, Python code or set JSON, into ready-to-run quantum programs across ten problem kinds and multiple hardware backends. Code, a ready-made parser model, test data, and a PyPI package are all out. The report maps item structure, setup steps, and run routes to the three tests.
arxiv-2604-04212: Meng Hua and Deniz Gündüz proposed a relay-assisted wireless physical neural network built on activation-integrated stacked intelligent metasurfaces. Each passive surface layer handling linear wave shaping is paired with a layer that performs nonlinear work in the analog domain. Relay boost and phase-shift matrices together serve as trainable network weights, while hardware-built activation functions supply the needed nonlinear twist. Simulations showed high classification accuracy, with hardware activation clearly beating purely linear designs.
arxiv-2604-04512: Jeans sums up current understanding of how detector ideas built for the International Linear Collider could fit other facilities. Detectors for the collider have been probed for years, giving a good grip on requirements and limits. With new Higgs Factory plans such as FCC-ee bringing new traits, the tweaks needed to use them there are now being probed.
arxiv-2604-04912: Chatterjee and four colleagues generalize the classic Dominating Set problem by adding quotas. They are given a graph, a size limit k, and for each vertex a lower and an upper quota. The task is to find a set of at most k vertices such that every vertex sees a number of chosen neighbors, counting itself, inside its quota range. The richer model fits settings where both under-coverage and over-coverage must be avoided. Examples include fault-tolerant infrastructure, load-balanced facility placement, and constrained communication networks.
arxiv-2604-05112: Polubarov and 13 co-authors present Vintix II, a pre-trained transformer that is a learner. Recent progress in in-context learning has shown agents can acquire new tasks at inference. AD pioneered this approach and was scaled to settings, although new tasks remained limited. It appeared as an option, showing stronger learning in domains, but its scale was untested. The authors extend it to domains, using Flow Matching as a training choice that preserves its reading as Bayes sampling.
arxiv-2604-05212: DeTone and six colleagues present Boxer, an algorithm that lifts 2D bounding boxes to 3D boxes from posed images and depth. At its core, BoxerNet, a network, lifts 2D proposals into 3D, then fuses views and filters geometry to give consistent boxes in world space. By reusing 2D detectors, BoxerNet focuses on lifting rather than detecting, cutting demand for annotated 3D training data. Trained on over 1.2 million 3D boxes, it beats CuTR in settings without depth, 53 to 1 on mAP, and on CA-1M with depth, 41 to 25 on mAP.
arxiv-2604-05512: The ATLAS Collaboration measures charged particles from proton-oxygen crashes at 9.62 TeV, a lab stand-in for cosmic-ray air showers. From 246 million picked events, they give a proton-oxygen cross section of 396 millibarns and an inferred proton-air inelastic value of 406 millibarns. Their counts beat gaps between shower models in precision tenfold, tightening air-shower models.
arxiv-2604-05912: Krumdick and ten colleagues offer FrontierFinance, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon financial modeling tasks across five core models, each averaging over 18 hours of expert labor. Built with professionals and graded by detailed rubrics, it tests industry-standard workflows. Human experts outscore current systems on average and more often deliver client-ready outputs.
arxiv-2604-06112: Xiong and five colleagues probe fast-fading core excitons in sodium fluoride with attosecond four-wave mixing. One extreme ultraviolet pump and two delayed near-infrared probes track bright and dark excitons at the sodium edge. The excitons lose coherence faster than the 8 femtosecond instrument limit, a speed the team links to strong coupling between excitons and lattice vibrations. Polarization control shows bright excitons carry s-like momentum while dark ones, reached by two-photon excitation, carry p-like momentum.
arxiv-2604-06212: Sounack and ten colleagues review code sharing in diagnostic and prognostic prediction model research, where code is essential for reproduction yet rarely available. Screening PubMed articles citing TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI, they assess 3,967 eligible studies with a language-model pipeline checking repo links against 14 features. Of those, 12.2 percent shared code, rising to about 16 percent in 2025. Shared repos usually hold a README but often lack dependency lists or modular structure, setting a baseline for the planned TRIPOD-Code guideline.
arxiv-2604-06312: Marks, Staelens, and Sperhake present a fully nonlinear study of binaries pairing one black hole with one boson star. They study quartic self-interaction plus a solitonic potential for the scalar field. They show equilibrated boson-star initial data matter for precise gravitational waveforms, and discuss ways to further reduce constraint violations. In head-on crashes, radiative output varies greatly with the scalar potential. Early inspirals show a suitable scalar self-interaction can suppress tidal disruption. The authors note implications for model-agnostic waveform banks for exotic compact objects.
arxiv-2604-06412: Bera and four colleagues show quantum states with intrinsically complex amplitudes gain an edge in telling states apart. They build five orthogonal three-qubit states, strongly nonlocal exactly with imaginary parts, locally indistinguishable even under joint two-part probes. That makes imaginarity a cryptographic resource, keeping encoded information secure. Replacing its product state with a biseparable state wipes out the effect, as entanglement dilutes it and it plays its role. The set, the smallest Unextendible Biseparable Basis, spans an indistinguishable subspace whose complement yields distillable entanglement, settling an existence question.
arxiv-2604-06712: Blain audits the open-source quantum simulator ecosystem in Broken Quantum, the first comprehensive formal security review of its kind. Using COBALT QAI, a four-module static analysis engine backed by the Z3 solver, he examines 45 frameworks from 22 organizations across 12 countries. The audit finds 547 issues, with 40 critical, 492 high, and 15 medium, spanning memory corruption, resource exhaustion, unsafe deserialization, and a novel QASM injection vector. All 13 vulnerability patterns verify formally, the 32-qubit boundary recurs as a threshold, and one case traces a flaw from IBM Qiskit Aer into Oak Ridge laboratory infrastructure.
arxiv-2604-06812: Luo and six colleagues quantify uncertainty in long-form generation with AGSC. Hallucination haunts long outputs, yet reliable uncertainty scores struggle across mixed themes, and fine-grained splitting costs heavily while missing neutral information. AGSC first uses NLI neutral probabilities as triggers to separate irrelevance from uncertainty, cutting wasted compute. Gaussian mixture soft clustering then models latent themes and weights topics for aggregation. Tests on BIO and LongFact show leading correlation with factuality while cutting inference time by about 60 percent versus full atomic splitting.
arxiv-2604-06912: Shi and four colleagues build Q-Zoom, a query-aware perception scheme for multimodal models. High-resolution inputs flood self-attention with redundant tokens, choking speed and ignoring query intent. Q-Zoom works coarse-to-fine, with a light gating network skipping high-resolution work when coarse features suffice, and a region proposal network pinpointing regions. It speeds inference about two and a half times on document and OCR tests and about four and a half times on high-resolution tasks at matched accuracy. Fidelity-first beats the baseline.
arxiv-2604-07012: Luo and four colleagues bring DTCRS, making summary trees on the fly. Search-boosted writing cuts made-up facts with knowledge, and repeat summing up builds summary trees by grouping text chunks for multi-step questions. Summary trees often hold extra nodes that slow building and hurt answers. DTCRS decides whether a tree is needed from question type, splits the question, and uses sub-question vectors as centers, cutting notes while lifting fit. The approach cuts build time and lifts results across three tasks.
arxiv-2604-07412: Schmid and three colleagues measure sound absorbers in place from near-field pressure and velocity data. Standard in situ methods struggle with noise, model error, and strict assumptions. Their deep net maps measurements, positions, and frequencies to sound fields while inferring one consistent surface admittance spectrum, with no explicit forward model. Helmholtz, momentum, and Robin boundary physics guide training as a check. Tests on two flat porous absorbers show accurate recovery and robustness to noise and sparse sampling.
arxiv-2604-07612: Karchkhadze and Dubnov present a framework for live human-AI musical co-performance, with a latent diffusion model playing accompaniment from context audio. A MAX/MSP front end handles audio input and playback, while a Python server runs the model via OSC/UDP messages. Accompaniment becomes a sliding-window look-ahead task: predict future audio from partial context under tight latency limits. Consistency distillation cuts sampling time 5.4-fold, with real-time operation for both. Both score well on coherence, beat alignment, and audio quality, degrading gently as look-ahead grows.
arxiv-2604-07712: Ding and four colleagues add CausalVAE to world models as a plug-in part. The part learns cause-and-effect links inside the model's hidden state. Plain forecasts stay strong, while guesses about what would happen under changes improve. The Physics test set gains 102.5 percent on average across eight paired baselines. Learned links also match sensible first-order trends in how objects act on each other, which aids reading the learned structure.
arxiv-2604-07812: Zhu and 11 colleagues prune visual tokens in multimodal language models with attention to which heads matter. Floods of visual tokens slow inference and strain limited hardware, and dropping redundant tokens is a natural fix. Past work treats all attention heads as equal contributors to vision. This study shows heads play distinct roles and capture different visual meanings. Their HAWK method weighs head importance and uses text-guided attention to judge token significance, keeping the tokens that matter most for the task.
arxiv-2604-08212: Kyem and three colleagues ask whether tuning on domain instructions can enable full pavement review with vision-language models. General-purpose vision-language models perform strongly in daily domains but struggle with expert fields that demand exact terms, ordered reasoning, and building standards. PaveInstruct, with 278,889 image-response pairs across 32 task types, merges labels from nine varied road sets. PaveGPT, a pavement base model trained on it, was tested against top models on sight, grasp, and reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2604-08312: Fyon and three colleagues study neuromodulation for rhythmic transitions in varied central pattern circuits with fixed connectivity. Key functions like breathing and walking rely on robust, adaptable patterns from certain network designs called connectomes. Rhythmic tuning is often tied to slow wiring changes via nerve flex, but such routes act too slowly for rapid transitions. Here, the team offers such control to reshape rhythmic firing in fixed-connectivity networks. The key challenge is reliable rhythm switching despite nerve degeneracy, where varied setting mixes act alike.
arxiv-2604-08812: Venkat, Henneking, and Ghattas present a scalable Bayesian framework for placing tsunami early warning sensors in linear time invariant systems. Reformulating the inverse problem in data space turns sensor choice into dense matrix subset selection. A multi GPU greedy algorithm with Schur complement updates solves it, overlapping input output with computation. The framework scales near perfectly on hundreds of GPUs across Perlmutter and Frontier. It optimizes a 175 sensor network for the Cascadia digital twin, taming a field of over one billion parameters.
arxiv-2604-08912: Gan and four colleagues defend quantum damping of cosmic shear in changed loop cosmos as generic. A prior note argued from single cases that the damping is not generic and the cosmos never becomes truly normal. The authors show those cases use mixed growing shrinking ways that do not stand for truly allowed falling Bianchi I worlds, yielding lower dimension post bounce shapes. Limiting to three dimension squeeze, quantum damping proves robust, with unevenness fading fast toward an even pull free of matter when the weak energy rule holds.
arxiv-2604-09212: Luo and Laban introduce SPASM, a stability-first framework for multi-turn dialogues with language model agents that keep their personas intact. Long chats often degrade as agents drift from roles, confuse roles, or echo each other. SPASM splits simulation into persona creation, dialogue, and stopping detection, adding egocentric projection, which recasts shared history into each agent's own view. Across three backbones and nine pairings, 4,500 personas and 45,000 dialogues show the projection cuts drift and removes echoing under human checks.
arxiv-2604-09512: Mickeler and seven colleagues move the attention mechanism's nonlinear step from digital logic into light. They use thin-film lithium niobate modulators as analog units. Softmax and sigmoid functions cause under 1 percent of a transformer's work, yet they slow inference. Running those functions with light instead keeps accuracy high in vision transformers and large language models. The system holds up even under tight 4-bit quantization of the analog units, at signal speeds reaching 10 GBaud.
arxiv-2604-09712: Tian and seven colleagues present LAST, a framework that sharpens spatial reasoning in multimodal language models. Data-driven scaling struggles to instill geometric priors, and reading diverse tool outputs poses a second hurdle. LAST-Box, an interactive sandbox, turns varied tool calls into atomic instructions and reusable spatial skills, giving back annotated images and text. A three-stage training path moves from understanding tool outputs to adaptive invocation. On four datasets, LAST-7B gains around 20 percent over its backbone and beats strong proprietary models.
arxiv-2604-09812: Panchendrarajan and Zubiaga present Claim2Vec, the first many-language vector model tuned for fact-check claims. Repeat claims challenge auto fact-checking, notably across borders, and grouping similar claims that share one fact-check remains new. The team fine-tunes a many-language encoder with paired learning on similar many-language claim pairs. Tests on claim grouping across three sets, 14 vector models, and 7 grouping methods show Claim2Vec clearly lifts grouping scores.
arxiv-2604-10112: Ge and eight colleagues enter the NTIRE 2026 infrared super-resolution challenge with a dual-branch system. It sharpens low-resolution thermal remote-sensing images while preserving target outlines, scene layout, and radiometric stability. A transformer branch and a state-space branch run in parallel. Test-time local conversion, eight-way self-ensemble, and equal-weight fusion combine the two outputs. On 12 synthetic fourfold samples from Caltech aerial thermal data, the fused result beats either branch alone. It leads on peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity, and overall score.
arxiv-2604-10212: Niu, Jin, Dolphin, and Dong turn hidden states straight into link graphs for market forecasts with Relational Probing. Prompting chains pay step-by-step reading costs and split graph building from downstream tuning. Their method swaps the model head for a link head making a graph from hidden states, jointly trained with a stock model. It learns meaning, preserves the induced graph's strict structure, and recasts outputs into task formats. Tests with Qwen3 bases of three sizes beat a pair-count rival each time at low run cost.
arxiv-2604-10412: Ge and Díaz widen orthogonal machine learning to odds and risk ratios. Group wise effects guide who gains most from a treatment, yet odds and risk tools lagged behind. Their work extends DR-learner and R-learner methods with orthogonal risk forms for both ratios. The fake outcomes meet second order remainder rules like those for average effects. Trials across hundreds of simulated worlds favor the new tools in hard cases, and a NHANES study shows hidden group gaps.
arxiv-2604-10712: Bian and four colleagues learn treatment rules tailored to each patient by pooling trials that share a comparator but test different arms. Single trials are often too small to catch how effects vary across patients, so pooling raises power for personal decisions. Their method blends study evidence through a regularized weighted risk score and lets study weights adapt to the data. Simulations show better estimates of value and benefit functions. In two depression studies sharing one serotonin-reuptake inhibitor arm, the pooled methods beat one-size-fits-all care.
arxiv-2604-10812: Mudireddy and Patibandla present PokeRL, training reinforcement learning agents for early Pokemon Red tasks. Pokemon Red offers sparse rewards, partial observability, and quirky controls . Recent PPO agents clear two gyms with heavy reward shaping, yet training stays brittle, with agents falling into loops, menu spam, or wandering. PokeRL contributes a loop-aware PyBoy wrapper with map masking, anti-loop and anti-spam layers, and a dense hierarchical reward design. The authors argue modeling failure modes like loops and spam is a necessary step toward full Pokemon League champion agents.
arxiv-2604-10912: Gao and six colleagues propose TAMISeg, a text-guided medical image segmentation frame using clinical prompts and semantic distillation to sharpen visual grasp while leaning less on pixel labels. It joins three parts: a consistency-aware encoder pre-trained with strong perturbations for robust features, and a semantic distillation module taught by a frozen DINOv3 teacher for sharper meaning. A scale-adaptive decoder segments anatomy across spatial scales. Tests on Kvasir-SEG, MosMedData+, and QaTa-COV19 show TAMISeg beats existing single- and multi-modal methods in qualitative and quantitative checks.
arxiv-2604-11012: Ding and five colleagues propose Min-k sampling, a dynamic cut-off rule separating truncation from temperature scaling. Mainstream top-p, top-k, and min-p methods balance diversity and accuracy but are sensitive to temperature. Recent logit-space approaches gain temperature invariance yet rely on global statistics open to long-tail noise. Min-k finds semantic cliffs in the logit distribution, sharp shifts from confident core tokens to uncertain tail tokens. A decay rate sets the boundary each step, and the authors prove strict temperature invariance.
arxiv-2604-11112: Li and four colleagues propose Quantum-Gated Task-interaction Knowledge Distillation for class-incremental learning. Class-incremental learning gathers knowledge from a stream of tasks into a unified classifier over all seen classes. Pretrained models perform well but struggle with tangled multi-task subspaces, causing severe loss when routing parameters are mistuned or representations are stiffly fixed. The framework uses quantum gating to guide inter-task transfer, with a quantum-gated modulation modeling links among task vectors. It captures sample-task fit for joint training and testing across streaming tasks.
arxiv-2604-11212: Béal and four colleagues survey sofic measures, also called hidden Markov measures. They compare equivalent definitions of the notion and sharpen the bound for deciding whether a sofic measure is a k-step Markov chain. For an invariant sofic measure with a linear picture of dimension n, the step count k need be at most n choose two. The bound is tight for alphabets of size three.
arxiv-2604-11312: Cau, Failla, and Rossetti study how network structure shapes opinion change among populations of debating language-model agents. Across networks with controlled homophily and group sizes, low homophily aids convergence through cross-group contact, while high homophily preserves distinct opinion states. The choice of model itself strongly affects the dynamics, and telling agents about their local neighborhood further shifts transitions, with models differing in sensitivity to local social context.
arxiv-2604-11712: Brumali and three colleagues propose a distributed algorithm tuning macroscopic behavior of multi-agent systems via small actions. They cast the task as bilevel optimization: the upper level sets a large-scale state through a score, shaped below by a compressed summary. The large-scale state uses an exponential-family distribution from small-scale setups. Agents rebuild the large-scale state through distributed estimation, with hypergradient-based updates of small states to improve group action. Convergence to stationary points follows via split timescales, and simulations confirm it.
arxiv-2604-11812: Périer, Blanchard, Döhler, Durand, and Roquain build confidence envelopes for false discoveries that stay valid when the user selects any subset of null hypotheses. Existing envelopes were built for homogeneous data, where null p-values spread uniformly, but heterogeneous discrete data break that pattern and can inflate false-discovery counts. The authors bridge old homogeneous constructions with new tools for such data, including a Bretagnolle inequality and a new Simes variant. Simulations compare the new envelopes with the older ones.
arxiv-2604-11912: Huang and five colleagues study how multi-token prediction helps language models plan, versus next-token prediction. On synthetic graph path-finding and realistic tests like Countdown and boolean satisfiability, multi-token prediction consistently beats next-token prediction. Theory on a simplified two-layer Transformer and a star graph task shows why: multi-token prediction drives a two-stage reverse process, first attending to the end node, then tracing nodes backward. That pattern stems from gradient decoupling, which gives a cleaner training signal, biasing optimisation toward robust, interpretable reasoning circuits.
arxiv-2604-12012: Cao and eighteen colleagues advance vision-language pretraining with TIPSv2, a family of image-text encoders tackling patch-text alignment. Patch-level distillation strongly boosts dense patch-text alignment, surprisingly pushing the student past its teacher. That insight drives iBOT++, where unmasked tokens also feed the masked image loss, dramatically improving alignment. Tweaks to the moving-average setup and caption sampling across granularities complete the recipe. Across nine tasks and twenty datasets, TIPSv2 performs on par with or better than recent vision encoders.
arxiv-2604-12112: Benatia, Molinié, and Pineau ask what drives differences in energy use across American states, combining decomposition, frontier analysis, and variable importance on 2006 to 2022 data. Per-person use fell 12.8 percent, almost all through intensity gains, with the demand frontier explaining 63 percent of cross-state variation. Prices account for roughly 26 percent and efficiency policies about 13 percent, plus a further 6 points through reduced inefficiency.
arxiv-2604-12312: Yang and seven colleagues present CompliBench, a benchmark testing whether language-model judges can spot and locate guideline violations in multi-turn dialogues. A scalable pipeline simulates user-agent chats and injects flaws in a controlled way. It yields exact labels for the violated guideline and turn, while adversarial search keeps the flaws hard. Leading proprietary models struggle badly, yet a small judge fine-tuned on the synthetic data beats them and generalizes to unseen business domains.
arxiv-2604-12412: Abdourahmane Diatta and El Hadji Abdoulaye Thiam prove that positive solutions exist for a doubly critical elliptic problem. The equation lives in a bounded region with a singular surface inside. Two Hardy-type terms carry distinct critical powers, breaking compactness. Local shape of the singular set and the potential near it prove decisive. Variational tools, with the mountain pass lemma, drive the proof. Tests built for the task handle the loss of compactness.
arxiv-2604-12512: Guanyi Qin and 52 colleagues run a challenge on judging high-quality images like human experts. Standard quality scores compress rich visual traits into one number. That compression hides fine differences between uniformly strong images. It also cannot explain why one image wins. The challenge asks multimodal models to pick the better image in each pair. Models must also give expert-level reasons for the pick. Nearly 200 teams registered, with over 2,500 submissions in total. Top methods pushed professional image assessment forward.
arxiv-2604-12612: Mikhail Zibrov and three colleagues study deuterium retention in tungsten irradiated at high temperature. Recrystallized samples took 20 MeV self-ion irradiation at 1350 K. Defects were then marked with deuterium from gentle plasma. Depth profiles came from nuclear reaction analysis. Below a tenth of a dpa, trapped deuterium runs lower than at 800 K. At higher doses it exceeds the 800 K values, peaking near 1.7 atomic percent. Microscopy finds nanometer voids unique to the 1350 K samples. Desorption spectra point to gas in voids and atoms at surfaces.
arxiv-2604-12712: Aelson Sobral proves a Weiss-type almost-monotonicity formula for variable energy functionals. Only mild smoothness of coefficients is assumed. The formula classifies blow-up limits for the Alt-Phillips problem with variable coefficients. It does so under weaker assumptions than Araújo and colleagues required. A distinct argument extends the free-boundary result. The paper closes with further extensions, including two-phase cases.
arxiv-2604-13012: Iania and Ricciardone compute gravitational waves induced by scalar-tensor mixing during matter-dominated eras, a possible source of the nanohertz background hum. In a purely matter-dominated age the energy density dilutes fast, but a brief early matter-dominated phase leaves a lasting signal. Scalar-induced waves still dominate the NANOGrav 15-year data, yet the mixed waves remain a viable target for the future Square Kilometre Array.
arxiv-2604-13112: Aglin, Muchiri, and Nkundineza introduce MM-IQA, a lightweight multi-metric framework for judging UAV image quality without a pristine reference image. It merges interpretable cues on blur, edges, resolution, exposure, noise, haze, and frequency content into one score from 0 to 100. Tested on five benchmarks, it reaches correlations from 0.647 to 0.830, runs about 1.97 seconds per image, and uses memory that grows linearly with image size.
arxiv-2604-13512: Fuad tests distance metrics and scaling functions using electron and photon events from decaying krypton-83, taken with an HPGe spectrometer under cryo-vacuum setup. He covers Hellinger, 1D Wasserstein, square-root Jensen-Shannon, L-inf, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, and Fisher-Rao metrics. First setting up a unit-free PoI, he makes spreads from the data and studies how steady PoI stays under sample size, binning length, and scaling functions. He also lists rules that a scaling function should have and uses them in the test.
arxiv-2604-13612: Kolesnikov, Maksimov, Moskvitin, and Semenova probe how internal noise disturbs spiking neural networks, testing additive and multiplicative noise at the input current, membrane voltage, and spike output. Multiplicative noise on the membrane voltage harms most, dragging voltages strongly negative and silencing neurons. A sigmoid input filter counters this best by keeping inputs positive; other noise settings then cost at most one percent accuracy, and networks tolerate shared noise better than independent noise.
arxiv-2604-13912: Burczak, Székelyhidi, and Wu build smooth, divergence-free flows that make a spreading scalar lose energy anomalously as diffusion fades toward zero. For any roughness exponent below one-third, their iterated homogenization setup keeps the scalar bounded in a matching regularity class while dissipation persists. The construction confirms a conjecture of Armstrong and Vicol and pins the Obukhov-Corrsin threshold as sharp in this setting. It also shows the dissipation anomaly stays steady in time, beating the classical Yaglom prediction for time regularity.
arxiv-2604-14112: Chang, Shen, and Zhou build a framework for the gravitational Sommerfeld factor, the broad correction that curved space imprints on waves from merging pairs. They recast sums over diagrams as a wave equation with a point source, deriving a closed form in terms of an effective-theory link matrix. They solve the factor's size and phase to tenth order in G for the lowest three partial waves. Its phase matches elastic scattering without tidal dissipation, and they derive a new evolution equation for radiative multipoles.
arxiv-2604-14312: Wang, Muñoz, and Yung measure dark matter halo biases at redshifts 6 to 19 from simulation data. Their values run about 3 to 4 percent above canonical low-redshift calibrations. The team offers an updated linear-bias fit for these early times, cutting the mean systematic offset to under 1 percent. The results back robust interpretation of early-Universe galaxy clustering seen by JWST, Roman, and intensity-mapping surveys.
arxiv-2604-14412: Rybkin treats the Korteweg-de Vries equation on the half-line for real initial data that are integrable and square-integrable. With Hankel operators and the left reflection coefficient on Hardy space, he derives a trace-type formula for the wave. Approximation by compact potentials, uniform convergence of reflection coefficients away from zero, and continuity of the Hankel operators carry the proof. The result gives an inverse-scattering construction beyond the usual short-range setting.
arxiv-2604-14612: Amer, Das, and Kurdahi propose ConfLayers, a plug-and-play draft model for self-speculative decoding that skips layers by confidence. It scores every layer for confidence and skips layers past an adaptive threshold. It checks each set and keeps the best until gains stop or iterations run out. Simple heuristic skipping often beats learned skipping policies, and ConfLayers avoids training a skipping policy altogether. Across models and datasets, it reaches up to 1.4 times the speed of vanilla large-language-model generation with steadier speed-quality trade-offs.
arxiv-2604-14812: del Valle, Bergold, and Kropielnicka extend logarithmic perturbation theory to time-dependent dynamics, expanding the wave logarithm in powers of a coupling constant. Corrections follow a hierarchy set by a gauge-rotated Hamiltonian, giving closed forms via Duhamel's formula and an energy shift. Dynamic shifts emerge as time-averaged pseudopotential means, as in AC Stark shifts and polarizabilities. The laser-driven harmonic oscillator recovers its exact solution as proof of principle, while the laser-driven hydrogen atom shows it at work on atomic systems, backed by tests.
arxiv-2604-15012: Yang and Liu present a method for detecting Faraday rotation measure flares in repeating fast radio bursts. Rotation measure shifts trace evolving environments around progenitors, and sudden flares can mark passing structures. Flares are hard to isolate because change ranges from smooth trends to chaotic noise with non-uniform sampling. Their pipeline separates transient perturbations from quiescent backgrounds for a uniform census. Applied to 15 bursts, only FRB 20220529A shows a detection under standard parameters; most other repeaters show intrinsic fluctuations or secular evolution.
arxiv-2604-15212: Tett and colleagues study magnetic colloidal dimers that carry both an induced moment and a weak permanent moment. In a steady uniform field, fixed pairs hop between two preferred in-plane angles, forming a two-peaked orientation pattern. Reversing the field periodically flips the response from tiny hops to full half-turn rotations on each flip. Combining axis-field misalignment, bifurcation strength, and short-time variance lets the team read off the net permanent dipole from microscopy.
arxiv-2604-15412: Hafjall and Ryttov study conformal quantum mechanics through its perturbative S-matrix, tracking UV divergences from the interplay of two couplings. Focusing on the inverse-square potential in one dimension, they compute the beta function to all perturbative and non-perturbative orders in both bound-state and scattering sectors. They give exact infinite-series results for the first few non-perturbative orders.
arxiv-2604-15512: Sabzevari and Khan mine 1,404 Stack Overflow posts to map how developers actually wrestle with quantum computing tools and algorithms. Topic models surface seven main topics, led by hybrid quantum-classical work and circuit building, with Qiskit and Q-sharp leading tool talk and Grover's and Shor's methods most cited. Hardness varies by topic, tool, and method, flagging where docs and teaching most need work.
arxiv-2604-15712: Chen and Yi prove Matsuki duality forms for loop groups. A one-to-one match links symmetric loop-group paths and real polynomial loop-group paths on affine Grassmannians or affine flag kinds. Along the way, they win path labels and tie them to vector bundles on real and twistor projective lines and Kottwitz sets.
arxiv-2604-15912: Zhou, Xie, and Wang study sensing of low-frequency electric fields with Rydberg atoms, whose dipole moments suit measurement. Current work targets microwaves, leaving quasi-DC and low-frequency bands largely unexplored. They build a Fisher information framework with the Cramér-Rao bound to set precision limits for EIT readouts. A DC-biased two-point scheme eases weak-field blindness, reaching a bound around one ten-thousandth of a volt per meter per root hertz. A Fabry-Pérot cavity version boosts Fisher information more than a hundredfold.
arxiv-2604-16012: Yaping Mao resolves the Erdős-Faudree problems by showing isolated vertices control their literal forms. For every graph, the tied sequence depends only on its isolate-free core. Problem 1 has a positive answer and Problem 2 a negative answer in their form. For connected graphs, Mao proves a limit theorem: for every alpha between 0 and 1, some connected bipartite family attains that limit. For Problem 2, the strengthened positive statement holds when the isolate-free core grows without bound. Every connected bounded-degree family thus tends to 0.
arxiv-2604-16412: Toutouh compares two cooperative evolution methods for sorting tables when only a tiny share of rows carry labels. His cooperative method evolves two feature views plus a pseudo-labelling policy, while a matched single-population baseline evolves everything jointly. Across 25 OpenML datasets at 1, 5 and 10 percent labelled data, both methods beat light semi-supervised baselines, with the widest gaps at the lowest label share. Most head-to-head tests ended as statistical draws, though the single-population search showed higher fitness and diversity as it ran.
arxiv-2604-16612: Kaur and colleagues propose FedLLM, a private model for clear traffic flow forecasts. Traffic forecasts support choices, jams and planning, yet most models train with clarity. FedLLM forecasts short-term flow to minutes ahead across varied clients. Four parts stand out: a mix score for freeways, and an adapted model on set traffic prompts. Training swaps only light LoRA plugins, and a prompt supports transfer. Each client learns patterns while adding to a model, cutting cost and keeping data private. Tests show better results over rivals, with clear outputs.
arxiv-2604-16712: Amenoagbadji and Weinstein study waves in flat honeycomb lattices cut by a line defect that does not line up with the lattice. Edge states must hug the defect while oscillating along it, yet the missing translation symmetry makes even defining them hard. By lifting the problem into a three-dimensional setting with a two-dimensional interface, they build approximate edge states and derive a resolvent expansion that seeds a later rigorous construction.
arxiv-2604-16812: Shenoy and colleagues train introspection adapters letting fine-tuned models report learned behaviors in natural language. Fine-tuning can induce unexpected, harmful or hard-to-detect behaviors far easier to audit if models describe them. Models from a shared base carry implanted behaviors, and one adapter is trained across them to verbalize them. The adapter induces self-description even in differently trained fine-tunes, generalizes to AuditBench at state-of-the-art, and detects encrypted API attacks. Introspection adapters scale with model size and data diversity for scalable audits.
arxiv-2604-17112: Hamidieh and four colleagues improve uncertainty scores for language models that sound sure while wrong. Self-consistency, the usual proxy for chance noise, collapses when an overconfident model repeats the same wrong answer. Their epistemic term compares answers across a small ensemble of similar-scale models, measuring the gap between inter-model and intra-model semantic similarity. Their sum improves ranking and selective silence.
arxiv-2604-17512: Deekeswar proposes ONTO, a columnar notation that trims the token cost of feeding operational data to large language models. JSON repeats field names on every record, so 1,000 sensor readings can burn about 80,000 tokens; ONTO names each field once and lines values up in pipe-separated rows. Tests on three synthetic sets cut tokens by 46 to 51 percent against JSON, sped inference 5 to 10 percent on Qwen2.5-7B, and kept task accuracy intact.
arxiv-2604-17612: Bollig, Függer, and Nowak introduce a language for coordinating LLM agent teams, based on message sequence charts. Multi-agent LLM systems are hard to reason about, and coordination errors like deadlocks or type-mismatched messages often escape testing. Their language keeps message-passing structure apart from human control points, LLM calls, and tool calls, whose outcomes stay unpredictable. A syntax-directed projection turns global specs into deadlock-free local programs, shown on a diagnosis consensus protocol, with a runtime planning extension and a Python implementation.
arxiv-2604-17712: Kimura and three colleagues study Y-Ca superhydrides YCaHn, n from 8 to 20, with density functional theory. For YCaH8, many phases differing in metal arrangement are nearly isoenthalpic. The equimolar ratio lifts Tc to 149 K and 170 K for P4/mmm and Cmmm YCaH8 at 180 GPa. YCaH12 is also predicted disordered, with ordered variants spanning 105 to 253 K at 200 GPa, so doping can raise or cut Tc. YCaH18 and YCaH20 each yield one dynamically stable superhydride.
arxiv-2604-17912: Ildiz and three colleagues tackle multi-attempt chain-of-thought reasoning, where a model gets up to K tries and each try builds on earlier ones after hard verifier feedback. Training for success by the Kth attempt seems natural, but weighting attempts naively by pass or fail biases gradients. Their calibrated attempt-level GRPO devises a weighting scheme that yields unbiased gradients while keeping variance small. Theory and experiments on synthetic and real data show it beats both vanilla GRPO and naive weighting.
arxiv-2604-18312: Bartlett, Gabillon, Healey, and Valko propose Platypoos, a planning algorithm for deterministic dynamics with discounted, stochastic, unbounded rewards. The optimal value function is unknown, so the algorithm adjusts to reward scale and smoothness it cannot see in advance. Its sample-complexity analysis improves on prior work and holds across wide spans of discount factors and reward scales with no advance knowledge of them. A matching lower bound shows the analysis is optimal up to constants.
arxiv-2604-18512: Shukla, Jandial, and Ross spot a gap in multi-image matching: current methods use preset indices for narrow reasoning, skipping global search and self-run cross-image comparison. They offer a Simple-to-Hard method building choice data at three levels: single-image focus, multi-image contrast, and global visual search. Unlike prior work relying on hallucinations or focus tricks, their approach uses harder prompts for chosen and losing pairs across models. Tests on LLaVA and Qwen-VL models show large gains over rivals while keeping single-image skills.
arxiv-2604-18712: Tsipidi and six colleagues probe language model representations for human reading times, using eye-tracking data in English, Greek, Hebrew, Russian, and Turkish. Early layers beat surprisal at predicting early measures such as first fixation and gaze duration, suggesting that low-level structural and lexical codes carry human-like processing signals. For late measures such as total reading time, plain surprisal stays ahead. The best predictor varies sharply by language and by measure.
arxiv-2604-18812: de Souza and 13 colleagues present sagui, an approach for multi band galaxy images, with synergies to integral field spectroscopy. Building on capivara for spectroscopy data, sagui extends it to imaging data for a treatment of spatial and spectral information. A starlet based decomposition masks objects across scales while suppressing noise, then spectral similarity analysis partitions the image into pixel groups. A statistical treatment recovers faint, diffuse low surface brightness components. It is demonstrated on morphologies and eleven James Webb galaxies in GOODS-South.
arxiv-2604-18912: Chang and seven colleagues propose Collaborative Contextual Bayesian Optimization, a framework for many clients to learn designs for each context jointly. Contextual optimization must map each context to its best design, weighing exploration across contexts with exploitation within each. The framework supports online collaboration and offline start from peer beliefs, with private messaging. The authors prove slow regret growth and test the method in simulations and a real hot rolling application. It beats existing approaches even when clients differ.
arxiv-2604-19012: Wang and Huang present Phoenix, a training-free multi-agent framework for vulnerability detection. Standard models collapse under strict deduplication because identical code can be safe or vulnerable under different project contracts. Phoenix splits detection into semantic slicing, Gherkin contract synthesis, and strict compliance judging. On PrimeVul Paired it reaches an F1 of 0.825 and about 64 percent Pair-Correct, beating prior methods with models up to 48 times smaller. Ablations credit the Gherkin specs as decisive, and some flagged false positives prove genuine concerns in patched code.
arxiv-2604-19212: Akbari, Souza, and Garg ask how logically expressive topological neural networks are. Graph neural networks lead learning on graphs, yet their power is limited, often framed through the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy or first-order logic. Topological networks add higher-order relational structure to message passing, promising more representational power. The paper pins down which binary classifiers such networks can represent, by analyzing isomorphism tests drawn from their inner mechanisms.
arxiv-2604-19412: Huang and colleagues propose Visual Contrastive Editing, a zero-cost post-hoc fix for object hallucination in large vision-language models. Such models often describe objects absent from the input image, a serious flaw for medical imaging and driving. Prior work traces the flaw to language priors, biases from pretraining that push models toward likely words. The new method spots and damps hallucinatory tendencies by testing responses to contrastive visual changes, using singular value decomposition.
arxiv-2604-19712: Stojnic links two views of hard search gaps in symmetric binary perceptrons, simple neural nets with binary weights. He proves upper bounds on constraint densities for multi-level ultrametric overlap gap properties. His proof joins a combinatorial part, cast as a convex problem, with a nested probabilistic part. The tightest first- and second-level bounds sit near past parametric estimates, backing conjectures that both views share one threshold in the limit.
arxiv-2604-19912: Liang and Peréz-Ríos model how dipolar fluids assemble into chains at low temperature, using molecular dynamics of Stockmayer particles with a purely repulsive core. Across broad regions of density-temperature space, chain sizes decay exponentially with a characteristic size captured by an effective free energy combining entropy, bonding energy, and crowding. Deviations from that scaling split the phase space into four regions, locating a regime of simple chain statistics.
arxiv-2604-20012: Du and seven colleagues propose EmbodiedMidtrain, a mid-training step that adapts vision-language models for vision-language-action robot control. Off-the-shelf vision models hold broad knowledge but sit far from action data, limiting downstream robot performance. Their data engine scores candidates from a large vision pool by proximity to action data, producing the EmbodiedMidtrain-1M set for mid-training before fine-tuning. Tests on simulated manipulation and real-world tasks show steady gains across backbones and action heads, even on tasks never used for selection.
arxiv-2604-20712: Zhao and five colleagues propose a visual-tactile framework for peg-in-hole assembly that learns from peg-out-of-hole disassembly. Disassembly is easier, needing only to beat friction with no exact alignment, so data costs less effort. A disassembly policy is trained first; its trajectories are reversed and action-randomized to provide expert data for assembly. Experiments show the policy attains about 6 percent lower contact forces than rivals. The framework reaches average success rates of about 88 percent on seen objects and about 77 percent on unseen objects.
