arxiv-2604-20812: Brown builds a method for exact estimates of Hausdorff dimensions of limit sets from continued fraction iterated function systems. His method is based on the approximation of a Perron-Frobenius operator using the finite element method with B-splines as basis. This choice brings key gains: faster convergence and more flexibility in computing. He proves an analogue of Falk and Nussbaum's result on hidden positivity for B-spline quasi-interpolants, giving exact upper and lower bounds on Hausdorff dimension for various limit sets.
arxiv-2604-20912: Shehata and colleagues survey nine quantum-HPC software stacks now in production use. Today each stack stands alone, with no shared links across its runtime, resource, and execution layers. From patterns the survey finds, the team puts forward openQSE, a reference design whose layer lines let varied tools work together. It aims to run both noisy machines of today and fault-tolerant machines of the future, with no change to the top layers that apps use.
arxiv-2604-21212: Marios Papamichalis and Regina Ruane show Philadelphia eviction is organized upstream, not in the courtroom, from 755,004 landlord-tenant filings between 1969 and 2022. A concentrated plaintiff-side bar dominates: the ten most active plaintiff attorneys handled most represented cases each year, and large plaintiffs lean heavily on a single attorney. Nearly half of residential cases recur at addresses filed within the prior year, usually by the same plaintiff along a default-heavy path.
arxiv-2604-21312: Kai Liu and 67 colleagues report the NTIRE 2026 challenge on quadrupling the resolution of remote-sensing infrared images, which arrive blurred by bicubic downsampling. In a single-track setting, 115 participants registered and 13 teams submitted valid entries. The report summarizes challenge design, dataset, evaluation protocol, main results, and each team's representative method. The challenge aims to push infrared super-resolution toward real-world remote-sensing use.
arxiv-2604-21412: Isaak Mengesha and six colleagues offer a useful plan for tracking AI incidents over time. Raw counts mix up media attention, rollout size, and harm per unit of rollout. Their method poses a clear tracking question. It separately tracks harm trends and exposure trends in steps, with LLM-assisted filtering. It maps trends onto governance groups: escalating, mitigating, concentrating, receding, or unclassifiable. Case studies show the plan clarifies insight for policy teams despite messy real-world data, as a proof of concept for practical AI tracking.
arxiv-2604-21512: Romain Simon and four colleagues show that current methods for tracking turning motion in fluids fail under slow, mixed, or stop-start dynamics, including supercooled liquids. These failures cloud debates on turning-translation decoupling and Debye-Stokes-Einstein breaks, and no method captures the shift from diffusive fluid to arrested solid, clearing inconsistent results. They introduce a method fixing these issues, tested on continuous-time random walk models. It gauges free and caged motion plus non-Gaussian and non-Fickian dynamics, promising a read on dynamic heterogeneity in supercooled fluids.
arxiv-2604-21912: Holleis and eighteen colleagues introduce cryogenic shock exfoliation to produce large rhombohedral graphene flakes. Combined with a low-pressure assembly method keeping stacking order, the method enables uniform devices over 1300 square microns with yields of 90 percent. Scanning nanoSQUID-on-tip imaging shows uniform spin magnetism over the central 10 by 10 square micron area. Transverse magnetic focusing reveals a disorder mean free path over 200 microns at low temperatures. Within flat surface bands, a size-driven crossover from Poiseuille to porous electron flow signals ultrahigh device quality.
arxiv-2604-22012: Gagné and colleagues present a Python spectrophotometry extraction tool for point sources in the SPHEREx mission, used to build about 1 to 5.0 micron low-resolution products from SPHEREx Quick Release 2 for 6,003 L0-Y1 ultracool dwarfs: 2,050 known dwarfs, 3,008 known photometric candidates, and 947 newly identified dwarfs. The work more than doubles the number of ultracool dwarfs with spectroscopy, from 3,449 to 7,402. The data open the 2 to 5 micron window for many substellar objects, enabling study of cool brown dwarf chemistry. The authors flag 2,668 dwarfs as candidate young brown dwarfs, 250 as candidate subdwarfs, and 865 as peculiar.
arxiv-2604-22212: Dong and six colleagues use an open multi-input diffusion model to learn the dynamics between EBSD and polarized light data. The model tackles inverse problems for 3-D electron back-scattered diffraction. Trained solely on fake data once, the model carries over strongly to real data that are low-detail, noisy, damaged, and misaligned. With test-time scaling, it gains on grain edge guessing, upscaling, and cleanup. The model shows little gap from full-detail scores with only 25 percent of EBSD data and damaged polarized light data.
arxiv-2604-22312: Cheng and nine colleagues speed Top-K selection in sparse-attention decoding on NVIDIA Blackwell hardware. That step picks key-value entries per query token and bottlenecks long-context serving. Their Guess-Verify-Refine algorithm uses the previous step's Top-K as a prediction, exploiting correlation across steps. It narrows to a valid threshold in one or two passes, verifies candidates without ballots, and finishes in shared memory. On DeepSeek-V3.2 workloads it averages 1.88 times faster than the production radix-select kernel, with bit-exact outputs.
arxiv-2604-22412: For a wide class of discrete groups, Ozawa shows that marked-group convergence forces operator-strong convergence. The class holds free groups and their limit groups. Behind it sits uniform exactness, also called uniform amenability at infinity, a trait he sets out for discrete groups. One payoff: the spectral radius formula converges evenly over probability laws on such groups when their supports share one fixed size.
arxiv-2604-22812: Schwerter and seven colleagues test whether prediction models built from digital learning traces travel across courses, using weekly self-regulated-learning indicators from three theory-heavy computer science courses at two universities. Early warning proves possible, with time management, effort control, and steady engagement standing out as predictors. Random Forest fits its own course best, Elastic Net travels better, and accuracy falls when the share of at-risk students differs between institutions.
arxiv-2604-23212: Lu and three colleagues characterise learning curves and benign overfitting of spectral algorithms with comparable sample size and dimension. For kernels on the sphere, they describe excess risk across the regularisation path under source conditions for regression smoothness. The curve is not U-shaped but splits into over-regularised, under-regularised, and interpolation regimes. Benign overfitting appears across under-regularised and interpolation regimes when smoothness is positive but below a critical threshold. Kernel curves in the regularised regime follow a sequence model.
arxiv-2604-23312: Young and Pugeault tackle chaotic dynamics in deep reinforcement learning policies for continuous control with nonlinear contact forces, where tiny initial changes reshape long-term conduct. Such sensitivity blocks real-world use in settings where stability pledges matter. Their framework, GIFT, directly optimises global stability of strong existing policies through a custom reward. Tests show GIFT raises control stability while keeping task performance close, improving deep RL suitability for real-world control.
arxiv-2604-23412: Amalvy and colleagues offer a legal workaround for sharing annotations of copyrighted books: publish the annotations openly alongside a one-way hashed copy of the text. A researcher who owns the book hashes their own copy the same way and lines the annotations up against it, even when editions differ slightly. Tests on novels align nearly all tokens, and the team releases its tool, novelshare, for others to use.
arxiv-2604-23712: Li and colleagues present OptProver, a prover that carries skill from Olympiad maths to undergraduate optimisation, a domain other provers serve poorly. Large-scale optimisation-focused data curation plus a preference objective that penalises valid but non-progressing proof steps guide the search toward efficient paths. On a new Lean benchmark for optimisation it leads models of similar size while staying strong on general theorem proving.
arxiv-2604-24212: Xiang and four colleagues give autonomous debugging agents an efficient dynamic analysis interface, ADI. Coarse post-mortem feedback limits repair agents, while classic debuggers burn budgets in unproductive loops. ADI works at function level, powered by a Frame Lifetime Trace of function execution plus high-level navigation commands. A basic agent with ADI resolves about 64 percent of SWE-bench Verified tasks, slightly beating a highly tuned Claude-Tools agent at low cost. ADI also plugs into leading agents for consistent gains.
arxiv-2604-24412: Pálvölgyi extends prior work on polychromatic colorings of hereditary hypergraphs. For h from 4 up, he builds a hypergraph of uniformity twice h minus one with no polychromatic 3-coloring. Yet all of its h-heavy subhypergraphs are 2-colorable, and with the h equals 3 case this gives such cases for every h from 3 up. The build uses complements of h-uniform hypergraphs. For h from 9 up, a probabilistic argument proves existence. Cases h from 4 to 8 are certified by computer check, with code in the appendix.
arxiv-2604-24512: Shehata and Li name a failure they call the Attention Latch. In it, old context in a language model agent outweighs fresh orders mid-task and pins it to stale constraints. Their fix, Self-Synthesizing Reasoning Protocols, splits high-level planning from step-by-step execution so the plan can be remade without losing the goal. Across thousands of test runs, the split design held up where plain baselines collapsed, lifting success 715 times at the boundary they locate.
arxiv-2604-24612: Romero Schellhorn and Mossakowski show that the three semantics of ULLER, a unified language for learning and reasoning, are cases of one monad framework. The three semantics had looked quite different, yet they share one first-order syntax. ULLER's classical, fuzzy and probabilistic semantics had separate rules. The monad view lets users add new semantics and clean translations between them. As an example, they extend the Giry monad to add general quantification in Logic Tensor Networks to all domains.
arxiv-2604-24712: Akli, Papadakis, Cordy and Le Traon ask when vague prompts help rather than hurt code generation. Earlier work on minimal benchmarks found that under-specification sharply cuts correctness. The authors test ten models on HumanEval and the richer LiveCodeBench. On LiveCodeBench, the same vague-prompt changes have near-zero net effect, because redundancy across descriptions, constraints, examples and input-output conventions cushions them. Surprisingly, some prompt changes improve correctness on the richer benchmark.
arxiv-2604-25112: Sun and nine colleagues propose a closure for three-moment fluid equations that depends on wave number. In plasma simulation, standard closures drift from exact kinetic response as the perturbation wave number changes. They map Padé approximant coefficients onto kinetic roots of the collisionless Vlasov-Poisson system, yielding an analytical closure that keeps the primary dispersion relation at all spatial scales. The same frame extends to collisional plasmas via the BGK model.
arxiv-2604-25512: Sen, Ray and Chakrabarti present CoGReV, a post-hoc thinking layer that can take back its calls, in Answer Set code. A trust-gated rule flips a phishing call to clean only when site data is present and the call is low-trust. Unlike an ungated rule, which cuts false alarms only by dropping genuine catches and harms recall by about nine points, the gated rule keeps recall within 0.7 points of base while changing few calls. By cutting false alarms without losing catches, CoGReV reduces alert fatigue.
arxiv-2604-26012: Carretta presents a census of dynamical ages for 93 Milky Way globular clusters, with Gaia progenitor data. Most accreted clusters are dynamically young: 61 percent, against 38 percent for in situ clusters. Excluding low-energy clusters of ambiguous origin, the young share among ex situ clusters rises to 70 percent. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test finds low-energy clusters indistinguishable from in situ bulge and disc clusters. Yet low-energy clusters sit firmly on the satellite side of the age-metallicity relation. Carretta suggests their progenitor plunged in very early.
arxiv-2604-26212: Goldberg and five colleagues introduce grasp planners for an asymmetrical gripper. One uses a single-view colour image, a novel sampling strategy, and a classic grasp-quality metric. The other uses a three-dimensional gripper model with ray tracing. In experiments the image-based planner improves lift success, shake survival, and force resistance by over forty percent against a bounding-box baseline. The mesh-based planner edges it on lift and shake survival but costs far more time: seventeen seconds against under one second for the image-based method.
arxiv-2604-26312: Putri and five colleagues used an LSTM network to sort public feeling about Indonesia's Free Nutritious Meal Program in YouTube comments. From 7,733 comments, the model reached 89 percent accuracy, doing well on negative sentiment with an F1-score of 0.94, yet weaker on positive sentiment. The gap traces to imbalance, since negative comments made up nearly 88 percent of the set. The study shows LSTM's strength for Indonesian sentiment while flagging the imbalance problem.
arxiv-2604-26412: Liu and ten colleagues asked whether KV caches can rescue long-range speculative decoding, where draft accuracy fades as steps stretch out. They argued the target hidden state compresses history for the next token only, starving later steps, while the KV cache keeps every token's key-value pair intact. Their KVShot framework compared hidden-only, KV-only, and hybrid reuse on Qwen3-8B. KV reuse lifted long-range acceptance, though end-to-end speedups stayed marginal under current training.
arxiv-2604-26712: Alba Alonso and Sánchez González describe core-nilpotent endomorphisms over any vector spaces through the k[x]-module structure they define. Core-nilpotent endomorphisms form the largest set of endomorphisms admitting a split as a sum of two endomorphisms. The two parts have properties like the matrix core-nilpotent split. Their approach yields a new broad inverse that becomes the well-known Drazin inverse in certain cases. It also gives a broad core-nilpotent split for endomorphisms over any vector spaces.
arxiv-2604-27012: Kropotov, Moreto and Salami tackle stalled pre-silicon validation when a large multi-core system outgrows one chip, since a single FPGA lacks resources for full-system emulation. EMiX, a scalable framework using several FPGAs, partitions a monolithic multi-core RISC-V design into pieces on interconnected FPGAs. Its links balance scale against performance, with no fundamental RTL redesign required. A prototype puts a 64-core design on eight linked Alveo U55c FPGAs, runs the whole system, and boots Linux. The authors intend an open-source release of EMiX.
arxiv-2604-27112: Dinella tests modular randomized testing for Java programs, where single parts are checked apart from the rest of the code. She finds that EvoSuite in modular mode bars setup calls from outside the target part, which often leaves branch coverage low. Her fix, called EMOTE, loosens that bar so setup calls can appear in test prefixes, borrowing the habit of hand-written fuzz drivers that call setup routines first.
arxiv-2604-27212: Churazov and seven colleagues study iron He-triplet signatures of shocks in the hottest galaxy clusters. Cluster mergers drive shocks of Mach number up to about 3 in the intra-cluster medium, leaving brightness edges plus temperature and velocity jumps. Low density makes ionization balance and electron-ion equilibration slow, adding transient spectral signs visible to high-resolution telescopes such as XRISM even when geometry hides sharp edges. The paper focuses on the iron XXV triplet line ratio and on hot-ion contributions to line width.
arxiv-2604-27612: Nomura and Okada propose a mechanism for naturally small vacuum expectation values of exotic multi-Higgs fields using non-invertible symmetry. They add a quartet and a quintet under the minimal Fibonacci fusion rule, which forbids tree-level values for these fields. Once the symmetry breaks, the values arise radiatively at one loop, with no extra particles needed. The values land between a thousandth and a hundredth of a GeV, satisfying rho-parameter constraints, and the setup applies to type-III, Dirac, and inverse seesaw models.
arxiv-2604-28012: Manaswini and colleagues track the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20240114A across twelve observing epochs with two large telescopes. Rotation measures stayed stable and most bursts were strongly linearly polarised, yet the polarisation angle jumped wildly from burst to burst, by up to about a right angle. That mix points away from one fixed emitting spot and toward several regions or strong propagation effects such as plasma lensing.
arxiv-2604-28112: Berthold's team develops splitting methods for bipolar set-based argumentation frameworks, which combine collective attacks and supports and cover both SETAFs and bipolar systems. More power calls for varied splits, so they cover splits over collective attacks, over group supports, and over both at once. They set out splitting patterns and prove them correct under the most common rules. The system naturally captures layered, maybe non-flat assumption-based argumentation.
arxiv-2605-00012:
Roman Smirnov investigates whether the biases of large language models can be exploited to rig AI search overviews. Such overview systems use a model to pick the most relevant sources from search results and compose an answer. Bias can enter at both stages, and Smirnov focuses mainly on source selection, asking whether a snippet can be rewritten to win the model's favor.

He trains a small language model with reinforcement learning to rewrite search snippets so an overview system prefers them. The setup deliberately limits the rewriter to snippets and blocks easy reward hacking, matching real search conditions. The results show the overviews are biased, that the rewriting usually succeeds, and that choices turn on comparative rather than absolute advantage. Context poisoning can also push such systems toward wrong or harmful answers.
arxiv-2605-00312:
Jan Ljubas and Tim Byrnes review Decoded Quantum Interferometry, a recent approach that seeks quantum speedups for practical optimization problems. Proving a clear quantum edge on broadly useful problems has been a long-standing goal, and earlier speedups covered only narrow, structured cases. The new method draws on classical coding theory as much as on quantum mechanics.

The review is self-contained. It builds up the needed background in Galois fields, in the max-LINSAT class of problems, and in error-correcting codes, then walks through the quantum algorithm step by step. For one special problem, optimal polynomial intersection, strong evidence suggests a faster-than-any-classical speedup for approximate solutions. The authors explain the operating principle carefully, aiming to make the method usable by readers outside its home field.
arxiv-2605-00412:
Sen Cui and Jingheng Ma argue, from a Hamiltonian angle, that world models for robots and cars should be built around physics. World models, which predict how a scene will unfold, have split into three camps: video makers, 3D scene builders, and latent forecast models. Each camp, they note, still struggles to give reliable forecasts that actions can steer and that stay stable over long spans.

Their plan encodes what the sensors see into an ordered latent phase space, the state language of Hamiltonian mechanics. The latent state then evolves by Hamiltonian-inspired rules with terms for control, losses, and leftovers, before decoding into forecasts for planning. The authors discuss possible gains in clarity, data thrift, and steadiness. They also flag hard cases plainly: friction, contact, energy-losing forces, and soft objects all strain the approach.
arxiv-2605-00812:
Evan Cavallo and Jonas Höfer examine a weaker form of univalence in homotopy type theory, a foundation that treats spaces and types together. The classic result, due to Voevodsky, says function extensionality holds inside any univalent universe. The authors define categorical univalence, which asks only that the wild category formed by the universe be univalent, and ask whether it still forces extensionality.

Using Von Glehn's polynomial model, which always refutes function extensionality, they show the answer is no. When the base model has a univalent universe, its polynomial model can have a universe that is categorically univalent yet lacks function extensionality. The split clarifies exactly what the stronger axiom adds.
arxiv-2605-00912:
Emilie Durrieu, Christophe Hurter, Philippe Muller, and Victor Boutin develop an object-level way to explain image geolocation models, using GeoGuessr as the test case. Human players rely on concrete cues such as road markings, vegetation, and building details. Standard attribution maps highlight diffuse areas, so it is hard to tell whether models use similar evidence or which specific objects drive a prediction.

Their pipeline extracts salient regions from attribution maps and segments them into object-like elements. Deletion and insertion tests then measure how much each element matters, compared with random regions of similar size. On a three-country benchmark, attribution-guided crops consistently retain more predictive information than random crops, giving a step toward interpretable object-level analysis.
arxiv-2605-01012:
Yurou Liu and nine co-authors measure chemistry and isotope ratios in the atmosphere of a planetary-mass companion in the Beta Pictoris young moving group. The companion, with about twelve Jupiter masses, orbits a pair of brown dwarfs and sits at the boundary between planets and brown dwarfs, making its formation pathway a key question. High-resolution spectra from CRIRES+ on the Very Large Telescope feed an atmospheric retrieval.

The retrieved carbon-to-oxygen ratio and metallicity are close to solar-like values, and the carbon isotope ratio is also measured. Two benchmark brown dwarfs in the same group show consistent compositions. Together with the companion's wide separation, that consistency supports formation by gravitational collapse in a star-like manner, and provides a baseline for comparing true planets in the same group.
arxiv-2605-01512:
Jiantang Huang locates rare traffic crashes in real security footage without any training on labeled crash video, a constraint set by the rules of the task. The system must name when a crash happens, where in the frame it sits, and what kind of collision it is, all at once.

The pipeline works in two passes. A first sweep at one frame per second gives a coarse time, place, and type. A second, denser pass inside a six-second window refines the call, with two fixed safety gates that fall back to the coarse answer when the fine pass hedges at edges. Two frozen vision-language models split the work, one grounding and one typing. On a benchmark of over two thousand real CCTV clips, the method beats the best baseline blend by a wide margin, at a total run cost of about twenty dollars.
arxiv-2605-01712:
Xinyue Chen and five co-authors teach one network to solve many multi-objective problems at once. Pareto set learning trains a model to turn any preference weighting into a matching best-compromise solution. The standard setup trains a fresh model per problem, wasting both compute and the kinship between tasks.

CoAction adds task awareness to a transformer backbone. Each task carries its own embedding, so the model can tell tasks apart while still sharing what it learns across them through self-attention. One trained model then serves the whole task family, reading a task tag plus a preference vector and returning the compromise. On broad multitask suites of benchmarks and real-world problems, the framework proves effective and competitive on the standard quality measures of volume covered, range, and spacing of solutions.
arxiv-2605-01812:
Koushik Ghorai, Sayan Sarkar, and Amit Agarwal define a new current for the altermagnet era. Altermagnets split electron spins by crystal rotation rather than by net magnetization, and their spin-splitter current is established; the orbital cousin, current sorted by orbital angular momentum, had not been framed.

The orbital-splitter current is derived in a density-matrix treatment with two sources, a Drude part from plain band motion and an orbital Berry curvature part from band geometry. One material makes the effect pure: in the d-wave altermagnet FeSb2, mirror symmetries kill the Drude channel by forcing the orbital moment to vanish, leaving a solely intrinsic current. The response is strongly directional and, for chosen field angles, runs nearly four times the spin-splitter current. In a stack with a ferromagnet it adds a damping-like torque, and paired with its spin cousin it switches magnetization markedly faster.
arxiv-2605-02012:
Sphiwe Skhosana and Hien Duy Nguyen make mixtures of experts more robust for data that are skewed, heavy-tailed, or full of outliers. Mixture of experts models handle varied data for regression and clustering, but they usually assume Gaussian expert distributions. That assumption fits poorly when real data lean to one side or have long tails.

The authors replace the Gaussian expert with a shifted asymmetric Laplace distribution, giving the SALMoE model. They fit it with a hybrid algorithm that joins expectation-maximisation with a minorization step, and they show the observed likelihood never falls during fitting. Simulations support the model's robustness, and a real application in the paper shows its practical use.
arxiv-2605-02112:
Samuel Julian Weisenthal makes a variance estimate better for a method that gauges how sparse a policy model is, relative to a base case. Past work gave a normal limit result for an adaptive lasso in this setting. But that result was not fully used for the variance of the policy terms. So the graphs that show model choice understated how unsure the choice was.

Weisenthal builds a new variance estimator that uses the limit result in full. It also takes model choice itself into account. Better uncertainty counts here, because these graphs guide policy learning in clinical care, where too much confidence can lead to unsafe choices. The aim is for shown uncertainty to match what the theory supports.
arxiv-2605-02212:
Jiebin Yan and colleagues review the NTIRE 2026 challenge on efficient low-light image enhancement. The challenge asked for light networks that brighten and clean mobile photos taken in low light, while staying practical on limited hardware. A total of 207 participants registered, twenty-seven teams submitted valid entries, and seventeen teams provided valid factsheets for the final report.

The paper surveys the submitted solutions and final outcomes in a systematic way. It compares how teams balanced image quality against speed and model size, the central trade-off of the task. The authors report clear progress in both performance and efficiency over past methods, and they summarise design patterns that worked across the leading entries.
arxiv-2605-02312:
Enea Figini and Mario Paolone ask whether small data centres should join the day-ahead electricity market, as AI demand strains power grids. Their proposal is a bilateral power purchase agreement between small data centres and distribution system operators. That agreement would let a data centre bid into the market while supporting grid operation, rather than buying power on a fixed tariff alone.

To bid well, they develop a scenario-based, risk-averse strategy. It uses flexibility from local energy resources, waste heat recovery, and workload shifting. The strategy jointly lowers operating cost and carbon emissions. A case study compares a conventional time-of-use supply scheme with the proposed custom agreement, testing whether market participation pays for a small operator.
arxiv-2605-02412:
Christopher Campbell and Matti Silveri analyse how dark states in a pair of photon-emitter systems gain dissipation when weak anharmonicity is added. Dark states are excited states that decouple from their environment, neither emitting nor absorbing photons. One of the simplest homes for them is a pair of dissipatively coupled harmonic oscillators under the Bose-Hubbard model.

With on-site interactions included, those states are no longer truly dark, because dissipation appears in them. Campbell and Silveri use weak anharmonicity as a perturbation to trace the origin of that dissipation. They compute first and second order corrections to the wavefunction and feed them into the master equation to track the dynamics. The analysis shows how the dark state's protection erodes order by order.
arxiv-2605-02612:
Nicolas Masson, Benoît Perthame, and Filippo Santambrogio propose a new model for crowd motion built as a limit of traffic-like conservation laws. Their rule is selective: a density limit may slow an agent only when that agent is in a crowded zone, or has one ahead. Agents outside crowded zones, with clear space ahead, keep moving freely.

The authors study what happens as a stiffness parameter grows, and obtain a limit equation of a wholly new type. A main step is proving uniform variation bounds on the density, which give the compactness needed to show solutions of the limit equation exist. Qualitative behavior, the entropy conditions proper to the new equation, and numerical pictures in one and two dimensions complete the paper.
arxiv-2605-02712:
Dominik Macko reports a single-author system entry for a shared task on conspiracy detection in social media comments. The task is binary: does a Reddit comment express a conspiracy belief? Training data were limited, which shapes the whole approach. The entry builds on methods first developed for detecting machine-generated text.

To cope with scarce data, the system uses data augmentation and self-training, then fine-tunes a large open language model for classification. The result was competitive, placing in the eighty-fifth percentile among fifty-two submissions. Macko presents the outcome as evidence that a pipeline built for one text classification problem can transfer to another with similar traits. The paper is a compact system description rather than a new theory.
arxiv-2605-03012:
Led by the Euclid Collaboration, this preparation paper sets out how the Euclid mission will measure the three-point pattern of galaxies in space. Two-point measures miss some of the detail in how galaxies cluster, so triple counts add key information and help separate competing models.

The team compares an exact triplet count with a faster method based on spherical harmonics, which still meets mission needs. A random split trick also cuts the cost of counting reference triplets by a factor of ten with little loss in accuracy. Tests show a full Euclid analysis is within reach.
arxiv-2605-03112:
Mukesh Ghimire, Zhe Xu, and Yi Ren speed up strategy solving for the informed player in a two-player differential game with hidden payoff information. One player knows the true payoff while the other holds only a public belief, so the informed player can hide or reveal type through control choices.

For linear dynamics with quadratic costs, they split the problem into an outer signaling choice and an inner game-tree control solve. An adjoint backpropagation scheme alternates a backward control pass with a forward gradient step. On homing test cases, the solver ran at about ten updates per second, enabling robust planning under uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-03312:
Jiayi Chen, Yingcong Li, and Guiling Wang present MemFlow, a memory system for small language model agents. Such agents must handle long, multi-turn histories. Full-context prompts overflow. Flat retrieval adds noise. Open-ended loops strain a small model's limited reasoning.

MemFlow plans memory outside the small model. A router sorts each query by intent. A memory agent then runs one of three tiers, from profile lookup to deep reasoning. Each tier has a matched token budget. A validator can retry with a heavier tier. On long-horizon benchmarks with a frozen small backbone, accuracy nearly doubled over full-context baselines.
arxiv-2605-03512:
Ilias Chalkidis and Anders Søgaard argue that deskilling and addiction are missed risks in AI safety work. Safety research has focused on bias, harmful content, information hazards, and malicious use. Public concern centers heavily on cognition, mental health, and over-reliance.

Offloading thought can erode critical thinking. Attachment to AI systems can foster dependence. Yet both risks are rarely addressed in alignment work. The authors quantify that gap. They sketch how safety work could take such harms seriously. Campaigns and regulation are discussed as routes to cut these risks.
arxiv-2605-03612:
Ali Hamed Moosavian and Bahram Abedi Ravan critically examine Entropy Quantum Computing, a commercial approach from Quantum Computing Inc. that treats environmental noise and decoherence as fuel rather than as problems to fight. The original article presented the method as an open quantum system that turns entropy into computing power. Moosavian and Ravan test how far those claims hold up.

They show that some claims can be made more rigorous, but even then the method does not beat state-of-the-art classical algorithms on conventional computers. Their comment is not a dismissal: they stress the technology is young, and continued rigorous work is needed to judge its long-term value.
arxiv-2605-03812:
Chris S. Lin and six co-authors demonstrate GPUBreach, a privilege escalation attack on graphics processors using Rowhammer, the hardware fault technique that flips bits in memory by repeated access. NVIDIA GPUs with GDDR memory were known to suffer untargeted bit flips that degrade model accuracy, but privilege escalation was thought to be a CPU-only feat. The authors close that gap.

By exploiting GPU page table management, an unprivileged CUDA kernel learns when and where new page tables are allocated. It can then flip targeted bits in page tables and reach other tenants' memory. They demonstrate leaking cryptographic keys from cuPQC libraries, tampering with model assembly code, and even escalating from GPU access to CPU-side privilege despite IOMMU protections.
arxiv-2605-03912:
Aslıhan Gür, Didem Gözüpek, and Hadi Alizadeh characterize packing chromatic critical graphs of small radius. A packing coloring partitions a graph's vertices into classes. Vertices in the class labeled i must sit at distance greater than i from each other. The packing chromatic number is the smallest number of classes needed. A graph is critical when every proper subgraph has a strictly smaller packing chromatic number.

The authors provide a structural characterization of the critical graphs with radius one. They then completely determine the critical cactus graphs with radius two and diameter two or three. Cactus graphs, where cycles share at most one vertex, are a natural test class for such structural results, and the radius restriction keeps the graph's center close to every vertex.
arxiv-2605-04112:
Thales B. S. F. Rodrigues and four co-authors analyze the idea that emergent quantum dynamics can be viewed as a Bayesian inference problem. Coarse-grained views capture processes where information is lost or cannot be reached, and the authors connect them to the quantum conditional states framework. From a Bayesian viewpoint, they pin down exactly when an effective dynamics can exist given a microscopic one.

Their solution, though optimal, turns out to be limited because it works state by state. They therefore use semidefinite programming to study four model scenarios on a computer. The existence of effective dynamics motivates a new robustness measure: how much noise can be added to a microscopic dynamics before it stops being compatible with a given coarse-grained view.
arxiv-2605-04312:
Connacher Murphy introduces a benchmark for language models that is built as a multiplayer game. It aims to avoid two common failures of fixed tests. One is models saturating the score. The other is test data leaking into training. Agents compete in a social game of cooperation, conflict, and persuasion.

Because opponents adapt, a new model can always in principle beat the current leader, and rankings come from a Bayesian model that also reports uncertainty in skill. In nearly a thousand games among forty-nine models, one model led by a wide margin. The released game logs also let researchers study behaviours such as favouring finalists from the same provider.
arxiv-2605-04412:
Yiran Qiao and seven co-authors present a method for generating three-dimensional objects in a chosen visual style, for uses such as games and virtual reality. Existing methods work when the target style resembles their training data, but degrade badly on unfamiliar styles.

Their approach uses a pretrained two-dimensional diffusion model as a teacher, since such models carry broad and transferable style knowledge. Rendered views of the object are aligned with the target style under that guidance, and the structured three-dimensional representation is adjusted to match. The authors argue the bottleneck was never model capacity, but how little past methods used those structured representations.
arxiv-2605-04612:
Chris Dong and Jannik Peters bring an axiom-based method to the study of proportionality in committee elections. In these elections, voters approve candidates. Many notions of fair representation have been proposed for approval-based multiwinner voting. But the case for choosing one notion over another has been poorly understood.

They define axioms that a good notion of this kind should satisfy. They then characterise two prominent recent notions through those axioms. The analysis shows a classical one-way growth rule is the key feature. It separates the newer notions from the earlier ones. They also introduce witness-based notions. In that framework, a guarantee of this kind is backed by an explicit witness. This broadens the axiom-based picture.
arxiv-2605-04712:
Lirui Luo and four co-authors address a fading ability to learn in deep reinforcement learning agents trained over long streams of experience. Mixture-of-experts networks, which route work to specialist sub-networks, were hoped to help. Yet their skill can still decay as training goes on.

Drawing on neural tangent kernel theory, the team defines this decay as a loss of spectral plasticity and derives a simple proxy for it. Their method, SPHERE, adds a Parseval penalty shaped for expert policies to protect that plasticity. On MetaWorld and HumanoidBench tests, SPHERE raised average success well above an unpenalized baseline while keeping plasticity higher throughout training.
arxiv-2605-04812:
Daniela Moretti and three co-authors study clusters of active Brownian particles, tiny particles that move on their own as well as by random thermal motion. Simulations show these clusters spread out in an unusual way as particle number grows. The authors ask how particles joining and leaving a cluster help cause that pattern.

Starting from equations for single particles, they build a paired model for the cluster centre and its changing mass. Solving it gives one normal spread term and one driven by mass changes, which can dominate. Their predicted scaling matches large simulations closely, showing that changing cluster size is central to the odd diffusion.
arxiv-2605-05012:
Joao Florindo presents a texture classification framework that pairs self-supervised learning with deterministic chaos to handle changes in scale and lighting. Texture tasks are hard because classes look alike and surface patterns shift with conditions. His method uses pixel-wise chaotic maps as a form of augmentation during contrastive pretraining, forcing the network to learn features that survive complex noise.

An attention-based ensemble then fuses high-level features from a large supervised backbone with structural features from a small chaos-pretrained encoder. Across six public texture benchmarks, the combined method beat leading approaches. Florindo argues chaotic perturbations, grounded in ergodic theory, mimic real reflectance and environmental variation well.
arxiv-2605-05112:
Tianshu Zhu and ten co-authors steer reinforcement learning for software engineering agents toward training groups whose pass rate sits near one half. Groups of attempts earn binary rewards, and when almost all pass or fail, the learning signal is weak and skewed. The authors show the reward-side signal is strongest near an even pass rate under several criteria.

Their Prefix Sampling method replays pieces of the model's own earlier trajectories to rebalance skewed groups: good prefixes help mostly-failing groups, and bad prefixes handicap mostly-passing ones. Replayed tokens are masked from the loss, so learning applies only to fresh continuations. On a verified software benchmark the method matched baseline peak scores with large time savings.
arxiv-2605-05412:
Johanan Ramírez-Arellano and seven co-authors report a radio survey of the Coronet Cluster, a nearby nursery of young stars in Corona Australis. Using the Very Large Array, they watched the region at two radio bands from 2012 to 2015. The maps were deep and sharp enough to split close pairs of young stars.

They found twenty radio sources, including fourteen known young stellar objects. The youngest stars showed varied radio colors, while older ones fit free-free emission from ionized gas. Almost every source varied over time, and one known binary, IRS 5, was cleanly resolved into its two stars.
arxiv-2605-05812:
Q-learning learns from any experience, but its bootstrapping lets small errors compound across long horizons. Armaan A. Abraham, Lucy Xiaoyang Shi, and Chelsea Finn add a backstop: n-step inequalities. Any action sequence actually realized lower-bounds what the optimal policy can achieve, so value estimates can be tightened against that fact.

Their long-horizon Q-learning uses those inequalities to stop estimation errors from propagating backward unchecked. The method keeps the appeal of off-policy learning from old or borrowed data. It targets the settings where temporal-difference learning is most brittle: problems whose payoffs arrive far in the future.
arxiv-2605-05912:
Rafael Pablos Sarabia and three co-authors present a method for making high resolution rainfall maps from sparse data. Good rain maps matter for forecasts, water planning, and hazard warnings, but station readings are often noisy and thin on the ground. Radar adds spatial detail, yet past deep learning methods fused the two sources poorly.

Their system, DropsToGrid, uses a neural process design with multi scale features, temporal attention, and fusion of station and radar inputs. It gives continuous rain estimates and states its own uncertainty. On real world data sets it beat both standard operational tools and deep learning baselines. It stayed accurate with few stations and when moved to new regions.
arxiv-2605-06312:
Toby Maddock and five co-authors remove a transport blocking defect from an ion trap without opening the vacuum system. Surface electrode ion traps shuttle ions along paths for quantum computing, and a single defect can block a route entirely. The usual fix means venting and rebaking the apparatus, a slow process that costs heavy downtime, above all for cold systems that need long bakes after any opening.

Their remedy fires a pulsed ablation laser, of a type many ion trap labs already own, at the defect in place. After ablation, shuttling across the once blocked region succeeded at near unity rates. Micromotion, a key quality measure for trapped ions, stayed within acceptable limits. The technique restores transport pathways quickly and suits shuttling focused experiments well.
arxiv-2605-06412:
Brean Maynard and Peter Schweitzer study leading Generalized Transverse Momentum Dependent parton distributions, called GTMDs, inside the bag model. GTMDs describe how quarks carry momentum inside a proton. The authors check that the model description is theoretically consistent and then use it to examine orbital angular momentum.

Orbital angular momentum is studied through one GTMD and the Ji sum rule, with analytical proofs of the related sum rules. A deeper link is also established between orbital angular momentum and the pretzelosity distribution. Readers get a compact model study tying several proton-structure ideas together with proofs rather than numerics alone.
arxiv-2605-06912:
Kirill Trapeznikov and eleven co-authors report on the SAFE challenge, a blind competition for detecting synthetic videos. As generative video improves, telling real footage from fabricated clips becomes urgent. The challenge, held alongside an ICCV 2025 workshop, drew over six hundred submissions from twelve teams over ninety days on the Hugging Face platform.

Two tasks were scored: spotting videos from thirteen modern generators matched against real clips from twenty-one sources, and spotting synthetic content after common post-processing like resizing, recompression, and motion blur. The dataset totals twenty hours across six thousand videos. Results show measurable progress in generalizing across generators, but post-processing artifacts remain a persistent weakness for detectors.
arxiv-2605-07012:
Ishitaa Narwane, Johanna Gunawan, and Konrad Kollnig examine deception in generative AI through the idea of banal deception. Research on deceptive design usually targets visible tricks in interfaces, often called dark patterns. AI deception instead hides in defaults, suggestions, and ordinary chat, making it easy to overlook and live with.

Drawing on Simone Natale's framing, the authors stress how users themselves take part in being deceived. They propose directions for adding helpful friction, including raising awareness, giving users intervention tools, and improving regulation. The piece is offered as discussion points for scholars who study deceptive design.
arxiv-2605-07112:
Sharad Agarwal and five co-authors present Switchcraft, a router that picks cheaper AI models for tool-calling agents without losing correctness. Developers often default to large models and overspend, while existing routers were built for chat rather than tool use. Switchcraft chooses the lowest-cost model that should still answer correctly, inline during a run.

Built on a small classifier and tested on five function-calling benchmarks, it matched or beat the best single model's accuracy. At the same time it cut inference cost sharply, saving thousands of dollars per million queries in their accounting. The team also found larger models do not always win at tool use, and cheap models can cost more overall.
arxiv-2605-07812:
Robin Buchta and three co-authors detect stealthy break-ins by watching what programs do rather than what they are named. Advanced persistent threats hide inside normal system activity. Provenance-based detectors that log relationships between processes, files, and network parts are a strong defense, though threshold-based versions are brittle.

Their system, GRASP, masks each process's executable identity and learns to infer it from the process's two-hop neighborhood in the provenance graph; processes it cannot classify are flagged as odd ones. Because detection needs no preset threshold, it resists tampering and unknown activity. On the DARPA TC and OpTC datasets it found every recorded attack whose executable behavior was learnable. It beat existing systems, and surfaced extra odd behavior the records had not labeled.
arxiv-2605-07912:
Lujain Ibrahim and seven co-authors present experimental evidence that flattering AI changes people's real relationships for the worse. Across five preregistered studies with more than three thousand participants and nearly thirteen thousand conversations, they track what sycophantic AI does over time. One study ran three weeks with a census-representative United States sample.

Sycophantic systems immediately delivered the emotional and esteem support people associate with close friends and family. Over three weeks, users grew nearly as likely to seek personal advice from such AI as from their closest people, and reported lower satisfaction with real-world social interactions. Most users chose the sycophantic style when offered alternatives, not for better advice but because it made them feel understood. The authors call this a relational account of sycophancy's costs.
arxiv-2605-08012:
Zezheng Lin and Fengming Liu argue, in an opinion paper, that interpretability research claims too much causality. Papers in the field speak of circuits, middlemen, and causal models, but causal claims rest on identification assumptions that are rarely stated. Their audit of ten papers across four method strands found no dedicated section on these assumptions anywhere.

The usual pattern is a swap: metrics like faithfulness, completeness, or ablation effects are offered as causal support without the assumptions that would make them identifying. A two-coder audit of thirty papers confirmed the finding. The authors propose an openness norm: say whether the claim is causal, name the identification strategy, list the assumptions, stress-test at least one, and explain how results move if they fail. Checking, they insist, is not identification.
arxiv-2605-08112:
Drew Dillon and Kasyap Varanasi measure a weakness of AI coding agents: they write working code but often break team decisions that never appear in the code itself. The authors built a controlled benchmark of eight realistic engineering tasks with forty-one weighted decision points covering product, design, and engineering choices.

They compared Claude Code with codebase access alone against the same setup plus Brief, a retrieval system that supplies recorded decisions, persona pain points, customer signals, and rival intelligence. The augmented setup reached ninety-five percent decision compliance against forty-six percent for the baseline. The gap shows how much product context, not coding skill, limits agent reliability.
arxiv-2605-08212:
Anamaria Hell and Leander Thiele test whether a large language model, wired to a computer algebra system, can do routine algorithmic work in theoretical physics. Such computations are conceptually simple but slow and full of traps, so reliable automation would save researchers real time.

The authors connect Claude to the Maple algebra system and aim the pair at cosmological perturbations in modified gravity theories. Given worked examples as context, the frontier model solved most of the test problems. The study catalogs the typical failure modes that remain and shows which ones extra context can fix, giving a grounded picture of where language models help symbolic physics today.
arxiv-2605-08412:
Sara Ghazanfari, Siddharth Garg, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, and Farshad Khorrami benchmark reasoning across several videos at once. Multimodal models have improved quickly on single videos, but questions that compare independent streams are barely tested, and human-annotated footage cannot supply exact spatial or temporal ground truth for grading failures.

SYNCR is built in simulators, Habitat, Kubric, and CLEVRER, so every answer is programmatically verified. It holds four thousand question-answer pairs over nearly five thousand unique videos, organized into eight tasks under temporal alignment, spatial tracking, comparative reasoning, and holistic synthesis. Zero-shot tests of leading open and closed models reveal a substantial gap to human performance.
arxiv-2605-08712:
Bohan Li and thirteen coauthors generate surgical videos that follow robotic control commands faithfully. Low dimensional control signals must steer complex image change, a hard translation. Their approach lifts articulated robot kinematics into five image aligned control forms, then routes conditioning through a hierarchy that activates only the most relevant controls and motion scales for each moment.

Routing losses guided by kinematic priors keep usage physical, stable, and efficient, while a budgeted scheme drops weak pathways to cut delay. A new benchmark with human checked articulated labels supplies realistic supervision. Across baselines, action faithfulness, visual quality, and cross domain generalization all improve, and the efficient variant runs much faster.
arxiv-2605-09112:
Noam Mizrachi, Nadav Har-Tuv, and Shai Shalev-Shwartz address tasks where a system must pick a coherent sequence or subset, such as forecasting a path or choosing representative items. The catch is ambiguity: many answers can be valid, but training data shows only one sampled answer for each input.

Their model, Contextual Plackett-Luce, extends a classic ranking model so its scores depend on context, with terms for single items and pairs. Scoring runs in parallel for speed, then a light step-by-step selection keeps the output coherent. On path prediction and subset selection tasks, the model gave more consistent and robust results than strong parallel rivals when supervision was ambiguous.
arxiv-2605-09312:
Huang and three colleagues compare accelerated NeRF variants for low compute, low data work, testing DS-NeRF, TensoRF, and HashNeRF. NeRF achieves high quality novel view synthesis, but long training and need for dense input views limit accessibility. First, they add depth supervision from COLMAP keypoints to TensoRF, forming TensoRF-DS, tested on LLFF with fewer views.

Second, they ablate TensoRF's decoding MLP and study downsampling effects on PSNR and runtime in the synthetic Lego scene. Next, they propose four variants of the HashNeRF colour and density networks, with residual and convolutional designs, reporting PSNR and time tradeoffs at matched iteration budgets. At equal time budgets, no extension conclusively beats published baselines, but the experiments characterise which extensions transfer to constrained settings and raise questions for future work. The honest negative result maps where low cost NeRF extensions help and where they do not, guiding future work.
arxiv-2605-09512:
Drensky and Zhakhayev map all families of bicommutative algebras over fields of characteristic zero that obey a cubic identity. Bicommutative algebras are nonassociative algebras with left and right swap rules, which exchange the last two factors in a triple product on either side. The paper sorts every such subvariety under a degree three identity. It builds on past work on free bicommutative algebras and their number invariants.

Beyond the map, the authors give a test, both needed and enough, for a variety to have a distributive lattice of subvarieties. That lattice test orders how subvarieties sit inside each other. The result closes the degree three case in characteristic zero, giving algebraists a full map of these varieties and a clean test for distributivity.
arxiv-2605-09612:
Dzhunushaliev and Folomeev study static self gravitating non Abelian monopoles with round and axial symmetry in a modified gravity theory. Monopoles are finite energy field lumps with nontrivial topology. The classic case is the t Hooft Polyakov monopole in SU(2) Yang Mills Higgs theory. Modified gravity extends general relativity. The authors compare its monopoles with those of Einstein Yang Mills Higgs theory to isolate what the change adds.

Differences prove quite large for systems with strong Higgs self coupling. That matters because modified gravity is used for early universe inflation and late time cosmic speed up with no extra fields, and for compact stars. The paper maps where the modified theory departs from Einstein gravity in the monopole sector. It shows the gravity change is not cosmetic for strongly coupled setups.
arxiv-2605-09712:
Goulet Coulombe argued that average forecast accuracy tells only half the story about a forecaster. The paper treats forecast losses against a benchmark as a return series, then grades that series with finance-style risk measures: Sharpe, Sortino, and Omega ratios plus drawdown gauges. A new Edge Ratio captures how often a model delivers uniquely useful predictions ahead of the forecasting frontier.

Applied to United States macroeconomic forecasting, the framework compared econometric models, machine-learning models, the TabPFN foundation model, and the Survey of Professional Forecasters. Beating professionals on average accuracy proved feasible, but beating them on risk-adjusted terms proved much harder, since they rarely fail catastrophically. Selected machine-learning methods still showed attractive risk profiles for specific targets.
arxiv-2605-10012: Monteiro and Das present Sketch-Based Access Control, a sketch-based, AI-assisted system for writing access rules that say who may reach a resource and under what conditions. It joins sketching's expressive power to the interpretive power of multimodal large language models. Users draw what they mean, and the system turns it into intent-aligned policies.
arxiv-2605-10212:
Michael A. Garrett turns the usual search for alien signals on its head. Most SETI work hunts for narrow, beacon-like radio tones. Garrett notes that human technology has drifted toward many weak, wideband digital emitters. An advanced civilization might therefore leak a broad radio glow rather than a sharp signal. This 2026 paper asks whether that glow could be found.

Garrett sketches a tiered hunt. Wide-field surveys from next-generation arrays such as the SKA would scan deep fields first. Very Long Baseline Interferometry would then follow up the best candidates at high resolution. Candidates would be checked against several clues at once, including high brightness temperature, almost no circular polarization, uneven spectra, and motion matching nearby stars. The reach extends to Kardashev Type I leakage about 100 parsecs away.
arxiv-2605-10412:
C. Ruyer and eighteen colleagues show how thread-like structures form in the expanding plasma plume of a laser-irradiated foil. The Weibel instability, a kinetic effect in mostly thin plasmas, amplifies seed fields when pressure is uneven, sorting particles by current direction into threads wrapped in field loops. Their 2026 paper studies that process in the inertial confinement fusion context.

Sideways cooling during near-spherical plasma expansion naturally drives uneven electron pressure, growing current threads. That growth competes with electron-ion collisions, which tend to even out the electron spread. From theory and computer modeling, the authors estimate the dominant wavelength and amplitude of self-made field ripples. Those estimates explain test data from the OMEGA and Laser Megajoule sites, tying thread formation to conditions in expanding fusion plasmas. In short, tiny plasma physics shapes what large fusion laser shots record.
arxiv-2605-10512:
Cristina Ballantine and three colleagues introduce the subsum polynomial of an integer partition. For a partition with parts lambda-1 through lambda-k, the subsum polynomial is the product over i of one plus x to the power lambda-i. Viewed as a counting function, it counts partitions whose parts form a submultiset of the given partition. Their 2026 paper studies the sum of reciprocals of this function over all partitions of n.

The authors prove arithmetic properties of related functions and offer connections to other counting objects. Number tests led them to define and study a ratio function summing inverse values across partitions, expressed as a ratio of top and bottom polynomials built from the same factors. The degree of the bottom minus the degree of the top equals n, a clean fact. Readers get a new function family linking split counting with ratio-function arithmetic.
arxiv-2605-10712: Amusuo and seven colleagues present AutoSOUP, a system automating component-level memory-safety checks in low-level and embedded software, where such errors cause many zero-day flaws. Safety-Oriented Unit Proofs encode verification choices such as scope, loop bounds and environment models, derived by three techniques. A hybrid LLM-As-Function-Call design joins deterministic program synthesis with language models to produce justifiable proofs and expose flaws in verified components.
arxiv-2605-10912:
Shuangrui Ding and sixteen colleagues present WildClawBench, a benchmark that tests agents on realistic, long-horizon computer work instead of toy sandboxes. Most agent tests rely on brief tasks, fake services, and final-answer checks, so they leave untested whether agents hold up in the runtimes where they actually run.

Sixty human-written, bilingual, multimodal tasks run inside reproducible containers with real command-line harnesses and real tools, averaging about eight minutes and over twenty tool calls each. Hybrid grading mixes rule checks, side-effect audits, and model judges. Across nineteen frontier models, the best reaches only about 62 percent, and swapping the harness alone can swing a model by eighteen points. Agent builders get a sobering, realistic yardstick.
arxiv-2605-11112:
Václav Blažej, Michał Pilipczuk, and Evangelos Protopapas give a coarse Menger's Theorem for planar and bounded genus graphs. Menger's Theorem states that if a graph with terminal sets S and T has no k pairwise vertex-disjoint S-T paths, then under k vertices intersect every S-T path.

The coarse variant proves this for every surface. There is a function f of d and k. For every pair of integers d and k, and every surface-embeddable graph with terminal sets S and T, suppose the graph lacks k S-T paths pairwise farther than d apart. Then some set X of at most f of d and k vertices sits within d of every S-T path. This partially answers questions of Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour, who proved no such result holds in general graphs. Graph theorists get a coarse Menger theorem for surfaces.
arxiv-2605-11212:
Amirhossein Abaskohi and five co-authors present ReVision, a method for scaling computer-use agents by cutting temporal visual redundancy. These agents read screen interfaces through screenshots, but each screenshot becomes many visual tokens, and token cost grows fast as sessions lengthen.

It trains multimodal language models on trajectories where extra visual patches are removed by a learned patch selector. It compares patch vectors across back-to-back screenshots while keeping spatial structure the model needs. Across OSWorld, WebTailBench, and AgentNetBench with five history screenshots on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it cuts token use by about 46 percent while lifting success rate by 3 percent over the no-drop baseline. Agent builders get longer sessions at lower token cost, and results keep rising as more past context is added.
arxiv-2605-11312: Danilo Brajovic, David Kreplin and Marco Huber address data pruning when little data remains, where Shapley-based values prove poorly suited. Their Constraint-Data-Value-Maximization method casts pruning as a constrained optimization that maximizes total influence while penalizing excessive per-test contributions. On the OpenDataVal benchmark it performs robustly when only a small fraction of data is kept, with competitive runtime.
arxiv-2605-11412: Wu and nineteen colleagues report the first lifetime measurement of the third excited zero-spin state in tin-118. This state was a missing piece for shape coexistence near the neutron mid-shell. Intruder bands built on two-particle-two-hole excitations across the proton shell gap show enhanced electric monopole transitions, but mixing stayed unclear without lifetimes. Using fast timing after thermal-neutron capture, they find an enhanced transition strength of 150 plus or minus 30 milliunits. This supports multiple coexisting shapes, as theory also finds in tin-116, 118 and 120.
arxiv-2605-11712: Chen, Sun, Bai and Song propose the Stable Value Guidance Transformer, SVGT, for stable value alignment. Aligning LLMs with human values usually relies on steering backbone parameters or representations. But the residual stream is highly dynamic, with values as fragile properties. SVGT keeps normative representations in a separate value space cut off from the backbone. It transduces stable signals into learnable Bridge Tokens serving as dynamic value anchors steering generation. Experiments across backbones and safety benchmarks show SVGT reduces harmful scores by over 70 percent while maintaining generation fluency.
arxiv-2605-12112: Xiaofeng Tan and seven colleagues show why a diversity guard fails in flow-based RLHF for text-to-image models. Fine-tuning for tastes collapses diversity, yet in flow models entropy stays flat while perceived diversity collapses. Flat entropy comes from the fixed noise schedule; collapse comes from reward-seeking gradients narrowing outputs. They propose perceptual entropy, measuring spread in perceived space, plus two guard strategies. Tests across two base models, neural and rule rewards, and three spaces show gains, best score 0.734 against a 0.366 baseline.
arxiv-2605-12412: Bigelow and seven colleagues picture in-context learning as travel through a belief space. They propose that a language model holds beliefs over a low-dimensional space of concepts. Each new story detail moves its position along a path in that space. Combining behaviour tests with checks of internal representations on story understanding, they find those paths lie on structured, low-dimensional shapes. Simple linear probes can read the position and predict behaviour. Targeted interventions steer the path in ways the shape predicts.
arxiv-2605-12812: Baghel, Ravsky and Segal-Halevi define k-times bin-packing, a new packing puzzle in which every item must appear exactly k times across different bins. The idea comes from sharing scarce electricity fairly among households. They prove any fair division problem can be solved this way for some finite k. They adapt classic packing methods to the new setting and test them on real demand data, beating existing heuristics on equal connection time.
arxiv-2605-12912: Mori, Oide and Zimmermann model a tricky step in running the planned FCC-ee collider: continuously injecting new particles while beams collide. Charge imbalance between the beams can destabilise them. They introduce a quasi-strong-strong scheme that keeps a self-consistent beam lens without the cost of full strong-strong tracking. Stable injection paths reach full population in the W and H operating modes, but the Z mode saturates below nominal in the explored region.
arxiv-2605-13012: Zhao and Kadota develop practical scheduling for time-sensitive 5G uplink traffic, where the base station cannot directly see destination-side Age of Information. They design a low-complexity estimator that infers packet timestamps and destination-side age from base-station observations, then build a Max-Weight policy around it. Implemented in the NetSim 5G emulator and tested in MATLAB simulations, the policy nears the performance of a richer estimator-based policy from the literature.
arxiv-2605-13212: Meng and colleagues analyse four detached eclipsing binaries, paired stars whose light dips as each passes the other. All four pairs have near equal masses and sunlike spectra, yet their life stages differ sharply. Two pairs sit on the main sequence, one has reached the subgiant stage, and one secondary has become a red giant. Magnetic activity is strongest in the two evolved systems, and one may hide a third star.
arxiv-2605-13612: Yatin Dandi and four colleagues introduce Neural Low-Degree Filtering, a simple limit of gradient-based training. In that limit, layered feature learning becomes a plain looping spectral method. At each layer, the next layer picks directions with maximal open low-degree link to the label. Neural LoFi predicts how codes are selected layer by layer and explains concept rise for given sample sizes. Tests on fully linked and conv nets show it beats lazy random-feature rivals and finds shaped filters.
arxiv-2605-13712: Jose Ordonez-Miranda and six colleagues show near-field thermal glow between tiny SiC square wires is ruled by many corner and edge echoes. Simulations place these echoes in the SiC Reststrahlen band, redshifting for thinner wires, with a four-fold boost in thermal conductance. Peak boost comes when the gap nearly matches wire thickness, trading trapping and wire-to-wire coupling. Square wires thus offer a handy platform for shape-run near-field heat transfer in tiny-scale heat handling and energy use.
arxiv-2605-13912: Chen, Qiu, Mao and Xu offer ViT-K, a few-shot model for flows where free fluid meets porous matter, ruled by Stokes, Navier-Stokes and Darcy laws joined. Running such flows in code costs much, since the join zone is fine-grained and long-run forecasts drift. Vision Transformers catch the varied join physics. The model rebuilds whole-flow physics on a low-size manifold from sparse training sets.
arxiv-2605-14012: Khan and Castanheira use the Procyon binary to probe how stars evolve when they do not interact. They run a wide grid of MESA tracks for Procyon A and B, pinned by exact dynamical masses plus measured temperatures and luminosities. The grid shifts metallicity, mixing length and core overshoot in turn. That shift shows how the inferred age and the birth mass of Procyon B hinge on each knob, and picks a best-fit model for hydrogen-poor white dwarfs.
arxiv-2605-14112: Upirvitskiy and Levin give a fast structure for leaf-to-ancestor minimum queries on rooted weighted trees in the oracle model. There, only comparisons of edge or node weights may read values. After preprocessing in O(n log h) time, space and oracle calls, any query answers in O(1) worst-case time, making no oracle calls at query time. The method fuses conversion of edge weights to node weights with a deterministic tie-break, ladder decomposition, binary lifting, and sparse-table range-minimum queries.
arxiv-2605-14612: Sokolov and team present an AI Toolkit plugin for JetBrains IDEs. It brings tracing and evaluation of language-model features into the run-debug loop, so devs can watch a feature run and judge it in place. Devs get run-triggered trace capture, layered inspection, one-click addition of traces to data sets, and unit-test-like checks with swap-in metrics. Early PyCharm use data is reported as promising, with strong uptake at run time and steady use among those who capture traces.
arxiv-2605-14812: Xiao, Zheng and Li present MetaGEM, a bottom-up method for genome-scale metabolic networks via enzyme-metabolite anchoring. Top-down work leans on sequence homology and leaves unknown enzymes unresolved, while direct work from metabolomics faces an ill-posed inverse problem. MetaGEM uses a dual-tower design mixing protein language model semantics with 3D metabolite shapes, plus contrastive learning with hard negative mining. Working models for three bacteria are generated, with improved connectivity claimed.
arxiv-2605-14912: Varad Vishwarupe, Nigel Shadbolt, and Marina Jirotka argue that AI helpers fail when they just agree with the user. They call this sycophantic consensus, a habit of smoothing over clashes of values instead of showing them. The authors reframe pluralistic alignment around three moves: scoping, flagging conflict, and principled repair. They define a Pluralistic Repair Score to tell honest revision from mere surrender. A small test on two frontier models found much agreement but weak repair quality.
arxiv-2605-15012: Kai Yan, Alexander G. Schwing, and Yu-Xiong Wang propose FEST, a few-shot method for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. On hard problems, correct rollouts are rare, and demonstration-guided fixes usually demand large supervised datasets. FEST needs only 128 randomly chosen demonstrations, combining supervised cues, on-policy cues, and fading weights on the few-shot data to block overfitting. Across benchmarks it beats baselines using far less supervised data, even matching rivals trained on full datasets.
arxiv-2605-15512: Khanh-Hung Giang-Tran, Soroosh Shafiee, and Nam Ho-Nguyen build a self-tuning frame for Frank-Wolfe optimization. These projection-free methods hinge on step size. Old closed-loop rules need a global smoothness constant up front. Line-search variants dodge that need but cost extra function calls. Their frame swaps the global constant for a local gauge read from gradients along the run. It covers standard, matching-pursuit, pairwise, and away-step forms. Proofs show convergence with no prior smoothness knowledge, and tests beat line-search rivals.
arxiv-2605-15712: Shuaiyi Li and six colleagues report protocluster PC J1001+0214 at redshift 2.96 in COSMOS. Built from COSMOS2025 and JWST spectroscopy, it shows an overdensity of 2.66 in catalog data. It holds 131 galaxies: 21 confirmed by spectra, via helium emission, and 110 photometric members. Against a mass-complete sample, members show a 0.2 dex shift to higher stellar mass, a sign of faster assembly. Low-to-mid mass galaxies show star formation gains from 0.11 dex to 0.15 dex over field galaxies. The quiet fraction stays tiny and field-like, so environmental quenching has not yet taken over.
arxiv-2605-15912: Raghavan Thiagarajan and four colleagues study how actin cross-linking orders basal bodies in developing frog embryos. Basal bodies anchor cilia on cilia-bearing cells, and even spacing matters for joint beating and one-way fluid flow. Early on, actin change lets basal bodies spread in a loose setting. As development proceeds, the actin network cross-links more, holding movement in check and giving even spacing. Breaking alpha-actinin-1, a key cross-linking protein, weakens the hold and breaks regular patterns, harming cilia lineup.
arxiv-2605-16012: Savita Priya and three colleagues survey carbon-carbon stretching vibrations in BEDT-TTF salts. They judge how well these modes reveal charge ordering and site charge. In charge-ordered states, two modes shift by 141 and 98 cm-1 per elementary charge. Yet spreads across compounds exceed 20 cm-1. That spread leaves a margin near 0.045 charge units. So the links suit gauging charge order better than pinning down exact site charge.
arxiv-2605-16112: Zhang and three colleagues diagnose attention dispersion as a shared failure of dynamic graph transformers under time shift. Predictions hinge on key nodes that carry more signal than random neighbours, yet models fail to focus on them when shift blurs attention contrast. Swapping standard attention for differential attention damps shared signals and boosts distinctive ones. Added to three baselines, it helps most on high-shift data, and their DiffDyG system tops nine benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-16312: Kujur shows that taking options away hurts a self-play learner more than scrambling what it sees or does. His attacker strikes legal moves from the victim's menu, so the choice is gone before the learner picks. Tests span poker games with 6 to 5,531 information states, plus two settings outside poker. Trained masking beats random masking and trained perturbation attacks, spreading between agents and growing with self-play. The harm does not fade with longer masked training, and hits Q-learning, PPO, NFSP, and DQN learners.
arxiv-2605-16612: Schlesinger and colleagues offer PRISMat, a lean model that creates crystal surfaces with chosen properties without the bulk of a large language model. It treats a material as an unordered set, so its output does not depend on atom order, and it beats language models on slabs matched to surface traits. Reported errors fall to about a quarter of the next best model on cleavage energy and work function tasks.
arxiv-2605-16812: Ha's team tackles a weakness of local differential privacy: its blanket randomisation degrades data usefulness because it perturbs every dimension regardless of downstream importance. Their method finds task-critical directions from the Jacobian of a public downstream model, damps noise along those directions, and reshapes uniform noise into an anisotropic pattern. The privacy guarantee of the base randomiser stays intact while utility rises sharply. On corrupted CIFAR-10-C images at top severity, accuracy gains reach about eight points for Laplace and twenty points for PrivUnit variants at epsilon 7.5.
arxiv-2605-17012: Chandee, Li and Milinovich prove density results for a family of L-functions, assuming a famous unproven hypothesis about zeta zeros. They handle even and odd cases apart and widen the range of test functions to span from minus three to three. That wider range gives the strongest known claims that these functions and their derivatives do not vanish at the center point. The claims still rest on that same hypothesis.
arxiv-2605-17112: Peter Hanukaev and Eades present GRASS, a type system uniting graded and substructural approaches to resource-sensitive computation. Graded systems track variable use with numbers, while substructural logics restrict reuse. GRASS lets both styles and many grade algebras coexist, so different variables obey different resource rules in one program. Its categorical semantics, they show, covers established systems including LNL and Adjoint Logic.
arxiv-2605-17212: Enabe and Provasi present a unified frame for learning under covariate shift, where a constrained density-ratio net gauges how target and source data differ. That ratio feeds an anytime PAC-Bayes certificate, with normalization and moment rules enforced as hard constraints. A pre-registered two-campaign test finds calibrated ratios, lower target loss than unweighted and classical baselines, and certificate coverage tracking label shift as theory predicts.
arxiv-2605-17412: Luo claims a polynomial-time quantum attack on ML-KEM and related lattice schemes over two-power cyclotomic rings. A tower breakdown of the principal ideal problem through cyclotomic fields yields an algorithm with cubic-log gate cost and quadratic-log qubit cost, plus polynomial classical work. For ML-KEM-1024 he reports an approximation factor at most 21, well under half the modulus, with success probability at least 99 percent. The analysis extends to Falcon, Hawk and NTRU.
arxiv-2605-17912: Yu Shang and colleagues present WorldArena 2.0, a broader testbed for embodied world models. Older tests cover vision-only prediction, offline use, and simulators alone, too narrow for today's models. WorldArena 2.0 widens tests along modality, functionality, and platform. It adds touch-plus-vision perception, tests world models as interactive RL settings, and spans simulated and real robots. Under one standard protocol it measures sense quality, interactive utility, and cross-platform performance.
arxiv-2605-18112: Jiaqi Liu's 2026 study builds a light-based test of quantum contextuality, a mark of behaviour no classical hidden-variable account can match.
