Single photons pass through linear optical nets and simple on-off detectors, with each shared measure done the same way in each setting. The tests break the KCBS bound and hold up well when photons are lost. The set-up can also probe photon counts and check single-photon sources.
arxiv-2605-18212: Jiro Murata's 2026 review updates short-range tests of the gravitational inverse-square law under one consistent formalism across scales. It gathers a decade of new data from tabletop force probes, Casimir tests, slow neutron work, and collider searches, building on the authors' earlier review. The unified treatment lets lab results speak directly to theories that extend general relativity. The paper also compares model parametrizations, including extra-dimensional models, and sets tabletop bounds beside high-energy collider bounds for Yukawa and power-law potentials.
arxiv-2605-18312: Sayan Sircar and Kabir Ramola study two-dimensional site percolation with an energy cost added to bonds between neighboring occupied sites. Their 2026 paper shows the cost shifts the percolation threshold smoothly and creates an energy-dependent cutoff in cluster sizes. Using simulations and renormalization-group methods, they trace how the correlation-length exponent moves from one half for dense clusters to four thirds for classical percolation.
arxiv-2605-18412: K. Piejko, J. Sokół, and K. Trcabka-Więcław examine Jackson's difference operator in a 2026 paper, for convex univalent functions in the unit disc, viewed as a Hadamard product of two power series. Jackson introduced the operator in 1908 for a real parameter q between 0 and 1, and the paper surveys its role in q-theory. The theory now reaches hypergeometric series, special functions, combinatorics, number theory, fluid mechanics, quantum mechanics, and physics.
arxiv-2605-18812: Varun Kotte presents PASC, a method that gives joint coverage promises for multi-stage language pipelines. Errors compound across stages, yet current methods either calibrate each stage alone or use a conservative union bound. PASC turns joint coverage into a single conformal problem on the worst stage score. It carries a finite-sample promise that all stages land inside their sets. On a three-stage entity pipeline it reaches about ninety-six percent end-to-end coverage, ahead of both rivals at the same set size.
arxiv-2605-18912: Luigi Accardi and four colleagues present a quantum version of Viterbi decoding for hidden quantum Markov models. Given results, the method finds hidden quantum paths that top a joint decoding score, the quantum twin of the classical Viterbi score. Unlike classical decoding over a finite state space, it searches a continuous manifold of pure quantum effects, using superpositions in hidden memory. The authors prove a strict quantum advantage: coherent paths can beat any classical strategy restricted to diagonal effects, even with identical data.
arxiv-2605-19012: Prabal Adhikari works out magnetic masses and decay rates for the eight mesons at next lead order in a steady field. The neutral pion mass falls just as in two flavour theory, while the neutral kaon mass stays put. Charged meson masses shift in step with each other. Axial and vector decay rates each climb steadily with the field, and low energy rules give strong cross checks.
arxiv-2605-19112: Sophia Roshal and Frank Pfenning generalise earlier work on ordered logics that relax the exactly-once resource rule. Earlier calculi used subexponentials inside a linear ordered logic; the authors instead use adjoint modalities to combine logics with different structural rules, including weakening, contraction, and mobility on each side. They show the resulting sequent calculus admits cut elimination. They also give a natural deduction version with implicit structural rules and show proof checking is decidable, making the system a base for an expressive adjoint programming language or logic framework.
arxiv-2605-19212: Katsunori Wakabayashi and two colleagues show transconductance in layered WSe2 carries a mark of K-Gamma valley reshuffle. It cuts the signal in bilayer WSe2 and flips sign in trilayer, absent in single-valley systems. Unlike trap-state filling or contact drag, the oddity leaves the turn-on slope as is, beyond single-valley models. Valley response, capped by a built-in heat limit, reaches about 0.20 per volt near threshold at room temperature. Its sign, size, and heat response give marks of valley physics, establishing it as a probe.
arxiv-2605-19312: Florian Moser and Léo Louistisserand design MultiBallot, a safe way to collect signatures online in Switzerland. Such drives can force binding votes, much like elections, so they need both secrecy and checks. Their plan meets both aims under fair trust rules, and it needs no hidden channel for signers. Its shield rests on a plain fact: many drives run at once, so one name hides among many others.
arxiv-2605-19412: Feng and colleagues improve language-agnostic program reduction, which shrinks failing programs to minimal test cases. Pure syntax-guided deleters often break meaning, so checkers reject the cut and force backtracking. DRReduce adds dependency reconstruction: it maps program dependencies, repairs those broken by a deletion, and hands further shrinking to a syntax-guided reducer. Built for C and Java, it cut programs far more than Perses, WDD and CDD on real bug cases, matched CReduce and Latra, and ran several times faster.
arxiv-2605-19612: Wu and team count the independent modes of a fluid antenna. Exact outage analysis needs a large integral, while block-correlation approximations understate outage odds. The spatial correlation matrix for aperture length W holds at most 2⌈W⌉+1 major eigenmodes, regardless of ports, a spatial analogue of Slepian-Landau-Pollak concentration. That gives an equivalent-degrees approximation matching selection combining over that many branches, plus a weighted-modes version. Both reach diversity order and never understate outage, turning exact at high signal-to-noise ratio, extended to capacity and planar arrays.
arxiv-2605-19712: Kamal Basha S and Nambiar present ACOUSIM, a physics-based framework for scoring synthetic sonar images. Synthetic sonar data offer a cheap alternative to real capture, yet lack strict validation. A Gazebo environment builds sonar-like images by setting seabed texture, shadowing, altitude and noise. Realism is scored against two public sonar sets using global intensity and local texture patterns gauged by three divergence gaps. Texture match proves strong, with KL below 0 point 07 across all classes, while plane brightness beats ship brightness, which suffers from shadow complexity.
arxiv-2605-19812: Fries, Nelson, Jung, Reichstein and Peters introduce FLUXtrapolation, a benchmark for extrapolating ecosystem fluxes beyond observed sites. Fluxes are flows of carbon, water and energy, measured directly only at sparse towers. Global estimates must upscale from observed sites using global inputs, facing shifts in inputs and in unobserved drivers. The benchmark defines temporal, spatial and temperature based scenarios with held out domains, varied aggregations and tail errors. A pilot finds baselines similar on median hourly error but separated on tail and multi scale measures.
arxiv-2605-19912: Huang and colleagues trace how a dark wrapped charged black hole scatters and swallows matter waves. In slow waves they match near and far views for the swallow rate, and in fast waves they work out bend to second order. More dark fluid cuts the swallow rate hard, and where waves gain energy the dark hole boosts them far more.
arxiv-2605-20112: Alessandro Agapito, Viola De Renzis and Michele Mancarella test whether spectral-siren Hubble constraints survive redshift evolution of the black hole mass spectrum. Spectral sirens combine waveform distances with redshift information in mass-spectrum features, making the method sensitive to assumptions. With the GWTC-4.0 catalogue, letting main mass scales evolve with redshift, they find no evidence for evolution at current sensitivity. Evolution shifts the Hubble posterior downward, but not significantly. Constraints are thus robust to mass-spectrum redshift evolution at current sensitivity.
arxiv-2605-20612: Ziye Chen and three colleagues propose Matryoshka Concept Bottleneck Models, a single model that can use more or fewer human concepts as needed. Concept bottleneck models ground predictions in ideas people can grasp, but fixing errors at test time costs expert time. One fixed concept set forces exhaustive checks, while many tailored models cost too much to build and keep. Their nested design lets one model adapt its concept use to the budget at hand.
arxiv-2605-20712: Kavya Manohar and three colleagues present SCRIBE, a diagnostic framework for speech recognition in Indic languages. Word error rate collapses distinct mistakes into one number and penalizes agglutinative languages, where valid word merges inflate scores. SCRIBE instead splits errors into lexical, punctuation, numeral, and domain-entity rates, using sandhi-tolerant alignment with domain vocabulary. Human checks confirm it matches expert judgment where word error rate does not, and rich transcription models are released for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada.
arxiv-2605-20912: D. Roussis, S. Sofianopoulos, and S. Piperidis develop parallel and monolingual corpora for machine translation in the scientific domain. Growing research volume demands communication across language barriers. Yet scientific text poses unique challenges from specialized words and complex sentence structures. Their corpora target Spanish-English, French-English, and Portuguese-English pairs, three major pairs. For each pair, they create a large general scientific corpus plus four smaller corpora focused on cancer, energy, brain science, and transport research.
arxiv-2605-21212: Aristeidis Amvrosiadis and colleagues test for dark matter substructure in the strongly lensed system PJ011646 with high-resolution ALMA dust-continuum data. Their lens model uses an elliptical power law plus third- and fourth-order multipoles and external shear, improving the fit sharply over a plain power law. A grid search then finds a subhalo candidate, with two image-plane spots mapping to one source-plane spot, suggesting only one is real. Its mass is about twenty-eight billion solar masses, a notable subhalo detection.
arxiv-2605-21412: Aarón Guillén-Villalobos and co-authors give a biquaternionic reformulation of Maxwell's equations via Fourier analysis. They analyze the parabolic Dirac tool in this setting, mapping its kernel via general div-curl systems and Cauchy-Riemann-type links between real and imaginary parts. Using Fourier transform tools, they map the Fourier transform of a basic solution. They construct a right inverse tool and derive direct vector solutions to the time-dependent Maxwell system.
arxiv-2605-22412: Martínez and Chacón explain two past findings with the ratchet universality law for biharmonically driven tunnel junctions. Joined with Heisenberg's uncertainty rule, the law yields a universal case of optimal quantum transport. The driving field boosts diode efficiency and widens the rectification range for the supercurrent. It also cuts excess quantum noise against the dc noise level, allowing nonclassical photonic states. The authors argue the law is key for optimal ratchet uses, from superconducting power electronics to electron quantum optics and quantum computing.
arxiv-2605-22612: Raman and team argue benchmarks are needed for health tests, but too thin for rollout scores. The gap arises not from poor benchmarks, but from hidden beliefs about user contact that benchmarks alone cannot surface. The team sorts beliefs into task, seen from chat data, and outcome, needing outcome data and conduct studies. Outcome beliefs depend on human conduct, which benchmarks cannot observe. In a health RCT, the team finds roughly equal task and outcome gaps. The team offers BenchmarkCards, listing beliefs, and staged tests, testing beliefs.
arxiv-2605-22712: Hughes puts forward a conjecture on boundedness for maximal functions over a sparse family of discrete spherical averages. Better bounds beyond the full discrete spherical maximal range have stayed open for 24 years. The paper states a theorem backing the proposed claim. The note is short and conjectural, not a full answer, and it sets a precise target for later work on these averages.
arxiv-2605-23212: Pritchard and Rondinelli study hydrogen and deuterium tunnel in niobium, tied to noise. Theory assumes a split between the guest and the lattice, never shown for H-like species. They show splittings of H and D in niobium fit a 5D Born-Oppenheimer model treating guest and lattice modes together. Recast layers in the model and tests against ab initio maps, the split holds only in the muon mass limit. For H and D, tunnel is joint and mixed. Guesses can predict the breakdown.
arxiv-2605-23512: Duarte and colleagues test how dust dims type Ia supernova colors, using light-transport simulations of supernovae in lifelike galaxies. The standard one-parameter exponential law fits poorly: it undercounts dim events and overcounts bright ones, and it cannot tell apart settings that differ a lot. Two-parameter laws, above all Weibull and exponentiated exponential forms, fit all mock settings better and split host shape from dust mass effects. With a two-parameter law, observed supernovae come out intrinsically redder.
arxiv-2605-23712: Zhang and Karniadakis propose operator learning with language model design to rebuild flow fields from sparse measurements, mesh-free. They recast reconstruction as sequence-to-sequence learning, treating sparse measurements as context and unseen spots as queries. The model learns the full flow field from sparse inputs, catching spatial correlations and long-range links. They test it on vortex street simulations, United States temperature data, blood flow simulations, and turbulent jet readings. Scores stay competitive even with under 10 percent seen, showing language models as robust tools for science work.
arxiv-2605-24212: Li and eleven co-authors propose DRUM, a transfer-learning frame for clinical prediction when key covariates vanish at deployment. Cardiac-arrest models trained on rich prehospital data often fail abroad. DRUM splits covariates into shared parts seen everywhere and missing parts seen only at the source. It optimizes worst-case performance over the unknown target distribution of missing parts given shared ones, using a neural generator. A bias-correction step steadies the result. Simulations show large gains, and United States to Asian registry transfers yield better predictions.
arxiv-2605-24312: Nguyen and six co-authors present MEntA, a query-efficient membership inference attack on retrieval-augmented generation. Grounding reduces hallucinations but leaks membership. Existing attacks rely on templated queries that detectors catch, or on many ones. MEntA asks low-cost questions and measures entailment between responses and documents, maximizing information per query. Across NFCorpus, SCIDOCS, and TREC-COVID, it reaches near-perfect AUC with only 5 queries. It stays effective under RAG defenses, while detectors either miss it or flag queries, and it cuts attack cost by up to 65 times.
arxiv-2605-24712: Beyazit Bestami Yuksel and Emrah Dikbiyik build hardware-aware federated learning for speech emotion recognition. Real deployments mix clients with different compute, memory, and latency, which stretches round times and system cost. Their loop combines hardware profiling, adaptive local epochs, and top-K client picks on session-partitioned IEMOCAP data. Against FedAvg, FedProx, and random client picks under non-IID data, it matches validation accuracy across 50 rounds and 5 trials. It cuts total training time by about 36.5 percent versus FedAvg and lowers cumulative communication cost by 40 percent.
arxiv-2605-24812: Zhihao Dou and co-authors improve multi-agent code generation with Collaborative Reinforcement Code, a framework for role-specialized language-model agents. Most code methods decode step by step without global planning, yielding locally coherent but globally weak solutions such as failing tests or slow code. CoRe-Code uses a simple Planner-Coder setup: the Planner drafts high-level plans and the Coder turns them into code. A collaboration-aware reinforcement learning stage sharpens specialization and alignment. Tests show it beats many baselines.
arxiv-2605-25312: Amanda Cercas Curry, Gianmarco de Francisci Morales, and Luca Maria Aiello release P1SCO, a collection of social media comments from three platforms labeled along ten social dimensions. The labels capture how people perceive social interaction, and the data stay split by comment, annotator, and platform. Rich annotator records add demographics, personality profiles, and political leaning to each judgment. Keeping individual viewpoints intact lets researchers study annotator agreement and how personality and politics shape interpretation. The set also supports cross-platform comparisons of social discourse.
arxiv-2605-25512: Nobutaka Ito unifies directional models for blind speech separation in one complex spherical Student's t mixture model. Existing angular models are defined separately, making density-shape effects hard to isolate. His cSTMM connects the angular Gaussian, Bingham, and Watson mixtures through freedom and eigenvalue constraints, with an expectation-maximization framework. On reverberated LibriSpeech mixtures, a freedom value of 1 beat the equivalent choice in all 18 conditions, gaining 0.25 decibels on average. It reduces to the angular Gaussian mixture at matched freedom and approaches Bingham and Watson mixtures at large values.
arxiv-2605-25612: Peng and colleagues explain why activation sparsity appears in the MLP blocks of trained Transformers. Earlier accounts blamed data or fitting, or leaned on strong assumptions that fail for deep models trained over many steps. They show sparsity equals augmented flatness divided by input norm times activation gradient. This ratio falls during training. They define derivative sparsity, which matches activation sparsity under ReLU but allows pruning in backward passes and stays more stable. Three tweaks that shrink the ratio yield much sparser activations on ImageNet-1K and C4 tests.
arxiv-2605-26012: Todorov and Sabatelli squeeze reinforcement-learning encoders through a fixed straight bottleneck. The bottleneck forces features into a low-dimensional slot, with no extra losses, pretraining or tweaks to the learner. Theory says that when the slot is wider than the true rank of the best value function, power survives and learning stays the same in low-dimensional form. Tests on single-task and multi-task trials match or beat baselines. The trick thus shapes what the learner sees, cheaply, without touching how it learns.
arxiv-2605-26412: Amir Jafari offers a diagnostic that checks whether flow geometry holds across two resolutions. For a pair of separated points, states, or theories, his method compares the field's jump direction after smoothing at each resolution. Averaging over sampled gaps gives a coherence matrix. The test stays tied to chosen variables and sampling plan. Synthetic swirl fields with matching spectra still yield unlike matrices. A wrinkled coordinate change shifts Lorenz drift shape but not the motion, and truncated renormalization flows lose cross-truncation coherence as more couplings switch on.
arxiv-2605-26512: Erin M. Cusson and twelve colleagues survey molecules in Gomez's Hamburger, a massive edge-on planet-forming disk, possibly unstable under its own gravity and hosting a forming giant planet. From Submillimeter Array wideband data near 1 arcsecond detail, they detect 11 molecules across 15 lines and measure disk-wide fluxes. Column densities for several species at fixed excitation temperatures broadly match other large planet-forming disks. A hunt for instability signs via gas-phase formaldehyde boost finds no firm evidence. The inventory should guide sharper studies of the candidate planet GoHam b.
arxiv-2605-26612: Jinze Li and seven others present LATTE, a personalization method that tracks how a user drifts from peers over time. Older tricks compress a whole history into one static profile, mixing stable taste, recent drift, and item quirks. LATTE instead subtracts a peer baseline for each past session, forecasts the next relative state, and feeds it to a frozen model through one soft token. On Amazon reviews it lifts ROUGE-L from 0.219 and 0.245 for rival baselines to 0.259.
arxiv-2605-26712: Boillet, Tarride, and Kermorvant present METATR, a benchmark for automatic text recognition that aims to mirror real documents rather than clean modern English print. It spans 29 languages with varied scripts and layouts, drawn from public collections, and sets standard prompting and normalization rules so results stay comparable. Tests of leading open and closed systems show proprietary models most consistent, yet performance still varies sharply across scripts and layouts.
arxiv-2605-27212: Pillai and Smith prove a conjecture about how fast the first columns of the transvection walk mix. The walk, on matrices, picks two rows at each step and adds one to the other. The conjecture held that the first k columns mix in steps scaling with matrix size times k times a log factor. The authors prove this uniformly, using a local-to-global entropy estimate plus a burn-in argument that sidesteps blocks with weak log-Sobolev constants. They extend the method to Heisenberg product-replacement algorithms.
arxiv-2605-27812: Keita Matsubara and Kazumasa Hattori sort the ways a crystal gains chirality, a handedness that breaks mirror symmetry, as its atoms shift. They write the key electric toroidal measures as functions of that shift, showing the first-order trend rests on the starting symmetry and the mode of shifting. The same trend appears in linked effects such as current-driven magnetism and split chiral vibrations.
arxiv-2605-28812: Jiahe Pan, Stelian Coros, Jitendra Malik, and Toru Lin introduce Center-of-Pressure, a tactile code grounded in physical rules keeping dense contact information for sim-to-real transfer. Current sim-to-real methods shrink tactile data into coarse features, losing richness complex handling needs. A sensor tuning scheme using smooth motion estimates taxel angles without force readings. Across peg-in-hole fitting and ball balance, policies tuned on Center-of-Pressure reach zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with a multi-finger hand, beating binary-contact and raw rivals.
arxiv-2605-28912: Xin Li and colleagues expose a blind false-data attack on power grids. An autoencoder learns the measurement pattern and crafts perturbations that slip past residual and time-series detectors. Their topology-informed Cycle-Space Detector instead uses the network's cycle space, with a minimum cycle basis, to tighten null-space estimation and sharpen the split between normal and attacked readings. Simulations on IEEE 14-, 30-, 57-, and 118-bus systems show the method detects these data-driven attacks under realistic noise without needing precise line parameters.
arxiv-2605-29512: Kevin Wang and colleagues present Mindgames, an arena for social and strategic thought in multi-agent language models. Static scenes and single-game tests miss long-run thought in multi-agent settings. Mindgames stages four games with an interface, skill ratings, and play logs. A 2025 cycle drew 944 agents from 76 teams across Colonel Blotto, iterated prisoner's dilemma, Codenames, and Secret Mafia. Analysis finds brittle rule following a bottleneck, with top systems relying on scaffolding. Secret Mafia shows a failure confound, with tens of thousands of games shared plus offline contest rules.
arxiv-2605-30012: Jarno Laakso, Armi Tiihonen and Patrick Rinke use machine learning to map where mixed lead and tin perovskite alloys stay stable. The work matters for solar cells made from these tunable semiconductors. Their two-step method pairs graph neural network potentials with energy forecasts from unrelaxed structures to chart free energy across mixes. Tin alloys hold stable mixes over a narrower range than lead alloys, and iodine-rich mixes reach peak stability.
arxiv-2605-30112: Jianing Shi examines why neural PDE solvers struggle when the Reynolds number shifts, on the forced two-dimensional Navier-Stokes benchmark. A trained Fourier Neural Operator errs by nearly half under a tenfold Reynolds shift, yet simple retrieval baselines matching states without any forward model do better. ConvAE-Relay matches states in a source-trained autoencoder space and borrows source dynamics, cutting error with no target fitting. Ablations pin matching quality as dominant, and a multi-scale U-Net does better still, suggesting representation geometry organizes cross-regime transfer.
arxiv-2605-30512: Nafiul Haque, Syed Nazmus Sakib and Shifat E Arman present PhyDrawGen, a hybrid flow splitting scene meaning from rule checks, starting from a typed scene graph. A fixed solver then turns this graph into a Planar Straight-Line Graph (PSLG), holding force balance, optical paths, and field shapes. Finally, a fine-tuned Qwen-VL model runs a propose-verify loop to correct rule breaks. Tested on 1,449 problems spanning motion, optics, and EM, PhyDrawGen clearly beats GPT-5-image, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Gemini 3 Pro.
arxiv-2605-30712: Feng and colleagues present ExpHarness to improve frozen language-model executors, leaving their parameters untouched. Agents gather experience across tasks that rarely flows back into the harness. It distills trajectories into skills and failure lessons within an experience graph. It trains a copilot deciding how broadly to explore the graph and how strongly to favor useful experiences over similar ones. The copilot learns from a reward based on score difference with and without experience. Tests show ExpHarness beats the baseline while cutting interaction steps by up to a fifth.
arxiv-2605-30812: Han, Chen, and Li model large-scale motion of tiny systems, where the state is inherently unordered, as in particle systems. Many approaches learn a latent state through an autoencoder trained for reconstruction, assuming an ordering of microscopic degrees of freedom. The authors adopt a permutation-invariant encoder and design the decoder to reconstruct mass distribution at observed points. They jointly learn dynamics of observables and latent states. The method proves effective and robust. Examples include energy dynamics in particle systems, mixing in fluids, and stretching from polymer video data.
arxiv-2605-30912: Hu and colleagues teach vision-language models to look at the right image parts, not just land answers. Outcome-only rewards cannot tell a grounded answer from a lucky guess or a language shortcut. Their EASE method turns evidence regions into a visual-token target and steers attention toward it during training, but only on high-reward paths. At test time, only image and question are needed. Across three models, EASE lifts scores over a baseline by two to three points across perception, hallucination, visual math and reasoning.
arxiv-2605-31112: Wang, Degen and Liang test a renormalization method for quantum thermodynamics against an exactly solvable single-site model. A careless continuum treatment invents a false self-interaction, they show, and a careful derivation names the correction that removes it. They compare several closures of the flow equations. Free energy proves forgiving, but chemical potential and fluctuations expose closure flaws sharply, with a maximum-entropy closure most accurate overall.
arxiv-2605-31312: Deng and colleagues reduce multimodal hallucinations with In-Context Visual Contrastive Optimization. Text-only preference optimisation lacks visual help. Visual taste methods suffer mixed-up goals and coarse bad cases that invite shortcuts. Placing paired images in a shared multi-image context makes the goal sound. An extra gated check aligns multi-image training with single-image use. Hard bad cases from precise semantic edits complete the method, which leads five benchmarks and proves the editing plan.
arxiv-2605-31512: Ali and team build a system for sorting orthopedic notes written as free text in English, Hindi, and Punjabi. Low-resource clinics face mixed scripts, gaps in evidence, and skewed labels. They test multilingual encoders, a DistilBERT baseline, zero-shot large models, and IndicBERT-HPA, an encoder with adapter heads for bone care. Under natural clinical prevalence, IndicBERT-HPA performs best overall. A verification layer then defers risky cases, beating accept-all prediction on held-out data.

arxiv-2606-04212:
Shauna Kwag, Anakha Ganesh, Tomaso Poggio, and Pierfrancesco Beneventano show in 2026 that the edge of stability does not act on a dataset as a whole. Training at this edge hovers near instability. The team finds it sorts examples instead.

Examples the model gets right with confidence are pushed down in loss. Examples it gets wrong are pushed up. The net effect is a quiet reweighting of the training set. This sorting explains odd effects seen before, such as sudden drops in test error late in training. It also links training dynamics to which examples a model ends up trusting. The authors argue that dataset-level views miss the real action.
arxiv-2606-04612:
Abouzaid, Wang, Lin, and Middleton combine three kinds of defense into one shield for language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI security. Models are vulnerable to hallucination and to adversarial manipulation. These problems are usually treated separately. Their hybrid framework joins entropy-based models, aimed at hallucination. It adds uncertainty-based and geometric-based models, aimed at attack detection.

On in-domain benchmarks including FEVER, HotpotQA, CSQA, and SIQA, the hybrid improved clean-task accuracy by up to 43 percent. Adversarial robustness rose by up to 65 percent. Attack success rates fell by up to 62 percent. On out-of-distribution sets it again improved robustness substantially. On prompt injection and jailbreak detection sets, it reduced attack success by up to 51 percent against state-of-the-art baselines. The authors conclude that combining entropy, uncertainty, and geometric features protects better than any single feature family. This holds across familiar and unfamiliar data.
arxiv-2606-04712:
Shangguan and colleagues search the nearby universe for the strange absorption signature that Webb's little red dots show, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. Balmer absorption lines in those distant objects may trace dense gas around rapidly feeding black holes. The team analyzes spectra of a representative parent sample of 14,584 low-redshift type 1 active galactic nuclei from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, hunting the same feature in homogeneously processed data.

They find just seven sources with robust Balmer absorption, an occurrence rate of about 0.05 percent, confirming the phenomenon is extremely rare nearby. Modeling with a partially covering absorber shows all robust cases need optically thick hydrogen absorption with moderate covering factors, while one little-red-dot analog shows a covering factor above 0.8, matching high-redshift measurements. Absorbers move slowly and vary over months to years.
arxiv-2606-04812:
Prashant and Easwaran generate test scenarios aimed exactly at the states where a learning policy's safety is unproven, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep RL policies can behave unsafely, and one verification approach builds barrier certificates by sampling trajectories. Tight bounds on violation probability are hard when perturbations push the agent into insufficiently explored states. The authors approximate the encountered state distribution with a variational autoencoder.

Using latent characteristics of states, they construct upper- and lower-bound barrier certificates. Sampling training states from the set difference between the two bounds, the non-robust region, tightens both bounds and sharpens the safety guarantees. The framing is a dual problem, and the authors describe the guarantees placed and demonstrate the tightness of their bounds. The work serves risk-aware deployment, where a safe certificate is the deliverable regulators need.
arxiv-2606-05612:
Kun Huang and colleagues made a fiber laser that emits swirling light beams on demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. The beams are vector vortex beams, whose polarization twists across the beam face. Such structured light serves imaging, sensing, and quantum optics. Making it usually needs add-on parts outside the laser. The team instead shapes the beam inside the laser cavity itself, using geometric phase control.

Tuning that phase maps polarization onto orbital angular momentum, the twist of the beam. The design switches among vector modes at any chosen point on the standard map of such states. Crucially, the tuning leaves the passive pulse locking undisturbed. Pulses lasted about eight and a half picoseconds, each far shorter than a billionth of a second. Math formulas for the beam profiles matched the bench results closely. The source stays compact while offering flexible, high-purity structured pulses.
arxiv-2606-05812:
Arghya Pal and Rajanala sharpen text-to-audio search with explicit logic in a 2026 arXiv paper. Shared embedding models like CLAP match captions to sounds well at coarse grain. Fine details still slip, because words and audio carry meaning so differently. FORTE rewrites each query as a first-order logic form. A constrained search then enriches the form with telling attributes while keeping its meaning fixed.

A light projection module aligns the refined query with audio embeddings. A final re-ranking step checks results for logical consistency with the query's predicates. Tests on AudioCaps and Clotho, two standard caption-audio sets, showed steady gains over strong baselines. The gains grew largest on the fine-grained cases that embarrass pure embeddings. Symbolic care and learned vectors, the authors argue, cover each other's blind spots. Retrieval precision benefits most where descriptions turn precise.
arxiv-2606-05912:
Jiahao Yang and colleagues build expressive 3D face avatars from strikingly little footage in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gaussian avatars model faces as clouds of soft blobs that deform with expression. Standard pipelines demand thousands of frames across many cameras and expressions. SAGE learns the deformations by itself instead. It optimizes flat Gaussian surfels together with a signed distance field, keeping blobs glued to the facial surface.

A self-supervised phase then replaces long expression sequences with geometric and appearance consistency rules. The savings cascade across capture setups. Multiview rigs need a single frame rather than thousands. A lone camera needs only head rotations, no expression takes. One-shot mode needs no pretraining or face priors at all. Quality matched state-of-the-art methods in the reported experiments. Data needs fell by several orders of magnitude. The authors pitch self-taught deformation as the route to avatars anyone can capture.
arxiv-2606-06112:
A reply in a scholarly dispute: Chong Qi answers a published Comment on his review of seniority conservation in semi-magic nuclei, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Comment raised objections to how the review treated an earlier paper's approach. Qi accepts some points as fair clarifications of wording and logic. He rejects the implication of scientific error.

None of the objections, he argues, identify a mistake that would mislead readers or misrepresent the criticized work's substance. The corrections live at the level of emphasis and phrasing, not physics. On the methodological dispute, he holds his line: emphasizing subspace decomposition and basis transformation adds little until someone identifies a unique operator that generates the partially seniority-conserved states directly. Terminology for the special states is also defended. Replies like this keep the nuclear-structure literature's record straight in public. The exchange turns on what counts as insight versus reformulation.
arxiv-2606-06212:
Rufat Asadli and co-authors benchmark language models at fixing broken computer networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. A single wrong line in a router configuration can take down large parts of the internet, and hand repair is slow and error prone. Plain language models, even strong ones, often fail on large tangled cases and introduce fresh faults. The team asks whether giving the model tools and an agent loop changes that record.

Their agents can retrieve context and call formal verification tools, which check a proposed repair against the network's stated requirements before it is applied. Across open and closed source models, agentic setups beat base models on repair success by twelve percent on average, and scored seventeen percent higher on safety. The authors credit the gains to managing context dynamically and validating each fix in rounds rather than answering in one shot.
arxiv-2606-06512:
Sharon Urieli compares binary images without being fooled by small shifts in this 2026 arXiv technical note. Comparing two pictures fails in practice because imperfect alignment looks like real change. Her tool comes from mathematical morphology, the set based study of shapes in images. The symmetric difference of two masks marks every pixel where they disagree. But it also flags every slight misalignment. Dilating that difference, expanding it slightly, absorbs the jitter.

Urieli defines the operator formally and proves it works: real differences are detected as long as the leftover alignment error stays within bounds tied to the dilation size. It needs no learning, just set operations on the two masks. As future work she proposes folding it into neural networks as a trainable layer, so the dilation radius could be learned inside a pipeline that also handles registration.
arxiv-2606-06712:
Most language models write one word at a time, in order. Diffusion language models instead start from a garbled draft and clean it up in parallel, but training them from scratch is costly. Xingyu Su and co-authors convert an existing orderly model into a diffusion model in this 2026 arXiv paper, avoiding that full retraining bill.

Earlier conversions suffered two problems: switching the training goal threw away knowledge the original model had learned, and training on randomly garbled text did not match what the model meets when generating. Their method has the student model produce its own drafts, while the frozen original grades each step, a setup called on policy distillation. The converted models needed fifteen to seven thousand times fewer training tokens than earlier diffusion baselines, while still performing strongly across a wide range of language tasks.
arxiv-2606-07112:
Skyrmions are tiny whirlpools of magnetization that could store bits at extreme density. Potkina studies their paired form in synthetic antiferromagnets in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two magnetic layers lock together with opposite alignment. That pairing cancels stray fields and steadies the bits. The question is how the pairs die, and how they can be born.

Using a reduced lattice model, she computes minimum energy paths for both events. Collapse destroys a written pair; nucleation creates one from a pinned reference state. The saddle energy barely moves with island size. The pair's own energy, though, carries a growing boundary penalty. For large islands, collapse proceeds layer by layer, sometimes through a single layer skyrmion. The reverse barrier for writing dwarfs the collapse barrier. That asymmetry favors assisted, layer sequential writing schemes. Barrier values reach roughly one electron volt for the largest islands studied.
arxiv-2606-07412:
Xiao and co-authors build a coding agent that improves itself using past attempts, in this 2026 arXiv paper on Socratic-SWE. Training data scarcity limits software engineering agents; synthetic tasks from bug-injection recipes ignore what an agent gets wrong. Their closed loop mines the agent's historical solving traces, distilling them into structured skills that summarize failures and repair patterns. Those skills then guide generation of targeted repair tasks inside real repos, validated by executing the code.

A solver-gradient alignment reward scores candidate tasks for being verifiable and useful for improvement. The updated agent produces traces, so the curriculum adapts round after round. Across 4 benchmarks, including the SWE-bench suites and a terminal-use benchmark, the method beat self-evolving baselines under equal compute budgets. On SWE-bench Verified it reached a solve rate above 50 percent after 3 iterations in their runs. Traces, discarded after scoring, become training data.
arxiv-2606-07512:
Cong Chen and co-authors split long-video understanding into watching once and reasoning many times, in this 2026 arXiv paper on MemDreamer. Vision-language models choke on hours-long video because feeding every frame explodes token counts and dilutes attention. MemDreamer streams the video once to build a hierarchical graph memory: a 3-tier structure whose graph records spatio-temporal relations, with semantic abstractions layered. At question time, a reasoning model explores that memory with actions, navigating tiers, searching nodes, and following edges in an observe-reason-act loop.

The framework plugs into models rather than replacing them. Across 4 benchmarks it reached top results, narrowing the gap to experts to under 4 points. It used 2 percent of the context that full ingestion would consume, gaining 12 points of accuracy over the end-to-end baseline. Statistical analysis linked models' logic-reasoning strength to their video performance, suggesting agent skill drives the gains.
arxiv-2606-07612:
Gupta and co-authors argue that claims of misalignment in AI models often rest on evidence too weak for the decisions built on it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Studies of deception, sycophancy, and emergent misalignment influence deployment and regulation, yet the authors show how conceptual ambiguity, datasets, design choices, and causal interventions invite reading too much into behavior. A behavior that looks like deception may be an artifact of how the test was framed, and without interventions the mechanism stays unknown.

Their remedy is a framework of evidence levels paired with a diagnostic checklist that studies can be graded against. The goal is standards strong enough that claims about AI risk rest on empirical foundations and discourse stays productive. The paper evaluates failure modes, showing where literature's evidence chain breaks. It serves as guidance for researchers, reviewers, and decision-makers who decide how much weight a misalignment demonstration deserves.
arxiv-2606-07712:
Yao and co-authors present MatMind, a single generative model built for many crystal-materials tasks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Materials AI has relied on narrow specialists: one model family predicts properties, another generates new crystal structures. A language-model backbone could in principle do all three in one place, but none had matched the specialists.

MatMind combines three ingredients: injected structure-activity knowledge, a dual head that trains language reasoning and numerical regression together, and physics-informed reinforcement learning that rewards stability, novelty, and diversity. Across three task families it posted the lowest prediction error for energy above hull, bulk modulus, and band gap, beating purpose-built graph networks. Its unconditional crystal generation reached a stability-novelty rate of about sixty-five percent. It also improved generation guided by magnetisation density, a task with only twenty-one positive examples among six hundred thousand training entries.
arxiv-2606-07812:
Feng and colleagues propose building AI from the bottom up in this 2026 arXiv paper. Today's large language models are built by a few organisations as monolithic systems, which poorly reflects the diversity of human knowledge and values. Under their paradigm, scaling participation, many stakeholders each train a small model on their own interests. Those small models then collaborate inside modular frameworks as one compositional system.

Across fifteen tasks, including reasoning and factuality, the participatory systems beat monolithic models by up to about fifteen percent, even surpassing models larger than all components combined. Diversity among contributors helped rather than hurt, and each model improved on the priorities it was built for. Most strikingly, the combined systems solved over fifteen percent of problems where every single model failed, an emergent capability no part had alone. The authors present this as a foundation for a more open, collaborative AI ecosystem.
arxiv-2606-07912:
Deshpande and Bhattacharya fix a quiet flaw in a popular uncertainty method, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polynomial chaos expansions write a random quantity as a series in special polynomials, letting engineers carry randomness through simulations cheaply. Standard coefficients come from projecting simulation output onto those polynomials. At low orders the resulting mean and variance, its first two moments, can come out wrong.

The authors instead choose coefficients by constrained optimisation, forcing the expansion to reproduce the true mean and variance exactly. Moment errors that biased risk estimates are removed by construction. In tests the new coefficients gave large accuracy gains over standard projection. The gains were largest at low orders, where expansions are cheapest and most used. The method keeps the speed of polynomial chaos while removing its most basic inaccuracy.
arxiv-2606-08112:
Xu Du, Shuting Wu, Karl H. Johansson, and Apostolos I. Rikos make a distributed optimisation method smarter about when to use costly curvature information, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Consensus problems ask many agents, each holding part of a problem, to agree on one solution, the setting behind federated learning and coordinated control. Their algorithm builds on the C-ALADIN framework, an augmented Lagrangian method with Newton-type steps.

Existing versions must fix their Hessian approximations in advance, sacrificing the benefits of fresh second-order information. The new variant adds a helper variable deciding when to update the curvature model, exploiting curvature where it helps without endangering convergence. Under smoothness and strong convexity, the authors prove global convergence. In logistic regression tests the method beat baselines using fixed or routinely updated Hessian information. The lesson is scheduling: when you refresh the model can matter as much as the model.
arxiv-2606-08212:
Saleh, Mili, and Boukadoum propose a free online platform that helps beginners solve machine learning problems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning means teaching computers to find patterns in data, a process that normally demands expert judgment at every step. Existing help comes as fully automatic tools, simple cheat sheets, or decision aids that rank single algorithms. The new platform combines the last two approaches and recommends a complete pipeline, the full step sequence from raw data to finished model.

The system reasons over a knowledge base of expert rules written in first-order logic, a formal way of stating facts and conditions. It also inspects each uploaded dataset automatically, noting problems such as missing values or lopsided class counts. Recommendations come back ranked by relevance, and a linked crowdsourcing site lets experts add fresh knowledge over time. The authors call it the first free public framework of its kind.
arxiv-2606-08312:
Ansarifard and colleagues teach reinforcement learning agents to obey rules stated in formal logic, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is offline reinforcement learning. The agent learns from stored experience rather than live trial and error. Its task constraints are written in LTLf, a logic for rules over finite traces, such as one action before another. Transformer-based policies treat behavior as sequence modeling. They optimize purely for reward and ignore such high-level rules.

The authors build a neuro-symbolic framework, mixing neural learning with symbolic logic. Each formula is compiled into a deterministic finite automaton, a small state machine. The machine tracks how much of the rule has been satisfied so far. A smooth form of that machine yields signals during training. A logic-based loss term penalizes the policy when it drifts from the formula. The constraint thus shapes learning continuously, not as a final check.
arxiv-2606-08612:
Spyridon Georgiou and colleagues survey a decade of teaching computers to read faces, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Facial expression recognition has progressed rapidly. The field shifted from handcrafted descriptors and shallow classifiers to deep convolutional networks, attention-based models, and foundation models. In parallel, large-scale benchmarks have grown to cover categorical emotions, ratings of feeling, compound expressions, and micro-expressions. The field's literature had so far been reviewed only along narrow axes.

This systematic multi-criteria review supplies the missing holistic account, organizing recent deep learning methods by models, datasets, and performance, and analyzing the challenges that persist. By comparing approaches on multiple criteria at once, the survey exposes where progress is real and where it is an artifact of easy benchmarks. The authors close with future research directions. The goal is a clear map of what works, what does not, and what to try next in the lab.
arxiv-2606-08712:
Hongyi Yu and colleagues improve the filling-in of missing gene expression values in tissue slices, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where in the tissue each value came from. But the data are noisy, low-resolution, and sparsely sampled. Deep neural networks can impute expression from histology images. Yet small sample sizes and uninformed augmentation constrain them, and most augmentation was designed for classification, not regression.

Their framework, SNR-ST-Mix, is a geometry- and expression-aware data-mixing scheme designed for spatial transcriptomics. Mixing, blending training examples together, is constrained to a spot's nearest neighbors. The blend adapts to each sample's own neighborhood structure rather than a global rule. Synthetic examples thus respect both the tissue's geography and its expression patterns, teaching the network plausible fills in each gap it meets.
arxiv-2606-08812:
Li and colleagues ask which tumor cell properties diffusion MRI can measure reliably, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion MRI tracks how water wanders inside tissue, and that pattern reflects cell size and crowding, signs of how a tumor responds to radiation. The IMPULSED method fits a five-parameter cell model, including cell diameter and the share of volume inside cells. Because fitted values wobble badly, the team first mapped each parameter's uncertainty in simulations.

The analysis found three robustly estimable parameters, each with relative uncertainty below one: cell diameter, intracellular volume fraction, and extracellular diffusion coefficient. Of the mapping models trained on transformed signals, a four-layer neural network performed best. Its average error was 1.7 micrometers for cell diameter and about five percent for volume fraction. In tests on cultured mouse tumor cells, its cell diameter error was 6.7 percent, supporting use for monitoring treatment response.
arxiv-2606-09112:
Fan and colleagues borrow Ising-machine dynamics to fix a weakness of a brain-inspired training method, in this 2026 arXiv paper. GPU training is energy-hungry, motivating physical, energy-based alternatives. Equilibrium propagation trains energy-based models with a two-phase rule, but its settling dynamics contract phase space, trapping training in poor local minima. They replace it with extended phase-space dynamics with conjugate variables, inspired by Ising machines, solvers that settle into low-energy spin states.

The learning rule stays untouched; only the physical route to equilibrium changes. The new dynamics lowers energy barriers, so training escapes shallow minima, converges faster, and resists noise. The team trained deep convolutional Hopfield networks on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10, matching backpropagation, whose energy costs motivate the enterprise. The result suggests a division of labor for future hardware: let physics handle the settling, with rules designed for physical dynamics.
arxiv-2606-09312:
Pan and colleagues evaluate compiler optimizations the way a world model would, by simulating how a program's state evolves under each scheduling decision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor compilers search huge spaces of program variants for the fastest one, and learned cost models score candidates to avoid slow on-device measurement. Those models judge candidates as static snapshots, blind to the transformations that produced them. Their framework rolls out scheduling actions in a latent space instead.

Instantiated in TVM's AutoScheduler with a learned state encoder and ranking model, the method improved representative-subgraph latency over the Ansor scheduler by 1.37 times on GPU and 1.54 times on CPU at the same 64-trial budget. It matched a 10,000-trial Ansor run within 2.2 percent using ten times fewer measurements. Full-model inference beat PyTorch baselines by 4.61 and 3.67 times in geometric mean, with peaks far higher.
arxiv-2606-09412:
Saee Desai and her co-authors build a teaching prototype that protects drug-safety data against future quantum computers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pharmacovigilance systems collect adverse event reports and clinical observations that must stay confidential for many years. That long lifetime creates a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk, where attackers store encrypted files today and open them once quantum machines mature.

The prototype pipeline links hospital, gateway, and pharmaceutical receiver components, with an attacker role included for testing. It establishes keys with ML-KEM-768, a standardised post-quantum method, derives an encryption key, and encrypts files with AES-256-GCM. Digital signatures from ML-DSA-65 guard against tampering, and all common file formats are handled as raw bytes with metadata preserved. Tests on synthetic datasets showed the post-quantum key step adds only a small constant overhead. Encryption and signing, not the new algorithms, dominate the running time.
arxiv-2606-09712:
Renjie Feng studies how close the zeros of a random polynomial sit to its nearest critical points in this 2026 arXiv paper. The polynomials are Gaussian SU(2) type, a standard random model tied to the sphere. Each zero has a gap to the closest point where the slope vanishes. The scale of that gap, and its spread across many trials, was open.

Feng works with the Fubini-Study distance, the natural ruler on the sphere. For a polynomial of degree n, he rescales each gap by n and gathers the whole set into a spread. He proves that spread settles, in a weak sense, onto a fixed law. That law is the spread of two over the squared size of a random draw from the sphere's own measure. The result gives a clean limit shape for a fine trait of random waves.
arxiv-2606-10012:
Vaikundaraman and colleagues study how complex gas flows inside planet-forming discs shape the growth of dust, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. Protoplanetary discs around young stars host winds, rings, and gaps when magnetic effects are included. Dust grains must grow and gather into traps before planetesimals, the building blocks of planets, can form.

The team post-processed a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulation with a Monte Carlo coagulation code that tracks dust growth and transport globally. Strong gas velocities advect small particles. A transition region in the flow acts as a dust pile-up, raising the pebble-to-gas ratio by a factor of about two and a half over a steady disc. Lowering the fragmentation velocity, the impact speed at which grains shatter, made the pile-up more stable but less concentrated. The trap forms without any pressure bump.
arxiv-2606-10212:
Soto and his team define covariance for data that lives on curved spaces, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Covariance is a basic second-order summary behind feature learning, shrinking inputs, and modeling links. But it is ill-defined for random objects on curved Riemannian manifolds, such as shapes or symmetric positive definite matrices. Their intrinsic Riemannian cross-covariance moves local variations to a shared tangent space by parallel transport, the geometry-respecting way to shift vectors along a manifold. The result is a descriptor free of arbitrary coordinate choices.

They show it inherits the prized properties of its Euclidean counterpart, and they chart its asymptotic limits. Studies on spheres and on spaces of such matrices back the claims. Real-data tests on heart valve shapes in Kendall's shape space show the estimators work well and confirm the stated claims.
arxiv-2606-10512:
Joubert and colleagues simulate how solar wind turbulence scrambles magnetic field lines in this 2026 arXiv paper in space physics. The solar wind carries the Sun's magnetic field outward in a spiral named after Parker, and charged particles from eruptions travel along those lines. Turbulence makes real field lines wander randomly around the ideal spiral, so the magnetic connection between the Sun and a spacecraft is statistical. The authors turn a convection-diffusion equation for field line density into stochastic equations and trace many spirals numerically.

At Earth's distance, one astronomical unit, the angular spread of field lines fits a two-dimensional Gaussian with a standard deviation close to twenty-five degrees. Tracing lines backward from a quarter of that distance cuts the angular uncertainty to about four degrees. Strong turbulence also leaves field lines underwound on average, a bias that matters for forecasting solar particle events.
arxiv-2606-10612:
Han, Luo, and Wan tackle digital forensics for three-dimensional assets in this 2026 arXiv paper. The assets are 3D Gaussian Splatting models, a format that builds scenes from millions of soft particles and is widely shared online. When altered copies spread, creators need provenance: a directed graph showing which version descended from which. GaussTrace builds that graph as an evidence-based reasoning problem. It profiles each model's parameters statistically, then simulates common editing operations for clues about transformation paths.

A large language model receives the evidence in a structured prompt and infers each relationship's direction, with a reason attached to every edge. Experiments show the framework reconstructs lineages accurately, without training or access to editing histories. The authors present it as a forensic tool for protecting shared three-dimensional content.
arxiv-2606-10912:
Vojtěch Staněk and colleagues ask what deepfake speech detectors actually listen to in this 2026 arXiv paper. Detectors output one score with no hint of which sounds drove it. The team applies Integrated Gradients to time-aligned self-supervised features, marking the moments that matter, then hand-labels the top regions on ASVspoof 5 for three WavLM-based detectors.

Despite similar accuracy, the three detectors lean on different cues: AASIST favors non-speech and background sounds, CA-MHFA homes in on local phoneme flaws, and SLS watches word boundaries and spectral integrity. Masking each detector's favorite cues hurts it most, confirming the readings are causal, not decorative.
arxiv-2606-11112:
Chinichian and Palm survey why industrial augmented reality still struggles to leave the pilot stage in a 2026 arXiv paper. It overlays digital guidance on real work. Factories have trialled it for design, training, assembly, maintenance, and quality checks. Dependable deployment at scale remains the exception. The blockers are software quality, integration friction, workload, and readiness, not display hardware.

The authors synthesize published evidence into a full-stack framework of six coupled axes. They cover value, technical constraints, human factors and safety, organizational and economic questions, data security and privacy, and governance. Within each axis they separate benefits, failure modes, and design considerations. A deployment checklist cross-links them for managers and vendors. They grade the evidence too: mature for assembly time and training efficacy, emerging for workload trade-offs, speculative for metaverse-scale governance.
arxiv-2606-11512:
Shi, Zhang, and Ye align the uncertainty language models express with how unsure they actually are, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models increasingly state uncertainty in words, yet these expressions often fail to reflect sampled behavior. The right uncertainty target for a prompt, they argue, should come from repeated model outputs, not one isolated response. But group rollouts alone give no useful training signal.

Their SAGE target builds an answer-conditioned uncertainty geometry over sampled responses, preserving answer distinctions while keeping a smooth, scale-preserving signal. A companion training framework, GUPO, supervises only the verbal channel rather than the full response. Across factual, mathematical, and multiple-choice tasks, including TriviaQA, MATH-500, and MMLU-Pro, it improves uncertainty ranking, lowers calibration error, and reduces overconfidence. The authors note the method aligns what models say with their behavioral self-uncertainty, a complement to correctness checks rather than a replacement.
arxiv-2606-11612:
A Yu Loginov studies a solitary wave in a gauge theory model in this 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. The object is a soliton of Q-ball type, a stable lump of field energy held together by a conserved charge rather than by topology. The model is a pure Chern-Simons Higgs theory, where a special term gives the gauge field mass without breaking its symmetry.

Working in the general case, where simplifying shortcuts do not apply, Loginov shows the soliton minimises energy at fixed Noether charge, the conserved quantity tied to a symmetry. He derives a relation linking energy, charge and the gauge field's boundary value, plus a linear relation between energy parts. He maps where solutions exist. One sharp condition emerges: energy and charge can grow without limit only when the field's self-interaction potential has two equal zero minima. Analysis and numerical work both support the picture.
arxiv-2606-12112:
Malte Kuhlmann and four colleagues give an ageing social robot a new lease of life in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Pepper humanoid robot is widely used in social robotics research, but its built-in computing and perception are dated. Replacing the platform would waste a large installed base, so the team designed PEBRE, an open-hardware add-on that upgrades it.

PEBRE integrates a modern Jetson Orin Nano computer, a high-quality webcam, a depth camera and two microphones into a modular package. Experimental verification shows the add-on considerably improves Pepper's perception abilities and computational power. Everything is open hardware and open source, so any lab can build, modify and repair it. The design also speeds up software development and simplifies connecting external components, the usual friction in robotics projects. The authors frame PEBRE as community infrastructure, keeping a relevant research platform functional beyond its expected lifespan.
arxiv-2606-12312:
Celada and co-authors show that future electron colliders can probe the top quark without ever making one, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The top quark's couplings to other particles are prime places for new physics to hide. Colliders like the proposed LEP3 and FCC-ee would run below the energy needed to produce top pairs directly. But virtual top quarks still ripple through quantum loops into other processes. The authors compute those effects for W-boson pair production within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, a framework adding small dimension-six interaction terms.

They include next-to-leading order electroweak corrections. The indirect sensitivity from W-pair production proves competitive. It rivals the Z-Higgs channel and stands well against current limits from LEP and the LHC. The work is a first step toward computing such corrections systematically for lepton colliders, so global analyses can weigh this channel.
arxiv-2606-12412:
Yang and co-authors argue that vision-language models should shelve unused image tokens instead of deleting them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models turn images into hundreds or thousands of tokens, making inference costly. Standard pruning ranks tokens and discards the low scorers. That is fragile: a token unimportant early can matter in deeper layers, especially for grounding questions about where things are. Their plug-in, Reroute, defers low-ranked tokens around decoder stages, letting them re-enter the candidate pool later.

Reroute needs no training and reuses ranking rules and schedules. It preserves the compute and memory budget of the pruning method it augments. Under reduction from 576 tokens down to 64, pruning collapses grounding accuracy. Reroute recovers it across three backbones, from LLaVA to Qwen models, while question answering holds up. The lesson reframes token reduction: not irreversible pruning, but recoverable routing that respects how importance shifts with depth.
arxiv-2606-12512:
Popp and co-authors warn that the fingerprints of exotic quantum matter can be forged by ordinary excitations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutron scattering probes magnetic materials, and broad smears in the spectra are often read as spinons, fractional particles signaling a quantum spin liquid. The team studies the XXZ Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice, a frustrated triangular pattern, using adiabatic continuity: tracking excitations smoothly as the model's anisotropy varies.

They find the low-energy spectrum carries two peaks that do not move with momentum. Their frequencies sit at multiples, about 3.4 and 6.3, of a hidden energy scale. That scale is set by a peak in the heat capacity, where frustrated magnets show spin-glass freezing. Crucially, the low-energy features arise from magnons, ordinary spin waves, not fractionalization. The result hands experimentalists a test: check whether supposed spin-liquid signatures match these magnon energies before claiming discovery.
arxiv-2606-12712:
Goldfein and Marzen ask whether the neuromuscular junction is designed to transmit as much information as possible, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The neuromuscular junction is the synapse where a motor neuron signals a muscle fibre, releasing neurotransmitter that produces an electric current. Treating that conversion as a communication channel, the authors use information theory to derive the distribution of neurotransmitter concentrations that would maximise information transmission, given known dose-response relationships.

They compare that theoretical distribution with an experimentally derived one from the fruit fly Drosophila, whose junction uses glutamate rather than acetylcholine. The two distributions show very little agreement. In particular, the fly's distribution of vesicle release probabilities does not look shaped for maximum information transfer. The authors conclude that other demands, such as reliability, speed, or energy cost, likely dominate the design, and they provide testable predictions for the cholinergic junctions found in vertebrates.
arxiv-2606-13012:
Israeli and colleagues formulate guarding a target against a faster attacker with a slower guard as a differential game scored by flyby distance, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Both players follow nonlinear, thrust-free aerodynamic motion in the plane. Because the guard is inferior in speed, capturability is the wrong question. Instead the attacker is constrained to terminate at its target. The game's value is the flyby distance, the closest the guard comes during the flight.

An auxiliary state variable records the players' minimum separation throughout the flight, making that quantity accessible at termination. Taking an indirect approach, the authors formulate the game's 2-point boundary value problem, solve it numerically, and identify several solution types. Imposing an attacker terminal speed constraint yields simpler solutions, reveals the trade-off between terminal speed and flyby distance, and shows that capture is possible in a relevant region of the parameter space.
arxiv-2606-13112:
Raza and colleagues study the initial coefficient differences of Ma-Minda convex functions, a class of univalent functions defined by subordination to a fixed starlike function, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For analytic functions normalised on the unit disc, bounding the difference between the absolute values of consecutive Taylor coefficients is a classical problem descending from the Bieberbach conjecture. The bound of 1 fails in general, so each function class needs its own sharp analysis.

The authors present sharp bounds on the absolute difference between the third and second Taylor coefficients for functions in the Ma-Minda convex class. They establish the same bounds for the coefficients of the inverse functions. They give conditions under which the bounds on the coefficient difference and on the inverse coefficient difference are invariant, that is, unchanged between a function and its inverse. They also give conditions under which they are not.
arxiv-2606-13212:
González Rodríguez and Ramos Pérez develop a theory of how algebraic structures deform in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are Hopf coquasigroups, which extend Hopf algebras, relaxing the associativity rules. Such structures arise in non-associative geometry, including settings linked to the seven-dimensional sphere. The authors introduce non-coassociative bimonoids with left and right codivisions, operations playing the role of division, and prove how these connect with them. This lets them define twists, modifications inspired by Drinfeld's method.

They prove that a twist deforms the coproduct, the operation splitting an element into a pair, and produces a new coquasigroup structure. Procedures are given for right and left versions, together with an analysis of the antipode, the analogue of an inverse map. Finally, the theory is applied to coquasigroups built from the seven-sphere. The construction yields new examples that are neither commutative nor cocommutative.
arxiv-2606-13312:
Jammal and Sharf present MagPlus in this 2026 arXiv paper, a pipeline for working with facial micro-expressions. Micro-expressions are brief, faint facial movements that can reveal emotion. They are hard to model or generate because labelled examples are scarce and the motions are weak. Rather than train a dedicated generator, MagPlus learns to magnify subtle facial motion into the range of ordinary expressions. Existing animation models, built for those stronger expressions, can then process, transfer, or synthesise the movement.

A companion module, DeMagPlus, scales the generated motion back down to realistic intensity while keeping its dynamics. This round trip connects two research areas that needed separate tools. The authors evaluate the pipeline on such tasks and report gains over methods trained directly on the limited data. Because the magnified signal matches what standard models expect, the approach reuses mature expression technology instead of replacing it.
arxiv-2606-13712:
Michael Chrzan and colleagues identify speakers in real classrooms by combining sound with meaning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated analysis of classroom dynamics promises feedback on student participation, but background noise and variable child speech confound acoustic-only models. The study anchors acoustic embeddings with semantic context derived from transcripts by a language model. It uses thousands of utterances from eight mathematics classrooms in a dataset. The acoustic baseline, a speaker embedding network, reached only about thirty-nine percent accuracy at naming the student speaking.

Adding transcript-based contextual anchoring to a gradient boosting classifier raised student identification to about half of utterances. For utterances longer than five seconds, accuracy climbed to roughly three quarters, well above the baseline, with the correct student in the top three guesses nearly always. The model also distinguished teachers from students with near-perfect accuracy. The approach advances feedback systems that consider individual participation.
arxiv-2606-14212:
Lange connects two theories of shape in a 2026 arXiv doctoral dissertation from the University of Greifswald. Coarse homotopy theory studies spaces up to large-scale equivalence, ignoring fine detail. Shape theory classifies compact metric spaces by their approximative behavior. The thesis links them through Euclidean cones built over compact spaces.

For a compact metric space, the cone's coarse homotopy groups are determined by the space's pointed shape invariants. They sit in an exact sequence involving Čech homotopy groups. Using inverse mapping telescopes and strong shape theory, Lange proves an equivalence. Two compact spaces are strong shape equivalent exactly when their Euclidean cones are coarsely homotopy equivalent. He also proves a coarse Whitehead theorem for cones. For arbitrary proper metric spaces the parallel theorem fails. The thesis constructs a counterexample showing why.
arxiv-2606-14612:
Claude and Luo claim a structural match between a Beethoven sonata and machine learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is the Moonlight Sonata. They argue its three movements instantiate three distinct learning designs. The claim rests on measured correspondence, not loose analogy. The analysis uses score features such as entropy and dissonance. It also uses self-similarity, memory decay, and pitch embeddings.

Four surprising findings emerge. Perceived musical warmth is governed by throughput, not by distributional width. The lightest movement carries the highest dissonance. The movements implement streaming, recurrent, and periodic positional memory schemes. One pitch class gains different contextual identities across movements. That mirrors contextual embeddings in language models. A reverse sonification back into MIDI shows steady loss as sequence order grows. This chirality effect is stronger in natural language than in music.
arxiv-2606-14712:
Atul and co-authors design a streaming analytics system for internet-of-things data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Connected devices produce continuous data streams needing real-time processing, but cloud-centric designs suffer network delays and heavy transmission overhead. Their framework, EdgeStream, processes data on lightweight edge nodes near the devices, with a cloud backend only for coordination and storage.

The system communicates over the MQTT protocol and distributes processing with built-in anomaly detection. The authors develop analytical models for latency, throughput, and bandwidth, then test the design experimentally against cloud-based systems. Their abstract reports improvements reaching above ninety percent on the headline measure, though the posted text is truncated mid-sentence at that figure. The work targets deployments where low latency and bandwidth efficiency matter more than centralized computing power.
arxiv-2606-15012:
Hwang and Coleman model coupled oscillator phases without assuming the system sits in equilibrium in a 2026 study. Coupled oscillators describe brain waves, stomach slow waves, and protein backbone angles. Standard estimators write the phase law in Boltzmann form, which fails when systems drift away from balance. The authors build their Kuramoto-von Mises model from Langevin dynamics instead.

Fitting the model by maximum likelihood has a closed-form answer when sampling is fast. Modern recording systems sample at kilohertz rates, so that regime is realistic in practice. Simulations show the method beats existing approaches in non-equilibrium settings and stays competitive in equilibrium ones. The team applies it to brain traveling waves under stimulation in cortical recordings. They also run hypothesis tests on stomach recordings taken from the body surface. One limit is a fixed base rate per oscillator, which suits the stomach better than broadband brain activity.
arxiv-2606-15112:
Guo and coauthors detect oriented, fine-grained objects in satellite video by learning temporal consistency in a 2026 study. Earlier detectors chase a few coarse moving categories and draw flat horizontal boxes around them. Objects in orbit footage sit at arbitrary angles and carry fine class detail. Treating each frame alone also breaks consistency across the video.

Their framework, TCL, joins three modules around the video's time structure. One module aggregates temporal and fine-grained features across frames. A structure encoder captures appearance plus shape cues for precise recognition. A temporal consistency constraint keeps representations stable from frame to frame. On the SAT-MTB benchmark, TCL sets a new best accuracy for oriented fine-grained detection, beating the baseline clearly. Existing image-based detectors also plug into the framework and gain accuracy. The authors present TCL as the first video detector built for this oriented, fine-grained satellite task.
arxiv-2606-15312:
Yu identifies an intrinsic decay length governing elastic localization in a 2026 solid mechanics paper. Localization concentrates strain into a narrow zone, as in bulging tubes or buckling rods. Theory models such states on infinite domains, ignoring boundaries. When a finite structure behaves like its infinite ideal form was unclear. Yu shows the answer hinges on one geometric measure, the intrinsic decay length. Once a structure's length exceeds it, finite and infinite solutions agree almost exactly.

The same length explains a puzzle about weakly nonlinear rules. Finite-domain expansions fail quickly as structures lengthen, while infinite-domain ones stay accurate. Beyond the decay length, solutions for different lengths differ by exponentially tiny amounts. That makes them nearly impossible to distinguish in numbers, a warning. Two problems validate the framework: bulging in membrane tubes and helical buckling in twisted rods. The result unifies localization shifts, approximation reach, and computation under one measure.
arxiv-2606-15412:
Mraz and coauthors test whether language models can extract relations from biomedical text with only a few examples in a 2026 paper. Relation extraction turns papers into structured knowledge by flagging links between entities, such as a drug and the disease it treats. Supervised systems do this well but need costly expert-labeled data. The authors compare two prompting styles: classifying each entity pair separately, or generating all relations from a passage in one call.
