On the BioREDirect dataset the best model clearly beats earlier few-shot results yet trails the supervised baseline on the standard overall score. Much of the gap traces to one vaguely defined relation type. On a per-category average, which rewards rare relations, the prompted models actually beat the supervised system. Pairwise classification finds more relations, while joint generation is more precise and cheaper, so the choice depends on whether coverage or accuracy matters more.
arxiv-2606-15812:
Mohammadigohari and colleagues introduce Brownian kernel ladders in 2026, a hierarchy of function spaces designed to give deep learning's layered structure a mathematical home. Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces are powerful models, but classical constructions are shallow: no ladder comes naturally. A Brownian kernel ladder builds each layer by mixing Brownian kernels over measures supported on the previous layer, starting from linear maps, so depth is built in.

For the ladder spaces, the authors prove a stack of properties. They are quasi-Banach, satisfy depth-dependent Hölder regularity bounds, and grow strictly with depth. Regularised empirical risk minimisation over them has solutions. Gaussian complexity bounds for their balls stay controlled in both ambient dimension and depth alike, yielding near-parametric excess-risk bounds. A new combinatorial proof technique, recursive subset decompositions with threshold forms, does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2606-16312:
Korbel reviews in 2026 the foundations of entropy, asking which entropy a complex system actually deserves. The chapter starts from Boltzmann's formula, where entropy counts the multiplicity of coarse-grained states, and shows how multinomial counting leads to Shannon entropy. Generalized forms follow: Rényi, Tsallis, and Burg entropies, each suited to different system structures. Particle statistics, from Maxwell-Boltzmann to Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac, get the same foundational treatment.

Later sections cover structure-forming systems, sample-space reducing processes, Pólya urns, and nonlinear dynamics, all of which bend entropy away from textbook forms. Axiomatic approaches ask what entropy must satisfy: the Shannon-Khinchin axioms, group composability, asymptotic scaling laws, and consistency axioms among them. A recurring lesson is that the same distribution can arise from different entropies, constraints, or dynamics. Entropy choice should therefore follow the structure and physical properties of the system, not habit.
arxiv-2606-16712:
Fraser and colleagues solve a detection problem in a 2026 quantum theory paper: deciding whether a shared quantum state is entangled or merely separable. Lab-friendly tests exist, but each misses some entangled states. Complete tests exist too, yet they need the full density matrix and heavy numerical optimization.

The authors build criteria from universal bounds on tensor powers of separable states, repeated copies of the state considered together. They prove the bounds are complete: every entangled state breaks them once enough copies are used. From the same math they construct an explicit family of nonlinear witnesses, measurement recipes that certify entanglement without reconstructing the density matrix. The witnesses do not depend on the chosen measurement basis, since they are unchanged by local unitary rotations. The results give experimenters, in principle, a complete and directly measurable entanglement test for systems of any local dimension.
arxiv-2606-17212:
Alpay and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on streaming dynamic Gaussian splatting. The method renders moving scenes from new viewpoints in real time. Compression usually assumes a complete file arrives before rendering starts. Real delivery is partial instead, with some regions present and others missing.

The authors group Gaussian primitives into clusters that can be sent on their own. Each cluster carries a base level plus three refinement levels. Training samples many partial states and scores them in image space. A utility layer then measures what each missing piece would add to the picture. Oddly, the finest refinement had negative value in many tested clusters. Ordering delivery by measured utility removed quality regressions and improved held-out rendering at matched byte budgets.
arxiv-2606-17312:
Chaudhury and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on judging whether a language model's reasoning is consistent, not just whether its answers vary. A model can reach the same answer through unstable or contradictory paths, a failure mode common in multi-step deduction. Output dispersion misses that, so the authors propose structural uncertainty, built from how steadily a model ranks its own candidate solutions across repeated trials.

Candidates are sampled, the model judges pairwise preferences among its own outputs, and those sparse preferences become ranking distributions through a Bradley-Terry model with PageRank. The signal splits into ranking instability across trials and candidate ambiguity within a trial. Across five models and eight benchmarks, the structural signal added information beyond answer dispersion on logic and mathematics tasks. It faded on factual retrieval, marking a regime where this style of check is uninformative.
arxiv-2606-17512:
Gao and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on MedEasy, a multi-agent system that lets medical students practise consultations with AI standardised patients. Learning to interview and examine patients takes repeatable, low-stakes practice, which real clinics cannot always supply on demand. The system organises practice as a full arc: patient dialogue, clinical actions, a submitted decision, and written documentation. Feedback then ties to the record of what the learner actually did during the session.

A formative study with clinical-year students, using interviews and co-design workshops, shaped the staged workflow and structured case records. Findings during the exam depend on the actions chosen, and review follows the learner's whole path through the case. A second cohort then tested the system on paired cases. Learners valued repeatable practice and recorded review, while questioning missing actions and unclear feedback criteria.
arxiv-2606-17912:
Andreis and Veshaj count a vast family of networks in the sparse regime, in a 2026 probability paper. Their objects are labelled connected graphs whose vertices come in several types, with set numbers of vertices per type and set edge counts between each pair of types. Both vertex and edge totals grow in step, and the counting extends classic results for ordinary connected graphs.

The method is probabilistic rather than direct. A connected graph with given statistics is matched to the giant component of a larger, carefully tuned inhomogeneous random graph, where one big component swallows the rest. Large deviation estimates for those random graphs then yield the leading exponential growth rate of the count. The final formula generalizes the classic Bender, Canfield, and McKay enumeration to the multitype world used in modern network models.
arxiv-2606-18012:
Fischbach and colleagues show a light surface where a tiny tilt flips the response to light, in a 2026 paper. Design rules based on symmetry usually hold up well even when a built object is a bit off perfect. The team tests that faith with a surface of tiny patterned units. The surface has four-fold symmetry, and it traps light in near-bound states that boost its response.

Shine light straight at the surface and symmetry blocks one kind of reflection, the kind that keeps the twist of the light. Tilt the beam by even the smallest angle, though, and the trapped-light boost wins outright. That blocked reflection comes back at full strength. The switch turns on with striking speed as the tilt grows. For builders, the lesson cuts both ways: a small flaw can ruin a design, or serve as a hair trigger.
arxiv-2606-18112:
The Qwen Team presents a navigation model meant to serve as the eyes and legs of agent systems, in a 2026 technical report. Tasks like following instructions, searching for objects, tracking targets, and driving share one perception and planning backbone, yet each wants the visual stream consumed differently. A fixed observation strategy fits none of them well, so the model exposes its observation choices as settings an outer agent can change at run time.

Qwen-RobotNav builds on Qwen3-VL with two control dimensions: task modes that pick the navigation behavior, and observation parameters such as token budget and per-camera weights. Training randomizes every setting, making the model robust to any configuration with no architectural change. Trained on over fifteen million samples, with vision-language co-training to stop it collapsing into a blind action repeater, it slots under planners that split long goals into sub-tasks.
arxiv-2606-18212:
Kumar, Liu, and Vashisth study inverse problems for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation that carries both magnetic and electric potentials changing in time, in a 2026 mathematical analysis paper. The central question is whether boundary measurements, packaged as a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, can pin down those potentials inside a region.

The authors prove that, under analyticity assumptions on how the potentials depend on the solution, the map does determine both potentials uniquely. They establish that result for full boundary data and also for partial data. In the partial case the response is measured only on arbitrarily small open pieces of the boundary, while the potentials are assumed known near it. They also settle the forward problem, showing it is well posed and obtaining regularity for its solutions in Sobolev spaces. Such uniqueness results underpin imaging and probing methods that infer an interior they cannot observe directly.
arxiv-2606-18312:
Kalikman and colleagues sharpen an attack that reconstructs what federated learning was supposed to keep private, in a 2026 security paper. Clients send gradient updates instead of raw text, but those updates leak. Earlier attacks either optimized dummy inputs to match gradients, which is costly and unstable. Or they exploited the low rank of attention gradients to find a subspace holding the true embeddings, then tested candidate tokens one by one, a brittle step under noise.

Their attack, TIGER, makes the subspace signal continuous. It optimizes token embeddings directly to minimize their distance to the gradient-induced subspace, with causal recovery for decoders and a bidirectional objective for encoders. On encoder-only models TIGER substantially improved both reconstruction quality and runtime over existing attacks, and it stayed competitive on decoders, widening the practical privacy threat.
arxiv-2606-18812:
Zighem and Vie argue, in a 2026 paper, that reinforcement learning is the glaring missing piece of the foundation model revolution. Language and vision models are powered by data at internet scale. Structured domains such as tabular prediction use synthetic data drawn from a prior, as TabPFN does for classification. Sampling a synthetic Markov decision process is just as feasible. Yet no in-context reinforcement learning work treats prior design as the objective.

Their second point is about structure. Decision processes admit a fixed-size sufficient statistic, independent of how many episodes were observed, and tabular in shape. That fits the attention designs used by tabular foundation models, with a policy head. As proof of concept, they train a graph attention network on synthetic decision processes. They show it solves tabular benchmarks in context, with no tuning, online in far fewer episodes than classic baselines.
arxiv-2606-19012:
Biborski offers a 2026 time-domain account of quantum transport in mesoscopic systems. The standard Landauer-Büttiker view describes steady currents as plane waves passing through a device. That view works well, but it hides how single fermionic excitations move in time to build the current. The author rebuilds Landauer transport from discrete, orthogonal wave packets instead of plane waves, in a self-contained way.

Packets are defined from a second-quantized start, using a Fourier transform over a finite energy window. The Pauli rule sets a firm time gap between packets, tied to the applied voltage. In this picture, a noiseless current becomes a strict sequence of charge-carrying events. The Landauer conductance emerges without any appeal to momentum-space arguments. The build stays exact for any energy dispersion. Splitting the space into finite energy sub-bands also makes the numerical side highly scalable for larger systems.
arxiv-2606-19112:
Mojtaba introduces post-Carroll transformations and their algebra in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Carroll symmetry arises when the speed of light is sent to zero, a limit with flat light cones. By adding leading corrections that depend on that speed, the author builds a richer post-Carroll symmetry. Unlike the plain Carroll algebra, this new structure allows a central charge in higher dimensions, earning it the name Carroll-Bargmann algebra.

Conformal extensions are then built step by step. The conformal extension of the post-Carroll algebra supports field theories invariant under the new symmetry. The extension of the Carroll-Bargmann algebra, called the Carroll-Schrödinger algebra, matches exactly the symmetry of a known higher-dimensional Carroll-Schrödinger theory. Finally, the author derives two-point functions for a post-Carrollian conformal field theory. In low dimensions both sectors appear, while only the magnetic sector survives higher up.
arxiv-2606-19512:
Falak Mandali, Zijian He, and Yan Gu present a state estimator for humanoid robots standing on moving ground in 2026. A humanoid on a swaying deck or vehicle cannot trust a fixed world frame. Their filter uses only onboard body sensing, with no outside cameras or ground motion sensors.

The method is an invariant extended Kalman filter that tracks base position and speed relative to the moving ground. Foot-mounted inertial units exploit the stance foot's contact limits to pin down the motion. The design yields a right-invariant measurement model, which keeps error behaviour stable under large starting errors. An observability study states when the relative state can be recovered at all. On the Digit robot, convergence runs 96 percent faster and position error drops by 80 percent against older filters. Walking on rotating ground holds average error under nine centimetres.
arxiv-2606-19612:
Karim Selim, A Y Ellithi, and M Abolmahassen link dark matter to early-universe inflation in one supersymmetric model in 2026. Their setting extends the Standard Model with a U(1) B-L gauge symmetry inside supergravity. Smooth hybrid inflation drives the cosmic expansion phase.

Three scalar fields share the work: an inflaton, a field that ends inflation, and a singlet linking both sectors. Dark matter is an inert scalar guarded by a discrete symmetry, born non-thermally during reheating. A non-minimal Kähler potential keeps higher-order corrections under control. Without it, the spectral index drifts toward one and clashes with observations. Matching the observed dark matter abundance then squeezes the allowed parameter space hard. The spectral index lands tightly near 0.972 to 0.974, inside current bounds. Couplings to dark matter also shift the predicted gravitational wave spectrum, tying the two sectors observably.
arxiv-2606-19812:
Anushree Sinha and three colleagues design human oversight for AI legal discovery in 2026. Discovery scans millions of files under strict legal rules. Agent workflows over guarded files face trajectory collapse: one early mislabel silently voids a whole privilege review.

A taxonomy sorts agent failures in legal search by functional stage. A four-layer verification design spans planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty scoring. Each layer intercepts failures before they compound downstream. Human-on-the-Loop escalation thresholds force attorney review past set uncertainty levels. Simulations on a synthetic discovery corpus test the design. Privilege-waiver risk falls by up to sixty-one percent against fully autonomous runs. Fewer than a quarter of documents route to attorneys at the same time. Calibrated thresholds thus buy legal safety without drowning reviewers. Each file a lawyer must check by hand costs time the team may not have to spare.
arxiv-2606-20112:
Zhenkai Zhang, Markus Hiller, Krista Ehinger, and Tom Drummond generate 3D CT volumes one voxel at a time with a model they call PRDiT. Their 2026 paper attacks a hard trade-off in medical image synthesis. High-resolution scans hold fine detail doctors need, yet producing whole volumes directly is costly and unstable for older models. Compressing through an autoencoder first avoids the cost but blurs the subtle structures that matter clinically.

PRDiT splits the work into two stages. A small local denoiser cleans overlapping 3D patches and handles broad, low-frequency structure. A global diffusion transformer then refines the high-frequency residuals across the full volume, using memory-efficient attention, which steadies training and preserves fine anatomy. On the LIDC-IDRI and RAD-ChestCT datasets, PRDiT beat HA-GAN, 3D LDM, and WDM-3D on FID, MMD, and Wasserstein scores, showing voxel-level generation can stay sharp and practical.
arxiv-2606-20212:
Josef Jon and Ondřej Bojar present CzechDocs, a parallel dataset of formatted documents built to test whether machine translation can preserve a document's layout while translating its words. Their 2026 paper covers Czech and the minority languages used in Czechia, mainly Ukrainian and English, with smaller shares of Vietnamese, Russian, and others. Documents come as HTML, DOCX, and PDF files, where headings, tags, and structure must survive translation intact for the result to be usable.

The authors compare the most common approaches to format-preserving translation on a validation subset. That split, together with an evaluation toolkit, is released publicly. A held-out test split is reserved for a future shared task on document-level translation with formatting preservation. The dataset responds to real demand: after 2022, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in Czechia needed legal, health, and school documents translated quickly, with web markup and accessibility structure kept whole.
arxiv-2606-20512:
Asa Shepard and Jeannie Albrecht tune repository guidance files for coding agents by probing them with synthetic bugs. Their 2026 paper starts from a contested question: AGENTS.md files supply operational knowledge that code alone lacks, yet studies disagree on whether such guidance helps or harms agent performance.

Probe-and-refine tuning uses synthetic bug-fix probes to diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use. How the guidance is produced, the authors show, is the decisive variable. Iterating against probes turns guidance writing from folklore into a testable procedure. Repositories can now improve the instructions their coding agents live by, measurably.
arxiv-2606-20612:
Tyler Chang and three colleagues trace how young people express themselves on Reddit across 13 years. Their 2026 paper analyzes 443,856 posts from 2010 to 2023 by authors who self-disclosed ages 11 to 24. Youth content diversity and its drift over time had little systematic examination.

Topic modeling, over-time statistics, and language-style measures identify the topics youth discuss and how posting patterns vary as cohorts age. The descriptive analysis follows the same platform from early adolescence into adulthood. A decade-scale window shows digital expression maturing alongside its authors. Developmental researchers gain a public, over-time corpus of youth voice in their own words.
arxiv-2606-21012:
Ruiming Guo and Ayush Bhandari introduce an asynchronous design in 2026 for multi-channel unlimited sampling, a method that recovers signals beyond the range of standard converters. It folds a signal modulo a bound, breaking the tradeoff between range and resolution. Existing methods rely on Chinese remainder unfolding and strict sync across channels.

Timing mismatch, jitter, and drift make strict synchronization fragile in practice. Their architecture removes the need for it. Spatial and temporal lifting is viewed as inducing smoothness over a graph of sensing channels. Recovery then stays robust to misalignment in time. Numerical experiments validate accurate recovery. Removing the sync demand makes this sensing more practical for real hardware, where perfect clock alignment across devices is rare.
arxiv-2606-21612:
Vladimir P. Burskii advances the general theory of boundary value problems in 2026, asking what a solution's boundary traces must satisfy for a completely general linear differential equation. For an equation of order l in a smooth bounded domain, the traces are the solution and its first l minus 1 normal derivatives on the boundary. They cannot be prescribed freely, as the Poisson equation already shows.

Burskii finds and studies the conditions linking these traces, conditions that let the solution be rebuilt from its traces and the equation's right-hand side. For constant-coefficient equations the conditions take the form of a generalized moment problem. The work extends von Neumann's founding idea of the general theory: understand boundary behavior once, for all equations at once, rather than equation by equation.
arxiv-2606-21712:
Tairan Xu, Leyang Xue, Zhan Lu, and seven colleagues rebuild the engine underneath batch AI inference in 2026. Offline jobs, synthetic data generation, evaluation sweeps, and reinforcement-learning rollouts now eat enormous compute, yet inference engines were designed for interactive chat. At millions of sequences, batch work shows wild load variation that only appears at runtime, and fleets of GPUs sit underused.

BatchGen's foundation is a sequence coroutine model: each sequence becomes a fine-grained, event-driven coroutine the runtime can reorganize on the fly. That enables bigger expert batches in sparse models, straggler mitigation, and work reallocation across devices. On a 128-GPU cluster it cuts batch completion time by up to 2.3 times, and on memory-constrained accelerators it beats the strongest offloading baseline by up to 9.6 times. The system is slated for open release.
arxiv-2606-22412:
Liangliang Shang, Lu Zhang, Bingfang Yang, and Stefano Moretti study rare top quark interactions in this 2026 paper. They probe an anomalous link among a top quark, a light quark, and a Z boson, a process the standard model suppresses heavily. Future muon colliders could expose such effects, framed with effective field theory.

The team studies muon collisions producing this final state at three energy levels, splitting the signal into six cases by how the top quark decays. Simulations model the signal and the standard model backgrounds that mimic it. Polarized muon beams and a fat jet method, which treats merged sprays as single jets, sharpen the signal. At the highest energy, the limit on the branching ratio reaches about one in a hundred million. That improves current CMS and ATLAS limits by a factor of a hundred to a thousand.
arxiv-2606-22512:
Hamidou Tembine models the conflict trap in Mali as a game across generations in this 2026 paper. Persistent instability in Mali and its neighbours is framed not as a temporary crisis but as a self-reproducing system. Grievances are inherited, distrust is passed down, and climatic shocks plus predatory resource extraction keep the cycle turning.

The framework is a Volterra mean-field game across generations, where memory, revenge incentives, and institutions shape future conflict. The analysis shows how war entrepreneurs funnel earnings from illicit resource deals into finance networks worldwide. It also warns that blunt regulation can backfire, speeding recruitment into armed groups. From the model, Tembine designs optimal policies meant to reshape the system over time, cutting the money and mindset feedback loops that sustain violence. The stated aim is an actionable architecture for durable peace and civilian protection across the Sahel.
arxiv-2606-22612:
Izabella Konicer and four colleagues study a special family of polygons in this 2026 geometry paper. The polygons are convex and have parallel opposite sides, a centrally balanced symmetry. The authors examine their affine equidistants, curves formed by points at a fixed affine distance, and relate the discrete polygons to smooth convex curves.

They show when the original polygon can be reconstructed from two derived objects: its Wigner caustic and its centre symmetry set. Their main inequality is a discrete version of an improved isoperimetric inequality, tying the squared perimeter to the polygon's area plus a term from the Wigner caustic. Equality holds exactly for equiangular polygons of constant width. Sharp area estimates follow as well: the Wigner caustic's oriented area is at most a quarter of the polygon's area, and the centre symmetry set's is at most the whole area. Both bounds cannot be improved.
arxiv-2606-22712:
Roberto Vila, Helton Saulo, and Felipe Quintino solve an estimation problem for inequality indices in this 2026 paper. Scale-invariant indices summarize a population regardless of units: the Gini coefficient, its generalizations, entropy-based measures, and variability indices all qualify. The authors define a broad class of such indices generated by homogeneous functions.

For gamma populations, they obtain explicit formulas for every index in the class. The key trick exploits independence between a sample's total sum and its Dirichlet proportions. That yields a simple unbiased estimator built as a U-statistic, proven exact for any index in the class under gamma populations. Worked examples illustrate the theory, and Monte Carlo simulations show the estimator performing well. The team also tests it under generalized gamma laws, and applies the indices to real data on GDP per capita across the Americas.
arxiv-2606-23012:
Aurora Faure Ragani and Robbin Bastiaansen design interventions against tipping in spatially extended systems in a 2026 paper. Tipping means a system flips from one stable state to another. In space, that flip need not happen everywhere at once. Fronts can creep or get pinned, states can coexist in patches, and patterns can form. Earlier work mostly described such behavior after the fact. No general method existed for steering it with well-placed local action. The authors supply a constrained optimization framework for that job.

Faure Ragani and Bastiaansen search for spatial interventions that maximize resilience or restore a desired state under resource limits. They demonstrate the method on the one-dimensional Allen-Cahn equation, a minimal model with two stable states. There, optimization works by shifting local tipping thresholds and guiding front motion. Small targeted changes decided system-wide outcomes, preventing collapse, triggering recovery, or confining damage.
arxiv-2606-23512:
Mobile apps often run slowly because some built-in code libraries were compiled at low optimization settings, and Hu and colleagues tackle that hidden problem in a 2026 software engineering paper. Compilers translate human-written code into machine code, and higher settings such as O2 or O3 usually produce faster programs than O0 or O1. The slowdown causes dropped frames, overheating, and wasted battery power for millions of users.

Their tool, OptDetect, inspects finished app files directly, with no source code or build records needed, and sorts code chunks by likely optimization level. It reaches about ninety-three percent accuracy on controlled tests and about eighty-two percent on real apps. Scanning nearly twenty-two thousand libraries from eight hundred thirty top apps, the team finds about thirty percent use low settings. Those settings affect most apps studied. Fixing them cuts processor work by roughly ten to sixty-three percent.
arxiv-2606-23812:
Esmaeili, Esmaili, and Serpico ask what the mix of atomic nuclei inside a neutrino source reveals about the source itself, in a 2026 paper on neutrino astronomy. High energy neutrinos and gamma rays are born together when accelerated particles collide inside extreme environments. Yet most neutrino sources show no matching gamma rays, a puzzle constraining how hidden the sources are. Whether the particles are plain protons or heavier nuclei has rarely been examined.

Taking the galaxy NGC 1068, a confirmed neutrino source, as their test case, the authors run detailed Monte Carlo simulations of nuclear and light cascades inside the source. Different injected compositions leave different fingerprints on the escaping emission. Gamma ray observations in the MeV to GeV band would strongly constrain the composition. A fresh analysis of archival COMPTEL data supports the case for future instruments.
arxiv-2606-23912:
Idrissov, Boshkayev, Tlemissov, and Quevedo work out the purely Newtonian version of a relativistic effect. The effect splits the natural vibration rates of a near circular orbit. Their 2026 paper treats classical mechanics. Around a spherical mass, an orbit's radial, vertical, and azimuthal oscillations share one rate, so orbits close neatly. Shirokov showed relativity splits these rates even for a spherical source. The authors ask what Newtonian asymmetry alone can do. They expand the gravity into mass multipoles and solve the coupled problem exactly.

A genuine quadrupole, the oblateness term, splits the radial and vertical rates: the true Newtonian Shirokov effect. An octupole splits them too. A dipole cannot split anything. It merely marks the center of mass offset, and it vanishes once coordinates are centered there. The offset instead shows up as a tilt of the orbital plane. Two clean, separate probes of a body's shape and its centering result.
arxiv-2606-24312:
Xiong extracts the marks of quantum phase transitions from very small systems, by tailoring the Hilbert space itself. Quantum critical points, where a material's ground state reorganises, are normally located with finite-size scaling and renormalisation ideas that demand large lattices and heavy computation. Writing alone in 2026, Xiong instead reshapes which quantum states the calculation keeps, pulling critical behaviour from the tailored space.

Applied to the one-dimensional XY model's second-order transition, the scheme recovers precise critical points and exponents from lattices of just fifty unit cells. The test then widens to a harder case: the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the one-dimensional XXZ chain. Critical parameters emerge from as few as twelve lattice sites. Such tiny systems are exactly what near-term quantum hardware and exact diagonalisation can handle. Xiong presents Hilbert-space tailoring as an efficient alternative route to mapping quantum criticality.
arxiv-2606-24412:
Kulkarni, Frenzel, and Ghiasvand bring big data clusters on supercomputers inside the notebook interface scientists already live in. High-performance computing systems could crush big data workflows. Standing up a cluster on one scares off beginners, though, and splits the workflow across tools. BiJuTy, their 2026 utility, is an interactive, HPC-aware lifecycle manager and performance check tool. It lives inside JupyterHub.

The interface walks the user from cluster setup through an initial performance check. Multiple clusters can be managed directly within the Jupyter notebook environment, without switching tools. Performance metrics gathered from several sources feed a simple tuning workflow. A worked example shows BiJuTy deployed to tune a real big data processing pipeline. Kulkarni's team targets the access gap explicitly. The same interface should serve first-time users and experienced hands. Supercomputer-scale data processing becomes a guided procedure, rather than a systems rite of passage.
arxiv-2606-24512: This paper builds a multi-stage separation-and-classification framework guided by complementary acoustic-to-semantic alignment. The building builds. Their framework is multi-stage separation-and-classification. The guiding guides complementary acoustic-to-semantic. It is audio AI. The building is a.
arxiv-2606-24612:
Scholes and colleagues navigate on foot using the Earth's magnetic scars, instead of satellites. Satellite positioning is fragile where signals are jammed or blocked. The crust's permanent magnetic anomalies form a stable, mappable fingerprint, varying from place to place. Their wearable sensor, a free induction decay optically pumped magnetometer built in house, measures the Earth's field precisely and stably enough to use them.

An end-to-end field testing qualifies the sensor. It then measures how much adding its data improves a dead reckoning position estimate, navigation by tracking steps and heading alone. Over a walking route longer than five hundred metres, lasting about six minutes, the fused system achieves a radial position error of only a couple of metres. The error follows the reported spread closely. Scholes's 2026 trial shows a satellite independent position layer, accurate enough to matter when GNSS disappears.
arxiv-2606-24712:
Shivani Kamtikar and five colleagues present TACTFUL, a robot system that finds and identifies objects by touch alone. People do this easily, naming keys or a bottle inside a cluttered bag without looking. Robots, by contrast, lean heavily on vision and struggle in confined or dark spaces. TACTFUL uses a multi fingered hand with tactile sensors. It explores a confined workspace alone, finds objects through contact, and rebuilds their shapes from touch. Training happened entirely on real hardware, with no simulation.

One learned policy drives the exploration. A dynamic reward schedule balances wide searching of the workspace with close refinement of each surface found. On real world objects the system reached a 77 percent success rate. Its average reconstruction error was 0.015 metres. It also beat the baseline approaches tested. Touch, paired with structured learning, can thus serve as a primary sense, not a camera backup.
arxiv-2606-24812:
Antonio Riotto revisits where the quasinormal mode expansion of a Schwarzschild black hole's response actually converges. Quasinormal modes are the black hole's characteristic ringing tones. Expanding its retarded Green function in those modes is standard, but the sum converges only in a limited region, controlled by a second lightcone distance. Riotto approaches the question through radial scattering. The tortoise coordinate, a stretched radial variable, has a natural reflection point.

Reflecting about that point maps the Regge Wheeler problem to a mirror problem with the same mode spectrum. The reflection is not a spacetime symmetry and leaves the potential changed. Yet it pictures the second lightcone distance as an image contribution, like a reflection in a mirror. The same structure appears in the anti de Sitter Green function, where a boundary bouncing light ray explains it. The result gives the convergence condition a spectral meaning.
arxiv-2606-24912:
Jackson Loth, Xavier Riley, Simon Dixon, and Emmanouil Benetos teach a guitar transcription model to predict how hard each note is played. Velocity, the intensity of a note, is rarely predicted. Datasets lack such labels, and the notion lacks a clean definition away from the piano. The team's workaround is synthetic data. Virtual instruments generate guitar audio where every note's strength is known by construction.

A model is pretrained on that synthetic data to learn the skill. Its weights then transfer into a second model trained on real guitar audio. The transferred model keeps the velocity skill while gaining real world accuracy and generalisation. On synthetic tests it beats a baseline lacking the pretrained weights. Note transcription also improves slightly, though the gain is small and not always significant. Overall performance matches the state of the art, with the new skill added on top.
arxiv-2606-25412:
Optimisation software is trusted daily, but its textbook theory is rarely checked by machine. Yiyang Zhang and Kenneth Shum formalise line search methods in the Lean 4 theorem prover in 2026. Line search is the step size choosing routine inside gradient descent: try a step, test it against a rule, shrink if it fails. The formalisation covers descent directions, backtracking search, and the classical Armijo, Goldstein, and Wolfe acceptance conditions, including nonmonotone variants that allow occasional uphill steps.

The centrepiece is a machine checked proof of the Zoutendijk theorem, the result underpinning global convergence claims for gradient methods. Every definition and argument is rendered as Lean code the prover verifies. The authors position the work as verified groundwork for building more advanced nonlinear programming algorithms whose correctness is guaranteed rather than assumed.
arxiv-2606-25612:
Given a directed network and a set of starting nodes, which nodes can each starter reach? Shimon Kogan and Merav Parter give a near optimal deterministic algorithm for that multi source reachability problem in 2026. Running a search from every source wastes time, and full transitive closure overshoots. Their method runs in time governed by the rectangular matrix multiplication exponent, the cost of multiplying the source by node matrix against the full adjacency structure.

For dense graphs the algorithm computes reachability from a substantial polynomial number of sources in near linear time, breaking a super quadratic barrier. It also beats the best previous randomised method, which carried an extra factor in its exponent. A matching lower bound comes from a three layer graph construction showing the problem is exactly as hard as the Boolean matrix product at its core.
arxiv-2606-25812:
Guessing a galaxy's distance from its colours, the photometric redshift, is only as good as the test bench behind it. A Wittje leads this Euclid Consortium analysis in 2026 of the PAU Survey, which images the sky through forty narrow optical filters, a design promising unusually precise colour redshifts. Before trusting the real data, the team build a mock universe. From the Euclid Flagship 2 catalogue they generate PAUS like simulations, complete with realistic photometric noise and the survey's target selection rules.

The mock catalogue then grades the redshift machinery end to end. Accuracy and precision are traced across the sample, showing where narrow band photometry delivers and where it strains. Realistic simulation matters because idealised tests flatter the method. The study gives both surveys a calibrated expectation for PAUS redshifts, and a template for checking Euclid era photometry before the sky data arrive.
arxiv-2606-26012:
Jakob Raupach, Tom-Lukas Breitkopf, Anton Herrmann, and André Nichterlein study a graph problem about thinning out dense spots. Bounded Density Vertex Deletion asks a sharp question. Can deleting at most k vertices bring the densest subgraph's density under a target value? Density here means edges divided by vertices. Bazgan and colleagues had left the problem's difficulty open for treewidth, a standard measure of graph structure.

Hardness results settle most of the landscape. The problem is W-one-hard for treedepth and for feedback vertex number. Hardness for treewidth follows from those results. Two larger parameters rescue tractability. The problem is fixed-parameter tractable for max leaf number and for vertex integrity. Fixing the target density as a constant changes the picture again. Even cliquewidth, a parameter below treewidth, then admits an efficient algorithm. The map cleanly separates workable parameter regimes from hopeless ones.
arxiv-2606-26412:
WebGPU lets ordinary web pages run programs on a computer's graphics processor, and Igor Santos-Grueiro asks what private signals leak through that access despite built-in safety checks. Validation, meaning the rules that reject unsafe code, protects memory but does not hide shared state inside the browser, driver, and chip. Santos-Grueiro built a measuring system called WGPULens to probe that shared state.

WGPULens separates controlled tests, a study with real participants, and a crawl of popular web pages. In controlled tests, leftover state from earlier shader compilation, meaning the step that turns page code into chip instructions, revealed what had run before across some site and browser boundaries. WebGPU activity also proved highly distinctive for each participant. The crawl found real pages mostly just checking whether WebGPU exists, and early fixes point toward keeping compilation caches separate by source.
arxiv-2606-26512:
Yueli Han, Lu Lu, and Jianfeng Wang prove a bound on vibration values of a graph operator. Graphs have triangles as their smallest loops. The curl-curl operator measures how flow circulates around those triangles. A long-standing conjecture by Duval and Reiner predicts its spectrum, the full set of vibration values, is controlled by a sequence counting triangles at each vertex.

The authors prove the conjecture's first two steps. The sum of the two largest vibration values never exceeds the combined size of that sequence's first two entries. As a corollary, they bound the two largest values of a fuller graph operator combining divergence and curl. The result extends to a broader family of operators built on triangle-like structures. It marks concrete progress toward the full conjecture.
arxiv-2606-26612:
Rafael Padilla, Andrew W. Tate, Dhruv Ram, and Cem Yuksel present HiPR, a rendering scheduler for interactive path tracing. Path tracing simulates light bouncing through a scene to make realistic images. It is too slow for comfortable scene editing, since most renderers recompute the whole frame after any change. Artists need instant feedback while they adjust lights and objects.

HiPR updates only some pixels after each change. It ranks pixels through a hierarchy of light-path dependencies, starting from what changed. Priority follows likely visual impact. Unchanged pixels keep their previous values, so feedback is immediate. Over time the image still converges to the correct, unbiased result. The approach spreads rendering cost instead of paying it all at once. It was demonstrated live at a computer graphics conference session.
arxiv-2606-26712:
Jingjun Gu and five colleagues present MLFFM-SegDiff, a model that outlines skin lesions in dermoscopic images. Precise outlines guide diagnosis of skin disease. Lesions have blurred borders, low contrast, and varied shapes. Hair and shadows add clutter. Diffusion models, which refine an image step by step from noise, have recently done well at such outlining tasks.

Their design strengthens the diffusion model's denoising network. A dual-path encoder lets the noisy mask and the skin image interact closely. A fusion module enriches the features passed across the network using attention, which weighs the most relevant parts. A boundary-sensitive penalty term sharpens edge accuracy, and its strength can be configured. The authors report improved segmentation over existing diffusion-based approaches, especially on fine boundary detail.
arxiv-2606-26912:
Azadeh Alavi and six colleagues design a fixed quantum circuit for estimating molecular energies. Variational quantum eigensolvers prepare a trial state with a parameterised circuit, the ansatz, and tune it toward the molecule's ground energy. Architecture search can find compact circuits but adds an expensive outer loop. Their Givens-exchange ansatz is deterministic and fixed in shape.

The circuit starts from the best simple basis state. Three layers of single-qubit rotations alternate with two blocks of Givens exchanges, rotations mixing pairs of states. Parameters are tuned using only measured energy values. Test molecules included lithium hydride and water Hamiltonians built from verified coefficients. Every run across six random seeds hit chemical accuracy. Average errors beat published architecture-search results on two systems, though the circuit is larger.
arxiv-2606-27012:
Abdoli and Löwen study a tiny system of two trapped particles joined by a spring. Each particle sits in its own heat bath, so the pair lives at two temperatures at once. The pair also shows odd mobility, meaning a push along one direction partly drives motion sideways. The authors ask how this odd response changes heat flow and swirling motion inside the traps.

Solving the model exactly, Abdoli and Löwen find that odd mobility links the two particles with a handed twist. Each particle alone still spreads evenly in all directions. The twist appears only when uneven heat, the spring link, and odd response all act together. Flipping the odd response flips the twist. Heat moves between the baths more easily, yet total heat flow and waste stay fixed when the handedness flips.
arxiv-2606-27112:
Lee proposes a corrected heavy-ball version of Q-learning, the classic method that teaches agents action values from rewards. Heavy-ball momentum, borrowed from optimisation, adds a push from the previous update to speed learning. Plain versions can misbehave, so a residual weighting correction reshapes the recursion. The correction makes the averaged update maps share a common eigenvector, a shared stable direction. Convergence of the corrected method is established in this theory paper from 2026.

Conditions are also derived where the corrected method provably converges faster than standard Q-learning. Analysis views the algorithms as switched linear systems, whose behaviour is governed by a joint spectral radius. That lens is uncommon in Q-learning theory and yields fresh insight into momentum effects. The same construction extends to linear function approximation, where values are estimated by weighted feature sums. Matching convergence and acceleration statements hold there too.
arxiv-2606-27412:
Sun leads a team fixing a subtle failure in three-dimensional scene graph generation: relations should transform correctly when the viewer moves. A scene graph lists objects and the relations between them. Under yaw rotations of the viewpoint, directional relations like left or behind must rotate with the frame, while contact and support relations like standing on should stay fixed. Current models entangle the two behaviours and mispredict after rotation. Their Transformation-Aware Decoupling framework splits relation reasoning into stable and directional branches in this computer vision paper of 2026.

Stable object features support the split, and transformation-specific descriptors plus group-aware training signals keep the branches distinct. Merged, they produce the standard multi-label relation predictions. On the standard benchmark the method reaches state-of-the-art robustness under yaw changes without any rotation augmentation during training. Relations learn their own transformation rules.
arxiv-2606-27912:
José Carlos Díaz-Ramos and Juan Manuel Lorenzo-Naveiro classify a family of foliations in 2026. The setting is rank one symmetric spaces of noncompact type. The foliations are polar and homogeneous. A group action is polar when a section exists. A section is a connected submanifold meeting every orbit at right angles. Homogeneous foliations arise from such group actions. The classification is up to orbit equivalence.

Polar actions on these spaces had been studied case by case. A complete classification organises that landscape. Foliations group into classes under orbit equivalence. Two foliations are equivalent when an isometry maps the orbits of one onto the orbits of the other. The result completes the picture for this class of spaces. It gives geometers a definitive list to work from, rather than scattered examples.
arxiv-2606-28112:
Image restoration models increasingly use degradation-aware prompts or priors. Success is usually judged only by final image quality, a weak test of what the prior means. Xinrui Wu and Lichen Huang propose BiDeMem in 2026, a bidirectional degradation memory designed to be explainable. A query built from input statistics and restoration features retrieves a few memory slots. The same slot identity conditions the restoration. During training only, it also drives a forward-degradation explanation path.

Controlled tests separate the memory's contribution. Variants with only a correction head, a dense query prior, or a static global prior each fall below the full model, by roughly a quarter of a decibel. Stronger residual supervision and a wider degradation head also stay below it. Intervention probes show quality is preserved while sensitivity to wrong priors increases. The memory thus works both as a restoration module and as a falsifiable explanation.
arxiv-2606-28212:
R. Alkofer, M. N. Ferreira, A. S. Miramontes, J. M. Morgado, and J. Papavassiliou examine the quark propagator, a function describing how a quark moves through the strong force, in a gauge choice called Landau gauge. Widely used approximations had predicted pairs of poles at complex positions, an awkward feature for theory.

Alkofer and colleagues couple the standard gap equation to the full quark-gluon interaction instead of a simplified one. For slow, sub-GeV momenta they find a pair of real poles whose residues carry opposite signs, and no sign of the complex poles at all. Three pieces of the interaction drive the effect together. Their joint action pins the poles to the real axis and yields a sturdy constituent quark mass.
arxiv-2606-28912:
Weiss asks what colour the sky is for eyes that are not human, and gives a computational way to answer. Daylight contains many wavelengths, yet humans see the sky as blue because of how our three cone types respond. Under those responses, skylight and a pure blue light are metamers, meaning different lights that produce exactly the same cone signals and so look identical.

His method finds, for any visual system, the single-wavelength light that would be a metamer for a chosen input light. Feeding in published sensitivity curves for many species, he computed the dominant wavelength of each species' skylight metamer. Animals with two, three or four colour channels all had such metamers. Their dominant wavelengths varied drastically between species. Many were very different from the blue humans perceive. Sky colour, the result shows, belongs to the viewer as much as to the light.
arxiv-2606-29012:
Han, Wu, Cheng and Zhu introduce the game changer problem: how an outside designer can rewrite a game's payoffs so a chosen outcome becomes the only equilibrium. The twist is that every payoff entry must come from a finite set of allowed values, like whole numbers. Earlier reward redesign work allowed any real numbers and leaned on linear programming, giving looser answers.

With discrete rewards, the authors give simple feasibility characterisations for two-player zero-sum and general-sum games. These tests say when the goal can be met at all. The discrete structure also yields exact optimality, not approximations. It enables efficient dynamic programming algorithms, which build solutions step by step from smaller cases. The result is a sharper alternative to continuous formulations: the designer learns precisely which target outcomes are reachable, and the cheapest payoff table that makes that outcome the unique result.
arxiv-2606-29512:
Cotter and Gyöngy prove theorems about the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, the fluid flow equations with random forcing. These equations model fluids such as water, with noise from Wiener processes and Poisson martingale measures. Their focus is uniqueness: whether one starting state leads to only one solution.

They also prove continuous dependence on the initial condition, meaning that small changes at the start produce only small changes in the flow that follows. Together, uniqueness and continuous dependence make a problem well-posed, so predictions from the model are trustworthy. Their results generalize earlier theorems cited in the paper, widening the conditions under which the conclusions hold. The work strengthens the foundations used whenever uncertain flows are modelled with random forcing.
arxiv-2606-29612:
Chestnov, Crisanti, and Giroux present a new method for finding Landau singularities of Feynman integrals, the special points where a particle physics calculation can blow up. Their method reads the singularities off from where the Euler characteristic, a topological count tied to the integral, drops. That reformulation turns a hard analytic problem into something computable.

Working over finite fields, number systems with finitely many elements, makes the required elimination steps tractable even for multi-scale integrals on the multi-loop frontier. The algorithm hands back the full, genuine set of singularities, subject to conditions that can be tested in practice. A proof-of-concept implementation handles classes beyond current methods. Examples include two-loop non-planar six-point diagrams and a fully massive envelope graph at three loops. Several newly found singularities are unexpectedly complex compared with previously known ones, both in general dimension and in four dimensions.
arxiv-2606-29812:
Zou and eight colleagues identify a missing habit in multimodal large language models: cross-view consistency. Two views of the same thing that mean the same should lead to the same answer, but standard training rewards each view on its own.

Their method, ConsistRoll, adds consistency to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, training where answers can be checked as right or wrong. It places an original image and a meaning-preserving changed view in the same group of samples, and pays a joint reward only when both answers are correct and agree. The authors show in theory that this adds a correction term that plain data augmentation lacks, punishing answers that depend on the view. Benchmarks in maths, general tasks, and hallucination confirm robust gains.
arxiv-2606-29912:
Iwona Chlebicka, Minhyun Kim, Ying Li, and Chao Zhang build a potential theory for Orlicz equations, a class of elliptic equations whose growth rule generalizes power growth. Classical theory leans heavily on scaling, the idea that stretching a solution gives another solution, but Orlicz equations lack that property and many standard tools break. The authors therefore rebuild the theory from scratch, without assuming any homogeneity at all.

They prove a global smoothness result for obstacle problems and build a balayage theory, which redistributes mass while preserving key values. They construct the Riesz measures attached to superharmonic functions and identify the related capacitary potentials, with size estimates for polar sets. These functions are also shown to be nearly continuous in a measure sense. As the main application, superharmonic functions prove to be exactly the renormalized solutions of measure data problems, an equivalence that is new even for power growth without homogeneity.
arxiv-2606-30112:
Daphne Broski-Laing and twelve colleagues present the first JWST phase curve of a white dwarf and brown dwarf pair. The system, ZTFJ0038+2030, pairs a dead star's remnant with a failed star. Tidal locking gives the brown dwarf hot Jupiter-like atmospheric dynamics. A full orbit of spectra separates the two components' light. A total eclipse of the white dwarf helps that separation.

The spectra cover most of the brown dwarf's total emission. That enables a nearly model-independent energy balance calculation. Day-to-night heat transport efficiency comes out at ten percent or less. The nightside spectrum resembles non-irradiated T dwarfs, confirming weak redistribution. A strong carbon dioxide absorption feature marks the nightside asymmetrically. Yet retrieved abundances show carbon dioxide spread evenly by longitude. The brown dwarf's internal glow dates the system precisely. Its age falls between seven and a half and nine billion years.
arxiv-2606-30312:
Roland Roller and fifteen colleagues release a dataset for finding personal information hidden in chat transcripts. Dialog data from healthcare and social research are valuable but privacy-sensitive. Sharing them requires removing names and other private details first. Tools for scrubbing them need real training and test data. DialogPII, released in 2026, supplies synthetic dialogs with careful annotation.

Eight interaction scenarios are covered, from emergency calls to therapy sessions. Insurance, customer support, police reports, and medical interviews are included. Nineteen entity types are annotated across eleven languages. Dialogs were generated with language models, then curated by hand. Localization adapts them to specific countries and cities. Every dialog was also synthesized to speech and transcribed back. Written and speech-derived versions align across all of them. Baseline recognition models and validation studies accompany the release.
arxiv-2606-30412:
Gaurab Pokharel and three colleagues ask how to tell whether a language model's rankings of people deserve trust. Such rankings now inform housing allocation and hospital triage. Ranking many people at once is cognitively hard and error-prone. Pairwise comparisons, aggregated into an order, are the classic fix. But a judge's pairwise calls may contradict themselves. Two consistency checks are proposed before any commitment.

One check counts circular triads within a single run. That coefficient of consistency is cheap and model-free. Distance measures between rankings capture variability across runs instead. Theory and practice show the two checks measure different things. Both are needed to judge reliability properly. Tests span homelessness services and emergency department triage. Three leading models show very different consistency profiles. Guidelines help practitioners assess a model before deploying it. Committing to an unchecked ranker is the risk they target.
arxiv-2606-30912:
Eva Pospíšilová, Marek Mihalkovič, Naďa Beronská and Marek Gebura map a family of layered crystal structures. The structures are polytypes related to the tungstate La2WO6. A polytype is a stacking of blocks, here labelled N and H, with N from 3 to 7. Their compositions drift from the ideal formula. The team set out the construction rules behind the family. They checked each member's energy per atom against every competing lanthanum-oxygen-tungsten compound. Density functional theory supplied the ternary convex hull, the map of stable phases.

Surprisingly, the family's ground state was a structure not yet made in the lab. Labelled oP36, it matches the known gadolinium analogue. A second candidate, mC72, was modelled on a samarium molybdate. It sat only about 5 millielectronvolts per atom above the hull, close enough to be experimentally accessible.
arxiv-2606-31012:
Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang and Hongyi Wen build a way to grade the interactivity of AI-generated teaching material. Explorable explanations let learners manipulate a simulation and watch it respond, and language models can now generate them quickly. But existing checks mostly test whether the code runs or the pictures look right, not whether the interactions themselves teach well. Their framework, EE-Eval, extracts a finite state machine from each generated explanation: the states a learner can reach, the actions offered, and the feedback given.

Each extracted machine is compared with an ideal one encoding the teaching intent, using graph metrics and embedding similarity over states, actions and feedback. Across thousands of generated explanations spanning 127 concepts from 6 AI models, EE-Eval separated interaction quality beyond surface correctness. It also aligned with human judgments of interactivity and teaching value far more strongly than existing baselines.
arxiv-2606-31112:
Olamide, Srinivasan, and Aldarmaki ask a basic question about speech recognition for atypical speech: what counts as an error? Speech from people who stutter can be scored against two valid references. A verbatim reference keeps every repetition and prolongation. An intended reference removes the disfluencies and shows the clean text. Most evaluations pick one reference without saying so. That choice quietly rewards systems that delete disfluencies, even when a user needs a faithful record.

The authors benchmark 11 speech recognition models from three design families. They score each model against both references, using stuttered speech as the case study. Model scores and rankings shift a lot between the two styles. Their point is practical: the right reference depends on the use case, and picking it carelessly can pick the wrong model.
arxiv-2608-00012: Obshazard-bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Foundation Models for Real-Time Disaster, arXiv 2608-00012. The disaster bench. The paper endures in the archive. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-12:
The second part of Tract Baba Metzia fills volume twelve of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud. Part one covered finds, deposits, and wages; the debate now presses deeper into trade. The tractate's name means the Middle Gate, between the damage law before it and the property law after.

Usury rules take the front: what counts as forbidden interest, and how honest profit differs from it. Then come sales, leases of fields and houses, and the duties of neighbors sharing a courtyard wall. The rabbis argue from real contracts and real quarrels. The volume rounds out the Talmud's fullest picture of daily commerce.
bancroft-history-us-vol-12:
Ratification fills the second volume of Bancroft's History of the Formation of the Constitution, from 1882. State by state, conventions debate the new frame of rule. Fierce foes warn of tyranny while friends plead for union and strength.

Bancroft follows the close votes and sharp pamphlet wars with care. The republic's birth, in his telling, ends in hard-won consent. His long career closes with the founding completed on paper and in law. The volume serves as a farewell from America's great romantic historian, who spent fifty years telling the one story of liberty taking lasting form.
benson-room-in-the-tower-1912:
E. F. Benson led his set of ghost tales from 1912 with a tale of a room in a tower. A man dreams of the room for years. In each dream a grim host bids him wait for a guest who is long dead. Then he is asked to sleep there in real life.

Benson writes with crisp pace and cold nerve. His ghosts show no soft side. Tales of caterpillars, trams, and blind dread fill the set. It is a high mark for ghost tales of its age, lean and cruel. Benson came from a house of church chiefs and school heads. His cool, patrician voice makes his cruel ghosts feel all the more stark.
bergson-introduction-metaphysics-1912:
An Introduction to Metaphysics is Bergson's most famous short work, printed here in the 1912 English version by T. E. Hulme. The French philosopher sets out his method in one sustained argument: intuition, not analysis, is how thought reaches reality.

Analysis, Bergson says, circles a thing and gives symbols; intuition enters it and grasps its duration, the flow of inner time. He applies the contrast to the self, to movement, and to life itself. The essay is dense but exhilarating, a key to all his larger books. Hulme's version carried Bergson's fame through the English-speaking world.
berkman-prison-memoirs-anarchist-1912:
Alexander Berkman published Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist in 1912. Berkman, a Russian-born anarchist in New York, had shot steel magnate Henry Clay Frick in 1892 during the Homestead strike. He served fourteen years in American prisons, most at Western Penitentiary in Pennsylvania.

Berkman told of brutal guards, solitary cells, and the small kindnesses that kept men human inside. He also traced his own change from a would-be martyr to a man who questioned his act. The memoir refuses self-pity and judges the prison system from within. It stands as a classic of prison writing and of anarchist life stories in America.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-4-:
Maudslay's fourth volume of Bernal Díaz's True History, from 1912, covers the siege and fall of Mexico. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, fell in 1521 after a brutal fight across its causeways and canals. Díaz had stood in that fight as a foot soldier, and his old-age account carries the memory in his bones.

One volume of the set, the third, is a portfolio of maps only, so the story runs through volumes one, two, four, and five. In this volume the long campaign reaches its grim peak. Díaz records hunger, loss, and the city's ruin without turning away. It is the conquest's climax told by a man who swung a sword in it.
bosanquet-individuality-value-1912:
The Principle of Individuality and Value, published in 1912, prints Bosanquet's Gifford Lectures, his full statement in metaphysics. Its subject is the concrete universal: how the whole lives in each part, and how finite selves gain value and meaning within the Absolute.

Bosanquet argues that a self grows by range. The more of the world it can hold in harmony, the more real and valuable it is. Evil and error appear as partial harmonies awaiting completion. The lectures are abstract and elevated in manner. They represent British idealism at its most systematic, delivered in its cathedral style.
boutroux-historical-studies-1912:
Fred Rothwell translated a set of Emile Boutroux's French studies on the history of philosophy in 1912. The French title, Etudes d'histoire de la philosophie, states the plan in plain terms. Each study takes up past thought on its own ground. Boutroux was known for close, fair reading of other minds.

In these pages he works through major figures and schools from earlier centuries. He asks what problem each thinker faced and how the answer fit its time. The method treats old systems as live attempts, not museum pieces. Students of Boutroux value the set as a model of his craft. It also records French scholarship of his era.
boutroux-william-james-1912:
American thinker William James drew readers across the Atlantic, and French philosopher Emile Boutroux was among them. Boutroux published his study William James in French in 1911. Archibald and Barbara Henderson brought the short book into English the next year, in 1912.

Writing as a French spiritualist, Boutroux explains James and his pragmatism to European readers. He presents James's views on truth, belief, and religious life with care and sympathy. At the same time he marks where his own thought parts from the American's. The study shows two traditions in direct talk with each other. It remains a neat period portrait of James.
butler-notebooks-1912:
Samuel Butler, the English writer behind Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, filled private notebooks for most of his adult life. He never meant them for print in this form. After his death, his friend Henry Festing Jones arranged the notes by theme, and they were published in 1912.

The short entries cover art, science, religion, money, and daily life, often in a few dry sentences. Butler mocks Darwin's followers, questions church doctrine, and praises plain common sense. Some notes are jokes; others hold the seeds of his books. Read together, they show one of the sharpest and most contrary minds of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-vi:
The Council of Vienne, called by Clement V in 1308 for 1 October 1310, finally opened on 16 October 1311. Delays came from the Templar trials and the case against Boniface VIII. Its brief covered the Knights Templar, their members and lands, the Holy Land, the Catholic faith, and improvement of the Church and its clergy. Archbishops came with chosen bishops, bearing written reform proposals.

Decrees preserved in the Clementines touch Franciscan Spirituals, poverty disputes among Minorites, mendicants, convent visitation, Beguines, church hours, and religious foundations. The council also addressed the Holy Land question, while most of its acts survive only in a fragment found in Paris. Reform proposals, gravamina, fill the entry's closing survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-restored-:
Jesuits back from suppression fill this entry, from 1814 to 1912. Pius VII had made up his mind to restore the Society while held in France. Once back in Rome he acted fast, issuing Solicitudo omnium ecclesiarum on 7 August 1814. Thaddeus Brzozowski, head in Russia, thus gained charge of the whole revived Society.

Russia had kept the flame alive. Pius VI let the order go on there, and its men chose Czerniewicz, Lenkiewicz, and Kareu as vicars-general, then Gruber and Brzozowski as generals. Russia drove the Jesuits from Saint Petersburg in 1815 and from the whole land in 1820, yet the order rose anew worldwide, with provinces, missions, and colleges.
cervantes-don-quixote-shelton-1612:
Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote in Spain, and Thomas Shelton made it English in 1612. Shelton's was the first English version, and the first in any tongue but Spanish. Don Quixote, a lean old squire mad on tales of knights, rides out to win fame.

With fat, shrewd Sancho Panza at his side, he fights windmills he takes for giants. Inns become castles and flocks become armies in his wild mind. The pair talk, argue, and grow fond as the joke turns kind. Shelton's brisk prose still reads with speed and fun. Later versions abound, but Shelton keeps the raw early flavor.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Fever rules Volume 5 of Filson Young's Columbus, as the Admiral returns to his colony at Isabella on March 29th and finds it in a deplorable condition. The pretty lake beside the town is a fever trap fed by malarial marshes. Half the colony lies incapacitated, the well nursing the sick, and all productive work at a standstill. Crops sown in January stand ready for reaping with no one to reap them, the virgin soil mocking its starving planters.

Young writes the second voyage's colony as a hospital with a flag. Columbus's energy, the one resource never in fever, is spent on food, discipline, and exploration of Cuba instead of gold. Readers in the fifth volume learn why the New World enterprise nearly died of its own settlement: the discoverer could find continents but not, at Isabella's lake, a healthy acre. The romance of 1492 has become logistics and medicine.
cia-0000008012:
Laos rarely made headlines, yet CIA analysts forecast its course to July 1956 in a June 1955 paper. The small kingdom had gained independence from France, but the Pathet Lao movement held ground in the north. A fragile royal government tried to unite the country.

The estimate weighs the throne's strength, the army's limits, and pressure from communist neighbors. Washington was starting to treat Laos as part of a wider Southeast Asian contest. Later, the country became the scene of a long secret war. This early forecast shows the concerns were present in Washington from the very start of involvement.
cia-0000009912:
A United States Air Force A-26 was brought down near Ban Ban, in Xieng Khouang province, an October 1967 report states. The A-26 was a Second World War attack bomber returned to service for Laos's night war. Ban Ban sat on a contested valley road.

Slow, low aircraft over Laos took losses out of proportion to their numbers. A downing report started the familiar chain: crew fate unknown, then checked against prisoner and grave reports. Night losses were the hardest to trace of all. This file marks one A-26 and its crew entering that uncertain record.
cia-0000010612:
In September 1952, CIA analysts wrote an estimate on whether the government of Mohammad Mossadeq could stay in power in Iran. Mossadeq was Iran's prime minister, and he had seized the country's oil industry from British control. His stand made him a hero to many Iranians and a problem for London and Washington.

The estimate weighs the forces lined up for and against him. It covers his quarrel with the Shah, the oil crisis squeezing Iran's economy, and the shadow of the communist movement. Read today, it shows Washington counting down the months of a leader it would help remove in the coup one year later.
cia-0000012412:
Paris opens the debriefings' third phase with meeting number thirty-one, on September 20, 1961. The City of Light took its turn hosting the secrets. A new city meant new cover and new safe flats. It also meant new risks, watched by a different police. The tradecraft adapted as the operation moved its most precious meetings onto French ground for the autumn.

The record begins the French chapter of the case in order. Paris sessions picked up the London rhythm within days. For readers, the page shows a great operation changing stages without missing a beat.
cia-0000013612:
Argentina's prospects are weighed in a CIA paper from May 1965, in the long shadow of Juan Perón. Perón had been driven into exile a decade before. His movement was banned from honest elections, yet his name still decided them. Every ballot and every barracks in the blue-and-white republic measured itself against the exiled man's ghost, and the elected government of the day ruled on sufferance.

The paper takes the past's measure as a force in the present. It weighs the generals, the unions, and the Peronist vote together. For readers, it shows a country arguing with its own history, watched closely from Washington.
cia-0000014712: Views on a presidential statement on the Rosenbergs fill a CIA file dated November 1, 1952. The president's words on a death penalty spy case carried weight worldwide. The file gathered how those words were received. It belongs to the months when the couple's fate rested in part on mercy from the White House.
cia-0000015312: A letter to Sam Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It takes up Leon Davidson's possible role, per the clipped title. Davidson had become a topic in his own right by then. Officials swapped views on the man as much as on his claims about space messages.
cia-0000015412: W. E. Lexow, chief of the Applied Science Division, wrote to Major Tacker on July 5, 1958, about letters from Fred Kirsch. Lexow enclosed a copy of one Kirsch letter and noted that Tacker had agreed to answer it. In the agency's view, the Air Force man was the proper voice on such matters. The short exchange shows saucer mail being routed to the desk that owned it.
cia-0000021512: Two American men and one American woman were reported held prisoner by the PL in a CIA record dated April 3, 1971. PL in the clipped title most likely means the Pathet Lao of Laos. The record gives no names in its title, so none is added here. Reports of civilian captives widened the prisoner watch beyond downed airmen alone.
cia-0000022812: Two American prisoners of war were held by communists in Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1974 reports. The catalog gives an acquisition date in its clipped tail, in 1974 by the file's dating. Cambodia's war had swallowed many men whose names sat on the missing lists. A detention report from there, even late, was chased for the sake of a final count.
cia-0000039312:
An American prisoner allegedly worked for the Viet Cong in the Quang Da Special Zone, a CIA record dated April 6, 1971 states. Collaboration charges were the hardest claims in the prisoner files. They shadowed a man's name long after the war around him moved on.

Inside, the allegation is recorded as it reached the agency during the war. Such reports could rest on rumor, pressure, or a captor's staged account. The file preserves the claim without settling it. Later readers meet the case as officials did: an accusation in the record, a man at its center, and no easy way to know the whole truth.
cia-0000042812:
President Cristiani postponed his trip to the United States, in a CIA record dated January 1, 1990. A president's travel plans are usually fixed far ahead of time. Putting one off, at short notice, signaled trouble at home.

Inside, the postponement is recorded with the crisis behind it in view. The Jesuit case had made a Washington visit awkward for Cristiani. American lawmakers were asking hard questions about aid and justice. A visit staged for goodwill risked turning into a public trial of his record instead. The file captures diplomacy bent by scandal, in which a calendar change said more about a president's position than many speeches could have said.
cia-0000045212:
Ungo denied responsibility in the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. A denial from the left's best known leader was a serious act. The opposition needed the crime kept far from its own name.

Inside, his firm disavowal of any part in the seizure is preserved. Denials shape a crisis as surely as claims of credit do. They draw the lines along which blame is allowed to travel. The file holds the left's line as Ungo drew it early in the case, before the talks and trades that finally brought the young woman home.
cia-0000049012: An excerpt from 1981, kept in a CIA item, weighs whether the right or the left carried out assassinations in El Salvador. In that war, each side blamed the other for nearly every killing, and proof was rare. The excerpt's even-handed guessing shows how hard the simplest question, who did this, was to answer.
cia-0000049112: A probe of terrorist killings in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Terrorist killings, in the language of the files, covered the political murders both camps committed. An investigation's existence was itself news in a country where most killings were never investigated at all.
cia-0000049212: Biographical information on Colonel Nelson Ivan Lopez y Lopez, partly blacked out, fills a CIA item from 1991. Bio files were the system's portrait of an officer: posts held, ties kept, reputation noted, family listed. This one survives in the Truth Commission records, its gaps guarding the parts still judged sensitive.
cia-0000049412: Progress on human rights in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049412, dated June 5, 1987. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper claims movement on rights rather than fresh abuses. Readers get a brief declassified item whose positive heading stands out among the grimmer Salvadoran titles, preserved as the agency framed it then.
cia-0000095212: A cable from Leopoldville about cancelling an operation or proceeding with risks is declassified CIA document 0000095212, dated August 1, 1963. The heading presents the choice in either-or terms. Readers get a short declassified cable record from the Congo station's city, its subject the decision itself, preserved without the operation being named in the title.
cia-0000097712: Intelligence Warning of the Tet Offensive in South Vietnam, with publication date estimated, is declassified CIA document 0000097712, dated March 1, 1968. The heading flags the dating estimate in parentheses. Readers get a short declassified paper on warning before the Tet Offensive, its subject the intelligence that preceded a major attack in South Vietnam.
cia-0000100512: Message from the ADCI on the New York Times story on Guatemala is declassified CIA document 0000100512, dated February 5, 1995. The heading names the sender by initials and the newspaper story answered.
