She advocates joining this training directly with local engagement programs. The aim is graduates who are skilled and ethically grounded.
pmc-13238612:
de Leon, Kikuchi, and Yasui-Furukori argue that Japan must loosen its tight monitoring system for clozapine, a last-resort drug for schizophrenia. The drug can cause a dangerous drop in white blood cells, so Japan surrounds it with blood checks and a central registry. The authors contend that this caution now costs more lives than it saves.

Adding ten thousand more prescriptions, they estimate, could prevent up to four hundred suicides linked to schizophrenia, at the cost of perhaps one death from the blood reaction. Clozapine is the only drug proven for treatment-resistant cases and for cutting suicide risk. Their plea reframes strict safety rules as a harm in themselves when they keep a life-saving drug from patients.
pmc-13239312:
Edouard Guez and team reported in 2026 the recovery of Nathan, a 24-year-old man with autism and severe intellectual developmental disorder. His challenging behaviors had led to two years of non-stop restraint and five antipsychotic drugs at once. He also suffered recurrent aspiration pneumonia from tube feeding and drug side effects. A special unit took over, with psychiatry, ICU, and ethics staff at one table.

The team chose a conservative plan: drugs cut down to clozapine, with an antidepressant added later. They added feeding support, speech help, and personal education, movement, and work in a set daily routine. Oral feeding returned step by step until the feeding tube came out, and restraints were dropped bit by bit. His behavior, self-control, mobility, and quality of life all improved a lot despite a grim first outlook.
pmc-13240112:
Hannu Pöysä, Esa Lammi, and Veli-Matti Väänänen ask whether milder winters can rescue declining boreal waterbirds in a 2026 study. Shorter ice seasons should ease wintering for lake birds, yet many northern breeding populations keep falling under other human pressures, so the team tested whether winter cold actually drives their numbers.

Counts spanning 1977 to 2022 covered fifteen species breeding on European boreal lakes. Winter severity barely influenced population growth for most species, with the common coot a clear exception that suffered after cold winters. Six species bounced back strongly after three harsh winters in a row. Body size, thermal niche, and life history did not explain resilience, so warming alone looks unlikely to offset other stressors.
pmc-13240212:
Zhou and colleagues use satellite readings of clouds to narrow how much the planet will warm. Cloud feedback is the biggest source of doubt in climate sensitivity, the warming expected from doubled carbon dioxide. One part of it, the brightening or thinning of clouds, should brake warming, yet models disagree on its strength and it has resisted direct measurement.

The team constrained that brake using the global share of ice in clouds, read by radar, laser, and combined satellite instruments. Feeding those observations into comparisons of the CMIP6 climate models pulled the estimate toward the middle. Their result supports moderate climate sensitivity, ruling out both the mildest and the most extreme model outcomes.
pmc-13240412:
Mingxi Gou and team build two machine-run blood tests to read pig immunity with more nuance in a 2026 study. Porcine circovirus 2 is a major swine pathogen. Standard antibody tests cannot split vaccine responses from signs that the virus is at work in a herd, so the team built a paired approach.

Both run on magnetic beads with light-based detection in a fully machine-run format. Each test agreed with standard lab tests in more than nine of ten samples, and the shell test beat the standard on sensitivity. Field samples showed the pair apart, split vaccine patterns from true exposure.
pmc-13240512:
Yosuke Nakatani and colleagues describe a 2026 technique paper on heart ablation in patients with a small left atrium. The Varipulse system uses a ring catheter to isolate the pulmonary veins, which can trigger irregular heartbeats. Keeping that ring steady against the back wall of the right veins is hard in a small chamber.

The authors lay out a four-step method that combines sheath bending, full ring expansion, partial withdrawal, and a clockwise turn. These moves set the ring nearly parallel to the sheath shaft. A smaller turning radius follows, so the ring sits flat and stable against its target. Clinicians facing tight anatomy gain a simple, repeatable workaround.
pmc-13241412:
Aboelmagd and a large Cairo-led team pooled studies of sealants preventing bleeding after gastric endoscopic submucosal dissection. Thirteen trials and observational cohorts covered two thousand seven hundred twenty-eight patients. Fibrin glue alone faced fibrin glue layered under polyglycolic acid sheets. Delayed bleeding was the outcome that mattered most. Three databases were searched through December 2025.

Overall, sealant strategies roughly halved delayed and total bleeding risk. The benefit concentrated in the sheet-plus-glue combination, which cut delayed bleeding by two-thirds. Glue by itself showed no significant protection at all. Acute bleeding and perforation rates were unchanged across groups.
pmc-13241512:
Mirza's team in Berlin and Jena built a system that reads molecular structures straight from raw spectra. Chemists piece structures together by hand from several test types. Their system, called SECS, pairs contrast learning with a breeding-style search. It reads nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared, and mass spectrometry data jointly.

The system aligns the three data types in a shared space, much as experts combine several views. It also reports confidence scores and nearby library matches. In a pilot comparison, SECS matched expert chemists on hard naming tasks. It even flagged wrong published structures, and it adapts to new chemistry by updating its library alone.
pmc-13241612:
Negash's team at Jimma report an infant whose kidney tumor wore a strong Wilms disguise. The boy, eight months old, carried a growing right-side belly mass. Scans showed a large renal tumor wrapping vessels and flecked with calcium. Those features pointed the team toward Wilms tumor.

Marker staining confirmed it, and neuroblastoma-directed chemo followed. The child reached full remission, but the authors urge biopsy when imaging looks atypical for Wilms. The first chemo was for Wilms.
pmc-13242512:
Galit Renzer and co-authors uncovered why a simple plant compound seeds ice so effectively. Their paper appeared in Communications Chemistry in 2026. Phloroglucinol, a small aromatic molecule with three hydroxyl groups, freezes water with unusual ease, but the mechanism was unclear. The team traced its activity to two pathways running side by side, one starting from solid crystal surfaces and one from dissolved molecules that cluster in solution.

Even below its solubility limit, the compound's nanoscale clusters could start ice forming. Alkaline conditions shut down both pathways by flipping the molecule into a different bonding form. Leaving solutions to age weakened their freezing power, while freeze-thaw cycles partly restored it by growing fresh crystals. The authors frame ice nucleation here as a moving chemical balance, not a fixed property. Their framework should help predict how similar organic molecules behave in clouds and in freezing technology.
pmc-13242812:
Anna Rudawska and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study using macrophages as delivery vehicles for boron neutron capture therapy of glioblastoma. This targeted radiation needs boron carriers that cross the blood-brain barrier, which few achieve. Immune cells naturally migrate toward tumors, so the team loaded them with boron carbide particles.

Macrophages of all tested activation states took up the particles, with the inflammatory state holding the most boron. Loaded cells crossed a model barrier layer toward fluid conditioned by tumor cells. They did not harm tumor spheres on their own, which fits their carrier role rather than a killing role. Loaded cells also avoided a shift toward a tumor-friendly state after tumor contact. The authors call the cells promising boron couriers.
pmc-13243412:
Tran-Lan-Khue Pham and a large team present a 2026 method for testing dental devices that find the tip of a root canal. Getting that length right matters for clean, well-sealed root canal work. Electronic locators are hard to judge because real teeth vary and hide the file tip from view.

The team scanned ten human premolars and printed 100 clear resin copies of them. Two motor systems with built-in locators were tested in two rinsing fluids, under still and moving conditions. A paired microscope setup tracked the file tip with fine precision. Readings agreed closely across modes and fluids. The clear models offer a shared yardstick for clinics, makers, and training.
pmc-13244512:
Jingmiao Wang and co-authors tested whether caffeine gum adds anything to a warm-up routine in basketball players. Their crossover trial appeared in the International Society of Sports Nutrition's journal in 2026. Fifteen male players each completed three conditions: placebo gum, a moderate caffeine dose, and a double dose, each followed by the squat-based priming session. Strength, jump, sprint, and agility were retested one, twenty-four, and forty-eight hours later.

Both caffeine doses beat placebo on the day itself, lifting isometric strength, jump power, sprint speed, and reactive agility, and players moved the priming barbell faster. The double dose bought nothing extra over the moderate one. By the next day, and again at two days, all caffeine advantages had vanished. The authors frame caffeine gum as a same-day tool only, with no carry-over into training. Whether caffeine alone without priming does the same remains untested.
pmc-13246712:
Satoshi Inagaki, Kenji Kato, and Hisafumi Yasuda ask why health apps struggle to win users in a 2026 survey from Japan. Health apps promise gains, yet few people start using them. The team compared views of health apps with everyday apps and probed reluctance toward each.

The survey covered 717 adults online. Health apps scored as moderately useful, near social media but below news apps. Reluctance toward a doctor-advised health app matched reluctance toward a discount shopping app. Storage limits and privacy worries topped the barrier list for both. Skill with smartphones stood out: skilled users saw more use in health apps and felt less resistance. Health status itself barely mattered.
pmc-13249012:
Williams and colleagues examined teachers' invisible care work during COVID-19, in a 2026 Public Health Ethics paper. Pandemic plans prized infection control and keeping services running, but they overlooked the personal care frontline workers would improvise. The authors interviewed thirty-two Australian teachers about what the crisis actually asked of them.

Teachers described inventing ways to reach isolated students and families, sometimes on their own initiative and sometimes because others expected it. Safety rules themselves often blocked the human contact that care requires. The authors argue planners must name care as shared public work, budget for the needs restrictions create, and support the workers who quietly hold society together.
pmc-13250012:
Lee and Kim review a steelmaking heresy: deliberately uneven chemistry, in a 2026 article. Steel tradition prizes uniform makeup. Chemically patterned steels instead plant controlled differences and keep them through rapid heating and cooling. The differences come from reversed phases, carbide particles, or layered structures, at scales the makers can tune.

Two payoffs follow. Uneven chemistry holds more of a helpful crystal phase in place, across a range of stabilities. The metal then stretches step by step instead of snapping. The chemical borders also block the tiny slips and cracks that weaken steel, adding strength and resistance to hydrogen damage. The authors suggest extending the trick beyond manganese, and even beyond steel.
pmc-13250212:
Faye and co-authors explain how Senegal raised contraceptive use faster than most West African neighbors. Their 2026 BMJ Global Health case study tracks modern contraceptive prevalence, which more than doubled between 2010 and 2023. The team combined trend analysis with policy reviews and interviews held across several regions.

Early gains rested on political leadership, task-shifting to lower-level health workers, community-based services, and a stronger supply chain. Campaigns and work with religious leaders and men shifted social norms and raised demand. Knowledge, schooling, and facility access were the strongest measured drivers of the progress. Since 2017, gains have leveled off, with adolescents and rural women still underserved, so the authors call for youth-focused and fairer services.
pmc-13252812:
Sally Lindsay, Gözde Öncil, and Sarah Leo review discrimination in housing for disabled people in this 2026 paper. Safe, affordable housing is a human right, yet disabled people more often land in homes that are inaccessible, insecure, or poor quality.

Searching six databases turned up over ten thousand records, of which 52 studies from 13 countries over 47 years fit. Discrimination showed up in scarce suitable homes, blocked viewings, and high costs. It was fed by ignorance about disabled people's needs and by overlapping factors like income, disability type, and policy design. Neighbourhood problems compounded the harm. The authors demand policy reform and real investment in accessible housing.
pmc-13253212:
Yizhe Pang and colleagues present RivDepth, an artificial intelligence model that maps river depth in muddy water, in a 2026 paper. Knowing depth across whole river reaches matters for tracking channel change and sediment movement. Satellite methods work in clear water but fail where suspended sediment clouds the view, leaving slow boat surveys as the only option.

RivDepth learns the tangled relationship among depth, surface reflectance, and sediment concentration from sample pixels, guided by an AI module that reasons over the patterns. Training and testing used the lower Yellow River, among the most sediment-laden rivers on Earth. The model's estimates tracked measured depths closely, with errors averaging well under half a meter. The authors offer the method for large-scale monitoring of turbid rivers that were previously unmappable from space.
pmc-13253712:
Isabela Ishikura and co-authors map sleep research growth in a 2026 analysis of journal output over 15 years. They checked the top 10 journals in six health fields, from child health to sports science. Sleep terms were tracked across three five-year spans, from 2010 to 2024, in a large database.

Sleep papers made up 0.4 to 2.2 percent of output in these fields. Their growth beat total journal growth by more than 1.5 times in four of six fields. Sports science rose 305.3% across the full span, and insomnia, sleep apnea, and sleep quality were the most used sleep topics.
pmc-13253912:
Beobmo Ku and colleagues test a magnolia extract in chicken sausage in a 2026 food study. Magnolia denudata extract was added at 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2 percent to chicken breast sausages. The team compared them with a plain control for cooking yield, water holding, taste, and storage changes.

Sausages with extract held more water and cooked with higher yield than the control. During storage, the 0.2 percent group kept the steadiest acidity and the slowest rise in a fat-spoilage marker. It also had lower volatile nitrogen, a spoilage sign. The authors propose the extract as a natural stand-in for synthetic antioxidants.
pmc-13254712:
Ivica Králová-Hromadová and colleagues genotype tapeworm larvae in fish from a western Norwegian lake in a 2026 parasitology study. Two broad tapeworm species, Dibothriocephalus dendriticus and Dibothriocephalus ditremus, mature in fish-eating birds and use salmonids as intermediate hosts. The count came out lopsided: 90.8 percent were D. ditremus, against 9.2 percent D. dendriticus, making this the first record of ditremus in the lake. The authors attribute the dominance to feeding ecology and to the abundance of the fish-eating birds in which ditremus completes its life cycle. The study updates the lake's parasite map with molecular certainty.
pmc-13254812:
Maryam Saeed and colleagues compare smile tastes across groups in a 2026 study. The golden proportion is a tooth width ratio used in smile design. Smile photos were altered across a range from 52 to 77 percent, and 128 patients and clinicians rated them on a five-point scale.

Patients accepted the widest range, the full 52 to 77 percent. Orthodontists accepted the narrowest, 62 to 67 percent, while restorative dentists fell between. Gender and experience rarely shaped ratings. The authors treat the ratio as a range, not a fixed value, and urge joint planning between dental specialties.
pmc-13255012:
Shiyu Hu and colleagues sequence the chloroplast genome of a rare tree in a 2026 study. Gleditsia japonica var. velutina is a Chinese tree variety with fewer than 10 wild individuals left. Combining long-read and short-read sequencing, the team assembled its full chloroplast genome, the DNA inside leaf energy organelles.

Genome size gaps across the genus, from 162.4 to 170.8 kilobases, came mainly from repeat growth in one region. Fast-changing stretches could serve as markers to tell species apart. Family analysis placed the variety closest to two relatives, and the authors offer the genome as a base for conservation.
pmc-13255212:
Bonelli and Van de Walle use this 2026 editorial to launch a new article type: plain language summaries of research papers. The summaries restate research findings in plain words so that busy vets, and readers outside the field, can grasp studies quickly. The editors present the format as a route to more readers.

The inaugural summary, by Forman and colleagues, covers a gene variant linked to itchy skin disease in dogs. The editorial notes the format grew out of joint work across human medicine, animal medicine, a media agency, and publishing. Future summaries will appear with chosen papers in the journal.
pmc-13255612:
Shubo Jin and co-authors present a 2026 survey linking water life to the nutritional quality of the oriental river prawn. The team sampled ten sites across China, five freshwater and five saline-alkaline, comparing plankton communities and the prawns' amino acid and fatty acid content. Plankton form the food web base that ultimately feeds the prawns.

The two habitat types differed clearly in both plankton makeup and prawn nutrition. Six plankton genera served as indicator species, three for each water type. In salty sites, two indicator groups rose and fell with potassium, calcium, and bicarbonate levels in the water. The authors say these plankton-chemistry links could eventually help farmers steer water conditions to raise prawns with better nutritional profiles for market.
pmc-13256012:
Massimo Mapelli and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter questioning the explanation offered for a recent case of mavacamten toxicity. Third, the patient's severe liver injury may itself have stalled drug clearance, creating a vicious circle. The writers agree on careful monitoring but urge caution before calling rifampicin the decisive cure.
pmc-13257612:
Vesna Zeljković and colleagues combine nitroglycerin with caffeine against stressed cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13259312:
Dipeng Ren and colleagues listen with a microphone modeled on a fly's ears. That bending mode hears from all directions, while the rocking mode favors two. Layered together, the modes paint shifting directional patterns, from split lobes to twin circles that gradually merge. A theory model tracks the whole transition neatly. Surprisingly, the separated circle patterns locate sounds just as well as the classic two-lobed one.
pmc-13259512:
Jiří Militký, Mohanapriya Venkataraman, and Şebnem Sözcü review germ grown cellulose in a 2026 piece. Germs grow this fiber as a pure nano web with none of the wood glue that loads plant stocks. Feed mix, growth air, and finish steps shape the end sheet traits.

Crystals run sky high in share and water hold tops half the sheet weight. Health uses lead the use list, from wound pads to fake skin. Drug pods form one more growth field. Cheap scale up stays the core block named in the piece. Fiber firms gain a full brief on a clean, high grade bio sheet.
pmc-13262612:

pmc-13263012:
Fadi Taher and colleagues chart hospital admissions for two aortic emergencies in Austria in a 2026 journal article. Using national hospital data from 2009 to 2023, they tracked admissions, deaths, and patient traits, and forecast trends to 2030.

Admissions for dissections more than doubled, rising from 430 to 872 cases, while their hospital death rate dipped slightly. pmc-13264012:
Jing Gu, Yunqi Cheng and Ziwei Nie present a 2026 dataset and model for finding oil well drill pipes and the small gaps at their joints in images. pmc-13264112:

Women tend to be older at first episode and present less typically, which can delay recognition in busy clinics.

Recurrence weighs more heavily on women, with more frequent and severe repeat episodes reported. Stronger links to autoimmune disease and greater use of steroid treatment, itself a recurrence risk, may help explain the gap. pmc-13264312:

pmc-13264412:
Ananya Chakraborty and colleagues review artificial intelligence methods for drug discovery and precision nanomedicine in a 2026 article. pmc-13264912:
Yananlan Chen and colleagues trace how a protein called USP1 helps bile duct cancer grow and hide from immunity, in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13265012:

pmc-13265212:

pmc-13265412:

pmc-13265812:

pmc-13266112:

pmc-13266712:

The authors urge closer watch for older patients and thicker growths.
pmc-13267312:

pmc-13267412:

pmc-13267612:

pmc-13268712:

pmc-13269512:

Sleepiness, daily function, and quality of life improved in both groups, with no differences between them. Weight loss differed only slightly at one month, by 0.7 percent, favoring the sleep test group. Since the oxygen check costs less and was equally safe, the authors favor it.
pmc-13269812:
Hee Jin Kwon and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on long-term blood pressure patterns and risk of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, in a Korean cohort. pmc-13270412:

pmc-13271712:

Three themes on living with these injuries were developed.
pmc-13271812:

pmc-13272012:

Most patients improve quickly when loose inner-ear crystals are guided back into place, yet some need many repeat sessions. Vitamin D status and vertigo subtype were candidate explanations.

Lower vitamin D levels predicted resistance mainly in the typical subtype, while prior vestibular nerve inflammation also mattered. Resolution gains flattened after three sessions. The authors suggest vitamin D may serve as a supporting marker of a fragile crystal system.
pmc-13272112:
Andreas Schäfer and coauthors set out in 2026 a trial protocol for reaching cholesterol targets quickly after a heart attack. Only about a fifth to a quarter of patients reach the guideline LDL cholesterol goal with standard care. The Hannover trial tests whether early, stronger drug combinations close that gap.

Patients arriving with high LDL who had not taken lipid drugs start a potent statin plus ezetimibe for six weeks. Those still above target then add bempedoic acid for eight more weeks, while patients at target continue the first pair. The design measures how far stepwise early escalation can push cholesterol control in routine post-attack care.
pmc-13272312:
Gargi Joshi and coauthors review in 2026 how gut microbes both suffer harm from antibiotics and store the drug resistance those drugs breed. pmc-13272412:
Shannon Q Fernandes and Mayuresh V Kothare build in 2026 a mathematical model of the gut-brain axis as it governs stomach function. Signals travel between brain and stomach through the vagus nerve and the gut's own nerve network, one branch promoting digestion and the other restraining it. A compartment model can simulate that tug of war cheaply.

Equations describe how motor neurons release transmitters and how stomach geometry and wall stress change during digestion. The authors present the model as a tool for testing regulation ideas before animal work.
pmc-13272512:
Youssef Fouani and a large team screened virus capsids for retinal gene therapy in a 2026 study. pmc-13272612:
Ding Quan Ng leads a 2026 study of delayed health care among cancer survivors in the United States. The team used the All of Us data set from 2018 to 2022, with 27,589 survivors. They asked how age, income, race and ethnicity, and insurance linked to reasons for delay.

Younger survivors aged 18 to 39, those on Medicaid, and those earning under 25,000 dollars a year delayed care most often. Cost was the top reason at 12 percent, followed by nervousness at 8 percent and transport at 6 percent. pmc-13273212:

pmc-13273412:
Michio Hirano and a large team assessed pyrimidine nucleoside therapy for thymidine kinase 2 deficiency in a 2026 pooled study. The team pooled 218 patients from trials, access programs, literature, and chart reviews, with 104 treated and 114 untreated. Most had symptoms start by age twelve. In that early onset group, treated patients lived far longer on average than untreated patients across thirty years of follow-up. Loss of motor milestones was more common before treatment than after it began. The study also tracked breathing and feeding support plus safety across the pooled groups.
pmc-13273812:
Santana and colleagues test dental filling materials that contain bioactive glass. Their 2026 journal article is an in-vitro study, meaning tests ran in the laboratory, not in patients. The team compared the new composites with standard resin fillings.

Tests measured surface hardness and water uptake. They also measured how much material dissolved. Color stability was checked after soaking in coffee. High-viscosity composites were the hardest. All materials stayed within the limits of the ISO 4049 standard. Bioactive glass may help teeth repair mineral loss. The authors say the composites behave much like standard ones. Lab success now needs testing in real mouths.
pmc-13274612:
Woncheol Jung and a large team present a 2026 journal article mapping how microplastic exposure injures mouse livers, neighborhood by neighborhood. Polyethylene is the commonest plastic, yet its liver effects were poorly defined. Exposure caused liver dysfunction on both diets, with gene changes spread unevenly across the organ. Spatial maps revealed inflammatory hotspots where cell variety shrank. One control switch, the nuclear receptor Ppara, stood out as a modulator. The team showed it directly regulates Anxa2, a gene for damage response and tissue recovery, suggesting targets for intervention.
pmc-13274812:
Marlis Reich wrote a 2026 primer article in PLOS Biology arguing that ocean carbon models overlook a major player: marine fungi. Fungi in the ocean are microscopic and hard to detect, so they were systematically neglected.

A new study by Trejos-Espeleta and colleagues, which this primer explains, shows fungi can dominate the uptake of labile dissolved organic matter, the fresh, easy-to-eat carbon in seawater. That flips the old assumption that such food belonged to bacteria alone. If fungi truly lead this uptake, models of how the ocean stores carbon need rethinking, Reich argues.
pmc-13274912:
Sanne H M Kremers and colleagues report a 2026 journal article evaluating an app-based health program for university hospital staff in Amsterdam. Hospital work carries distinctive stress, and the Recharge360 app targeted several lifestyle behaviors with a team competition twist. The single-arm study followed 532 employees, ninety-one percent women, over five months with three five-day program weeks.

Recruitment proved feasible, and well-being scores rose slightly but significantly by the final measurement. The weak spot was staying power: dropout reached up to seventy percent by the last program week, and participation faded over time. The authors conclude hospital-wide app programs can recruit broadly and help a little, but keeping a diverse workforce engaged is the hard part.
pmc-13275112:
Parag N Patel and Didar Singh report a 2026 case report of sudden tophaceous gout, chalky uric acid lumps under the skin, in an eighty-seven-year-old woman. She had started bempedoic acid, a cholesterol drug for people who cannot take statins, four months earlier. Painful nodular swelling had grown over two to three weeks on two fingers of her right hand.

A standard causality scale scored the drug link as probable. The drug was stopped and a short steroid course given. Within two weeks the nodules shrank and uric acid normalized, with no return at two months.
pmc-13275512:
Ellene Yan and a large team present a 2026 journal article profiling which thinking skills are weakest in older patients before surgery. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment is a thirty-point screening test spanning seven domains, from memory to naming. In a post hoc analysis of a screening study, the test was given before surgery to 382 patients with a median age of seventy-three.

The group averaged 25.9 points, and thirty-five percent screened positive for probable cognitive impairment. Those patients scored worse across all seven domains, not just memory. Having twelve or fewer years of education was tied to weaker scores in several domains, including executive function, naming, and language. Outcomes were tracked at thirty and ninety days after surgery for later analysis.
pmc-13275612:
Karina C Manz and colleagues present a 2026 journal article measuring clot risk in polycythemia vera, a blood cancer that overproduces red cells, using German health insurance claims from 2021 to 2023. They tracked blood-clot events, bloodletting frequency, and failure of the standard drug hydroxyurea, sorting patients into four risk groups by age and prior clots.

Patients with both risk factors, prior clot and age sixty or over, clotted at 82.4 events per thousand patient-years, over six times the low-risk rate. Their three-year clot incidence reached 21.1 percent. About twenty-two percent of hydroxyurea users showed intolerance or resistance after a median of 337 days, and they clotted more often than patients switched to ruxolitinib.
pmc-13276012:
Roeder and co-authors test a bedside blood-clotting monitor in bonobos, an endangered ape rarely kept in managed care. Their 2026 paper compares the VCM Vet device, a point-of-care viscoelastic monitor, with thromboelastography, the standard test that tracks how a clot forms and dissolves. Bonobos face clotting-related risks from heart disease, stroke, and tumours.

Compared with dog reference ranges, the bonobos appeared prone to over-clotting, a pattern also seen in chimpanzees. Bonobos treated for high blood pressure clotted less strongly than those with normal pressure. The authors present the monitor as a practical option for tracking clotting in this species.
pmc-13276312:
Heidi Roth and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how flies evolved to navigate by polarized skylight. Many insects read patterns of polarized light in the sky as a compass. A specialized eye region, the dorsal rim area, detects that light, but its form varies across insect groups.

In fruit flies, a gene called homothorax switches on in this eye region. The team found a short DNA control stretch that drives that pattern. pmc-13276512:

Gene variants turned up in seventy-seven babies; forty-nine carried disease-causing variants and the rest carried variants of uncertain meaning. pmc-13276612:
Helen Opdam and a large expert panel present 2026 consensus standards for organ donation after circulatory death. In controlled donation, organs are retrieved after life support is withdrawn and the heart stops. Practice varies widely between countries in law, ethics, and bedside routine.

Multidisciplinary teams should judge donor suitability, and trained specialists should lead family communication. Comfort and dignity during withdrawal of treatment rank alongside organ quality. Steps taken before death need careful weighing of benefit and burden with families.
pmc-13276812:

One compound, labeled 8o, slowed growth in cervical, colon, and breast cancer cell lines at very low doses. It broke up the cell skeleton, halted division, and triggered cell death. Early checks also suggested it fits common rules for drug-like compounds. The work is still at the cell stage, so animal and human tests would come next if it holds up.
pmc-13277412:
Seon Hee Woo and colleagues present the first aid section of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. First aid was newly added to this guideline edition after a systematic evidence review. The advice is tuned to Korean field conditions, law, and health system realities.

Seven emergencies receive priority coverage, from chest pain and stroke to asthma attacks, seizures, shock, and fainting. Core advice stresses fast recognition, quick calls to emergency services, and minimal delay to definitive care. pmc-13278612:
Diana Buitrago-Garcia leads a 2026 validation study of AI classifiers that sort clinical trial abstracts by intervention type, drug versus non-drug. The team tested two zero-shot models, which classify text without task-specific training, plus a prompted large language model, on 1,054 rheumatology trial abstracts against a human standard.

The best zero-shot model reached about eighty-eight percent accuracy with simple labels. The prompted model scored slightly higher. Such models could support one reviewer in screening work, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278912:
Kabinuer Keyimu and colleagues build a risk chart for outcomes in sepsis-related kidney injury, in a 2026 study. It kills many patients and leaves a share of survivors with chronic kidney disease. Simple bedside tools to forecast each patient's outcome have been missing.

A selection method called LASSO narrowed the predictors to four: age, organ failure score, creatinine, and blood potassium. Each of the four shaped outcome on its own in the final model. pmc-13279012:

pmc-13279312:

pmc-13279512:

pmc-13279712:

pmc-13279812:

pmc-13279912:

pmc-13280412:

pmc-13280912:

pmc-13281412:

pmc-13281812:

pmc-13282212:

pmc-13282312:

pmc-13282412:

pmc-13282512:

pmc-13282712:

pmc-13283212:

pmc-13284012:

Change patterns did not differ clearly across any measured outcome.
pmc-13284612:

pmc-13284912:

pmc-13285312:

pmc-13285512:

The authors call the work early proof of an anti-follicle effect and urge dose, safety, and fertility studies before any human claim.
pmc-13285712:
