The authors present NDVI as a practical tool for variety testing, most informative where conditions are hardest.
pmc-13285912:
Lu Lu and Yu Zhang review blood markers of inflammation and metabolism in older adults with cancer in a 2026 narrative review. Tiredness, pain, and appetite loss weigh heavily on this group, yet standard geriatric checks miss the biology behind them. Cheap blood ratios and scores might flag who carries the heaviest symptom load.

Three measures anchor the review: two ratios built from white cell counts and one score pairing an inflammation protein with albumin. High values track with frailty, weaker daily function, appetite loss, and the wasting syndrome of cancer. The authors link the pattern to lifelong low-grade inflammation plus tumor-driven shifts in fuel use. They advise adding the markers to full geriatric checks, while warning that mixed study designs and missing standard cutoffs bar solo use for now.
pmc-13286012:
Ali Aytemur, Ayşen Esen Danacı, and Osman İyilikci test timing shifts in schizophrenia in a 2026 experiment on action and perception. Brains constantly fix small delays between a movement and its seen result, a quiet repair job called temporal recalibration. The team asked whether patients lean on that repair more than healthy people, and whether leaning too hard could itself breed symptoms.

Stable patients and healthy controls judged which came first, a hand action or its visual echo, after training with set delays. Patients shifted their sense of sameness far more than controls did after the training blocks. When the trained delay shrank, patients often felt the result had come before their own action, a reversal controls showed less. Timing sharpness stayed alike in both groups. The authors read the stronger shift as a helpful patch that can misfire and shake the sense of causing one's own acts.
pmc-13286212:
Dorra Abdelmalek and colleagues hunt borrowed drugs for cancers driven by the normal form of a growth receptor in a 2026 computer study. Most approved blockers aim at mutated versions of the EGFR receptor, leaving patients whose tumors run on the standard form with few choices. Since a sister receptor shares both shape and cancer roles, its approved blockers became the hunting ground.

Five candidate drugs from that shelf all docked into the standard receptor's fuel pocket in flexible fitting runs. One, coded D4, gripped best, touching two anchor points that govern the pocket's shape. A long motion simulation kept the pair stable, and energy sums backed the strong grip with hard numbers. Bench proof still lies ahead, but the authors name D4 as the lead worth testing first against this stubborn target.
pmc-13286912:
Chantal M. Kapteijn and co-authors test a horse-based program for veterans with PTSD that standard care failed to help. The 2026 study ran twelve weekly group sessions. Fifty-eight veterans stayed in the final count. Sessions mixed calm time with horses and set tasks such as grooming and ground work. No one had to retell their trauma.

Surveys showed PTSD signs fell after the program. Sleep got better and life quality rose. Gains held at a check three months on. Heart measures showed no fixed shift from start to end. In sessions, though, heart rate eased and its pattern calmed after week one. The team thinks that learning to settle while stressed may be how the program works.
pmc-13287012:
Alyssa Imani and co-authors test whether a tissue-chewing enzyme and routine blood measures track with breast cancer spread in patients in Central Java, Indonesia. The 2026 cross-sectional study, run at the region's main referral hospital, compared patients whose cancer had metastasized with those whose had not. Reliable spread markers would sharpen risk judgment in everyday practice.

Tumor grade was the only basic feature tied to spread. Patients with spread showed higher levels of the enzyme MMP-2 and certain other measures, plus lower red cell size and uric acid. In adjusted models, MMP-2 and platelet count stayed independently linked with spread, in opposite directions. Platelets also related to estrogen receptor status. The pair may serve as accessible biomarkers, the authors propose.
pmc-13287912:
Assala Helal and colleagues report bivalent vaccine designs against two dangerous coronaviruses in a 2026 study. One virus caused COVID-19, and the other causes MERS, for which no approved vaccine exists. Each design fused the binding tip of both virus spikes onto an antibody tail piece. The tail helps the immune system grab and present the vaccine. Three versions differed in which tip sat at each end and in tail mutations.

In mice, the version with tail changes that boost cell uptake worked best. It raised strong antibody levels against the MERS tip after two doses. Responses against the COVID variant tip grew more slowly and reached moderate levels after a third dose. The vaccine also produced antibodies that cross-reacted with the first SARS virus. The authors propose the design as a broad platform for future coronavirus threats.
pmc-13288212:
Zhiyong Bai, Junhua Luo, and Kang Min Ok argue a design point in a 2026 perspective. Pairing flat organic ring systems with pyramid-shaped inorganic units is, they say, a smart way to build crystals. Such crystals double the frequency of ultraviolet laser light. Single families tend to trade one wanted trait against another: clear range, strong doubling, and beam splitting rarely peak together.

Three hybrid families built on guanidinium, melamine, and a hydroxy-pyridine base are reviewed in depth. Their combined blocks reached wide ultraviolet transparency, strong doubling, and adjustable beam splitting at once. The authors map how structure drives each trait and urge chemical tuning of the organic half as the fastest path forward.
pmc-13288712:
Ahmed I Kamal and co-authors combine a patient story with a literature review on a rare, dangerous blood disorder in a 2026 article. Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease can take a severe TAFRO form marked by low platelets, body-wide swelling, fever, marrow or kidney problems, and enlarged organs, and it can kill quickly when missed.

Their case involves TAFRO disease with acute kidney failure, treated successfully, and the review gathers what is known about kidney tissue findings and injury routes in this subtype. Interleukin-6 drives much of the illness, making its blocker siltuximab the recommended first treatment. Because diagnosis lacks a clean marker test, the authors push for early suspicion and fast nephrology involvement.
pmc-13289012:
Samuel Jacobs and colleagues profile the NASA astronaut cohort in 2026. The cohort holds all 360 chosen US astronauts. Picks run from the first class in 1959. The last class in the set is from 2022. Health and work data are tracked for life.

Crews are picked for skill, schooling, and fitness. Each class starts with a distinct health base. Data cover heart health and eye changes. Clot risk in space is also tracked. Checks run before, during, and after flights. Moon and Mars plans will grow the record. The set helps weigh the risks of space work.
pmc-13289112:
Amani Isa and colleagues map training for sex education teachers in 2026. Their scoping review spans six databases. Full sex education covers mind, body, and social life. Good teaching needs trained staff. The team sought gaps and blocks in training.

The set held 74 studies in all. About half used counts or mixed methods. Training before service worked best. Best length varied by place and context. Blended online and in-person formats helped. Follow-up support also helped a lot. Two regions stood out as gaps. They are the Eastern Mediterranean and Southeast Asia. The review offers steps for strong programs.
pmc-13289312:
Mahdokht Naghash led a 2026 cohort study on wealth, schooling, and place of living versus cancer risk in northeastern Iran. The Golestan Cohort Study enrolled 49 776 people in 2004 to 2008 and followed them until March 2021. The team asked how money, education, and rural or urban home each tie to specific cancers and cancer deaths.

Over a median of 14 years, the richest quarter faced lower esophageal and stomach cancer rates than the poorest, but higher breast cancer rates in the models. More schooling linked to lower rates for several cancers, including esophageal, stomach, liver-biliary, and lung sites. City living lowered esophageal risk yet raised colorectal risk. One-size prevention will miss these split patterns, the authors imply.
pmc-13289412:
Chizaram Onyeaghala headed a 2026 survey on mpox knowledge and vaccine willingness in Rivers State, Nigeria, among people living with HIV and men who have sex with men. Data were thin for these vulnerable groups where HIV and mpox overlap. Fieldwork ran from late August to September 2024 at two health facilities using web forms.

Participants totaled 290 people living with HIV and 14 men who have sex with men in the sample. Most had heard of mpox, yet over half showed poor knowledge on testing. About six in ten saw mpox as serious and a similar share would accept vaccination if offered. Fear of side effects and distrust in health systems were the top barriers named.
pmc-13289812:
Ysoline Beigneux led a 2026 study testing brain magnetic signals as markers of myelin and nerve function in acute optic neuritis. Optic nerve inflammation is a model for repair trials in multiple sclerosis, but standard electrical tests can vanish or prove unreliable early. Magnetoencephalography records magnetic brain responses to a flashing checkerboard and may fill that gap with steadier measures.

Patients with one-sided acute optic neuritis had eye exams, brain scans, and magnetic recordings at a median of 54 days in the excerpt. Two readouts mattered: timing of a key response wave and richness of steady response tones. Repeat runs in one visit checked steadiness, and links to short-term vision recovery were tested. Reliable early markers would sharpen repair trials.
pmc-13290012:
Marcia Spindler and co-authors test printed cleaning splints for teeth in a 2026 crossover pilot study. Interdental brushes clean between teeth, yet many patients aim them poorly. Each participant with periodontitis received a 3D-printed splint shaped from a mouth scan to guide brush placement. Thirty people used brushes with and without the splint in two two-week rounds, swapping methods midway. Plaque and gum measures were taken after each round.

The splint plus brush cut plaque far more than brush alone, by a change score of about 1.38 against about 0.23 on the index used. Gum inflammation gains appeared mainly in younger participants, and bleeding on probing did not shift overall. Perceived stress seemed to blunt the splint's effect on bleeding scores. Statistical models confirmed the splint effect on plaque after adjustments. The authors call custom splints a promising aid for interdental cleaning at home.
pmc-13290512:
A man whose melanoma spread to his pancreas and spleen, two rare destinations, survives long-term in a 2026 case report and literature review by Yanhua Mou and colleagues. The 55-year-old had a lower-leg melanoma removed, only for widespread metastases to appear within five months.

He cycled through several regimens, including immunotherapy with toripalimab, combinations with anlotinib, and temozolomide, before surgeons removed the pancreatic and spleen lesions. Testing of that tissue found a BRAF V600 mutation, which opened the door to targeted drugs, dabrafenib plus trametinib. At last follow-up on March 6, 2025, he remained stable. Mou and colleagues stress molecular re-testing, persistence with treatment, and team-based care for such complex cases.
pmc-13290812:
Emotion, more than immersion, decides whether phone visitors return to a virtual Great Wall, Dan Liu and Jungho Jung report in a mixed-methods study from 2026. Using the Great Wall E-tour mini program on WeChat, they modeled how technical appraisal, story design, and experiential value shape what users intend to do next.

A grounded-theory qualitative phase grounded the constructs, then a post-experience survey was tested with factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Technology perception, narrative design, and experiential value each fed emotional arousal and cultural value identification, which in turn related to psychological immersion. When outcomes were modeled, emotional arousal held the steadiest direct link to behavioral intention, while immersion's role was weaker and shifted between model versions. Liu and Jung advise heritage apps to build emotional hooks and clear action bridges, treating immersion as support, not the engine.
pmc-13290912:
Fermentation transforms stinky tofu's nutrition and aroma in measurable steps, Jinming Meng and colleagues track in a study of the Jianshui style from 2026. Open fermentation makes this traditional food inconsistent, so the team monitored chemistry, flavor compounds, and microbes through solid-state fermentation to ground quality control.

Acidity climbed as microbes worked: crude protein fell about 15% while amino acid nitrogen quadrupled. Health-linked compounds surged, with polyphenols up about 30% and flavonoids up 162%. Free amino acids reached 402.07 mg per 100 g, with essential ones up sixfold. Fifty-three volatile compounds were catalogued; ketones and ring-shaped compounds carried the signature aroma, and unusually high phenol emerged as its key source. A strong protein-cutting fungus, Mucor circinelloides, was also isolated for future starter use.
pmc-13291012:
Fluid collections near the pelvis after surgery for gynecological cancer are the subject of a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis led by Ting-yu Zhao. Such lymphoceles follow lymph node removal in many patients, and severe cases can delay further treatment, so the team hunted for factors that raise the risk.

Eight databases were searched through August 15, 2025, yielding 64 studies with 15,739 patients and a pooled occurrence rate near three in ten patients. Older age, higher body mass index, and diabetes each raised risk modestly, while open surgery and removal of more than 20 nodes raised it far more strongly. Wider node removal and removal of the omentum also counted as risk factors, giving surgical teams clear targets for prevention.
pmc-13291312:
Printed teeth aligners need one shared safety test method. Koen Tenge leads a 2026 scoping review of cell harm tests. Home and clinic printers now make aligners and retainers. Resin safety worries persist among dentists and patients.

World standards exist for such lab cell tests. Yet labs use them in loose, varied ways. The team charted 25 studies from 2020 to 2025. Most said they followed the standards in full. Others cited them in part or not at all. Test styles split between extract, direct touch, and mixed. Reporting gaps block fair study comparisons. Shared rules would make safety claims trustworthy.
pmc-13292012:
Bryan Tysinger and co-authors present a microsimulation model for United States dementia costs in a 2026 methods paper. Dementia's burden spreads across medical bills, long-term care, unpaid family help, and lost earnings. The model follows virtual individuals over time rather than counting group averages. It draws on the national Health and Retirement Study for adults over fifty, plus Medicare and other national data. Outputs cover prevalence, care costs, caregiving value, quality of life, and earnings for patients and care partners.

Counterfactual runs estimate what dementia itself subtracts from quality of life and earnings. Internal validation showed simulated outcomes lining up with observed data. The team stresses transparent methods so others can replicate or extend the model. Policy users can test how new treatments or care changes might shift costs over time. The framework also shows who bears each cost, families or public payers.
pmc-13292112:
Daniel Ortega Quijano and co-authors ran a 2026 one-year randomized pilot trial of an anti-hair-loss serum for men recovering from hair transplantation. Thirty men with androgenic alopecia, median age 40, were split evenly between the serum plus neutral shampoo and shampoo alone. The serum mixed milk thistle extract, Lespedeza capitata extract, and manganese PCA, and checks ran from two weeks to twelve months.

Serum users reported less painful scalp discomfort at one month and better hair condition, judged by both patients and investigators. Investigators also rated overall scalp appearance as improving faster from month one, and hair growth as stronger from month six onward. Tolerance and patient acceptance were rated excellent. The authors call the serum a safe cosmetic sidekick for post-transplant care, while noting the pilot scale.
pmc-13292312:
Irene Boateng and a large team report a 2026 multicentre cohort study, NURTuRE-CKD, on how stacked long-term conditions shape life with chronic kidney disease. All 2,996 recruits from 16 UK nephrology centres already carried multiple conditions by the study's definition. The median comorbidity count was three, and the commonest companions were hypertension, pain, obesity, and diabetes.

More conditions meant higher death risk in a stepwise pattern, with adjusted hazard ratios climbing to 1.80 for people with five or more conditions versus one. Burden did not, however, predict progression to kidney failure. Quality of life worsened as counts rose and with certain specific conditions. New pain, anxiety and depression, and cognitive impairment appeared most often during follow-up. The authors say multimorbidity management deserves center stage in kidney care.
pmc-13292412:
Rajesh Raj argues in a 2026 commentary that frailty deserves treatment status in kidney care. Kidney medicine usually orbits numbers like filtration rates and electrolyte levels. Frailty, a whole-person state of accumulated damage, fits that world awkwardly. Raj discusses a trial by Chang and colleagues in 242 older adults with nondialysis kidney disease. A year-long personal program of nutrition, psychological support, and exercise followed full geriatric assessments.

Nearly one in three treated patients reversed their frailty, against about seven percent under routine care. Gains spread across physical performance, thinking, nutrition, and daily activities. Raj notes the trial ran at one Beijing hospital in fairly early disease, and frailty was scored soon after hospitalization. A full assessment-based program also demands trained teams and protected clinic time. Still, the result challenges the assumption that frailty cannot be undone. He urges clinics to treat it as a target, not background noise.
pmc-13292512: Mohammad Saadatian, Abbas Hassani, and Samad Nejad Ebrahim issued a 2026 correction to their BMC Plant Biology article on vegetal protein hydrolysates easing salt stress in sage. The notice repairs the Figure 1 caption, which lost text during production. The full caption spells out the treatments: fertigation and foliar spraying at set concentrations, plus untreated control plants, under differing salt levels. The original article has been corrected. Only this caption fix is available here, so the study's findings on growth, nutrients, and oil yield cannot be described from it.
pmc-13293312:
Roger Y. Kim and co-authors study whether an artificial intelligence tool helps advanced practice providers judge lung nodules, in work published in 2026. Nurse practitioners and similar clinicians often estimate cancer risk for spots found on chest scans and decide who needs a biopsy. Six such readers reviewed three hundred scan cases, first on their own and then with help from a commercial imaging analysis program.

With the tool, average diagnostic accuracy rose by nine percentage points. Cancerous nodules were more often rated high risk and more often sent for biopsy or surgery, which fits appropriate care. Benign nodules were somewhat more often rated low risk, with no real change in procedure referrals. The authors say prospective trials should now test the tool in everyday practice before routine adoption.
pmc-13293412:
Josephine Katharina Mommertz and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, what drives HIV testing and daily preventive pill use among youth at a Malawi university. Malawi sees about 9000 new infections a year in youth, and the pill, called oral PrEP, has been open to youth since 2022.

A total of 377 students aged 18 to 24 answered a questionnaire framed by the Health Belief Model. Older youth, ages 21 to 24, were more likely to have tested. Pill uptake linked to seven factors, led by knowing about the pill and feeling at risk. Peers and social media were the main information sources, so outreach should work through them.
pmc-13294212:
Aleksandra J Wierzba and colleagues improve live RNA imaging probes with peptide nucleic acid linkers in a 2026 protocol. The popular MS2 protein tag is bulky and can distort RNA behavior. Their Riboglow probes use a cobalamin dye unit plus a synthetic PNA linker that grips a chosen sequence while the probe shape adds a second recognition check.

Four parts cover probe synthesis, a glow turn-on test for binding strength, a SHAPE footprint test at single-letter resolution, and live-cell assays for stress granules and U-bodies. Dual recognition raises affinity and specificity with less disturbance to natural RNA. The method offers a leaner rival to protein-based imaging.
pmc-13294412:
Omar Almaadawy and a large team pool survival after valve replacement when hidden heart amyloidosis coexists with aortic stenosis in a 2026 meta-analysis. Stiff protein deposits often hide in narrowed valve patients, and catheter valve replacement is standard care, yet long-term effects were murky. Five databases were searched through April 21, 2026, for studies with survival curves that could be rebuilt into patient-level data.

Seven studies held 2,747 patients. With broad deposit definitions, amyloid cases faced higher death risk after the procedure in pooled hazard terms. Restricting to confirmed cases erased clear significance. Pacemaker need and valve leak rates matched between groups. Definition quality drives the answer.
pmc-13294612:
Sandip Sinharay opens the April 2026 issue of Psychometrika with a letter to readers. He notes the next IMPS meeting, set for Seoul, Korea, and walks through what the issue holds. The first part holds thirteen pieces in the Theory and Methods section.

The previews span new work on adaptive tests, cause-and-effect paths, and firm ways to gauge how far results stretch. Three pieces on factor analysis follow, plus work on structural models and item response theory. Read as a whole, the letter maps live themes in the study of tests, scores, and mental measurement.
pmc-13295112:
Santosh Bhatta and a large team gather views on disaster readiness in Nepal in a 2026 study. Floods, landslides, earthquakes, and harsh weather strike the country often, harming health, buildings, and community strength. Meetings in 2025 with national agencies, local officials, and residents of two hard-hit towns fed the work.

Laws and policies exist at national level, yet putting them into practice locally stays patchy with thin staff and budgets. Local action leans toward relief after events rather than preparation before them. Residents showed limited knowledge of prevention but strong willingness to plan, and priorities included better coordination, clearer legal guidance, and warning messages shaped for each place.
pmc-13295212:
Darciane Coelho Cordovil and colleagues study high-risk HPV types in Amazon women in a 2026 survey from Brazil. The virus drives cervical cancer, and women in remote parts of the Amazon face distance, poverty, and thin services. Those barriers help explain the heavy cancer burden in the region.

Smears came from women across 18 municipalities, tested first for the virus and then for exact types. Infection was found in 182 of 1,315 women, with the highest town share above one fifth of those tested. Younger age, being unmarried, and not using condoms raised the odds, guiding where screening and vaccination efforts should aim first.
pmc-13295412:
Meng Zhang and co-authors turn wearable motion sensors into a fall risk score for people with Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 exploratory study. Falls injure many patients, yet clinics still judge the risk largely by eye. Ninety-two patients wore inertial and photoelectric sensors on limbs and trunk while performing standard motor examination tasks. The team used mutual information, a measure of how much a signal reveals about a label, to link movement features to disease stage, which itself tracks fall risk.

The weighted combination of the most informative features became their fall risk stratification score. Adding that score to a classifier lifted test accuracy from one half to over four fifths, and a standard discrimination measure rose sharply as well. The authors caution that the work is exploratory, but they argue sensor-based scoring could give clinicians objective evidence for targeting prevention at patients with the shakiest balance.
pmc-13295612:
Zhiquan Li and colleagues map research on a cell sensor in eczema in a 2026 bibliometric study. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor shapes skin barrier growth, immune balance, and responses to the environment. Drugs that activate it are reaching clinics for atopic dermatitis, yet the field's overall shape was unmapped.

Publications from 2005 to 2025 in two large databases totalled 306 after cleaning, mixing original studies and reviews. Output grew fast after 2020, led by the United States with Japan and China following. Keyword groups covered immune control, barrier and environment, microbe links, and receptor-targeted treatment, showing a drift toward clinic-ready work.
pmc-13295712:
Cuilan Hu and colleagues test a way to make lung tumors easier to kill with radiation, in a 2026 study of non-small cell lung cancer. Tumors short of oxygen resist radiation, a main bar to cure. The team mimicked low oxygen followed by fresh oxygen in cancer cells and found the swing fires up a backward flow of electrons in mitochondria, the cell power plants.

That backward flow made a burst of reactive oxygen that harmed the cells. A compound called dimethyl succinate fed the flow and deepened the harm, cracking DNA and breaking the power plant web. Cells so treated died more readily under radiation, and in mice the pairing of high oxygen, the compound, and radiation slowed tumors. The authors name the flow as a target worth aiming at.
pmc-13295912:
Olamide Todowede and co-authors outline a 2026 review protocol on how joined-up care is organised for adults living with several long-term conditions. Such patients need many services at once, and health leaders back integrated care, but the best set-ups remain unclear.

The planned review will search three databases for studies from high-income countries published since 1990. Two reviewers will screen and judge each study, then sort findings by how services link across levels and within them. Results should show which structures and daily processes help integrated care work in practice.
pmc-13296312:
Lei Xia and colleagues map how depressive symptoms connect with biased thinking about the future in a 2026 network study. Participants were 1,162 university students who completed self-report measures of depression and prospection bias. Network analysis treats each symptom as a node and estimates how strongly symptoms relate to one another.

Suicidal ideation, blurry future imagery, low energy, and catastrophic thinking about the future sat at the centre of the network. Suicidal ideation, imagined future self-harm, and guilt formed the main bridges between depression and biased prospection. The network looked similar for men and women in the comparison test. Such maps may help campus services spot at-risk students earlier and aim support at the most connected symptoms.
pmc-13296912:
Nikolaos I Davanellos and colleagues describe a case of Lemierre syndrome, a rare but dangerous offshoot of throat infection, in a 2026 report. A healthy man of thirty-four had lasting fever, a sore throat, hard breathing, and a tender neck despite antibiotics given at a clinic. Scans found many small lung spots, several hollowed out, matching infected clots that had spread from the neck.

A sound scan confirmed a clot in the left inner neck vein, the mark of the syndrome. Blood cultures stayed blank, which made the scans decisive. Broad antibiotics that also cover germs shunning air began, then blood-thinning drugs once the clot was sure. The man moved to a specialist centre. The authors urge care teams to suspect the syndrome when throat illness will not settle.
pmc-13297112:
Georgeta Stefan and colleagues review, in 2026, how the foodborne germ Listeria monocytogenes picks up new traits by swapping genes sideways between cells. Such transfers spread drug resistance and harm factors across farms, food plants, soil and animal guts.

The bacterium causes severe illness in vulnerable people and animals despite low case numbers, and its mobile gene pool helps it persist in tough settings. The review gathers evidence on transfer routes and their role in the germ's evolution. A joined-up human, animal and environment lens guides the authors' advice for food safety and veterinary practice.
pmc-13298012:
An inflammatory signal in the blood rises in step with hepatitis B virus levels, report Jayakrishna Pamarthi and co-authors in a 2026 hospital study. They measured interleukin-6 and viral DNA in 293 patients who tested positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen.

IL-6 climbed significantly across viral load categories and ran higher in patients positive for the e antigen, while showing no pattern by age, sex, or cirrhosis. Its correlation with viral DNA was r = 0.40, and regression kept viral load as the independent predictor of IL-6. Links to ordinary liver injury markers were weaker, leading the authors to propose IL-6 as a supporting marker of disease activity.
pmc-13298412:
Teresa Pinho, Martim Novais, and Maria dos Prazeres Gonçalves follow children treated with clear aligners during early mixed dentition, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Interceptive treatment aims to reduce malocclusion severity while teeth develop. Records for 55 children covered baseline, end of treatment, and at least eighteen months of follow-up, scored with a standard rating index.

Scores fell sharply after treatment and held steady during follow-up, with no significant change between those visits. A smaller group with paired head measurements showed large drops in case complexity, especially for dental targets, while skeletal and molar changes improved less. The authors stress the design had no control group.
pmc-13298712:
Maria Beatrice Galavotti leads a pilot study adding exercise and education to lung cancer care, in a 2026 report. Cancer-related fatigue burdens quality of life and physical performance during treatment. One group began the three-month supervised programme at the start of anticancer therapy, while another started three months later.

Adherence was high and no adverse events occurred, which supports feasibility and safety. Both groups saw better health outcomes during the programme. Interestingly, the later-start group showed more sustained quality-of-life gains at long-term follow-up. The authors argue exercise plus symptom education belongs inside routine cancer care to keep patients active and support well-being.
pmc-13299412:
Zunair Ahsan and others review how honeybee detox and immunity work as one connected system, in a 2026 survey. The fat body, midgut, and kidney-like tubules coordinate gut microbes, innate defences, and chemical detox pathways. Colony behaviour adds another defensive layer above single-bee workings.

Combined pressures from infection, pesticide exposure, and poor nutrition can slowly erode that strength. Even low-dose gene-level disruption may shift behaviour and reduce colony output over time. The authors argue bee health research must treat these body and ecological mechanisms as one rather than as separate problems, above all under the stacked pressures colonies now face worldwide.
pmc-13299512:
Ting Lv and colleagues sequence the complete chloroplast genome of an alpine plant found only on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, in a 2026 genomics study. The genome shows the typical four-part structure and encodes 132 unique genes. Comparison across eight relatives found size differences driven mainly by one single-copy region, while repeat boundaries stayed highly conserved in this species.

Repeat analysis found dozens of marker loci, and two genes stood out as most variable, which makes them useful for identification work. Most genes sat under purifying selection, though seven showed positive selection signals. Family analysis placed the species nearest a garlic mustard relative, splitting in the middle Miocene.
pmc-13299712:
Alma Trnacevic leads a team testing which patient factors predict urinary tract infection with rapid urine flow cytometry, in a 2026 records-based study from Tuzla. Culture remains the gold standard, yet resistance and empirical treatment complicate care in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Records for 200 symptomatic adults paired blood markers with automated urine bacterial counts.

White cell count, neutrophil count, and age each independently predicted infection, while a common inflammation marker and gender did not. A high urine bacterial count multiplied the odds of a positive culture many times over. The authors argue combining these measures sharpens rapid screening and diagnostic accuracy in routine practice.
pmc-13300212:
Sidi Bao and co-authors review polymer-based delivery systems for messenger RNA medicines in a 2026 article. Lipid nanoparticles carried the first successes in patients, yet they tend to gather in the liver, store poorly, and can be hard on the body. Polymers can be tuned by design, shaping how RNA is packed, kept safe, let out, and aimed at set tissues.

The review works through the main polymer families. These include polyethyleneimine and its kin, poly(beta-amino ester)s, poly(amino acid)s, polyesters, dendrimers, and charge-altering releasable transporters, plus hybrids that mix lipids with polymers. Design tricks covered include tweaks to structure, materials that respond to cues, and fast screening of many candidate polymers. Hurdles that remain are immune reactions, spread through the body, and making the carriers at large scale. The authors say those hurdles will decide whether the systems reach patients.
pmc-13300612:
Stubborn styes that resist warm compresses might yield to a chemotherapy drug used in tiny local doses. Mengzhe Qin and colleagues describe a 2026 case series of four women with persistent eyelid nodules in the hordeolum–chalazion range. Each received an injection of six-fold diluted 5-fluorouracil directly into the lesion.

Two patients cleared fully within three to seven days after a single shot. A woman with both eyes affected improved fast, though one side kept a firm lump despite a repeat dose. The fourth, a long-standing case after earlier drainage, shrank notably but never vanished. No side effects appeared, and the authors call for controlled trials on dosing and safety.
pmc-13301012:
Doonyah Alucozai and Elizabeth Kwo review how chronic opioid use disrupts women's hormone systems in a 2026 article. Opioids disturb three control axes governing reproduction, stress, and thyroid function, producing irregular periods, infertility, early menopause, thinning bones, adrenal failure, and changes in mood and sexual function. The authors stress a stark evidence skew: across the major studies they reviewed, almost every participant was male.

Because of that skew, female specific mechanisms, prevalence figures, and screening thresholds remain guesswork, and guidelines barely address the reproductive, skeletal, and adrenal fallout in women. The review separates what is actually established from what is extrapolated from men or animals. It then proposes a practical screening framework covering the three hormone axes, bone health, and fertility, with defined roles for the specialties involved. The authors close with a plea for sex sensitive research and routine screening.
pmc-13301312:
F Zoppo and co-authors map the electrical anatomy behind a common racing heart rhythm in a 2026 study of ten patients with AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. Treatment burns the slow pathway through the AV node, a target sitting close to the fast pathway that must be spared. Using a mapping system, the team paced from three spots around the triangle of Koch. They timed how quickly the impulse reached the His bundle recording, sketching the fast pathway's position and behavior.

Timing lengthened in a gradient from front to back of the triangle at baseline, exactly the signature expected for the fast pathway's location. After slow pathway ablation the same gradient persisted with statistically unchanged timings at all three sites. The authors suggest activation mapping can display the node's dual physiology alongside the standard study, marking safer ground for ablation and confirming the fast pathway's conduction survives the burn.
pmc-13301412:
An industrial solvent that poisons mitochondria also slows rats down, Tarek M. Abdelghany and colleagues report in a 2026 toxicity study of the ionic liquid M8OI. In dishes, the compound choked oxygen use in SH-SY5Y nerve cells and pushed them toward sugar fermentation. Rats then drank M8OI-laced water for twenty weeks before behavior testing and tissue measurement.

Exposed rats moved less in open-field tests yet showed no anxious behavior. Their brains held far less M8OI than the kidneys did, roughly thirty-fold lower, and brain levels sat at least a hundred-fold below dish doses that killed cells. The mismatch warns that chronic low-level exposure may alter behavior through routes other than outright nerve-cell death.
pmc-13302212:
N Radovanovic and co-authors look for predictors of staying in normal rhythm one year after a successful electric shock treatment, in a 2026 study. Cardioversion reliably ends persistent atrial fibrillation or flutter, yet many patients slip back within months. Knowing who holds rhythm could shape follow-up and drug choices.

The review included 297 patients treated between 2011 and 2023, with shocks succeeding in about ninety-two percent. Only about forty percent of those successes still held normal rhythm at one year. Shorter time since the episode began, a smaller left upper chamber, and not smoking each favoured lasting success. Having no previous cardioversion and using rhythm drugs around the procedure also helped, while a higher risk score hurt.
pmc-13302912:
Reagan Aviha and Gymama Slaughter review, in a 2026 paper, the electronics that run electrochemical sensors, known as potentiostats. These circuits hold an electrode at a set voltage and read the resulting current, forming the heart of glucose monitors and many other tests. Demand for wearable and bedside devices has shrunk them from bench boxes to chips.

Coverage spans sensing theory, analogue front ends, signal conversion, and wireless links from Bluetooth to NFC, treated as one system rather than separate topics. Design tensions around size, noise, power draw, and reproducibility are weighed using real platforms. The authors chart a path toward smart, connected sensors for clinics, environmental checks, and industry, with practical guidance for builders.
pmc-13303312:
Where a child's bone breaks through a hidden lesion hints at what the lesion is, Clemens Clar and colleagues show in a 2026 single-center review. Records of 235 children treated for pathological fractures between 1999 and 2021 were split between upper and lower limbs and compared for age, sex, accident setting, trauma energy, and underlying disease.

Arms and legs each supplied about half the cases at a median age of eleven. Lower-limb fractures more often arrived with no trauma or a trivial one, and girls were overrepresented there. Malignant lesions also trended higher below the waist, at 9.6 against 3.3 percent. Arm fractures mostly followed ordinary falls. The authors urge location-aware suspicion during workup.
pmc-13304012:
Yuan Gao and a large team engineer, in a 2026 study, bacteria that mass-produce tannase, an enzyme that breaks down the bitter tannins limiting some animal feeds. A tannase gene from a lactic acid bacterium was loaded into two Bacillus subtilis hosts using two plasmid designs, creating three candidate strains. Growth, plasmid stability, and enzyme output were compared head to head.

All three strains grew like their parents and peaked in activity at the same mild temperature and acidity. One pairing stood far above the rest, topping four hundred sixty activity units per millilitre with the most stable plasmid carriage. That strain kept its plasmid far better over ten generations than the weakest design. The authors offer it for industrial enzyme production.
pmc-13304112:
Haneul Lee, Youngeun Lim, and Seon-Heui Lee pool trials of digital brain training for mild memory loss and dementia in a 2026 meta-analysis. Drug options for sharpening thinking are few, so screen-based programs draw growing interest.

Ten databases were searched through May 2025, and 37 studies entered the pooled analysis. Digital programs improved overall thinking scores against all comparison groups combined, yet the gain vanished against active comparison activities. People with mild impairment gained clearly, while results for dementia stayed uncertain. Computer-based training worked, giving families a low-cost option worth discussing with clinicians.
pmc-13305412:
Racheal Agaba and co-authors measure uptake of the recommended eight pregnancy check contacts in Mbarara district, Uganda, in a 2026 facility study. The World Health Organization advises at least eight contacts to catch risks early, yet few women complete them.

Mothers at postnatal and baby clinics in five centers answered surveys checked against their clinic cards in spring 2025. Only a small share of 433 women reached eight contacts. Starting care in the first three months of pregnancy towered over other factors, and living near a facility or earning more also helped. Bringing first visits forward could lift completion sharply.
pmc-13305612:
H Bayliss and C Aherne report, in a 2026 conference abstract, that focused teaching sharply raised pharmacists' antimicrobial stewardship work in a large teaching hospital. Four clinical pharmacists in acute medicine received monthly hour-long sessions over ten months, covering common infections and simple stewardship moves like switching intravenous drugs to oral ones. Their logged actions were compared across periods before, during, and after teaching.

Actions averaged two per month before teaching, peaked at eight during the sessions, and held at seven monthly for six months afterward. The mix also changed: pharmacists began stopping unneeded antibiotics, relabeling doubtful penicillin allergies, and pushing IV-to-oral switches, habits that persisted after teaching ended. The authors present targeted teaching as a durable lever for building stewardship inside pharmacy teams.
pmc-13306612:
Angelo Troia introduced a second journal volume on water plants of inland waters in a 2026 overview. Rivers, lakes and wetlands cover under 1% of Earth's surface yet hold about 10% of known species in the cited figures.

Freshwater life is vanishing faster than in many land or sea habitats under pollution, habitat loss, broken rivers, invaders and climate shifts. Nearly one quarter of freshwater species face extinction risk in recent counts quoted here. The volume gathers new work on plant knowledge and care, tying plant management to wider water protection. New papers in the set add fresh cases from lakes, streams and wet lands.
pmc-13306912:
Hong Zhang and a large wheat team uncover in 2026 a gene pair that helps wheat tolerate cadmium, a toxic metal threatening crops and food safety. The transporter TaPROT2 moves proline, a protective compound, and raising its activity increased proline in engineered wheat. A partner gene, TaERF3, switches the transporter on.

Binding tests confirmed that TaERF3 attaches to a control element in the TaPROT2 promoter. Engineered plants with more of either gene accumulated more proline, activated antioxidant enzymes, and took up and moved less cadmium. Lower metal content in the plant is exactly what breeders want for safer grain. The authors propose the pair as a target for breeding low-cadmium wheat. Food-chain exposure through wheat makes the trait valuable beyond the field.
pmc-13307012:
Irma Zeljkovic tested whether gene variants in immune brakes alter risk of asbestos disease in a 2026 case-control study. Cases held people with asbestosis, pleural plaques or mesothelioma, while controls were exposed workers who stayed free of disease.

Nine variants across three genes, PDCD1, CD274 and CTLA4, were typed in all subjects by a competitive assay in the reported design. These checkpoints keep immune tolerance, and faults can open paths to cancer after asbestos exposure. Results weigh inherited immune tuning as one layer in why only some exposed people fall ill.
pmc-13307112:
Faisal Khaled Aldawood reviewed 3D printing of drug-releasing blood vessel stents in a 2026 survey. Six printing families are compared, from fine light-cured resin at 25 μm detail to direct energy deposition for metals.

Materials span stainless steel, cobalt-chromium, degradable plastics and shape-memory stocks in the gathered work. Newer multi-axis and stimulus-responsive printing enables programmed release and adaptive device behaviour. Design cycles shrank by 85 to 95 percent against conventional making in cited gains, with tooling costs for complex shapes removed entirely. The survey also maps gaps where bench proof still lags far behind bold design claims made by teams.
pmc-13307512:
Xiaoli Han and colleagues compare leaf strategies of male and female Euphrates poplars in a 2026 desert study. Thirty-one leaf traits were measured across growth stages and canopy heights, then mapped as networks. Sex, development, and their combination each explained different slices of trait variation.

Development drove most change in leaf size, weight, and photosynthesis traits, while sex shaped nutrient and resistance markers. Male networks grew more connected during development, with core traits shifting toward transport functions. Female networks stayed more modular, centred on area, biomass, and structure. Higher in the canopy, male networks reorganised strongly while female hubs moved toward structure-metabolism balance. The authors label males acquisitive and females conservative. Their reading offers a framework for how desert trees split survival strategies by sex.
pmc-13308412:
Hui Min Charlotte Choo and co-authors present a 2026 regional audit of osteoporosis care across twenty-two Asia Pacific countries and regions. Rapid ageing will swell fracture numbers, so the audit gathered questionnaires, registries, official statistics, and expert estimates across twelve domains. Two osteoporosis organisations coordinated the exercise.

Only six countries treat osteoporosis as a national health priority, which limits funding and coordination. Fracture surveillance is patchy, diagnostic access uneven, and payment rules often misaligned with patient risk. Care after a first fracture, the cheapest chance to prevent the next, remains limited almost everywhere. The panel's remedies include fracture registries, post-fracture care pathways, country-specific guidelines, and payment tied to risk. Their verdict is blunt: the region suffers an implementation gap, not an evidence gap. Governments get a roadmap for fairer fracture prevention.
pmc-13308712:
Aliya Moreira and co-authors survey in 2026 North American infectious disease doctors on shorter tuberculosis care plans that guidelines now favour over long courses. Their poll went to 1501 members of an emerging infections network, and 349 doctors sent back full replies for study.

Nearly all who replied chose short plans for silent infection, with few doubts about how well they work in that setting. For active lung disease, almost none picked the new four month plan, and few had ever used it in real care. Doubts about gains, drug harms, clashes, and patchy supply all slowed uptake. Shared choices and closer harm watch could help clinics adopt the new plans.
pmc-13309112:
Md Rahat Shahriar Zawad and co-authors pilot in 2026 a web test that reads mouse traces to screen for Parkinson disease from afar, where brain doctors are scarce. Their set held 261 people from Hawaii town groups: 73 who told of the disease, 155 without it, and 33 with suspected signs.

Each person traced a straight line, a sine wave, and a spiral on screen while the tool logged each cursor step. Models that joined trace traits with trace images did best, led by a mixed vision model in the main test. Models trained only on suspected cases still foresaw self told cases fairly well. Weak labels may thus seed useful screens for poor areas.
pmc-13309612:
Limin Shang and co-authors propose a wider frame for artificial enzymes in a 2026 article, naming the field eco-nanozymology. Natural enzymes have driven Earth energy and matter cycles for billions of years. Lab-made nanozymes copy enzyme action with sturdy materials, and uses now reach beyond medicine into energy and cleanup work.

The frame treats nanozymes as parts of whole ecosystems of energy and matter flow, not lone catalysts. Gains cited include cleaner water treatment, greener energy conversion, and steps toward carbon balance. Design advice follows from that wider view, favoring materials that fit natural cycles. The authors invite chemists and ecologists to build the field together.
pmc-13309712:
Aparna Khamatkar and colleagues pool orthodontic studies in 2026 comparing two ways to push upper front teeth upward in deep bite correction: small temporary anchor screws versus conventional intrusion arches. Nine studies qualified, including three randomised trials, with searches running to the end of 2025. Both methods had to show true incisor intrusion.

Both approaches corrected deep bite, yet pooled results favoured anchor-supported mechanics for speed, amount of intrusion, and bite correction. Treatment length did not differ meaningfully between the two routes. Anchors also preserved back tooth position better, while arches more often tipped molars outward and flared incisors forward. Some anchor protocols reported their own side effects. Evidence certainty rated low to very low overall. The authors call for stronger long-term trials before the preference hardens into guidance.
pmc-13309912:
Nobue Sato and co-authors report a leukemia patient whose disease returned after a second drug-free break in a 2026 case article. Stopping therapy safely is now a goal in chronic myeloid leukemia once the disease signal falls very low. Data on breaks after the newer drug asciminib remain scarce.

The man, in his 60s, had lived with the disease about 15 years and reached a deep response on his first drug. After a failed first break and a stroke on a second drug, asciminib kept the signal undetectable for over three years. Eight months after stopping asciminib, the signal rose past the relapse threshold. The authors add the case to guidance on watching patients after stopping.
pmc-13310512:
Husam Hamshary and co-authors report two incidental findings of an underbuilt brain membrane in a 2026 case article. The tentorium cerebelli is a dural sheet between the upper brain and the cerebellum, and its underdevelopment is a rare birth variant. Most cases surface by chance on scans done for other reasons.

The first patient, a 16-year-old boy, was scanned after a road accident caused bleeding under the skull. The variant appeared alongside brain tissue dipping into a nearby cistern, without symptoms from it. The second, a 3-year-old with spread nerve tumor, showed the same variant on scans, again without nerve deficits. The authors counsel calm follow-up plus a check for linked brain malformations.
pmc-13310612:
Mohammad Ghalib Riziq and co-authors describe long-term pain control through a repurposed spinal catheter in a 2026 case report. Cancer that invades the sacrum, the base bone of the spine, can cause burning pain that heavy pills barely touch. Implanted spinal pumps work well but demand surgery many patients cannot face.

A 54-year-old man with returned rectal cancer and a 6 cm tumor invading sacral nerve passages suffered burning pain across back, buttocks, and legs. High-dose opioids and add-on drugs barely helped, and emergency visits repeated. A catheter normally used as a spinal drain was adapted for lasting use with an external pump after team review. The report follows how the setup eased his pain over the long term.
pmc-13310712:
Santiago Besa reports early results from a new Ross operation program in South America in a 2026 study. The Ross method moves a patient own lung valve to the aorta, which suits young adults who need a lasting fix without blood thinners. Few centers in Latin America offer it due to its difficulty and scarce donor tissue.

Care covered 29 adults treated from July 2024 to April 2026 at a hospital in Chile. Most had narrow or leaking aortic valves, and many had two leaflet valves from birth. No deaths occurred during follow up, though three strokes were noted early. Longer study must confirm lasting safety.
pmc-13310812:
Mohamed Elsayed Gabr and Hoda Soussa assess groundwater quality and health risk in Qalyubia, Egypt, in a 2026 study. The crowded Nile Delta governorate relies on groundwater for drinking and farm use. The team tested whether water is safe by broad quality scores and by metal focused scores.

Samples from ten sites were checked for thirteen chemical traits. Broad scores rated water as good for drinking and farm use, while a metal score rated it as moderately affected. A pollution score stayed low, and no clear non cancer risk was found, though children were more at risk than adults. Regular metal checks are urged as an early warning.
pmc-13310912:
Nils Bertram and Dejana Mokranjac discuss protein quality control inside mitochondria in a 2026 review. Mitochondria make energy and build key cell parts, yet most of their proteins arrive from outside and must fold correctly in a tight inner space. Helper and cutting proteins guide import, folding, and disposal.

When the system is swamped, faulty proteins clump together. Some clumps aid recovery, some wall off harm, and some turn toxic. Stress inside mitochondria also sends signals to the rest of the cell that reshape defense. Knowing how clumps form and how alarms spread may clarify many diseases tied to faulty proteins.
pmc-13311212:
Yi Long and co-authors describe their 2026 method for mapping how much carbon forests store above ground. Plain satellite images tend to flatten out in dense forest, while space laser data leave gaps, so the team joined both sources.

Laser height data from TECIS were merged pixel by pixel with Sentinel-2 image features to build new three-part indices. A random forest model using these indices plus laser measures reached the best fit, with an R2 value of 0.764 across the map. Error fell by about 14.8 percent compared with image-only models. Better carbon maps help track forest change and support climate policy.
pmc-13311312:
Mohammad Sorowar Hossain and co-authors report the 2026 study of delays in breast cancer diagnosis in Bangladesh. Many women there learn they have cancer only at a late stage, when care works less well.

The study drew 355 women at two large cancer centers in Dhaka. Over half, 55.7 percent, waited more than four months from first signs to treatment start in this group. Delays by patients linked to low schooling, low income, and having no breast pain. Delays by providers linked to living in the countryside and having nipple discharge. The work names clear points where the system could speed up.
pmc-13311712:
Madison E Geeves and co-authors survey lung function services across the United Kingdom on oscillometry use in a 2026 study. The breathing test needs only quiet breathing, which suits patients who cannot manage forced blows.

Forty-two NHS respiratory services replied. Of these, 40 percent owned a device, and most owners already used it in clinic, chiefly for asthma and for patients who fail standard spirometry. Half of services without a device were weighing a purchase within five years. Funding was the top block, and most services said their consultants understood the test little. Training may matter as much as gear.
pmc-13311912:
Jose A. Céspedes and colleagues, in 2026, report a lab study on magnetic nanoparticles for testing beta-lactam antibiotic allergy in a dish. Current lab tests miss many true allergies and mislabel others.

The particles pair a magnetic core and silica shell with branching antigen carriers. Blood serum from 50 patients allergic to amoxicillin and from 44 tolerant people was tested. The new assay caught 98 percent of allergic cases, far above standard RAST at 38 percent and a commercial test at 17 percent in this cohort. It also separated selective from cross-reactive allergy cleanly. Magnetic pull-down shortens handling, aiding clinic use.
pmc-13312012:
Manuela Montatore and colleagues, in 2026, present an imaging case of massive mitral annular calcification tracked over eight years. Calcium buildup on the mitral valve ring is common in older adults, but massive forms carry real diagnostic weight.

The patient, a 76-year-old woman with past transient ischemic attacks and fainting spells, arrived with growing breathlessness on exertion. Early chest films showed a faint curved density that grew into a bold ring over time. Ultrasound found kept heart function with valve leaks, while cardiac CT gave the final picture: dense, merged calcium with a crescent shape and no soft tissue mass. Multi-method imaging over time secures the call.
pmc-13312312:
Stanley Yaidoo and colleagues present a 2026 case report from Ghana on treating a woman carrying three serious infections at once. The 37-year-old, who was living with HIV, came to a clinic in the Central Region with symptoms pointing to lung tuberculosis. Testing confirmed rifampicin-resistant disease alongside chronic hepatitis B and kidney impairment.

Her course was rough: drug side effects, worsening kidney problems, and antiretroviral supplies that ran out and interrupted her HIV treatment. Even so, she finished a 12-month multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimen and reached documented microbiological cure. Her HIV therapy continues, while hepatitis B and kidney disease are monitored without specific treatment because of cost. The authors use the case to argue for integrated, team-based care and to expose stockouts, thin diagnostics, and money barriers in low-resource systems.
pmc-13312812:
Kathryn Dalzell and colleagues report a 2026 veterinary case of a brain bleed in a dog whose MRI looked like almost anything except a simple hematoma. An 8-year-old German Short-haired Pointer arrived with sudden blindness, behavior changes, and weakness on one side, signs pointing to the left forebrain.

The scan showed a sharply circular, well-demarcated lesion with mixed signals, patchy contrast uptake, and a heavy mass effect. That geometry is unusual for hemorrhage, and it raised tumors, inflammation, and even parasite migration as possibilities. The owners chose euthanasia right after imaging, and pathology settled the question: an organizing hematoma in the thalamus, fibrous at the center with fresh bleeding spreading outward. The authors ask radiologists to add this round, centrally enhancing pattern to the known spectrum of dog brain hematomas so the next case is read correctly.
pmc-13312912:
A 2026 installment of the First Person interview series profiles Shamsun Nahar, a researcher in Jae-Wook Jeong's laboratory at the University of Missouri. She is first author of a Disease Models & Mechanisms paper on endometrial cancer. The series invites first authors to speak for themselves about their work and how they came to it.

Nahar traces her path to her mother's encouragement to help others and a growing conviction, formed during undergraduate laboratory work, that science improves human health. Her paper asks how two genetic changes, activation of beta-catenin and loss of the tumor suppressor PTEN, conspire to make endometrial tumors aggressive and metastatic. Using uterus-specific engineered mice with imaging, tissue analysis, and gene profiling, her team showed the pair switches on epithelial-mesenchymal transition and invasion. The route runs through WNT and Hedgehog signaling, exposing possible therapeutic weak points.
pmc-13313112:
Márcia Paulliny Soares Bahia and colleagues report, in a 2026 descriptive study, allergic reactions that followed Brazil's national dengue vaccination campaign in Belo Horizonte. The tetravalent vaccine TAK-003, sold as Qdenga, rolled out in 2024 to children and adolescents, and post-licensure watchfulness picked up more hypersensitivity than trials had led officials to expect.

Linking adverse event reports with vaccination records for ages 6 to 14, the team counted 28 hypersensitivity reactions among 146,115 doses, a rate of 191.6 per million in their calculation, including nine cases of anaphylaxis and two of anaphylactic shock. Every event followed a first dose, struck children averaging 9.4 years old, and began about 31 minutes after injection on average. The authors conclude the rates topped expected vaccine-associated levels and argue pharmacovigilance must stay intense as the campaign continues.
pmc-13314612:
Lin Ran and colleagues build a joint immune-inflammation score to sort relapse risk after cervical cancer surgery, in work published in 2026. Standard clinical traits miss how the tumor immune setting and body-wide inflammation shape who relapses after an operation.

The team studied 612 patients who had primary surgery from January 2020 to December 2025, as counted in the report. They graded immune cells in tumor stroma on stained slides and worked out a systemic immune-inflammation index from blood counts before treatment. Blending both gave three types: favorable, intermediate, and poor. Survival curves, flexible risk models, and adjusted hazard models tested the blend, and tissue staining checked the result. The joined score aims to flag high-risk women for closer watch or extra therapy.
pmc-13314912:
Dominika Oziębło and a large team trace inherited hearing loss through many Polish families in a 2026 study. Dominant hearing loss can spring from scores of genes, and big well-mapped European family sets were scarce.

They studied 108 families with clear dominant passing of the trait. A tiered plan ran gene panel sequencing of 237 hearing genes, genome-wide linkage, whole genome reads, family checks in 437 people, and lab splicing tests, as the report lists. A firm molecular answer came for a share of 52 percent of families in the figures given. A share of 67 percent of the faults found were new to science, as stated in the report. Genes such as MYO6, TBC1D24, and WFS1 recurred, while many families held lone faults. The sweep sharpens testing for families like these.
pmc-13315112:
Mia E Martin and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, years of dengue in Santa Marta, Colombia, hunting for the environmental signals that precede transmission. Colombia is hyperendemic for the mosquito-borne disease, yet analyses were scarce. The team linked 9,237 case reports from 2009 to 2023 with measures of vegetation, surface water, land temperature, rainfall, and population density. Effects were tested delayed by one to four weeks in models.

Greenery was the risk signal: higher vegetation index values associated with more dengue, and the effect strengthened where people live densely. Heat and water worked the other way at delays. High daytime temperatures a week earlier, warm nights four weeks earlier, surface water a week earlier, and rainfall four weeks earlier all tied to fewer cases. The authors interpret the pattern: heat and rain can suppress mosquito survival or breeding. They propose the lagged signals as ingredients for a One Health early-warning system.
pmc-13315212:
Samya Mitra and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a reference chart for peak nasal inspiratory flow in Indian children. The meter reading, how fast a child can sniff air in, helps diagnose allergic rhinitis and its blocking form, but norms did not exist. The team measured 573 children aged six to seventeen in a clinic, classifying rhinitis by international criteria, and modeled flow against age, gender, and body mass.

Average flow across all ages came to 67.95 liters per minute. Flow rose significantly with age and differed between age bands. A cutoff of 65 liters per minute served to flag allergic rhinitis and its blocker form, with accuracy varying by age group. It proved most useful in the youngest and oldest children and for obstruction past age ten. Their regression equation turns age, gender, and body mass into an expected value for any child, giving Indian clinicians a yardstick for Indian clinics.
pmc-13315312:
Juan Jose Hernandez-Gonzalez and co-authors review in 2026 the living partnerships found inside fungi, where one organism lives within fungal cells. These links matter for ecology and evolution, yet they have drawn far less study than similar partnerships in other life forms.

The review gathers evidence across major fungal groups, covering who the inner partners are, what they do, and which host systems show them. It also looks at attempts to build such partnerships in the lab and their possible uses in biotechnology. The authors propose a step-by-step frame that sorts partnerships by how fully the inner partner is merged into the host.
pmc-13315612:
Sigit Dwi Maryanto and a large team share gene activity data in 2026 from oil palm seedlings grown with varied phosphorus doses. Phosphorus is the second most used plant nutrient in oil palm farming, and breeding palms that take it up better could ease shortages, but the gene patterns behind dose response were unclear.

Three-month-old Dumpy seedlings grew in water culture for 180 days at five phosphorus levels, from none to the standard best dose used in nurseries. Leaf RNA was sequenced for each level. The dataset maps how gene regulation shifts with phosphorus supply and can support work on uptake efficiency.
pmc-13316212:
Atul Malhotra and colleagues describe in 2026 the design and starting traits of ATTAIN-OSA. That is a phase 3 program testing a daily oral drug for moderate-to-severe sleep apnea in adults living with obesity or overweight. Airway pressure therapy helps many, yet poor adherence limits it, and injectable drugs bring their own barriers.

Orforglipron is a once-daily oral GLP-1 receptor drug that may be easier to take and keep taking. The master protocol runs two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, one for people unable or unwilling to use airway pressure. Earlier tirzepatide trials showed apnea severity can improve with weight-focused therapy.
pmc-13318712:
Minfan Li and co-authors review, in 2026, cellular ageing in worn spinal discs. Degeneration of these discs is the top pathological driver of low back pain. Current care only eases symptoms and cannot reverse the process. The review blames programmed cell senescence driven by faulty gene regulation.

Ageing disc cells lose their identity and release harmful signals. Those signals, called the SASP, feed a destructive cycle. DNA methylation, histone changes, and non-coding RNAs together form an epigenetic ageing clock. The authors assess ways to reset that clock. Options include clearing senescent cells, editing gene marks, and reprogramming cells. They propose a staged plan: clear, prime, then seed new cells for repair.
pmc-13319712:
Eleni Ntantou and co-authors compare heart artery care plans in a 2026 study of a key branch near its start point. Narrowing at the mouth of this branch threatens a large share of heart muscle, and many patients also have narrowing in other vessels. Whether treating one extra vessel at the same time adds risk was the open question.

Records from one center split 276 people treated at the branch alone from 218 treated at the branch plus one more vessel. The wider treatment group was a bit older on average. After a median follow up of 756 days in the reported count, rates of major bad events were alike in both groups. Extra vessel care did not lift long term risk here.
pmc-13320012:
Mike Reichert and co-authors test whether a fake presenter teaches as well as a human in a 2026 feasibility study with engineering students. Short explainer clips are a staple of college teaching, and software made presenters are now cheap to produce. Whether the swap changes learning or how the clip feels to watch was still open.

Thirteen students each watched two clips on fuel cell basics, one with a human host and one with a software made host, in random order. Short quizzes before and after each clip tracked gains, and a standard form scored how each clip felt to use. Both hosts gave strong short term gains in the first round, which the team read with care due to repeat test effects. The design proved workable for a larger trial.
pmc-13320412:
Amy R Fumo and co-authors hunt liver made signals that shrink muscle in fatty liver disease in a 2026 study joining mouse and human data. Fatty liver and muscle loss feed each other, each worsening the other odds and outlook. Liver gene reads from two mouse disease diets were crossed with muscle protein reads to spot signals the sick liver sends to muscle.

Three liver signals ran high in blood of sick mice with muscle loss and in people with advanced liver disease and muscle loss. Muscle cells dosed with liver secretions or with two of the signals shrank and burned fuel in a skewed way, and human muscle models lost function too. Muting the lead signal in mouse liver eased muscle loss, while boosting it made loss worse.
pmc-13320512:
Akwasi Appiah and colleagues explore, in 2026, what life is like for young people with epilepsy attending a teaching hospital in Cape Coast, Ghana. Epilepsy brings physical, thinking and social challenges, and limited resources add problems with medicine access and stigma. Twenty people aged twelve to twenty-five gave in-depth interviews.

Six themes emerged from their accounts. Diagnosis brought shock, fear and sadness. Getting medicines and care involved cost, availability and long queues. Schooling, work and social life were disrupted, with occasional low self-esteem. Coping drew on lifestyle changes, faith practices and recreation. Friends and family provided crucial support, including during warning auras. Despite the burdens, participants held clear hopes for education and careers. The authors urge better medicine access, less stigma and stronger psychosocial support.
pmc-13321012:
Laurenz Nagl and a large Austrian team describe, in 2026, complete disappearance of a lung cancer after targeted antibody-drug treatment in a patient with limited spread. The cancer carried a rare HER2 gene insertion. The linked drug, trastuzumab deruxtecan, is proven in previously treated patients, but its use as first treatment in oligometastatic disease was undocumented.

The 66-year-old woman had a lung mass and one symptomatic brain metastasis, which was removed and irradiated. She declined standard chemotherapy and immunotherapy. An individualised plan used the targeted drug alone first. After four cycles, imaging showed major shrinkage. Surgery on the lung tumour then found no living cancer at all in the removed tissue. Drug treatment continued afterward. The authors call for prospective trials of this approach.
pmc-13321212:
Jim X. Leng and a large multi-centre team compare, in 2026, survival after two different problems that can follow focused radiation for brain metastases. Radiation necrosis is treatment damage to brain tissue, while local recurrence means the tumour regrew. The two look alike on scans and are hard to tell apart, yet their outlooks may differ greatly.

The cohort held 1,383 patients treated between 2015 and 2020. At irradiated sites, ninety-six patients were ultimately judged to have necrosis and forty-seven to have recurrence after multidisciplinary review. Recurrence appeared sooner after treatment and carried far worse survival, with median survival less than half that of the necrosis group. Symptomatic patients in both groups presented earlier and fared worse. The authors say the gap should inform monitoring and counselling.
pmc-13322812:

pmc-13325112:

pmc-13325312:

pmc-13325912:

pmc-13327612:

pmc-13327912:

pmc-13330612:

pmc-13331712:

pmc-13332012:
Senait Muluken and co-authors surveyed clinical ethics practice among health workers in Addis Ababa public hospitals for a 2026 cross-sectional study. pmc-13332612:

pmc-13332812:

pmc-13333312:

pmc-13333412:

pmc-13333512:

pmc-13336812:

pmc-13342212:

pmc-13342912:

pmc-13346112:

pmc-13348212:

pmc-13348712:

pmc-13349812:

pmc-13351712:

pmc-13352112:

pmc-13352412:

pmc-13352512:
