pmc-13354112:
Daniel Balderrama reports hidden flesh-eating infection behind a severe diabetes crisis in 2026. Necrotizing fasciitis spreads fast and kills, yet early signs can be faint. A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on long steroid therapy arrived confused and dehydrated with severe high blood sugar, newly found to be type 2 diabetes.

No clear infection source showed beyond mild leg swelling, so fluids, insulin, and broad antibiotics began. Sugar measures improved, yet lactate stayed high, blood pressure resisted treatment, and leg swelling grew with crackling gas under the skin. Scans revealed deep tissue gas matching necrotizing fasciitis, prompting emergency surgery. She recovered and went home, a warning to recheck crisis patients who stall.
pmc-13354812:
Sameer Pandey led a 2026 meta-study of lymph node spread in the most advanced oral cancers. Clinico-radiologic T4b oral squamous cell cancer forms the most advanced group of mouth cancers, and whether cancer has reached the lymph nodes strongly affects living and care choice. The anatomical extent of disease also determines who is offered surgery with curing intent.

Databases with PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from July 2005 to July 2024, with manual searches of specialty journals. The pooled study estimates how often nodes are positive and what living follows curing surgery. Surgeons gain a firmer basis for advice people with very advanced oral cancer about the value and limits of operation.
pmc-13355212:
Quentin Allibert and others studied whether the menopausal shift affects cutaneous lupus flares, ran the look-back study of sixty-four women in 2026. Sex hormones are thought to shape lupus, and body-wide lupus often quiets after menopause. Skin lupus, however, has a lower female predominance and later onset, and data on its conduct around menopause were scarce.

The team tracked disease action across the menopausal shift and after menopause, testing whether flares cluster in the late shift and whether action falls afterward. Results challenge any simple assumption that menopause calms all lupus. Dermatologists gain guidance for advice women with skin lupus about flare risk during this life stage.
pmc-13355712:
Lishu Guo reviews in 2026 how a process in mitochondria, the cell's powerhouses, acts as a switch for cell stress and death. The process, called mitochondrial permeability transition, opens pores that can either guard the cell or amplify harmful oxygen signals. It is tightly linked to ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage.

At low levels, oxygen signals help cells adapt and survive, but excess levels damage fats, proteins, and DNA. Recent work shows two mitochondrial parts working together to coordinate pore opening. The review maps how the switch flips between defense and death, with clues for future treatments.
pmc-13356612:
Chen Chen and colleagues contrast how Brazil and China built primary health care systems that last, in a 2026 commentary. Primary care underpins universal coverage and health equity, yet sustainability stays a global challenge. The authors compare the two countries across community roots, funding, continuity of care, and digital support.

Brazil's Family Health Strategy, built on community teams and a rights-based frame, cut deaths from preventable causes and widened access, but faces underfunding and political swings. China's state-driven digital model scaled coverage and financial protection fast, yet struggles with trust in frontline clinics and fragmented continuity. The pairing shows two viable paths, each with a distinct equity trade-off.
pmc-13359012:
Muskan Bansal and co-authors test two ultrasound methods for early kidney damage in diabetes in a 2026 study. Diabetes drives much of the world's chronic kidney disease, but standard blood and urine tests mostly show damage after it is done. The new methods measure kidney stiffness and blood flow resistance during a scan, which may reveal scarring sooner.

They studied 150 diabetic patients at a hospital in Ambala, India, including some with kidney disease and some without. Scan results were compared with standard kidney measures. If the scans track disease well, doctors could catch kidney scarring while steps to slow it still count most.
pmc-13359612:
Teiji Kuzuya and co-authors study what to do when first liver cancer treatment fails in a 2026 paper. For inoperable hepatocellular carcinoma, first care now pairs immune drugs, but the best next step is unsettled. The team evaluated lenvatinib, a targeted pill, given after two different immune-based first treatments in real-world practice.

Lenvatinib still shrank tumors meaningfully, even in patients whose cancer had grown straight through the first treatment. Shrinkage looked greater in patients whose first plan had not included a blood vessel-blocking drug. The findings support careful sequencing of treatments, and guarding liver function so patients stay fit for later lines.
pmc-13359912:
Jiaojiao Fan and co-authors build a cell model of chemotherapy heart damage in a 2026 study. Doxorubicin cures many cancers but can age heart cells early, a process called senescence that limits the drug's use. The team exposed rat heart muscle cells, H9C2, to a low dose of the drug and produced a stable senescence model with clear aging markers and faulty mitochondria.

They then tested SS-31, a compound that targets mitochondria. It reversed key aging signs and lowered cell stress in the model. The setup gives drug hunters a reliable screen for heart-protective candidates, and SS-31 itself emerges as a promising shield.
pmc-13360612:
Qin Zhang and co-authors tested a friendly bacterium as fish feed in a 2026 study of young tilapia. The fish were juvenile GIFT tilapia, a bred strain of Nile tilapia raised widely on farms. Their feed was laced with Bacillus subtilis, a safe microbe used as a probiotic. The trial ran for 60 days and covered several dose levels.

Fish on the added bacterium grew better and used feed more efficiently. Their digestion enzymes worked harder, stress defenses rose, and inflammation signals fell. The bacteria in their guts also shifted in a healthier direction. One dose level gave the steadiest gains across all checks. The authors say the microbe is a practical feed add-on that can support healthier, more sustainable fish farming.
pmc-13361312:
Wanhai Zhou and co-authors built an active food wrap for pears in a 2026 materials study. The film blends two base plastics and gums with a mushroom polysaccharide from Antrodia cinnamomea and tea tree oil. The team cast the films from solution and tested their strength, structure, and protective powers. The goal was a wrap that keeps harvested 'Yuluxiang' pears fresh longer.

The mushroom ingredient stiffened and strengthened the base film. Adding both extras improved water resistance, blocked ultraviolet light, and slowed oxygen and vapor passing through. The film clung well to pear skin and showed strong antibacterial action against Staphylococcus germs. Wraps like this could cut fruit losses after harvest without relying on synthetic sprays.
pmc-13361812:
Yong Oh Kim and co-authors asked whether chest shape should shape CPR guidance in a 2026 study. Guidelines call for the same compression depth, five to six centimeters, for every adult, ignoring body differences. The team reviewed 431 adults whose hearts stopped in hospital and who had chest CT scans. They measured body mass index and the chest's front-to-back depth, inside and out.

About four in ten patients survived to 28 days. The team split cases by how long CPR lasted and tested whether chest measures linked to survival differently across those windows. Early results showed the links shifting with resuscitation time. If body shape truly changes what works, future CPR guidance might fit compression depth to the patient instead of using one number for all adults.
pmc-13363112:
Gabriel Poirier and others linked mental impairment to disrupted motor planning in older adults, in 2026. Neurocognitive illnesses often accompany motor impairments that may precede obvious mental decline, but most motor markers are coarse and do not separate global deterioration from given control disruptions. Motor planning, drawing on both motor and mental stock, may be mainly at risk.

Fifty-seven older adults, with twenty-seven cognitively impaired and thirty healthy people, were tested with a gravity-based motor planning task. Planning deficits distinguished impaired people beyond general motor slowing. The study offers a process-given marker that could flag mental decline through movement, earlier than standard tests.
pmc-13363612:
The journal Materials issued a 2026 correction to a 2025 paper by Sisi Chao on how crossrib shape affects the bond between high-strength steel bars and concrete. The notice fixes two record items. First, one of the author's affiliations, a Xi'an key laboratory for low-carbon urban construction at Chang'an University, was left out of the original paper and is now added in full.

Second, the funding line is rewritten to name the correct fund, the open fund of that same laboratory, under the central universities' research funds. The notice states that the paper's science and conclusions are untouched by these record fixes. The editor approved the correction, and the original paper has been updated.
pmc-13363812:
Mohamed El Amine Kouadri and colleagues present a 2026 study of Fusarium fungi behind dry rot in stored potatoes in the Mascara region of Algeria, the first such survey there. They purified 118 isolates from rotting tubers gathered from stores in early 2025. They sorted them into 28 look-alike types and tested one from each type for how much rot it causes on a standard potato variety. Image analysis scored the damage.

Just over half of the types caused real rot, with strength varying widely, and gene reads named the worst offenders, including Fusarium sambucinum and Fusarium redolens. Common types were not always the most harmful, so counting isolates alone misleads. The authors urge storage surveys that join looks, harm tests, and gene identification.
pmc-13364212:
Cheng-Yu Lin and colleagues present a 2026 study on watching a motor's vibration state change with a single fiber Bragg grating sensor when its mounting angle shifts. The packaged sensor sits off the shaft, so its light signal blends the motor, fixture, glue, and boundary state into one trace. The team tracked the trace's moving frequency pattern with adaptive decomposition, and separately fed raw windows to three autoencoder networks trained on steady-angle behavior.

Fixed angles gave steady yet distinct signatures, while angle changes produced local trace shifts and alarm-worthy stretches. A simple threshold baseline caught more transitions but cried wolf more often, and the CNN-LSTM autoencoder was the most selective. The authors frame the setup as relative state watching, not fault diagnosis.
pmc-13364412:
Jiyou Zhu and Hongyuan Li study 2026 street trees that grow near air conditioner exhaust vents in a city. The hot, dry blast from a unit two steps away forms a harsh micro zone. The pair matched such trees with calm site kin and read nine leaf traits on each.

Exposed leaves grew thicker and denser, with more but smaller breath pores and less green tint. The shift fits a save mode, where the tree spends less and guards its water. Plain leaf traits like these could serve as cheap flags for heat stress checks on city trees.
pmc-13365112:
Tatiana Mencarini and co-workers probe in 2026 how tiny bits shed by blood plate bits change clot growth on vessel wall goods in flow. Plate bits clump on bare wall spots to seal harm, but too much clump drives heart ills. The team runs blood through fine tubes lined with four wall goods.

pmc-13369812:
Marta Graell and colleagues untangle the genetic links between dyslexia and school results in a 2026 study. Dyslexia, a reading disorder that often appears in school-age children, is tied to weaker school performance and less schooling overall. The team first confirmed a negative genetic link between dyslexia and years of schooling, then tested genetic scores in 4,274 school-age children.

They split dyslexia risk into a part shared with schooling and a part unique to dyslexia. Both parts shaped language results in similar ways, but maths results followed a different pattern. The dyslexia-only part was tied to poorer outcomes on its own. The work helps explain why reading genes affect subjects unevenly, and it points to reading support that is tuned to a child rather than to a single score.
pmc-13370712:
Samaneh Ahmadian-Moghadam and colleagues review how stress before conception may shape child brain development in a 2026 paper. The focus is on two conditions, autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and on whether risk can be set before pregnancy begins. Human and animal studies were gathered and compared.

The review finds that stress before conception can alter chemical marks on genes in reproductive cells, shift early development of the calming GABA system, and reset the body's stress hormone axis. Those shifts may change how the fetal brain matures. The authors argue that the months before conception deserve more attention in prevention, alongside the far better studied months of pregnancy itself.
pmc-13373112:
Volkan Demircan and co-authors checked side harms of joint care in breast cancer in a 2026 study. The cancer type in view lacks three common marks and has the worst outlook of the breast types. Women with tumor left after first drug rounds face high return risk, and a pill can cut that risk.

The study held 95 women at eight centers who got the pill and beam care at the same time from 2018 to 2024. Harms were graded with a set scale, and math checks kept false hits low. Joint use is well known in gut cancers but less so here. The counts help teams weigh gain and harm for this group.
pmc-13373512:
Ikram El Moubarik and co-authors timed how long a joint drug holds in a 2026 study. The drug is used when first joint drugs fail in sore joint disease. It works well, but the sore can come back at a wide range of times.

The team tracked patients from 2021 to 2025 at one center and timed the gap from the last drug round to a flare. Charts gave health, lab, and care facts to test what made the gap long or short. A clear time map helps doctors plan the next round and helps patients know what to expect. It also shows who may need a switch sooner.
pmc-13375212:
Ustinova and colleagues develop a multi-specialty method for spotting avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, known as ARFID, in children with autism, in 2026 child psychiatry research from Russia. Children with autism often eat restrictively, and ARFID adds bodily harm: weight deviation, nutrient deficits, and daily-life complications beyond picky eating. The team clustered the criteria, then built a standard exam algorithm. They applied a full assessment to a group of autistic children to test the approach.

Selective or restrictive eating patterns appeared in 71 of the 80 children examined, 88.8 percent of the group. Somatic disorders accompanied the eating, including body weight deviating from the norm and carbohydrate metabolism problems found during the exams. The authors argue ARFID is underdiagnosed in both psychiatric and child health settings despite frequent clinic encounters. Their method assigns roles to psychiatrists, pediatricians, and nutrition specialists so the somatic side is not missed while eating is treated.
pmc-13375412:
Neilmegh Lakshman Varada and co-authors share two rare blood cancer cases in a 2026 paper. The ill drives blood counts of one white cell type sky high for months. Gene tests split it from kin ills, and a famed pill helps those with the right gene marks.

The two cases lack those marks, the group where care rules are thin and proof is sparse. The paper logs how each case was found, what drugs were tried, and how each fared at one large US med center. Old counts gave this ill a near half death rate at five years. Each fresh set of cases helps teams pick care with less guess.
pmc-13379512:
Swainson and colleagues give the first full account of genetic counselling in Aotearoa New Zealand. Counsellors have worked there since 1995. They now serve both public and private care. Their work rests on Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the treaty that shapes public life. It also draws on Māori views of health and family. Counsellors hold family meetings, called hui, so kin can decide as a group.

New Zealand teams helped find the CDH1 gene, a key gene in some stomach cancers. Still, the field faces hard limits. Training places at home are few. Demand keeps rising. Māori and Pacific staff stay too few for the need.
pmc-13380412:
Muhammad Nabeel Shafqat, Ali Hassan, and Muhammad Shahzad describe a 2026 case of cancer of the lower bowel and anus spreading to the penis, a very rare site. Their patient was a middle-aged man whose cancer was already advanced, with spread to the liver. During combined chemotherapy and radiation he developed a painful ulcer and a firm lump on the penis.

Scans showed several lesions inside the penile tissue, and tissue tests confirmed they matched the original cancer. A specialist board advised major surgery, but his overall condition declined quickly as the disease progressed. Care therefore shifted to comfort measures. The authors note that such spread usually signals a poor outlook.
pmc-13382712:
Masaki Nakamura and co-authors present a 2026 study testing a scan measure for judging risk in small lung cancers treated with radiation alone. The measure compares the solid part of a tumour with its total size on scans, including hazy areas called ground glass. Good risk sorting helps tailor treatment intensity.

The study included 265 patients with tumours of three centimetres or less and no spread, treated between 2015 and 2022. Patients fell into three groups by the ratio, from hazy-dominant to fully solid. No patient in the hazy-dominant group saw the cancer return or died during follow-up of about four years. The authors compare the ratio against standard staging for predicting outcomes.
pmc-13382812:
Brandon Loshusan and colleagues report a redo chest operation using a new fenestrated graft in a 2026 case report. The patient, a 62-year-old man, had leftover chronic tearing and a widened 65 mm thoracic aorta after earlier repair. His left subclavian artery sat deep, and his left vertebral artery followed an unusual course.

The team moved the vertebral artery, then placed a hybrid frozen elephant trunk graft with a window for the deep artery branch. A bridging stent kept that branch open, as later scans confirmed. The case shows how careful planning and a tailored graft can solve anatomy that makes repeat arch surgery risky.
pmc-13383012:
Bromberger and colleagues report robotic-assisted decortication, peeling a fibrous rind off a trapped lung, in lung transplant recipients, in 2026 thoracic surgery research. Lung entrapment after transplant can defunctionalize the graft under scarred pleura. The series reviews 26 consecutive robotic cases from 2019 to 2024, performed a median of 516 days after transplant. It measures lung re-expansion, breathing test gains, chest tube duration, hospital stay, and complications graded by the Clavien-Dindo surgical scale.

No case required conversion to open thoracotomy. Median chest tube duration was 4 days and median hospital stay 6 days across the series. Complete lung expansion was achieved in 88 percent of cases, with a median improvement of 315 milliliters in forced vital capacity and 235 milliliters in one-second expiratory volume on breathing tests. The worst complications were one return to theater for air leak and one re-intubation. Bromberger says the robotic approach safely reverses entrapment.
pmc-13383512:
Tingting Tao's team describes four practical fixes for loosened knots during heart surgery, in a 2026 technical paper. Knots can slip unexpectedly at awkward angles or poor depth perception, especially in valve replacement, and a loose knot can cause paravalvular leak or force reintervention. The paper presents four simple techniques for knots that loosen mid-operation.

Each technique addresses loosened knots or the leaks they cause without reopening the repair. By avoiding reintervention, the methods help surgeons manage intraoperative emergencies calmly and safely. The paper gives cardiac surgeons a small toolkit for a stressful moment that every operating room eventually faces.
pmc-13386012:
Kai Ni and co-authors present an on-column method to cap reactive thiols on engineered antibodies in 2026 work. Such antibodies, called ThiomAb, carry a deliberately free cysteine that lets drug payloads attach at one exact site. In cell culture, that free spot gets capped unevenly, which varies charge and risks clumping or mix-ups.

Capping the thiol while the antibody sits on its capture column steadied the product early in processing. High-throughput screening tuned buffer and redox settings, guided by mass and charge profiling. Free thiol counts fell sharply, charge profiles evened out, and stability improved, which offers makers a scalable control step.
pmc-13387612:
Jonathan Munera Lopez and co-authors show that removing two tip components paralyzes the parasite Toxoplasma gondii in 2026 work. The parasite's apical polar ring anchors its internal rails and gates the moving conoid used in cell invasion. The team cataloged new ring parts, including the widely conserved protein APR9.

Losing APR9 alone only mildly dented the parasite's growth cycle in their tests. Losing APR9 together with KinesinA froze movement, blocked invasion and exit, and piled up cell defects. Conoid extension faltered and release of a key adhesion protein dropped, which marks the ring as a core motility hub.
pmc-13389812:
Hiroaki Fujita and a large team report, in 2026, fertility care after surgery for an extremely rare fallopian tube tumour. The growth, a mature cystic teratoma, was found in the right tube during keyhole surgery and was removed while keeping the tube in place.

A dye test three months later showed the tube was open, though fluid lingered in the pelvis, hinting at adhesions around the tube. Timed attempts at natural conception failed, so the couple moved to in vitro fertilisation. A further keyhole check before embryo transfer found a swollen tube, which was then removed, and a frozen embryo transfer achieved pregnancy. Fertility specialists gain the first account of conception care after this rare diagnosis.
pmc-13390212:
Zoilo Emilio García-Batista's team tested the PHQ-9 low-mood survey for adults in the Dominican Republic, where local test-based evidence had been missing despite the tool's global use. Without a locally tested tool, screening hit rate and grade-setting suffer, hampering both care and research.

In 914 adults, the team examined the survey's structure with factor checks, its consistency with omega and alpha scores, and its matching soundness against related gauges. Establishing that the nine-item scale behaves soundly in this group gives local clinicians and disease trackers a brief, free tool. They can trust it for screening and grade tracking.
pmc-13390612:
Hafsa Zahoor and Rameez Ahmed link, in 2026, women's digital access with women's health outcomes across Indian states. Mobile phones and the internet can shape how women find health information and reach services, but state-level proof for India has been limited.

Using aggregated national family health survey data from 2019 to 2021 for 36 states and union territories, the authors compare women's internet use and personal phone ownership with several health outcomes. The outcomes cover menstrual hygiene, anaemia, maternal care, and contraception. Because the analysis is ecological, it compares state averages rather than individual women. Public health readers gain a map of where digital gaps and health gaps coincide.
pmc-13391012:
Cheng-Hung Yang's team reviews how release spray charging mass scans imaging, DESI-MSI, grew from rapid screening into a precise exact marker-work platform. The method maps compounds across tissue sections under room conditions, but data quality hinges on sample handling.

The review traces a model shift from no prep work to tuned prep work, covering keeping, setting, washing, drying, and on-tissue tagging, plus rules that tame matrix effects and signal drift. pmc-13392012:
Jin Li, Chunjiang Zhao, Jian Gao, and Hui Guo design, in 2026, a carbon fibre hydrogen storage cylinder and simulate its stresses. Type IV cylinders, with a polymer liner fully wound in carbon fibre, are central to hydrogen vehicles, and their burst strength must be predicted reliably.

Winding layers were optimised with grid theory, with close attention to dome thickness, and a progressive damage model forecast a burst pressure above the design target, confirming the layup. The team also varied length, dome shape, and boss support dimensions to map stress effects. Hydrogen engineers gain design rules for trading weight against safety in high-pressure storage.
pmc-13392712:
Pan and co-authors describe, in 2026, a continuous-flow method for making molybdenum carbide nanoparticles, catalysts that mimic costly noble metals. Precursors flow through a reactor while instruments record spectra in real time, but the overlapping signals are hard to untangle by ordinary math. The team trained several machine learning models to convert those spectra into moment-by-moment amounts of precursor, intermediate material, and the end product.

A multilayer perceptron, a type of neural network, performed best, matching X-ray scattering checks with a mean error of only 9 percent across the validation runs. Its concentration profiles revealed a two-step pathway: the precursor first becomes an amorphous, disordered intermediate, and that material then crystallizes inside the particles. The first step limits the speed of the reaction. The authors present the setup as a step toward self-driving reactors that monitor and steer their production.
pmc-13392912:
Chaowalit Monton, Thaniya Wunnakup, and Jirapornchai Suksaeree hunted for the best liquid blend to dissolve an extract of Albizia myriophylla. Early tests showed the stem extract halting the germ at low strength, and propylene glycol dissolving it best among single liquids.

A statistical mixture design then balanced ethanol, propylene glycol, and water, targeting at least ninety percent recovery of lupinifolin. The winning recipe, dominated by propylene glycol with a moderate ethanol share, recovered essentially all the compound across checks, and the finished five percent extract still killed the target germ. The authors offer the blend as a foundation for future anti-cavity oral sprays.
pmc-13393812:
Yingying Wang, Qi Wang, Lijie Chen, Xiaomei Dong, and Tianchao Xu tested how emotional faces hijack attention in major depressive disorder using an emotion-induced blindness task. The setup measures how long an emotional image blinds viewers to what follows.

Patients identified targets less accurately overall, and the dip ran deepest at the shortest gap, pointing to stronger early interference. Disgust faces hurt accuracy most, out-interfering fear and sadness, and performance after disgust and fear distractors tracked who had depression. The authors suggest disgust carries a particular attentional grip in depression and that task performance under those faces might serve as a behavioural marker of the condition.
pmc-13394612:
Karnirius Harefa and others test butterfly pea and moringa plant brews against diet-driven artery harm in rats in a 2026 study. Artery harm is a long, low-grade vessel illness marked by vessel lining flare and slow thickening of the inner wall.

Blood signs of lining flare and defense flare were read, and inner wall width was gauged under the microscope. The paper offers plant leads for slowing early vessel harm before it hardens.
pmc-13395312:
Qin Li and co-authors build, in 2026, a platelet-cloaked carrier to ferry a statin into stroke-damaged brain. The cloaked particles cleared harmful radicals and nudged immune cells toward a healing mode. In animals they shrank the dead brain zone far more than free drug. Movement and sense recovered faster over three weeks, and weight loss eased. The authors pitch the cloak as a lower-dose route to lasting brain guard.
pmc-13395912:
Tomas Rosén and a large team present, in 2026, an X-ray method that films tiny flows in three dimensions plus time. Single particles were tracked in thin mixes, and flow fields were read in dense ones. The films can check the maths models used to design mixers and medical tools. Effects such as particles lining up in flow became visible live. With AI rebuild tools, the authors see a new speed frontier for flow science.
pmc-13396112:
Jian Gao and co-authors review how CT scans can map the stiffness and stretch of injured lungs in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Paired scans taken at different breath points can be aligned by software so each small region's change in air content and shape is tracked. From those maps, models estimate local strain, reopening of collapsed tissue, and stress. The aim is ventilator settings tuned to protect fragile regions, since pushing air too hard into stiff lungs causes further injury, a harm called ventilator-induced lung injury.
pmc-13396412:
Yuanyuan Jin and colleagues grow large single-crystal hybrid perovskite films by two-dimensional melt growth in a 2026 study. Melt growth normally yields bulk crystals, but extending it to ultrathin films with precise thickness control had been difficult.

A vapor-liquid-solid process reacted a pre-deposited inorganic seeding layer with organic precursor flux to form a two-dimensional molten phase, which spread and crystallized uniformly without lattice matching requirements. Both single-layer and quasi-two-dimensional ferroelectric films were grown on silicon wafers at low temperature. Materials scientists gain a substrate-agnostic route to large perovskite films.
pmc-13396512:
Asef Darvishi and co-authors scored the land of Qeshm Island, in Iran, for how well each area suits farming, using maps and a structured weighting method. The model folds together soil, slope, geology, water access, current land use, and sensitive ecological zones. A technique called analytic hierarchy process turns expert judgments into weights for those layers, and geographic software stacks them into a suitability map. Landscape ecology principles run through the design, so keeping habitat connected counts alongside yield when farmland is zoned.
pmc-13396612:
Aldossari, BinMayouf, and Alfuraih present, in 2026, a case of hemifacial cutaneous sarcoidosis, a rare one-sided facial form of the granulomatous disease sarcoidosis. Imaging additionally revealed silent lymph node findings inside her chest, showing the skin lesion was the visible tip of systemic disease. Treatment began with intralesional triamcinolone injections, two sessions eight weeks apart at 10 and then 2.5 milligrams per cubic centimeter, plus topical steroid step-down. Partial regression showed at one-month follow-up, with care continuing.
pmc-13396712:

Both sexes were studied, some on a background that also lacks a bile-modifying gene, and some dosed with the FXR drug obeticholic acid. The humanized mice answered the drug in their own pattern, distinct from ordinary mice, which the authors offer as a better preclinical test bed.
pmc-13397412:
Mutsuki Furukawa and co-authors tell the story of a nine-year-old girl whose leg muscle cancer returned, unusually, in her breast. Their 2026 case report covers alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, the most common soft tissue cancer of childhood and, in this subtype, an aggressive one with a poor outlook.

Surgeons removed the leg tumor widely and cleared nearby lymph nodes, and chemotherapy plus proton beam radiation brought complete remission. Three months after treatment ended, a lump appeared in her right breast and imaging pointed to spread of the original cancer. Breast spread from this tumor is extremely rare, and no standard local treatment exists, which is why the team documents their course.
pmc-13397612:
Mátyás Béndek and colleagues report a rare pancreatic tumour that looked, on scans, like one of the deadliest cancers. The scan showed a growth narrowing the pancreatic duct where body meets tail, and computed tomography strongly suggested ductal adenocarcinoma.

Its cells carried grainy pink interiors, stained for S100 and SOX10 proteins, and crept along tissue planes enough to pinch the duct. pmc-13413812:
Eri Tsunoi and colleagues fix in 2026 a quiet measurement error in chip-based digital PCR: DNA sticking to the chip's silicone walls. The rubbery PDMS surface grabs biomolecules, thinning the reaction and skewing counts in closed chambers, an effect poorly characterized until now. The team compared adding chemicals to the mix against baking water-loving agents into the plastic itself, testing three additives on DNA counting accuracy.

Beef protein, bovine serum albumin, won clearly: at 1.1 percent it lifted the measured copy number about 2.3-fold over the plain mix in their runs. The two rival additives changed little. Dilution series with plasmid and cell-line DNA both straightened out under albumin, with tighter linearity across the range. The authors recommend solution additives over plastic modification for this platform.
pmc-13414012:
Sylwia Drzymała and co-authors survey in 2026 the mental health of two hundred people living with post-COVID-19 syndrome. Recovery from the infection does not always restore health, and anxiety and depression ride along for many. Participants aged eighteen to eighty completed three standard psychological questionnaires while the team logged their other illnesses, hunting for who faces the highest risk.

By the hospital scale, anxiety touched 41.5 percent of respondents and depression 39.5 percent in this group. A dedicated screen flagged generalized anxiety in 36.5 percent of those surveyed. Diabetes alongside the syndrome tripled depression risk compared with having no extra illnesses. Among women who smoked and had diabetes, the modelled risk of depressive disorder passed ninety percent. The authors demand targeted psychological screening for such patients.
pmc-13414512:
Fatouma Mohamed Abdoul-Latif and co-authors screen plant chemicals on a computer in 2026 for a way to keep toxic dichromate out of crops. Hexavalent chromium sneaks into plants through the very transporters that carry sulfate and phosphate, so blocking those doors could starve the poison. Forty-nine compounds from ten Djiboutian medicinal plants were docked virtually against both transporter structures and ranked against the ions they might displace.

Binding scores varied widely, and several compounds latched onto the transporters' key residues in their models. One molecule from Aloe djiboutiensis, cyclohexanepropanoic acid, bound both transporters most strongly of the set. Safety and drug-likeness predictions looked favourable, and hundred-nanosecond simulations kept the winning complexes stable. The authors offer the candidates as a theoretical basis needing bench proof.
pmc-13415412:
Radan Kassab and Amal Hasan present early clinical observations of a refined tooth preparation protocol for fixed crowns, in a 2026 technical note. Their modified approach shapes teeth below the gumline using piezoelectric ultrasonic tips, then polishes the area with silicone points. Four patients received zirconia crowns across thirty-five teeth.

Crowns went through a strict four step ultra-polishing routine before placement. Gum measures were tracked at one week, then at three, six, and twelve months. Margins stayed stable with no visible recession at any site. Gum thickness rose most in thin tissue, from about 0.59 to about 1.14 millimeters on average. Bleeding stayed minimal across follow-up.
pmc-13416312:
Matteo Lusardi and co-authors test an anti-inflammatory compound in a flowing, pressurized model of hypertension, in 2026. Their bioreactor grows vessel lining cells under pump driven circulation and pressure pulses, separating chemical from mechanical stress. The test compound, an imidazo-pyrazolyl urea called 3l, is known to inhibit cell chemotaxis.

Angiotensin II, a vessel tightening hormone, switched on the inflammatory master switch NF-kappaB in the cells. Compound 3l cut that activation significantly under static, flowing, and pressurized conditions alike. Release of the messenger IL-8 also fell in static and flowing setups. Splitting stress types clarifies where drugs act, the authors note.
pmc-13416912:
Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of a herbal capsule called Bazi Bushen and its effect on the aging womb lining. With age the lining responds less well to pregnancy signals, and good treatments are scarce. The team tested the capsule in naturally aged mice and in aged human womb-lining cells, using gene-readout tools and computer models of its ingredients.

The capsule improved how well the lining received an embryo and how its cells changed to support early pregnancy. It acted through a cell energy pathway, AMPK and SIRT3, that guards mitochondria, the cell's power units. One ingredient, luteolin, stood out: it helped clear worn mitochondria and curbed a protein that splits them apart. Other named ingredients included several ginseng compounds. If it holds in women, it could raise fertility chances for older mothers.
pmc-13418512:
Ciais and colleagues proposed in 2026 a global observing system to cut uncertainty in methane emissions. Current monitoring is too sparse to track trends, above all in remote regions where natural emissions may grow with warming. The authors combine emission inventories and process models for 2014 to 2023 to show where the unknowns lie.

Human-caused emissions remain uncertain by about a third worldwide. Wetlands in the tropics and Arctic, fires, and inland waters carry far larger uncertainty as natural sources, around seventy percent, with trend uncertainty near double that. The authors match fixes to source types: sharp satellite views for point sources, more flux towers and wetland maps for diffuse ones. They calculate that about twenty new air-measurement stations per key tropical region could cut continental uncertainty at modest cost.
pmc-13418612:
William H Cook, Anas A Linjawi, and Veronika van Dijck report throat cancer spreading to the thyroid after apparent cure, in a 2026 case report with literature review. The patient, a 55 year old man, had p16 positive oropharyngeal cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy and a complete response. Nine months later throat pain and hoarseness led to scans showing an enlarged thyroid.

Needle sampling confirmed the same cancer inside the thyroid, with no return at the original site. Surgery removed the thyroid and neck nodes, finding spread in 13 of 22 nodes and involved margins. The authors call it the first such report and urge more cases to guide care.
pmc-13419412:
Nosheen Nasir and colleagues build and trial ComBact, a phone-based decision aid that helps doctors in Pakistan prescribe antibiotics more carefully. Resistance grows fastest where prescribing lacks specialist backup, a common gap in busy hospitals. The tool covers seven infection syndromes at a private tertiary hospital in the study.

Development and rollout were studied with a mixed design that joins usage data with doctor interviews. Registration, uptake, and detailed use counts came straight from the system itself. Interviews, read through a standard thematic method, captured how doctors judged the tool's help at the bedside. A homegrown aid fitted to local practice may spread stewardship further than imported rules that ignore local drug supply.
pmc-13420312:
Mingyu Sun and colleagues test a routine twist on freezing ablation for atrial fibrillation: parking the mapping catheter in different branches of each lung vein. Balloon freezing to isolate the veins works well, yet widening the treated ring may improve results for stubborn cases. Their study enrolled 709 patients with non-valve-related fibrillation treated between January 2020 and August 2022.

Of those, 293 procedures used different vein branches for support and mapping, while 416 stayed in the same branch per vein. The spiral catheter steadies the balloon and reads vein signals as the freeze proceeds. Comparing the two habits on real outcomes tells labs whether the extra maneuvering earns its time. Atrial fibrillation is common and returns often, so small technique gains multiply across many patients.
pmc-13420512:
Emily Dyer and colleagues report a patient with HIV whose virus grew resistant to a key drug class after treatment for silent tuberculosis. Short rifamycin-based courses for latent TB finish far more often than the old nine-month course. Trials report completion of 78 to 92 percent for the short courses, against half or less for the long one. Those same rifamycins force changes to HIV therapy, where the risk in this case hid.

Resistance surfaced only when the team checked the patient for a switch to long-acting injectable HIV treatment. Old genotype records proved decisive in judging what could still work. Before the TB course, the viral load had fallen to 33 copies per milliliter on the prior regimen in the value reported. The case warns teams to plan HIV drug swaps around TB treatment with resistance firmly in view.
pmc-13420712:
Ela Ahmad and colleagues report a case of sudden cardiac death rhythm triggered by very early heartbeats from the Purkinje network, finally quieted by the drug flecainide. This form of ventricular fibrillation strikes young people with no structural heart disease and no channel disorder to explain it. Emergency crews reached the patient within three minutes and found no pulse and no breathing.

The resting heart tracing afterward looked normal in its intervals, with no warning pattern visible. Short-coupled early beats from the heart's conduction fibers were identified as the trigger on rhythm analysis. Drug suppression succeeded where the trigger could not be mapped to a single burnable spot. Cases like this one guide emergency and rhythm teams toward drug options when ablation has no target.
pmc-13421012:
Simon Weinmüller and colleagues argue that diffusion, long treated as a helper, is in fact mandatory for the contrast seen in steady-state FLASH imaging, a workhorse MRI method. Textbooks credit radio wave and gradient spoiling for its tissue contrast. Simulations in their study told a different story when diffusion was switched off.

Without diffusion, the simulated spinal fluid signal overshot white matter, flipping the expected contrast in the synthetic brain used. A printed brain phantom filled with low-diffusion oil confirmed the effect in real scans. Earlier work had cast diffusion as a useful extra for spoiling; the new results promote it to a core actor. Scan designers and model builders must include diffusion or their contrast predictions will mislead.
pmc-13421112:
Wentao Zhao and colleagues build a prediction chart for failure of bone healing after fusion surgery for infected spine disease. Nonunion after such surgery runs far higher than after clean spine operations, and older models lacked both validation and infection-specific factors. Their cohort holds 224 patients treated with cleaning and instrumented fusion from January 2020 to December 2023.

The chart separated future nonunion cases sharply, with an accuracy measure of 0.936 on the standard curve in the reported validation, and its risk estimates matched observed rates well. Internal checks stood in for the external test the authors say must follow. Surgeons can now counsel patients with numbers before the operation and plan graft and follow-up choices for those at highest risk.
pmc-13421612:
Rachel Pereur leads a ten-author team studying, in a 2026 paper, how the Fgfr3 gene keeps the seams between skull bones healthy. Those seams, the cranial sutures, must stay open while the brain grows, and faults in the FGFR3 pathway cause sutures to fuse too early, though its everyday role was unclear.

Zebrafish lacking Fgfr3 developed abnormal sutures. Microscopy showed a disorganised collagen network, and reporter lines revealed that the gene limits the pool of bone-forming precursor cells while helping mature bone cells finish their work. Its loss switched on the Wnt signalling pathway inside sutures, and a drug blocking that pathway during development partly restored the picture. Crosstalk between the two pathways emerges as central.
pmc-13422312:
Taisuke Ishii and four colleagues compare, in a 2026 nationwide Japanese study, how patients on dialysis fare with chemotherapy after cancer surgery versus similar patients not on dialysis. Doctors often soften or skip adjuvant chemotherapy for dialysis patients, fearing toxicity through failing kidneys, yet hard evidence on the trade-off was missing.

Merging the hospital cancer registry with national claims data, the study covered adults newly diagnosed between 2013 and 2015 with colorectal, stomach, breast or lung cancer. Survival analysis began ninety days after surgery, counting chemotherapy started within that window, and statistical models separated the effects of dialysis status and treatment. The authors present the work as a basis for fairer, evidence-led drug decisions in this group.
pmc-13422812:
Bailly and colleagues set out a study protocol in 2026 for peer support for medical residents in Lyon, France. Residents often face anxiety, depression, burnout, and suicidal thoughts, and existing support has shown limited benefit. The PAESSM study will place Mental Health First Aid-trained peers inside a first-year resident cohort. About a tenth of first-years will train as certified supporters for their classmates.

The design follows two cohorts for twelve months: first-years with the peer network and second-years with usual support. Questionnaires every three months will track well-being on a standard scale, plus anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, job strain, and help-seeking. A qualitative part will explore supporters' own experiences and how the scheme runs in practice. Because groups are not randomised, the authors plan careful statistical adjustment and sensitivity checks.
pmc-13424012:
Scott M Friedman and eight colleagues present a plain-language summary of a statistical comparison between two eye injection drugs. The drugs are aflibercept 8 mg and faricimab. They treat diabetic macular edema and wet age-related macular degeneration. Both block vessel growth signals, and both promise longer gaps between injections, yet they have never met in a head-to-head trial.

The underlying study used a network meta-analysis, a method that chains trial results together to compare treatments indirectly. Outcomes were the number of injections needed, changes in vision, and changes in retinal thickness, which should fall when treatment works. The summary walks patients and clinicians through what the indirect evidence can and cannot say about the two regimens.
pmc-13424112:
Fabiana Moresi and colleagues tested palbociclib as first-line therapy in 2026 across 22 esophageal squamous cancer cell lines, a disease with few good options. CDK4/6 blockers had shown little benefit as second-line drugs, yet their first-line, subtype-specific effects were uncharted.

Cell lines split into resistant, delayed, and arrested responders tied to Rb-pathway status, and delayed responders accumulated DNA damage that triggered interferon genes and drew immune cells into tumor spheroids. The paper nominates early palbociclib for molecularly defined esophageal cancer, pairing growth arrest with immune recruitment in molecularly defined subtypes.
pmc-13424212:
Annica Heyne and three colleagues work out how self-driving laboratories, robot platforms that screen materials around the clock, can judge corrosion resistance quickly without losing predictive power. Full corrosion tests can take months, far too slow for early screening. The team therefore compared four alloys in salty water, including stainless steel and high-entropy mixes. Their aim was a short test sequence.

Their method starts by naming which long-term property a quick measurement must predict, then qualifies shortcut experiments against the slow gold standards. The result is a minimal electrochemical routine fit for automated platforms, aimed at corrosion protection and energy materials. The paper frames qualification, not just speed, as the missing discipline in materials acceleration.
pmc-13424312:
Li Yang and six colleagues uncover how the developing liver links cell division to the plumbing that drains bile. In mouse and human models, the tiny bile channels began forming exactly where liver precursor cells divided, and the channels lengthened in step with oriented divisions as the cells matured.

A polarity protein, PAR3, proved central: it gathers a partner protein at tight junctions and holds a growth signal, ERK/MAPK, in check along the cell's lower surface. With that restraint in place, channels elongate properly and hepatocytes mature. Without it, both falter. The authors present the pathway as a stage-by-stage mechanism tying liver architecture to function, with lessons for regeneration and metabolic liver disease.
pmc-13424512:
Larsdotter and colleagues surveyed in 2026 Swedish adults on palliative care, asking what people understand by it and where they would prefer to be cared for and die. A random sample of 3,750 people aged 16 to 90 years was drawn from the national register, and just under half replied. Grouping methods sorted respondents by their grasp of palliative care, care that eases suffering when cure is not possible.

Larsdotter found home was the top choice for both end-of-life care and death, picked by about six and five in ten respondents. Five understanding groups emerged, from full grasp to no opinion. People who understood that such care supports families leaned toward home or hospice. Those who wrongly believed it hastens death leaned toward hospital or nursing home. The full-grasp group held more women, older people, and university graduates. The authors link better public understanding to care that matches wishes.
pmc-13424612:
Aileen H. Hsi leads a ten-author study of whether social vulnerability, the neighbourhood-level burden of poverty, housing, and access problems, predicts survival in aggressive brain tumours treated at MD Anderson between 2020 and 2025. Cohorts held 398 patients with glioblastoma and 62 with a related grade 4 astrocytoma, with vulnerability scored at county and neighbourhood level from a national index.

In glioblastoma, vulnerability showed no association with survival at either geographic scale. The picture differed for treatment: patients from more vulnerable neighbourhoods had higher odds of missing complete tumour removal and lower odds of receiving treatment on a clinical trial. No survival link appeared in the smaller astrocytoma group. Reaching a top centre, the authors imply, does not erase access gaps.
pmc-13424712:
Lloyd and co-authors present a mathematical model in this 2026 engineering paper for a soft robotic catheter steered entirely by magnetism. Their design wraps soft magnetic rings around braided sleeves nested inside each other. A strong external field, such as the one inside an MRI scanner, then bends the device. No motors or cables are needed.

The team derived an energy-based model coupling magnetic torque to sleeve curvature. It captures awkward real behaviors like hysteresis, where the shape lags behind the command. It also captures bistability, where two shapes are stable at once. Testing inside a 7-tesla preclinical MRI scanner, predicted shapes matched measured deformation with a root-mean-square error of 4.4 degrees across the experiments reported. The authors position the framework as groundwork for closed-loop control and systematic design of magnetically steered medical robots.
pmc-13425712:
Jacquelina Achkar and coauthors tested a carbon monoxide breathalyzer for spotting smokers before joint replacement in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Smoking delays wound healing and raises prosthetic joint infection risk, yet patients often underreport use and clinics lack objective screening. Patients with end-stage arthritis listed for surgery at one academic center completed a smoking questionnaire and then blew into a validated handheld device.

Breath carbon monoxide was classed as low at 0 to 6 parts per million, borderline at 7 to 9, and high at 10 or above. Comparing answers with breath values shows how often self-report misses recent smoking before arthroplasty.
pmc-13426012:
Foster and colleagues tested in 2026 whether crossing two separated populations of a biocontrol moth could restore its vigor. The moth, Hypena opulenta, is released against invasive swallow-wort vines in North America, but control agents often lose genetic diversity through small founding groups and long lab rearing. One population had spent twenty-eight generations in the lab, another fourteen in Canadian fields.

Whole genome sequencing showed the two groups had already diverged genetically, and both carried low diversity. Their hybrid offspring carried significantly more diversity. Hybrid females also produced more pupae in the lab and stripped more leaves from host plants. In the field they produced the largest second generation of the three groups. The authors propose deliberate outcrossing before release as a practical way to strengthen control agents.
pmc-13427312:
da Cruz and colleagues used Brazil's 2023 national oral health survey in 2026 to study who has dental implants. The survey covered adults aged 35 to 44 and older adults aged 65 to 74. They compared two measures: what people reported themselves and what examiners actually saw during clinical checks.

Implant prevalence ranged from about one tenth to one fifth of the sample, depending on the measure used. For self-reported use, older age, higher income, private dental care, and seeking treatment or rehabilitation all raised the odds of reporting implants. For clinically observed implants, only the number of missing teeth showed a significant link. The authors say implant use reflects both access to services and real clinical need, and they urge fairer provision through the public system.
pmc-13427712:
Su and colleagues built in 2026 a neural network that finds and grades tertiary lymphoid structures, immune cell clusters that form inside tumors, on whole-slide microscope images. Grading these clusters matters because their maturity can forecast how a patient answers immune therapy. Slides are enormous, so models usually read small patches and miss the context around each patch.

Their network, GCUNet, uses a graph structure to pull in long-range and fine detail from beyond the target patch, then fuses that context with local detail. The team built four datasets across four cancers, covering hundreds of slides and more than fifteen thousand structures. On all four, GCUNet beat the best rival methods by a clear margin.
pmc-13427912:
Knut Asbjørn Solhaug and co-authors ask whether far-red light, wavelengths just beyond visible red, powers photosynthesis in the shade-dwelling lichen Lobaria pulmonaria. This old-forest lichen lives under dense canopies where far-red light is enriched. Their 2026 study combines light measurements under the canopy with gas exchange experiments.

Far-red photons made up as much as 32 percent of the usable light under the canopy, against 11 percent in open areas. Far-red light alone supported moderate carbon dioxide uptake, and rates rose sharply when it was combined with background red light, a synergy known as the Emerson enhancement effect. Per absorbed photon, far-red light was even more efficient than red light. The authors recommend sensors covering the extended range for ecological studies, and warn that standard electron transport calculations overestimate activity under strong far-red light.
pmc-13429112:
Yumeng Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, screening models that flag depression risk in older people on long-term dialysis. Depressive symptoms affect over half of this group in many surveys, and early warning could speed support. The team recruited 226 older maintenance hemodialysis patients at a Chinese university hospital and its branches. Questionnaires covered mood, symptoms, nutrition, physical performance, self-management, and self-reported sight and hearing.

Just over 54 percent screened positive for depressive symptoms. Five learning models all separated high- and low-risk patients about equally well. A simple Naive Bayes model calibrated best overall. Its top predictors were vision problems, hearing loss, symptom burden, nutrition score, and self-management. The models were checked only inside the same hospital system, so outside testing must come before clinic use.
pmc-13429312:
Anna Gilbertson and colleagues set out the MADE study protocol on food changes made by breastfeeding mothers in England when allergy is feared. A balanced, varied diet suits nursing mothers, yet beliefs that maternal foods cause infant symptoms are old and widespread.

Many mothers restrict foods thought to upset the baby's gut, and rising allergy worry now shapes those choices more strongly. Cow's milk allergy poses a known diagnostic puzzle in community care, where infants often show vague signs. This mixed-methods protocol aims to count how often diets change and what those changes cost mothers and babies.
pmc-13430812:
Jia Ji and colleagues compare two bleeding-control strategies for total knee replacement, where blood loss is common. Standard tourniquet use and controlled low blood pressure both aim to cut bleeding during surgery and avoid transfusions.

Ninety patients having one-sided knee replacement under general anaesthesia at one centre were split in two. A standard tourniquet group held 49 patients, while a combined group of 41 paired controlled low pressure with a low-pressure tourniquet. Red cell counts, haemoglobin falls, drain output, total blood loss, and transfusion rates led the outcomes, with operating time and hospital stay also tracked. Surgeons get a head-to-head test of gentler pressure control.
pmc-13432812:
Pan Lu and co-authors mined a United States vaccine harm report bank in 2026 for links between shots and a joint disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own joints. Reports spanned 1990 to 2026 and topped eleven million. Joint-linked reports formed a tiny slice, near five thousand people in all.

Women filed most reports, and adults in the broad mid-age band led the counts. Most harms touched muscle and joint themes, and near half struck within a week of the shot. The COVID shot drew the most reports yet only a weak math flag. Three older shots drew far stronger flags: one for a tick-borne disease, one for German measles, and one against anthrax. The authors stress that the bank is passive: it can flag leads, never prove cause.
pmc-13433212:
Shuai He and co-authors told a 2026 case of a 33-year-old woman. She slid toward an adrenal crisis picture two days after surgery. The surgery cut out an adrenal tumor that tests had called non-working. One small dose of a steroid drug, given in surgery to block sickness, sits at the center of the time line. Her stress hormone and its driver both read crushed low as she worsened.

Her signs fit many post-surgery faults, from infection to clots to fuel swings, so no single cause could be locked. She rose on broad support care plus stress-dose hormone cover. Workup before surgery had skipped a key overnight test, so a quiet hormone leak from the tumor could not be ruled out. The authors urge full gland checks before such cuts.
pmc-13433612:
Antonella Muscella opened a 2026 collection on motor skill care for kids with growth disorders of the brain and body, framing clumsiness as a whole-web trait rather than a side fault. Skill grows from brain webs, sense loops, body states, and world offers in live trade. In autism, focus faults, and palsy alike, weak motor skill marks the core build.

Pieces in the set share a turn: motor acts voice deep webs that weigh forecasts, pick acts, and gauge body state. Brain scans in autism show wide web breaks, not lone path faults, behind the motor gaps. One thread runs through fitness, since motor skill may reach social life by way of body health rather than head on. The editor calls for care that treats the full web.
pmc-13434012:
Jianhua Cai and co-authors split a two-job catalyst in 2026 into two stages in space to turn light gases into ring stocks that anchor the chemical trade. Two-job builds rule plant work, yet steps tangle when sites sit cheek by jowl, a flaw the old closeness rule missed. The test road runs propane to the ring trio of benzene and kin.

Stage one strips gas to light links, while stage two stacks and rings those links in step with the feed. The split hit near-full gas burn and high ring share at strong heat, with the prized trio near the whole take. Live light reads and rate math back the match. Ring by-products from cracks shrank to a whisper, and cost reads held firm.
pmc-13434412:
Miao Li and a large team lift the power yield of organic solar cells in 2026 with a new electron taking molecule. Ring free designs are cheap to make but move charge poorly, which caps their yield. Side arms with phenyl rings were added to guide how the molecules stack.

The arms form extra weak bonds with the ends of nearby molecules. Fluorine on the arms adds still more contact points. Tight, neat stacks open charge paths in many directions at once. The best cell reached a yield of 19.12 percent. That mark sets a record for this low cost class.
pmc-13434712:
Houyu Wu and Eng Hoe Wee survey 350 university teachers in China in 2026 about trust and worry over artificial intelligence tools. Both scores sat well above the middle of the scale. Teachers felt able to use the tools yet uneasy about what they mean for the job.

Trust and worry moved in opposite ways with a strong link. Women reported more worry and less trust than men. Computing teachers felt most trust and least worry of any field. The mix suggests training should build skill and answer job fears at once. One size support will miss half the picture.
pmc-13434812:
Wentao Xu and coauthors add hydrogen to carbon double bonds with electric drive and shape control in 2026. Nickel, a cheap and common metal, carries the reaction with a tight fitting coat. Protons plus electrons supply hydrogen, so no high pressure gas is needed.

Shape purity runs high across conjugated esters and allylic alcohols. The coat must hold a nickel hydrogen unit firm, else hydrogen gas wins or nickel plates out. Computer work points to a nickel one hydrogen as the active form. Weak sticky contacts with the coat set which shape wins. Green synthesis gains a safe route to chiral stock.
pmc-13437712:
Yang Sheng, Yao Yao, and Hengcang Wang argue heart and vessel disease should be read as an immune and metabolic disorder steered partly by non-coding RNA. These RNA strands never build proteins, yet they tune gene activity across many cell types. Their 2026 review sorts patients by dominant mechanism rather than by disease label alone, sketching types such as artery inflammation, sterile injury, and fibro-inflammatory remodeling.

Short and long RNA species, plus ring-shaped ones, govern cholesterol handling in macrophages, inflammation alarms, vessel lining activation, and heart muscle scarring. The same molecule can protect in one cell and harm in another, which defeats simple good-versus-bad labels. Spilled RNA in blood could serve as a liquid biopsy, and RNA-based drugs are in reach. They frame the endotypes as research tools, not clinic tests, until trials sort patients by them and prove the sorting helps.
pmc-13439612:
Hua Tian surveys how everyday online life shapes Chinese netizens' sense of their festivals' world reach, reporting in 2026. Cultural soft power is often told as state messaging, yet ordinary users form their own judgements while scrolling and sharing. A survey of 1,540 domestic netizens measured online engagement habits, media format leanings, and feelings about traditional festivals abroad. Statistical modelling then traced links among engagement, perceived influence, group pride, and a sense of cultural empowerment.

More frequent online engagement tracked with stronger belief that the festivals carry weight worldwide. That belief in turn carried part of the link between engagement and collective self-esteem. A chain ran onward from esteem to feeling culturally empowered. Neither a taste for video over text nor time spent overseas changed the core pattern. Tian argues that daily interaction frequency, not media format, drives the effect.
pmc-13440012:
Jiaming Ye and colleagues count genital mycoplasma carriage and drug resistance among women in Hangzhou, China, reporting a 2026 review of laboratory records. These small bacteria can colonise the cervix without symptoms, and carriage in pregnancy raises clinical questions. The team analysed 1,177 cervical samples collected between 2017 and 2023, spanning pregnant women, new mothers, and women at routine checks.

Just over half of all samples carried mycoplasmas, with pregnant women highest at well over half. Ureaplasma species dominated by far, while Mycoplasma hominis stayed rare in every group. Carriage peaked among pregnant teenagers in the data. Resistance testing worried the authors: most isolates resisted gatifloxacin, with large shares also beating ciprofloxacin and roxithromycin. The findings give local clinicians current carriage and susceptibility figures for guiding treatment in pregnancy.
pmc-13440312:
Kanai and Ichihashi grow self-copying RNA strands in the lab to test how parasites shape change. Parasite strands copy fast but make no useful product. Host strands do the work that keeps both alive. The team grew six groups of strands. Some groups held many parasites. Others held few. Groups with many parasites changed fast between groups. Yet hosts inside each group stayed much alike.

Groups with few parasites split, for a short time, into up to three host lines. The team reads this as loose pressure when hosts copy about as well as each other. Parasites kept hosts sharp but held back new forms inside a group.
pmc-13441512:
Nobutaka Doba and colleagues stop stubborn puncture bleeding after variceal injection therapy by pressing with an extra-long scope cap, reporting a 2026 case. Injection sclerotherapy seals bleeding veins in the food pipe, yet the needle holes themselves often bleed, sometimes hard. Balloon pressure is the usual first rescue. Their patient, a 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and returning varices, bled from the first puncture site during treatment with ethanolamine oleate.

Balloon compression failed to settle the bleeding. Direct pressure with a long transparent cap, protruding twelve millimetres against the standard four, achieved prompt control. At the second puncture in the same session, the team applied the long cap immediately after needle withdrawal as a planned step, and bleeding stopped again. The authors argue that the rescue deserves routine status, and they note that compression timing for this method is barely documented.
pmc-13441812:
Tong Xin and colleagues build a prediction model for brain dysfunction during sepsis in arthritis patients, centred on a blood ratio. Rheumatoid arthritis patients face raised sepsis risk, and sepsis-associated encephalopathy is hard to spot early. The neutrophil-to-albumin ratio bundles inflammation and nutrition into one number. Records from eighty-nine patients at two centres built it, with thirty-seven more at a third centre held back for outside testing.

Brain dysfunction struck about a quarter of the building group and carried far higher twenty-eight-day mortality. Three machine learning methods agreed on six predictors: organ failure score, infection markers, stay length, age, and the ratio itself. The chosen model discriminated strongly in both the building data and the outside cohort. A web tool packages the calculator for bedside use. The authors present the ratio as a worthy addition to early warning in this group.
pmc-13442712:
Thaiz Batista Azevedo Rangel Miguel's team tested ultrasound-processed cashew apple juice in 2026 for hidden toxicity, using brine shrimp and zebrafish models. High-intensity ultrasound preserves liquid foods without heat, yet it may create or release toxic compounds, a risk rarely checked. Juice treated at three power levels and varied durations was tested for acute and developmental toxicity against unprocessed juice.

Brine shrimp showed no acute toxicity from any juice. Zebrafish revealed parameter-dependent developmental harm from sonicated juice only, including heart swelling, spine curvature, and stunted growth, worse after short five-minute treatments than longer fifteen-minute ones. Food technologists get a sensitive-model warning: ultrasound settings can alter juice safety, so vertebrate checks should precede industrial rollout.
pmc-13443212:
Subrat Pattanaik and colleagues assess a 2026 survey of integrated farming in coastal Odisha, India, where smallholders face volatile weather, fragmented plots, and shaky markets. The team gathered primary data from 208 farm households across three coastal districts from 2020 to 2023, then used factor analysis and probit regression to find what drives adoption.

Credit access, schooling, market links, labor supply, and family type raised adoption odds, while older age and larger holdings lowered them. pmc-13443512:

pmc-13447112:

pmc-13448112:

pmc-13448212:

pmc-13448412:

pmc-13449612:

pmc-13449812:

pmc-13450012:

pmc-13451812:

pmc-13451912:

pmc-13455112:

pmc-13455412:

pmc-13457212:

pmc-13462212:

pmc-13462812:

pmc-13463012:

pmc-13463112:

pmc-13463512:

Rong Wei, a hematologist, reflects on a transplant patient whose test results spelled success while the overall outcome turned catastrophic, in a 2026 essay. pmc-13467112:

pmc-13467912:

pmc-13468612:

pmc-13468912:

pmc-13469012:

pmc-13469312:

pmc-13470012:

pmc-13470112:

pmc-13470712:

pmc-13472912:

pmc-13473112:

pmc-13474612:

pmc-13474712:

pmc-13474812:

pmc-13478612:

pmc-13479612:

pmc-13480112:

Schizophrenia and attention deficit cases gained a small to fair amount. Parkinson's disease and deep depression showed no clear gain at all. The catch was quality: near half of all outcomes sat in the weakest proof grade. The authors urge big, shared trials before wide clinical use.
pmc-13482212:
Nina Randolph-Koranteng and co-authors present a 2026 policy comparison on support for teen girls and young women in small-scale mining areas of Ghana and Uganda. These young workers face poor sexual health outcomes tied to poverty and thin clinic access. The team read fourteen global and twenty-seven national policy papers from 2010 to 2023 across mining, health, gender, and youth themes.

Global and national papers aligned on teen health, universal care, youth jobs, and child labour bans. National papers stressed services, schooling, and trade skills yet never named mining-community teens as a distinct group with stacked risks. Without that naming, their mix of money and health needs stays off budget lines. The authors urge policy writers to flag these young women as a priority group in plain terms.
pmc-13483612:
Zhuoya Zhang and co-workers sort blood pressure patients on a high plateau in China into self-care types. Their 2026 study took place at a hospital in Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture. Care was checked from late 2024 to mid 2025. The team used a grouping method that finds hidden types, then asked what traits place a patient in each type.

Three types came out of the data. One type did well on all parts of care. One type was weak on drug use and pressure checks. One type was weak on habits such as smoking, drink, and work stress. Trust in one's own skill played a part in all three types. Help, health knowledge, and faith in self also played roles. Care that fits the weak spot of each type should beat one-size advice.
pmc-13485612:
Carlos Cifuentes-González benchmarks a specialty-tuned language model against general models and medical students at screening papers for a systematic review. Published in 2026, the comparison sits inside a registered review of retinal vasculitis, using 1,030 randomly drawn records from an initial haul of 5,533. Two eye experts supply the gold standard, with disagreements settled by adjudication.

The tuned model, named UveAItis, reached 93.3 percent accuracy with strong agreement scores, clearly beating the base general model, a rival general model, and final-year students. It recovered 65.4 percent of expert-included papers after consensus, while students recovered only 22.3 percent. Fine-tuning on a narrow specialty task, rather than raw model size, drove the gap. Review teams facing thousands of abstracts gain a validated shortcut that still needs expert oversight.
pmc-13487212:
Rony and co-authors built a lightweight network that outlines organs and lesions in medical scans without needing a data-center computer. Outlining, called segmentation, demands both crisp boundaries and whole-image context, which small models usually trade against each other. Their 2026 framework, SwiftMSeg, mixes a convolutional encoder with a transformer module that shuttles between local detail and global context, then decodes at several scales.

Tested on colonoscopy, pathology, ultrasound, and MRI datasets, the model scored overlap values between about 0.85 and 0.90 across the four scan types. Its boundary error on MRI was the lowest figure highlighted, at about sixteen units on the distance measure used. Performance held up on an external dataset the model had never trained on. Rony pitches SwiftMSeg for clinics whose hardware cannot run giant segmentation models.
pmc-13487912:
Melinda Cservenak and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on learning after birth, carried out with an automated home cage system called IntelliCage. Female mice were compared across pregnancy, the period after giving birth, and a nonpregnant state. Tasks measured place learning, reversal learning, where a learned rule changes, and drinking on a fixed schedule over a long observation period.

Mothers after birth learned places faster, adapted better when rules changed, and kept learned information more reliably than the other groups. The authors link this gain to the demands of caring for pups, such as finding food and responding to changing needs. Results may inform wider research on how reproduction shapes brain function.
pmc-13488212:
Yu Nosaka and colleagues report a 2026 case pairing two rare infected aneurysms in a 58-year-old woman in Japan. Infection of a heart valve had sent infected clots to the lungs and blocked the heart's outflow path. Scans during antibiotic treatment found a small infected bulge in a lung artery branch, at high risk of bursting. Heart imaging struggled to tell a birth defect hole apart from a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. That is a bulge at the aorta's root.

Doctors first sealed the lung artery bulge with coils through a catheter, lowering the risk of catastrophic bleeding on the heart-lung machine. A probe ultrasound through the food pipe then confirmed the aortic root rupture, and surgery repaired it successfully. Two years on, no infection or growth had returned.
pmc-13490412:
Lukomska and colleagues hunted a rare cell population in the mouse retina marked by the protein nectin-3, hoping it might hold regenerative potential. Such marker cells maintain reserve populations in other tissues, but the retina's version was unmapped. Their 2026 study sorted the cells from embryonic stages through adulthood, counted them, read their gene activity, and located them under the microscope at each age.

The cells formed a small but persistent slice, about one percent of viable retinal cells before birth. Their share peaked near four percent shortly after birth, settling near one and a half percent in adults. Adult cells switched on a battery of early retinal development genes while lacking the transcripts for mature synaptic wiring. Microscopy placed them with the ganglion cell layer, distinct from the retina's support scaffolding. Lukomska reads them as a specialized neuronal lineage with basal identity.
pmc-13490512:
Ghosh and team studied a vivid atomic partnership in solution between the blue donor, an charge-rich blue hydrocarbon, and p-chloranil, an charge-hungry partner. When donor meets acceptor, a charge-transfer complex forms and drinks in near-deep-red light. Their 2026 study measured the pairing with uptake and glow methods, then modeled its structure and excited states with quantum chemical math in gas and solvent.

The complex announced itself with a distinct uptake band centered near 808 nm, in the near deep-red. Two reading approaches returned strong binding constants, both in the tens of thousands on the reported scale, confirming tight bonding. Math showed the partners align so their charge clouds overlap efficiently, explaining the strong coupling. Ghosh extracts the complex's switch strength and breakup energy as reference values for sensor and materials designers.
pmc-13490612:
Kathryn La Capria and colleagues run an attention experiment on cannabis vape advertising among young adults in a 2026 United States study. More than two thousand young adults who use such vapes or might try them viewed six ads online in 2024, clicking the message that drew their eye most in each. Ads rotated nine pitch types, from creativity and relaxation to health benefits, social gains, flavor, convenience, and high potency.

Noticing physical health benefit claims tied to stronger use intentions and rosier beliefs about body and mind effects in adjusted models. Noticing social effect claims showed a similar pattern, with the largest intention link of the pitches tested. Creativity claims linked only with intentions. The authors warn that benefit framing may pull new users in.
pmc-13491812:
Dingkang Wang leads a ten-author team profiling in 2026 how a salt-loving yeast used in fermented foods rewires its chemistry under salt stress, and whether added functional protein helps. Zygosaccharomyces rouxii thrives where salt would kill most microbes, yet the full metabolic picture was missing. The team used high-resolution mass spectrometry to compare yeast chemistry with and without protein supplementation at high salt.

On its own, salt forced a large metabolic reorganization, and adding protein pushed the cells into a distinct state beyond the stress response. Amino acid handling, antioxidant defenses, and nutrient transport all strengthened, while membrane fat pathways were tuned toward more flexible membranes. The practical message for fermentation is that the right protein feed makes a hardy yeast tougher still.
pmc-13491912:
Edith K Wakida and six colleagues explore in 2026 whether district health management teams could champion suicide prevention in rural Uganda under the World Health Organization's LIVE LIFE framework. Suicide there is criminalized and stigmatized, and surveillance is weak, so national strategies stall before reaching villages.
