Younger age, separation from a partner, unemployment, and weak social support showed the same pattern. The authors argue that screening for depression belongs inside routine maternal and child health visits, where mothers already receive care, so that support can reach them earlier.
pmc-13576012:
Richard Sean Lee and colleagues surveyed 100 hospitalized patients with end-stage kidney disease who were receiving maintenance hemodialysis at one hospital. Each patient answered a five-item questionnaire about their own dialysis care, and the answers were checked against the electronic health record. On average, patients answered just under three of the five items correctly.

Lower education lined up with trouble naming one's own dry weight and primary outpatient kidney doctor. A primary language other than English lined up with trouble naming the dialysis facility. The authors point to plain-language teaching, better hand-offs between hospital and outpatient teams, and stronger patient engagement as practical ways to close these gaps.
pmc-13576212:
Anqi Liu leads a 2026 study presenting ResSAT, a model that predicts gene activity maps of tissue from ordinary stained microscope images. Spatial transcriptomics measures which genes are active at each spot in a tissue slice, yet the process is slow and costly. Standard H&E stained images are cheap and routine, and tissue structure in them tracks gene patterns.

ResSAT blends image features, spot locations, and a transformer step that lets spots attend to each other, with residual network parts carrying the image reading. Benchmark tests on ten public Visium datasets put it ahead of rival methods. The predicted maps kept the spatial patterns that matter for biology, according to the authors. They present the model as a cheaper, faster route to many gene activity profiles.
pmc-13576412:
Terrell and colleagues ran a community-engaged trial in 2026 testing whether a weight-loss drug can lower body stores of persistent organic pollutants. The community studied was heavily exposed to a flame retardant called PBB. One hundred participants were randomised, blinded, to the fat-blocking drug orlistat or placebo for six months, with blood tests at set points.

Eighty-nine participants finished the study, a high retention the authors credit to community dedication. The orlistat group lost about two kilograms more than the placebo group on average. Despite that extra weight loss, blood levels of PBB and other pollutants did not differ between groups or fall over the six months. The authors conclude that mobilising fat with orlistat did not translate into lower pollutant burden in this timeframe.
pmc-13578312:
Nasir Assad and colleagues grow tiny manganese oxide particles with help from a plant extract, in a 2026 clean water study. Factory dyes stain waste water and resist normal treatment. Juice from a horsetail plant both formed the particles and kept them stable, replacing harsher chemicals. Tests confirmed round particles a few dozen nanometers wide with a steady surface charge.

Under sunlight the particles broke down two dyes and one toxic compound at close to nine tenths removal within about one hundred minutes. The same batch kept working through five reuse rounds with little loss of power. Dose and acidity both shaped the results, with plain neutral water working best. The authors pitch the plant made particles as a cheap, green option for dye laden water.
pmc-13581612:
Lee and colleagues report a 2026 study of how bacteria sense the proteins of phages, the viruses that infect them. Many bacteria carry STAND defense proteins, which switch on when they detect a foreign protein inside the cell. The team mapped the family across bacteria and archaea and tested what each branch senses.

The survey found at least 90 distinct STAND families tied to antiviral defense. One unstudied family, Avs7, detects the main shell protein of tailed phages. Three structure images show it forming a butterfly-shaped four-part unit around its target, with a host protein built in as support. Screens of 687 phage genes showed 13 more families sensing 13 conserved phage proteins, covering most core parts of tailed phages. Bacterial immunity watches the whole phage toolkit, not just one part.
pmc-13583212:
Su Li Goh and colleagues report a possible paradoxical drug reaction: retroperitoneal fibrosis arising during etanercept therapy for ankylosing spondylitis. Paradoxical reactions, where an effective drug triggers the opposite of its intent, are increasingly recognised with modern rheumatology drugs. This 2026 letter describes a 44-year-old woman treated first with adalimumab, then secukinumab, then etanercept for a decade of spinal disease.

After seven years on etanercept, she developed back and loin pain, and CT showed fibrous tissue encasing the aorta below the kidneys, with right-sided urinary blockage. The lesion could not be biopsied, IgG4 levels were normal, and she improved on steroids with a stent and a switch to bimekizumab. The authors present the case as a caution that new loin pain on biologics warrants imaging.
pmc-13584112:
Pasold and colleagues release in 2026 a satellite image dataset for spotting energy, transport, and storage infrastructure across Germany. Existing remote sensing benchmarks rarely capture how these structures appear together in real scenes.

The collection holds 10,000 true-color image chips from the Sentinel-2 satellite, each showing a square of land just over five hundred meters across. Every chip is labeled independently for substations, power plants, storage tanks, railway lines, and major roads. Several labels can therefore apply at once. Candidate sites came from OpenStreetMap, sampling was balanced across the country, and deliberately confusing empty scenes near real infrastructure were added as hard negatives. Predefined spatial folds keep neighboring images in the same group during testing, preventing inflated scores from look-alike nearby scenes.
pmc-13585912:
Grace Sanger and colleagues test a red seaweed against cervical cancer cells in this 2026 study. Cervical cancer hits hardest in poorer countries, so cheap natural sources of new drugs draw real interest. The seaweed, Halymenia durvillaei, was gathered in North Sulawesi, Indonesia, soaked in alcohol, and split into four chemical fractions for testing on brine shrimp and on HeLa cancer cells.

All fractions slowed the cancer cells, cutting growth by between seventy and just over ninety percent at the doses tried. The chloroform fraction was the strongest killer in the shrimp test. Chemical reading found oleic acid as a major ingredient, and computer models showed it fitting stably into a protein tied to cervical cancer growth. The authors say the seaweed deserves deeper work, with single compounds pulled out and tested on their own.
pmc-13587312:
P. Falcón-Urrutia and a large team show that a guidance molecule helps a childhood brain tumor renew itself. Medulloblastoma is a tumor of the cerebellum, and one subtype is driven by a growth pathway called Sonic Hedgehog. Their 2026 study proves that a molecule called Netrin-1 is switched on directly by that pathway's GLI switches, a link that had not been shown before.

Where the pathway ran hot, Netrin-1 ran high, and it fed the tumor's stem-like cells, the hardy minority that can regrow the tumor, through a signaling route called ERK. Measuring Netrin-1 also split the Hedgehog subtype more finely, marking tumors with the strongest pathway activity and the most stem-like character. The authors offer it as both a sorting marker and a possible drug target for this subtype.
pmc-13590912:
Nima Yazdankhah and four colleagues ask, in 2026, whether the fat pad behind the kneecap relates to knee pain in women past menopause. The pad can release irritant signals and may feed joint pain. The study enrolled 47 women aged 50 to 85 who were not obese, with a range of knee pain. Each woman had knee scans by two methods, plus pain and function questionnaires and physical tests.

A smaller, denser fat pad paired with a larger total volume pointed to more pain and worse daily function, once age and joint damage were taken into account. Yazdankhah and the team call this a long, dense, thin shape. They suggest pad shape, not size alone, deserves study as a pain source.
pmc-13591912:
Xia-Ying Xu leads a 2026 study of a combined blood index and death risk in American adults. The CALLY index blends three routine values: an inflammation marker, a nutrition protein, and a type of white blood cell. Data came from a national survey run from 1999 to 2010, covering 11,797 adults. The team tracked deaths from all causes and from heart and vessel disease over time.

Adults in the top quarter of the index died at markedly lower rates than those in the bottom quarter. The protective link bent in a curve rather than running straight. Adding the index to standard risk models sharpened forecasts slightly, though sorting single patients improved little. Xu and the team pitch it as a helper beside classic risk factors, not a stand alone test.
pmc-13592312:
Maximilian Böhm and six colleagues give, in 2026, the first portrait of an enigmatic enzyme family branch that barely burns carbon monoxide. These enzymes normally swap carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, powering microbe carbon cycles. The branch B version came from a gut bacterium and needed a fully air free imaging workflow the team built for the purpose. Its frozen structure emerged at fine detail.

The portrait shows blocked gas tunnels, a broken proton path, and a warped metal cluster, which explains activity thousands of times below a classic cousin. Family tree checks hint the enzyme instead serves cargo imported by a partner transporter. Böhm and the team read the scaffold as repurposed by evolution for a new, still shadowy job.
pmc-13593612:
Bodyl A. Brand and Robert A. McCutcheon review how sex and hormones shape thinking skills in people with psychosis. Writing in 2026, they note that memory, speed of thought, attention, and planning are heavily affected in psychosis. Women and men show the same broad pattern of strengths seen in the general population.

Their focus is on change over time rather than fixed differences. Hormone shifts across the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and the time after birth, and menopause all appear to nudge cognition, with estrogen standing out as a likely influence on the brain. Women with psychosis face these transitions on top of an already heavy cognitive burden. The authors therefore propose that hormonal state may be an overlooked driver of when symptoms and thinking problems worsen.
pmc-13594312:
Robert Morey leads an eighteen-author team mapping the diversity of cytotrophoblasts, the progenitor cells of the early placenta, at single-cell resolution. Their 2026 study sequenced cells from placental tissue at six to eight weeks and at twelve to fourteen weeks of pregnancy. They compared the fetal-side and maternal-side regions. The results were set against lab-grown trophoblast stem cells.

Location shaped identity: progenitors clustered near the maternal plate and leaned toward becoming invasive cells, while fetal-side cells leaned toward the fused surface layer that exchanges nutrients. Stem cell lines grown in dishes most resembled precursors of the invasive type, and they lost the marker genes of the true starting state as they adapted to culture. The findings matter for anyone using these stem cells to model pregnancy, since the dish-grown version represents only part of the original population.
pmc-13596912:
Tong Wu leads a ten-author team reading the sugar coatings on antibodies to sort idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, a family of autoimmune muscle diseases that no firm molecular test can sort. Looking back, the team profiled subclass-specific antibody glycosylation in blood from 145 patients and 52 healthy controls. They used mass spectrometry to do it.

Patients showed heavier core fucosylation and changes across thirteen antibody sugar forms. A clustering pass split patients into three sugar-defined endotypes dominated by muscle, skin, or joint disease, each with its own signs and blood profile. Certain antibody forms tracked with muscle injury markers and with complement deposits in tissue, hinting that the coatings help steer immune damage. A seven-marker model could assign patients to the types with fair success. The authors present these sugar patterns as a hidden layer of disease variety worth building tests on.
pmc-13611012:
Alyona N. Bortsova leads a large team testing a light-based method to grade the crystallinity of star-shaped plastic building blocks. The materials are lactide oligomers, short chains radiating three or six arms from a core, used in biodegradable products such as medical goods. How crystalline they are steers their behavior, so a fast check matters. Raman spectroscopy, which reads molecular vibrations from scattered light, had worked for straight-chain versions; this study asked whether it holds for star shapes.

The stars varied by arm number, arm length, and unit handedness, and the pure L-form was examined in semicrystalline and amorphous states. Raman-derived crystallinity agreed well with X-ray diffraction values. Crystallinity rose as arm number fell and arm length grew, giving makers two clear design levers. Raman spectroscopy can monitor these oligomers' crystallinity reliably, the authors conclude, including live control during annealing.
pmc-13612412:
José Luis Socorro-Cumplido leads a thirteen-author team validating a test battery for fibromyalgia. Questionnaires dominate assessment, but cannot show what a patient can actually do. Eighty-seven women from four Spanish specialist hospitals completed four performance tests: a six-minute walk, handgrip strength, a timed up-and-go, and a balance scale. They also completed symptom questionnaires and a week of activity tracking.

Factor analysis pulled the measures into four clean constructs: physical function, activity behavior, emotional distress, and pain impact, together explaining 67.1 percent of variance. Correlations behaved as theory predicts, strong within domains and weaker across them. Accelerometer data formed its own construct, proving wrist-worn activity counts add information no clinic test duplicates. The battery covered body functions and activities broadly. The authors recommend the combined approach for tailoring rehab and tracking whether treatment changes real-world function.
pmc-13613012:
Abdullah Avcı and Mükaddes Avcı review what research says about aromatherapy as a way to ease stress and anxiety among intensive care nurses. These nurses face heavy strain at work, and scent-based therapy is cheap, drug-free, and easy to try. Searching Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library with no date limits, the pair looked for trials and similar studies of aromatherapy used with this exact group of nurses.

Five studies involving 254 participants in total met their rules, and two reviewers picked studies, pulled data, and judged quality on their own before comparing notes. The authors present their review as the first focused only on intensive care nurses. Readers weighing scent-based support for staff get a compact account of how thin or strong the current proof is.
pmc-13614712:
Han and colleagues present in 2026 ConMIL, a framework that classifies whole slide images by letting written descriptions steer the computer's attention. Whole slide images are gigapixel scans of stained tissue used in pathology. Standard methods learn from slide-level labels alone and cannot say which regions drove the call.

ConMIL feeds paired positive and negative pathology text descriptions into the attention mechanism, so regions matching the described disease pattern gain weight while regions matching its opposite lose it. Human experts can refine the prompts in the loop to sharpen the wording. A special classifier network then exposes its learned curves for visual inspection. On three public slide collections covering lymph node and breast cancer, the method beat representative baselines while producing attention maps that matched pathologists' expectations of where disease sits.
pmc-13615312:
Anna Paolillo, Ally Memon, and Vittorio Edoardo Scuderi review in 2026 how safety climate shapes behaviour in health care. Safety climate means shared views of how much safety matters at work. The review covers both staff and patients. Most past work looked at patient safety through staff eyes alone. Their model treats safety as a joint product, so they searched the literature widely: 15,663 papers were screened and 43 met their rules.

A good safety climate for workers spilled over, lifting patients' own sense of safety, drive, and willingness to join in safety efforts. Patients who took part in turn raised staff compliance with safety rules. The loop puts patients at the centre of safety work rather than treating them as passive recipients. Hospital leaders get a research-based case for inviting patients into safety programs as partners.
pmc-13616312:
Xu Chen and colleagues build a layered nanomaterial to heal bone defects in diabetic patients, where high sugar stacks three problems at once: oxygen waste, local acid build-up, and confused bone immunity. Single-job materials cannot fix all three together. Their platform mounts a cerium-based nanozyme, a mineral particle that acts like an enzyme, onto an alkaline layered base rich in calcium and aluminium.

The base neutralises acid around the defect and slowly releases calcium that bone stem cells need, while guarding the nanozyme's activity. The cerium cycles between two states to soak up excess oxygen waste, calming the inflammatory tilt of immune cells. In tests the pairing restored bone balance better than either part alone. Craniofacial surgeons treating diabetic patients could gain a filler that repairs the wound's chemistry, not just its shape.
pmc-13616912:
Xianwen Shang and eleven colleagues report a 2026 analysis of how daily functioning changes in the years before and after a stroke. They pooled four long-running ageing studies from China, England, the United States, and Europe, matching each stroke case with two people of the same age and sex who had no stroke. Memory, mood, mobility, frailty, and basic daily activities were tracked over time.

People who later had strokes already showed steeper memory decline and more limits on daily activities several years before the event. After the stroke, gaps in memory, depression symptoms, and daily functioning widened for about five years, then leveled off or narrowed. Women fared worse than men on mood, mobility, and frailty measures. The authors say these timelines mark a critical window for prevention and for support after stroke.
pmc-13617312:
Thang Nguyen Ngoc and five colleagues present three cases of hospital-acquired pneumonia caused by multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that shrugs off many antibiotics. Intravenous drugs often reach the lungs poorly, so the team added high-dose inhaled colistin followed immediately by an inhaled aminoglycoside antibiotic, on top of standard body-wide therapy. Doses were set for each patient's kidney function, and delivery was timed to the breathing cycle.

All three very ill patients improved clinically, their scans cleared, inflammation markers mostly fell, and the bacterium was eventually eradicated. This held even though laboratory tests had called the strains resistant to the inhaled drugs. No kidney damage or airway spasm appeared, though hearing was not checked. Because body-wide antibiotics ran alongside, the authors cannot credit the inhaled pair alone, and they ask for prospective dosing studies.
pmc-13620112:
Nannan Wang and ten colleagues built the first living atlas of proteins that partner with VCP inside mouse tissues, in a 2026 study. VCP is a ring-shaped cellular machine that pulls damaged proteins out for disposal, and its failure links to muscle, nerve, and cancer diseases. The team engineered mice whose VCP carried a tag, fished out its partners from eight tissues, and identified them with advanced mass spectrometry.

The survey captured 923 confident partner proteins. Known helpers appeared alongside new candidates tied to energy production and protein quality control. Two liver partners received direct confirmation in human liver cells, one of them a regulatory piece of a major energy sensor. Because partners differ by tissue, the map may explain why one machine serves so many cell jobs. The authors offer the dataset as a resource for hunting drug targets in VCP-linked disease.
pmc-13621412:
Thomas Aaron Ricks, Elisabeth Jacob, and Louisa Lam surveyed the casual teaching staff who keep Australian nursing programs running. Sessional teachers fill gaps as nursing enrollments grow, yet little research asks how the work feels from inside. Their online survey drew eighty-four sessional staff with at least a year in pre-registration programs, answering a standard psychosocial work questionnaire.

Most respondents were women, over half were past fifty, and most had under five years of sessional work behind them. Only about a quarter planned to chase a permanent academic post. Experiences overall rated favorably. Job satisfaction rose hand in hand with support from supervisors, support from colleagues, and a sense of community at work. The authors argue that development chances, good leadership, and belonging are the levers that keep this workforce from drifting away.
pmc-13621712:
Ze Zhou leads the author list of a 2026 study asking which spine levels give a practical bone density check from routine CT scans. Doctors can read Hounsfield units, a measure of how dense tissue looks on a scan, from images taken for other reasons. The goal is to spot osteoporosis, the disease that thins bones, without extra testing.

The team studied 300 patients, half men and half women, and compared single vertebrae and grouped segments, from the upper spine down to the sacrum, against standard bone density scores. Averaging the whole spine matched best, but one mid-back vertebra and the segment joining chest and lower back performed nearly as well. That shorter segment also held up across men and women. The authors present it as a handy option when only part of the spine is scanned.
pmc-13623812:
Manon Monfort and colleagues use gene editing to breed soybean lines that flower earlier, a trait Europe needs if the crop is to spread north. Soybean is a short-day plant: long summer days at high latitudes delay flowering, leaving too little time before autumn cold. Rather than cross-breeding for years, the team knocked out several flowering-time genes at once with CRISPR editing.

Starting from two established maturity groups, the edited lines flowered up to four weeks earlier under controlled long days, and two generations were enough to produce a spread of new maturity classes. A field trial backed the greenhouse picture, with edited lines flowering about one to two weeks ahead of their parent lines. The authors say the approach creates targeted variety inside elite breeding stock quickly, and they offer the lines and their gene records as material for testing across European environments.
pmc-13624312:
Chuangjie Cao leads a multi-centre study building an artificial intelligence model that forecasts colorectal cancer survival from whatever patient data a hospital has. Rich prediction blends tissue slides, gene data, and clinical records, yet many centres can afford only the slides, and models trained in one hospital often falter in another. The team's framework, called DAIMS, was designed for that reality.

During training the model learned from three data types together; at prediction time it can work from slides alone, inventing stand-ins for the missing inputs from what the tissue shows. Validated on 842 patients from European and East Asian cohorts separate from its training data, it beat competing methods at ranking survival risk, with gains in accuracy on both test sets. Its risk splits held across disease stages, molecular subtypes, and treatment groups. The authors aim it at routine practice, where incomplete data is the norm.
pmc-13625312:
Hikmettullah Batgi and colleagues share real-world results for a modern myeloma drug in patients whose kidneys had failed. Four people on hemodialysis, aged sixty-one to eighty, received elranatamab, an antibody that links immune cells to a marker on myeloma cells. Each had already failed a median of six earlier treatment lines, including the three main drug classes, and dialysis patients are usually shut out of the trials that approve such drugs.

Every patient responded, two completely, and all four stayed on treatment at the report's cutoff. One had a mild, self-settling fever reaction, and one survived severe pneumonia in intensive care, then resumed the drug and kept the complete response. The small series hints the therapy can work even when kidneys cannot clear drugs normally.
pmc-13625712:
Erin MacIntyre and colleagues tell the story of a 66-year-old man told he needed both knees replaced. Long-standing osteoarthritis in both knees had brought pain, swelling, and night pain, and joint replacement was the advice on the table. Instead he joined a trial that wove pain science education into a personal, slowly graded exercise program. Sessions ran weekly at first, then by video call, with later top-ups. He set a bold goal: walking the Camino de Santiago trail in Spain.

By one year his knee pain had fallen by over four-fifths, function and daily activity had climbed steeply, painkillers were dropped, and swelling and night pain had gone. A year after the trial he walked 320 kilometers of the Camino in fourteen days. The case is shared as proof of how far good non-surgical care can reach.
pmc-13626312:
Siva Nageswara Rao Gajula led a 2026 rat study asking whether the herbal supplement echinacea disturbs blood levels of two antiviral drugs, favipiravir and atazanavir. Echinacea is widely taken for colds and immune support, often alongside prescribed drugs, and herb-drug interactions can push drug levels too low or too high. Male rats received echinacea daily for ten days or a control liquid, then a single oral dose of one antiviral, with blood levels tracked by validated lab methods.

Echinacea did not significantly change peak levels or total exposure for either drug, and clearance, half-life, and residence time also stayed steady. The authors conclude that repeated echinacea, under these conditions, caused no pharmacokinetically relevant interaction with either antiviral. Clinicians and patients get reassuring animal evidence, with the usual caveat: rat dosing and a single antiviral dose do not settle the question for long-term human use.
pmc-13627212:
Radhika S Amin and colleagues review what talk and behavior therapies can do for chronic ocular pain, a grinding eye pain that drops and surface treatments rarely touch. The condition, once filed under dry eye, is now seen as its own pain disorder, often riding with depression, anxiety, trauma symptoms, poor sleep, and a sensitized nervous system. The authors gather the wider chronic pain literature on therapies from cognitive behavioral work to mindfulness, acceptance therapy, and pain education.

Those approaches ease distress and disability in other pain conditions, yet not one formal study has tested them in ocular pain itself. The review therefore makes a careful case: borrow the tools inside team-based care that treats the pain system, and run the missing trials to learn which patients gain most. An understudied lever may be hiding in plain sight.
pmc-13630412:
Jan Sebastian Dominic Rodriguez and eight colleagues show that catalyst particles rearrange their surfaces in response to voltage. Their study appeared in 2026. The particles mix platinum and gold. Which metal sits on the surface decides how well they drive fuel cell reactions. That layout had been treated as fixed.

The team used X-ray spectroscopy inside a working cell. They watched platinum enrich the surface at moderate voltages. Then gold surged outward once higher voltages made its oxidation possible. Gold overtook the slower platinum. Every shift reversed cleanly, even at room temperature. The authors warn that catalyst design must reckon with this restless behaviour. The working surface is a moving target set by running conditions.
pmc-13632012:
Emily E Heming and four colleagues compared bodychecking and head contact across Canadian youth ice sports. They examined girls' ice hockey, boys' ice hockey, ringette, and para ice hockey, a seated sled version played by athletes with disabilities. Some of these sports ban bodychecking outright. The team analyzed video from one hundred forty-four games played between 2008 and 2022, counting checks, head contacts, and suspected injuries per minute of play.

Checking rates were surprisingly high in the sports that prohibit it. Girls' hockey and ringette both showed far more bodychecking than the boys' non-checking comparison group. Head contact rates were also higher in those sports. Para ice hockey did not differ clearly on either measure. Very few player-to-player head contacts drew penalties in any sport. The authors call for stronger enforcement of existing rules to cut injury and concussion risk.
pmc-13632612:
Mu-Cyun Wang and four colleagues studied two overlapping conditions of aging muscle and body fat in Taiwan. Sarcopenic obesity combines low muscle mass, low strength, and obesity. A related form, dynapenic obesity, pairs low strength with obesity alone. Earlier studies often mixed the two up. The team followed older adults from a Taiwanese aging study between 2015 and 2019, testing thinking skills at the start and again two years later.

Three hundred sixty-six adults aged sixty-nine and over took part. Everyone with the strength-based form also met the fuller definition. Both conditions were tied to weaker overall thinking scores, plus poorer memory and attention results. The links stood out among women and among people without a known genetic risk variant for Alzheimer's disease. Measuring grip strength alongside body size may help flag older adults at higher risk of early cognitive decline.
pmc-13632912:
Xiaoyan Zhang and four colleagues interviewed clinical nurses in China about working with artificial intelligence tools. Hospital AI promises lighter paperwork and decision support. Frontline nurses report a mixed reality, where help arrives together with new burdens and stress. The team spoke in depth with registered nurses who use clinical AI daily at several general hospitals. They sorted the answers using a framework that weighs job demands against job resources.

On the gain side, nurses described faster workflows, stronger clinical thinking support, and growth in professional standing. On the drain side, they described muddled thinking from overreliance, thinner contact with patients, and a rat race of rising performance targets. Personal coping habits, firm professional boundaries, and supportive organizations softened the harm. The authors urge hospital leaders to govern AI across its whole life cycle and to protect the human core of nursing care.
pmc-13635212:
Brain scans can reveal new genetic links when a machine-learning model learns their patterns without preset measurements, Islam and colleagues argue. Linking genetic variation to brain structure usually relies on hand-chosen features, which may miss subtle patterns. The team trained a vision transformer autoencoder on magnetic resonance images from more than six thousand UK Biobank volunteers. This model compresses each scan into a compact numerical summary, which they then used in genetic studies of nearly twenty-three thousand people.

The approach uncovered sixty-three genetic locations, including twenty-four missed by an earlier convolutional method, and interpretation showed the model captured both local detail and whole-brain patterns such as left-right symmetry. Those broad patterns, picked up through the model's attention mechanism, set it apart from the earlier approach. Islam and colleagues conclude that transformer-based image summaries offer a richer route to gene discovery.
pmc-13639012:
Hewei Ge and seven colleagues report a 2026 multi-center study on how a breast cancer feature called HER2-low affects immunotherapy results. Their focus was triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive type with few treatment options.

Patients whose tumors had low HER2 levels responded worse to immunotherapy given before surgery than patients with no HER2, while chemotherapy alone showed no such gap. Two outside trial groups confirmed the pattern. Single-cell analysis showed the HER2-low tumors were less visible to the immune system and had quieter T cells. The authors say HER2-low status could help predict who benefits from immunotherapy.
pmc-13641712:
Rose A. Gogal and twelve colleagues present a study on judging whether gene changes of unknown meaning cause hereditary deafness through protein misfolding. A public deafness database holds hundreds of thousands of such uncertain variants across 224 genes.

The team built probability models that weigh prediction scores, each gene's tolerance for change, and computed effects on protein stability. Adding folding stability improved accuracy and gave a physical reason for harm. Nearly twenty-nine thousand uncertain variants crossed a high-confidence threshold for likely harm, and twelve patients had their diagnosis upgraded as a result. The framework offers labs a principled way to sort uncertain findings.
pmc-13643612:
Kensuke Takaoka and six colleagues present a 2026 study of how gene changes in one cell pathway shape the course of acute myeloid leukemia. Such changes are common when the disease is found. Their weight for care and survival was not clear.

The study covered seventy-four patients at the University of Iowa. Sixty-two of them got first-round drug care. Five-year survival stood below thirty percent. A change in the KRAS gene meant worse survival and shorter time free of disease. It did not change the odds of reaching remission. The authors ask for checks in larger groups at more centers.
pmc-13643912:
Zheng Ni and thirteen colleagues present a review of how Tembusu virus, an avian flavivirus spreading through waterfowl, may reach and damage the brain. Evidence of nerve signs and virus in neural tissue is growing, yet the entry route and timing remain unclear.

The authors compare better-studied relatives, including Japanese encephalitis, West Nile, Zika, and dengue viruses. Those cases show blood-brain barrier failure involves vessel activation, junction loosening, enzymes, immune traffic, and glial amplification, with no single shared script. They argue Tembusu disease should be read as a staged sequence from body infection to barrier failure to brain injury, separating steps often blurred together.
pmc-13645512:
Aslak Steinsbekk and three colleagues present a study comparing two ways to measure how strongly students in health and social care programs identify with their future profession. A popular nine-item scale tends to bunch scores near the top, hiding real differences between students.

All students at one university were invited, and 864 from eleven programs answered both the nine-item scale and one plain question with positively tilted options. The single question spread scores about twice as widely and still tracked the longer scale closely. It also separated first-year from final-year students more sharply. Both tools flagged study year and first-choice admission as the strongest links. Brevity favors the single item, the authors say.
pmc-13645712:
Xuhui Liu and five colleagues study a blood inflammation score in patients with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a rare clot in the brain's drainage veins. Their records cover 213 adults treated at one center, about a quarter of whom had disturbed consciousness during the acute illness. The score, called the systemic immune-inflammation index, is built from platelet, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts. The team tested it alone and inside prediction models.

Higher scores went with clearly higher odds of disturbed consciousness, and patients in the top quarter of scores stood out sharply. A small three-factor model sorted patients about as well as a larger eight-factor one. The score also beat any of its single cell counts at telling the groups apart. The authors present the index as a cheap bedside signal of severity, while noting the work rests on one center's records and needs outside confirmation.
pmc-13647312:
Venkatesan Narasimman and Gunabalan Madhumitha build a light-driven catalyst for making quinolines, a ring family common in medicines, without harsh metals or heat. Their material anchors nickel cobalt oxide particles onto sheets of graphitic carbon nitride. Three loadings were brewed and compared under a small blue LED lamp. The middle loading performed best, and tests confirmed the two parts truly formed a joined structure.

The chosen catalyst delivered an eighty-two percent yield of the target quinolines and kept working across five reuse cycles. Radical trapping experiments revealed which reactive species carry the chemistry. The method tolerated a broad range of starting materials under mild conditions. The pair present the catalyst as a green stand-in for conventional metal-catalyzed routes, built from earth-abundant ingredients and powered by visible light.
pmc-13648312:
Alessandra Colella led a 2026 evaluation of JOINclusion, a mobile game designed to build empathy across cultures in children aged eight to twelve. Empathy supports kind behavior and reduces prejudice, and middle childhood is a sensitive window for both empathy and prejudice formation. The game, grounded in social emotional learning, offers a narrative story mode and a team play mode that practice reading feelings, seeing others' viewpoints, and kind choices.

The team tested the game before and after play with 286 children in Italy, Greece, and the Netherlands. Most children reported perceived gains in empathy-related skills. Latent change models showed a clear rise in empathic perspective-taking, with a small rise in empathic feeling and expression, regardless of gender, age, or family origin. Teachers get a promising model for empathy training through play, with the authors noting limits that call for stronger controlled trials.
pmc-13649212:
Diane Maria Scherer Kuhn Lago and three colleagues examine grief among nurses through the lens of psychoanalysis, drawing on Freud and Lacan. Nurses face death and loss repeatedly at work, and the essay asks how grief is processed when the lost bond belongs to patients rather than family.

Grief is framed as pain triggered by losing a significant bond, extending beyond death to symbolic losses across a life. Working through it demands slow psychic effort and re-signifying what was lost, while grief that stalls can harden into melancholia. The authors discuss resilience, adaptation, and reconnecting with the world, arguing that understanding these processes matters for nurses' mental health and collective well-being during crises such as pandemics and wars.
pmc-13649412:
Yan Liu and four colleagues weighed Chinese medicine options for poor sleep against Western drugs and talk therapy. They searched nine databases for trials up to early 2026 and merged the results in a network analysis, which lets many treatments be ranked at once.

Twelve trials with 1,260 people were included. Pairing Chinese medicine with Western drugs ranked first on two sleep scores and beat both dummy pills and drugs alone. Chinese medicine on its own also worked well and ranked second for overall benefit. Side effect rankings favoured Western drugs alone, though. The authors judge the paired and solo Chinese options useful, with fair safety, for managing poor sleep.
pmc-13650012:
Ninoslav Begovic and nine colleagues report the case of a baby boy, about six months old, with a painless lump growing under the skin of his right armpit and upper arm. The lump turned out to be a fibrous hamartoma of infancy, a rare and harmless soft-tissue growth whose look varies enough to imitate infections, blood vessel growths, and even cancers.

Clinicians first suspected an infected lymph node linked to a tuberculosis vaccine, yet drawing fluid found no pus, and repeated ultrasound scans showed steady growth. Magnetic resonance imaging measured a well-bordered mass, and surgeons removed it whole while sparing muscle and nearby nerves and vessels. Microscope study showed the growth's signature three-part pattern, confirming the diagnosis. The authors stress that tissue proof matters, since a firm diagnosis spares infants harsher cancer-style treatment.
pmc-13650612:
Mary Wickenden and two co-authors introduce a collection of papers on the lived experience of people with intellectual disabilities, read through an intersectional lens. The idea, borrowed from legal scholarship, is that disability never acts alone: age, gender, race, culture, sexuality, income, and place overlap to shape each person's chances and treatment.

Six papers from varied settings cover sexuality and gender diversity, housing, humanitarian crises, living arrangements, sexual and reproductive health, and the skills of support workers. One study asks how knowledge and direct experience affect staff confidence in supporting LGBTQ+ people with intellectual disabilities. The editors note that terminology differs by country and discipline, with some authors writing about learning or cognitive disability instead. Their shared argument is that single-axis views that see only the disability miss most of what marginalizes this group across a lifetime.
pmc-13650712:
Seiichi Ota and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, evaluate plastic slabs that sit against the patient to shorten proton beam range during treatment of shallow tumors. Proton machines cannot fire low enough energies for surface targets directly, so a range shifter absorbs some energy first. Placing it at the patient side helps when nozzle-mounted versions do not fit the setup.

Two slab materials, an acrylic and a dense polyethylene, were tested in a water phantom with gaps between slab and phantom ranging from touching to wide. Dose accuracy held up well while the gap stayed within eighty millimeters, even under strict comparison rules. Wider gaps at shallow depths produced failed checks and dose errors above three percent. Deliberately shifting the slab by up to a centimeter barely mattered. The authors recommend the gap limit as a practical rule for clinical use.
pmc-13650812:
Matthew E Modes and seven co-authors, in 2026, develop the Family Perspectives Project, a program that sends hospital chaplains to support families of critically ill patients in intensive care. Guidelines say families should receive emotional support from the care team, yet few do, and chaplains are an underused resource already skilled in that work.

Twelve stakeholder interviews first refined the design. Chaplains then visited families, offered emotional support, and wrote structured reports on family views for clinicians to read. A single-arm trial in one unit enrolled nine patient-family pairs, and the program was given with high fidelity. Those taking part rated it both feasible and acceptable on validated survey measures. The authors argue the model is ready for a larger randomized pilot, giving intensive care units a practical route to a guideline they currently miss.
pmc-13651512:
Hannah M Hansen and ten co-authors measure how covalently actinide metals share electrons with their ligands, a property that decides how these radioactive elements behave in separations and materials. Two trusted spectroscopic tools had never been applied together to the same compounds, so the team joined them on thorium and uranium borohydride complexes.

X-ray absorption at the boron edge showed a dominant signal that calculations assigned to covalent bonds in which hydrogen bridges metal and boron. Those bonds are built mainly from the metal's 6d orbitals, with the famous 5f orbitals contributing far less. Nuclear magnetic resonance measurements on the thorium compound and matching calculations agreed with that picture. The work marks the first joint use of these methods on actinide bonding and argues they fit each other well. The X-ray method reads orbital detail straight, while resonance spectroscopy sits in nearly every chemistry lab.
pmc-13652512:
Geraldo Ishak and seven colleagues examine how lymph nodes respond when stomach cancer is treated with chemotherapy before surgery. Chemotherapy first is now standard for locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma, and whether cancer remains in the nodes afterward strongly shapes the outlook. The team reviewed records of patients treated with the combined approach over a six-year span at their institution and compared staging before and after therapy.

Patients whose tumors shrank in stage after treatment were checked against the state of their lymph nodes at surgery. Since leftover nodal disease often survives even when the main tumor responds. The analysis links downstaging to nodal involvement and helps clarify which patients truly benefit from the preoperative course. For surgeons and oncologists planning care, nodal response after chemotherapy offers a practical signal for prognosis and for deciding how aggressive follow-up should be.
pmc-2222612:
Tennant, Hiller, Fishwick, and co-authors develop the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale, known as WEMWBS. Interest in mental well-being, beyond the absence of illness, was growing worldwide. Governments needed tools to track well-being across populations and to judge health promotion efforts.

The team describes how the scale was built and tested in the United Kingdom. Its questions aim to capture positive feelings and functioning in daily life. A short, tested scale lets surveys and programmes share one measure, so changes in public well-being can be tracked over time and compared between places.
pmc-2885312:
Janssen and LeBlanc review the health benefits of physical activity and fitness in school-aged children and youth. Their review had two aims: gather the evidence linking activity, fitness, and health in young people, and turn the findings into recommendations. They focused on a set of key health indicators.

Across the studies, more activity and better fitness track with healthier bodies and minds in childhood. The authors translate that evidence into guidance on how much activity children need. Schools and health agencies use such reviews to set activity targets and defend time for sport and play.
pmc-3278112:
Eysenbach and the CONSORT-EHEALTH Group set out guidance for reporting evaluations of web-based and mobile health interventions. Such interventions deliver behaviour-based treatment or support through the internet or phone platforms. They include many forms of digital health tools now in wide use.

Reports of their trials varied greatly in quality, making results hard to compare or trust. The guidance aims to improve and standardise those reports, extending the CONSORT approach to digital settings. Standard reporting helps health systems judge which apps and online programmes truly work before adopting them.  Reporting items cover the intervention itself, not only the trial around it.
pmc-3848812:
Gale, Heath, Cameron, and co-authors explain using the Framework Method for analysing qualitative data in multidisciplinary health research. The method was becoming an increasingly popular approach for managing and analysing interview and focus group data. Confusion existed, though, about where it fits and what its limits are.

The article discusses when adopting the method is appropriate and walks through its stages, from familiarisation to charting themes in a matrix. Its structured approach suits teams where several researchers share analysis. The paper became the standard citation for the method in health studies.
pmc-5870712:
Jake Conway, Alexander Lex, and Nils Gehlenborg introduced UpSetR in 2017. Scientists often need to show how sets overlap, for example genes shared across conditions. Venn diagrams become unreadable once more than a few sets are involved.

UpSetR uses a matrix layout that stays clear with many sets and large counts. Bars show the size of each overlap, and users can sort and filter by set traits. The package runs in R and is free to use. It quickly became a standard choice for overlap plots in genomics and survey research alike.
pmc-6941312:
Davide Chicco and Giuseppe Jurman argued for the Matthews correlation coefficient in judging classifiers in 2020. Binary classifiers are often graded by accuracy or the F1 score. The authors show both can flatter a model, above all when classes are unbalanced.

The Matthews coefficient uses all four cells of the confusion matrix in one balanced number. It stays honest when a rare class matters most, as in disease screening. Worked examples show rival scores crowning the worse model. Machine learning practitioners cite the paper when choosing how to report classifier quality.
pmc-7145712:
Bijay Jassal, Lisa Matthews, Guilherme Viteri, and coauthors gave the 2020 update of the Reactome pathway knowledgebase. Reactome maps cell processes as an ordered network of molecular changes. It covers signaling, transport, DNA copying, and metabolism in one model.

Curators added pathways and refined disease-related content for this release. Users can overlay experiment data to see which pathways light up in a condition. Diagrams make complex cascades readable for students and clinicians alike. Reactome remains free and is one of the most used pathway resources in the world. Disease pathway pages link each step to the drugs known to act on it.
pmc-7779012:
The Gene Ontology Consortium reported in 2020 on the progress of its long running effort to describe gene function in a shared, computable language. The Gene Ontology gives every gene product standard terms for what it does, where in the cell it acts, and which larger process it serves. The consortium calls it the most complete resource of its kind.

The article covers advances from the previous two years, including a newer annotation framework that can capture richer statements about how gene products work together. It also describes growth in the underlying knowledge and in the tools that use it. Nearly every modern study that asks what a set of genes is for leans on this shared vocabulary.
principia-mathematica-vol-2-1912:
Volume two of Principia Mathematica came out in 1912, from Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell. The first volume had built the logical frame and the theory of classes. This volume turns to cardinal and ordinal arithmetic. Cardinals count how many, while ordinals capture order and sequence.

The theory of series receives long treatment, since order runs through all later math. Step by step, the authors prove results most readers take on trust. Their notation stays dense, and the pace stays slow and exact. The volume holds the middle of a three part work. It shows the logicist program at full stretch. Endurance is the price of entry.
ptolemy-almagest-manitius-1912:
Claudius Ptolemy of Alexandria built the ancient world's full system of the heavens in the second century. The Almagest, in Karl Manitius's German rendering of 1912 and 1913, gives that system whole. For some fourteen centuries, this book ruled how men reckoned the sky.

Ptolemy shows, with tables and proofs, how circles set on circles can track the sun, moon, and planets. His star lists and tools let any trained reader cast the heavens for a given date. Manitius's version opened the Greek master to modern German readers. The Almagest stands at the summit of Greek science.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: The twelfth volume of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte opens here with nothing beyond a publisher's plain-text header. That header names the title, credits Constant as author, and states that the text is in English. No line of the memoir, no contents list, and no preface follows it in the pages at hand. Whether this final-numbered part closes Constant's account or what scenes it holds cannot be judged from such a front page alone.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-2-1912:
The second volume of Principia Mathematica, published in 1912, carries Whitehead and Russell's logicist program into arithmetic proper. Here the abstract machinery of volume one is put to work on number itself, step by careful step.

Cardinal arithmetic comes first: what it means for two classes to have the same number of members, defined without counting. Ordinal arithmetic follows, treating order and series with the same rigor. The symbolism remains forbidding, but the achievement is plain. Whole branches of mathematics are rebuilt as logic, step by audited step, in the founding work of modern mathematical logic.
sancta-veritas-hermetica-seu-concordanti: Sancta veritas hermetica of 1712 sought harmony among philosophers. The holy hermetic truth, concordant. The alchemical concord. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
scheible-das-kloster-vol12:
Band twelve, cells forty-five through forty-eight, closed Das Kloster in 1849. Johann Scheible's anthology had run to twelve bands of complete reprints in five years. No other German editor of his century matched that scale in saving folk print from decay.

The last cells hold the usual rich stock: grimoires, Faust books, and Höllenzwänge in full text. Folk charms and chapbooks, the cheapest print of past ages, stand preserved beside them. With this band the cloister door, so to speak, swings shut on a full house. Workers on German magic still enter by Scheible's door, because so many texts live nowhere else.
schiller-formal-logic-1912:
Formal logic claimed to state the pure laws of thought, above human mess and error. F. C. S. Schiller attacked that claim in Formal Logic, published in 1912. The subtitle names logic a scientific and social problem. Schiller, the Oxford humanist, treats logic as a human instrument instead.

He argues that real thinking serves aims, faces risk, and works with rough material. Rules of logic, on his view, are tools judged by how well they guide inquiry. The attack drew sharp replies from defenders of the old logic. His case remains a bold pragmatist challenge. It asks what logic is for.
schliemann-how-i-found-atlantis-1912:
Readers of the New York American on October 20, 1912, met a bold front-page claim: a young man said he had found lost Atlantis. Paul Schliemann presented himself as a grandson of Heinrich Schliemann, the famed digger of Troy. His letters told of a sealed envelope left by his grandfather, not to be opened lightly.

Inside the tale sit an owl-headed vase, coins of a strange metal, and clues said to point across the ocean. No proof ever backed the story, and it is now read as a famous newspaper hoax. Kept as a record of the Atlantis myth itself, the piece shows how eagerly the lost city gripped the public mind.
schopenhauer-world-will-idea-vol-2-1912:
Arthur Schopenhauer wrote The World as Will and Idea as his great work. R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp gave it English dress in three books. Book two holds his attack on the Kant scheme and adds to Books One and Two of the main work. Schopenhauer held Kant the peak of thought past him.

His gripe with Kant turns on how the mind shapes the world it knows. The adds deal with the senses, with thought, and with man's place in nature. Will, blind and blind still, drives all things in his bleak scheme. The book is key to the whole of his dark, clear thought.
schopenhauer-world-will-idea-vol-3-1912:
Book three of Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea ends the Haldane and Kemp set. The book gives adds to Books Two, Three, and Four of the main work. Schopenhauer kept at his one great book all his life. Its fame came late, when he was an old man in Frankfurt.

The adds take up life and death, art and music, and the denial of the will. Saint and monk stand as the mark of the soul that quits the chase. Schopenhauer's prose is clear, fierce, and full of scorn for cant. The book ends one of the great schemes of thought of its age.
shahnama-warner-vol-6-1912:
Volume 6 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1912, the sixth of nine volumes of the first complete English Book of Kings. Firdausi's epic, finished around 1010, runs to some fifty thousand couplets in Persian. Arthur and Edmond Warner rendered it for readers who had no other way to reach the whole poem.

The historical shahs take up more of the tale here, with wars against Rome and Turan and the splendor of the Sasanian court. Alexander and other foreign rulers enter Persian memory in Persian dress. The volume shows the epic changing tone as myth gives way to chronicle. It also shows the Warners' steady method: close translation, full notes, no cuts.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Volume XIV of the Slave Narratives, South Carolina Narratives, Part 1, gathers talks with former slaves. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 for South Carolina, and the Library of Congress project put the set together at Washington in 1941. The list of those who spoke gives page numbers, beginning with M. E. Abrams, Ezra Adams, Mary Adams, Victoria Adams, Frank Adamson, and Frances Andrews.
soldan-heppe-geschichte-hexenprozesse-vo:
W. G. Soldan and H. Heppe wrote the classic German history of the witch trials in the nineteenth century. Max Bauer revised their work, and this first volume appeared in his edition of 1912. It traces the trials from antiquity through their medieval foundations, the long road to the great persecution.

Soldan and Heppe treat law, theology, and folk belief as one tangle. Their history is sober, documented, and vast in scope. German scholarship's great reckoning with the persecution begins in these volumes. Volume one ends where the machinery stands built and ready. Modern historians of witchcraft still build on the Soldan-Heppe foundation, even when they correct it.

The second volume of Soldan and Heppe's history of the witch trials, in Max Bauer's edition of 1912, takes the terrible main act. It covers the great persecution at its height and its long decline. Genuine trial documents illustrate the narrative, letting courts and accused speak in their own records.

Readers follow the hunts through Germany's worst decades and into the age of the critics. Spee, Thomasius, and the slow turn of the law all find their place. The volume closes the classic German accounting of the trials. Together the two volumes form the founding modern historiography of witchcraft. Their care set a standard that later, fuller archives have only extended.
spanish-constitution-1812:
The Cortes of Cádiz adopted Spain's first liberal constitution in 1812, while the city held out against Napoleon's armies. Deputies from Spain and its American colonies wrote the charter under siege, in a port city swollen with refugees. Spaniards know it as La Pepa, because it was proclaimed on Saint Joseph's day.

The text declares that sovereignty rests in the nation, limits the king, and gives the Cortes the making of laws. It promises freedom of the press and equality before the law across the Spanish world. Restored King Ferdinand abolished it in 1814, and soldiers later forced it back on him twice. The charter of Spanish liberalism for a century, born under siege and murdered by restored kings, also taught liberals across Latin America their trade.
spr-proceedings-vol24-1910-1912:
Parts sixty and sixty one, with an appendix, form volume twenty four for 1910 to 1912. The SPR Proceedings reach thirty years from the founding in this stretch. Telepathy research persists, refined by decades of criticism. The society's case files on apparitions grow by steady additions.

Mediumship reports, led by the Piper record, remain the most argued pages. Physical phenomena receive brief, guarded notices, as usual in this era. The appendix handles society matters and odds of evidence. Volume twenty four shows the archive near its First World War pause. Its contents fed the survival debate for years after. Method and patience mark every report.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5012:
Thomas Jefferson gives eight yearly addresses, from December 8, 1801, to November 8, 1808, parted by three stars. The first brings glad news to the nation's great council: the wars and troubles that have grieved sister nations for so many years have at last come to an end. Roads of peace and trade open again among them, and thanks are due for that turn.

Jefferson adds a sharper thanks that America's own peace was kept through so risky a season. The folk were left free to till the earth and to better the arts that add to their comforts. Word from all powers with whom the states hold chief ties had bred trust that peace would hold. The end of wrongs done to neutral trade, he hopes, will firm that trust and ground fair claims for the past.
talbot-in-the-shadow-of-the-bush-1912:
Percy Amaury Talbot surveyed the peoples of southern Nigeria in In the Shadow of the Bush, published in 1912. Talbot, a colonial officer in the Cross River region, writes of the Ekoi and their neighbors. Secret societies, juju, in the period's word, and village religion stand at the center of his account.

Masks, shrines, and the law of the Egbo society pass through his observant chapters. Talbot aimed to help rulers understand the ruled, a colonial purpose plain on the page. Even so, his record of Cross River belief and custom remains a rich early source for the region.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Two verse tales at the expense of lecherous churchmen fill the twelfth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Monks of Catalonia and The Cradle. The monks of the first tale work their wills in a Catalan valley.

The poet asks leave to detail the feats of the holy fathers there, who showed such charity to wife and maid that the women thought they had gained paradise. Such men, he adds, know how to surprise young and easy minds and to get possession of the feeling heart, working in the holy vineyard with full success. The Cradle plays the companion trick: a lover hidden where a baby's cradle should rock, in one of Boccaccio's most retold jests.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-12:
Volume 12 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XXI with a fresh trial in the Court of Justice. Rustem, trusted with the jeweller's gold by Mary, makes ready for a journey to save Paula's life. The charge is grave: Orion, son of the Mukaukas, is said to have made away with a costly emerald left to the Church by his father, against the patriarch's ban.

He speaks his own defence, then, to end the odious affair, lays Paula's emerald before the judges. The Kadi hands it to Bishop John, who is not content. He cites the written word of the widow Susannah: the dead Mukaukas named all the jewels in the Persian hanging as his gift to the Church, in Orion's hearing. Suspicion of fraud still hangs on the young man.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-12:
The Caxtons moves house in Part XII, and Pisistratus moves with it as narrator. Son of a scholar, he chronicles his family in the first person. Books, ponds, and poultry fill this stretch of the picture, in the novel's gentle manner.

The family's move is done, and all have settled in the old Tower. The father's books arrive by wagon and fill his rooms, his bed chamber, and two lobbies besides. The household duck arrives under Mrs. Primmins and settles at the old stewpond. The father finds a walk there that makes up for the lost peach wall, and he makes friends with the carp, whom he may feed once the duck is fed.
the-complete-works-of-brann-the-iconocla: Etext 569, dated June 1996, presents volume 12 of William Cowper Brann's complete Iconoclast works. Like its companions, it opens with a Gutenberg header, and that header's inner line wrongly names volume 1. The set, readers are told, runs to twelve volumes in all. No page of Brann's text follows, so this final volume's contents cannot be summed up.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Volume 12 of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions closes his life story in twelve books, in an edition privately printed in London in 1903 for members of the Aldus Society. Book XII opens in a dark mood. Rousseau says that for eight years he has lived inside a plot he cannot see clearly, struck by blows whose source stays hidden from him.

He tells readers that the roots of his troubles lie in the books before this one. Anyone who wants the full truth, he says, should reread the three books just before it and trace each plot back to its first mover. The book then turns to his stay at Yverdon and his warm friendship with the Roguin family.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: The Great Events by Famous Historians retells world history in the words of eminent historians. Rossiter Johnson was editor-in-chief. Charles F. Horne and John Rudd were associate editors. This record is Volume XII. The National Alumni published it in 1905. Only front matter is present here: the title page and the start of a contents list. The contents open with an outline narrative. No single event or author is named beyond that head. The volume's own pieces cannot be told from what is here.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Part 12 of Don Quixote, Miguel de Cervantes' novel, appears in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter thirty treats the address displayed by the fair Dorothea, with other matters pleasant and amusing. The opening picks up a claim about a deed as the curate finishes speaking.

Sancho breaks in with faith that the man who did the deed was his master, and not for want of warning from Sancho himself. Dorothea's part in the rescue plan now comes forward. Cervantes gives the stage to a quick-witted woman whose address must persuade a knight lost in penance to leave the Sierra.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio: Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote The History of England from the Accession of James II. The record shows Volume III of 5, chapters XI to XVI. Porter & Coates printed it at Philadelphia. The contents outline chapter eleven in detail. The chapter opens with William and Mary proclaimed in London. It covers ministerial arrangements and the first Mutiny Bill. It also covers abolition of the hearth money. Religious disputes close the outline. Only the title page and contents outline are present here.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-12:
Book Twelve of Edward Bulwer Lytton Warwick novel takes its name from the Battle of Barnet. Edward and his army reach St Albans while Westminster sanctuary fills with Yorkist friends. London falls into fear, its mayor feigning illness and his deputy Sir Thomas Cook fleeing.

The Archbishop of York parades the frail King Henry through Cheapside to stir loyalty. Henry vacant eyes and drooping head win pity and scorn instead, fresh from a fit. Two thousand Yorkist gentlemen pour from sanctuaries as the rival kings near a final clash north of the city.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 286 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, December 8, 1827, opens with an engraving of Caxton's house in the Almonry at Westminster. To praise printing at this time of day, the editors say, would be wasteful and ridiculous excess. Instead the number introduces a coming memoir of Caxton, the first English printer. The house view serves as a frontispiece to that promised life.

The article locates the house southwest of Westminster Abbey, where the abbey's alms were once distributed. Howell's Londinopolis is quoted: the abbot permitted Caxton to set up his press in the Almonry, a name the spot still retains. Newcourt's Repertorium confirms the account. The memoir to follow will add antiquarian testimony from the Archaeologia, scarcely a volume of which lacks something on Caxton. Readers are primed with place before biography. The magazine treats a printer's workshop as a national shrine worth engraving.

Number 321 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, July 5, 1828, opens Volume 12 with Eaton Hall in Cheshire, seat of Earl Grosvenor. The mansion is praised as a princely specimen of Gothic architecture, completed within a few years. The article calls the earl's taste and generosity as a patron of the fine arts well known. His house realizes Sir Henry Wotton's idea of a home as a theatre of hospitality and private princedom.

A footnote follows the earl's picture collection, among England's finest. Its nucleus was the purchase of Mr. Agar's pictures for 30,000 pounds, and a new gallery is rising by his Grosvenor Street mansion. The public may view the private collection on specified days. In the Eaton drawing-room hangs Claude Lorraine's Our Saviour on the Mount of Olives, his largest known painting. Readers get aristocratic collecting presented as a national asset.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, November 8, 1828, No. 339, visits Great Milton near Thame in Oxfordshire. The village earns notice as the family seat of the Miltons, ancestors of the epic poet. One ancestor forfeited his estate in the Wars of the Roses; Dr. Johnson could not say which side he took. The poet's grandfather, under-ranger of Shotover forest and a zealous Papist, disinherited his son for turning Protestant.

Cut off from the property, Milton's father left Christ Church, Oxford, for London and became a scrivener. Eminent in music and classical learning, he grew rich and retired. His younger son Christopher became a bencher of the Inner Temple and a judge, while John, born in Bread Street in 1608, became the poet. A footnote from Dr. Burney rates the father equal in science to the best musicians of his age.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, January 10, 1829, No. 351, illustrates Macclesfield Bridge in Regent's Park. The bridge crosses the canal toward the park's northern verge, opposite the road to Primrose Hill. Mr. Morgan designed it, and its construction is called appropriate and architectural. Its piers are cast-iron columns of the Grecian Doric order, from which the arches spring over towing-path, canal, and southern bank.

Mr. Elmes, the architect quoted, praises the bridge's beautiful, light appearance. He calls it an improvement in execution on Perronet's design for a bridge of orders. The centre arch serves the canal and towing-path, while the two outer arches carry foot-passengers. Fastidious critics, Elmes allows, may object to pure ancient Doric degraded into supporting modern arches. Readers get industrial ironwork defended in the language of classical taste.

Rare Arctic birds open volume 19, No. 550, dated June 2, 1832. Engravings show a white-horned owl, a cock of the plains, and the legs and feet of a mountain grouse. The writers begin broadly, arguing that animals draw more public interest than maps alone after new lands are found.

Behind the pictures stood the final overland expedition to the Polar Sea, led by Captain Sir John Franklin. Its natural history collections grew too large for an appendix to the voyage narrative. Dr. Richardson, the expedition's surgeon and naturalist, prepared them for separate publication with Mr. Swainson's help. A government grant of one thousand pounds paid toward the costly engravings the bird volume required.
the-parisians-volume-12:
Book XII of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens in the last period of the siege of Paris. The last book closed with the Parisian sortie of November 30, followed by hard fighting on December 2. Hope that Trochu would break the iron circle faded as Ducrot recrossed the Marne and Moltke announced the defeat of the army of the Loire.

Winter and famine settled on the city, yet the narrator praises its people. The old noblesse sent sons to the front and women to nurse in ambulances, and opened their houses to the homeless. The thrifty bourgeoisie bore growing privation without a murmur. Courage, he says, became the mark of every class.
the-sunny-side-of-diplomatic-life-1875-1: Lillie de Hegermann-Lindencrone, author of In the Courts of Memory, wrote this memoir of diplomatic life from 1875 to 1912, published by Harper and Brothers in October 1914 with portraits and facsimiles. Only the title pages, contents, and a list of illustrations are present in this record, showing sections for Washington, Rome, Stockholm, Paris, and Berlin, and frontispiece and plate portraits including Mrs. U. S. Grant, so the memoir itself does not appear.
the-third-string-odd-craft-part-12:
W. W. Jacobs lets his night-watchman hold forth on love in The Third String, a story from Odd Craft. Watching one skipper try to hook a passing barge, the watchman declares he has suffered enough through love. He jokes that love needs teetotalers with ribbons, like drink, since the two mischiefs constantly lead into each other. Sailors, he says, fall hardest because they see so little of women.

He tells of a castaway who cherished his sweetheart's photograph for fourteen years on a desert island, then shot her for altering in looks. Then he turns to Ginger Dick, who fell in love while lodging in Wapping with Sam Small and Peter Russet. Jacobs's waterfront philosopher frames a comic tale of romance gone wrong.
the-war-with-the-united-states-a-chronic:
William Wood wrote The War with the United States as volume fourteen of the Chronicles of Canada, published at Toronto in 1915. The series, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, runs to thirty-two volumes. Contents chapters move from opposing claims and forces through Brock at Detroit and Queenston Heights to Lundy's Lane, Plattsburg, and the great blockade.

Chapter one warns that wars rarely divide absolute right from absolute wrong; they pit opposing rights against each other. Britain fought Napoleon for life and liberty while America sought unrestricted trade with both belligerents. Napoleon's Berlin Decree and Britain's Orders-in-Council left no safe place for an unarmed neutral, Wood argues, especially with Britain overwhelmingly strong at sea.
the-works-of-henry-fielding-vol-12: Volume twelve of The Works of Henry Fielding, edited by George Saintsbury, is represented by its title and contents pages. The volume forms the second book of Fielding's Miscellanies. Contents include The Author's Farce and The Tragedy of Tragedies. That play tells the life and death of Tom Thumb the Great. Pasquin, an essay on conversation, and numbers of The Covent-Garden Journal follow. The pieces themselves begin beyond the pages shown.
the-works-of-the-right-honourable-edmund: Volume one of Burke's writings and speeches, in John C. Nimmo's twelve-volume London edition of 1887, is shown through its contents. A Vindication of Natural Society opens the volume. His inquiry into the sublime and beautiful follows. That early work includes a discourse on taste. A Short Account of a Late Short Administration closes the list. The works themselves begin past the pages included here.

Nimmo's 1887 twelve-volume Burke continues with a second volume represented here by its contents list. The Speech on American Taxation of April 1774 leads. Bristol speeches from the same year follow. His speech on conciliation with America, from March 1775, is included. A letter to the sheriffs of Bristol on American affairs appears. Letters on Irish trade bills close the portion of the list shown.

Volume four of Burke's works, in the 1887 Nimmo edition, appears here through a contents list alone. A letter to a member of the French National Assembly opens it. Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs follows. Letters on Irish Catholics and the penal laws are included. Thoughts on French Affairs also appears. The letters and essays themselves do not follow in the pages present.

A contents list is what this record holds for volume five of Burke's works in Nimmo's 1887 edition. Observations on the Conduct of the Minority opens the volume. Thoughts and Details on Scarcity follows. A letter defending Burke's pension against attacks in the Lords appears. Three letters on peace with revolutionary France begin near the end of the list. Their texts do not appear in the pages shown.

Volume six of Burke's works, Nimmo's 1887 edition, is represented here by its front pages and contents. A fourth letter on peace with the French directory opens the volume. A letter to the Empress of Russia, dated 1791, follows. Earlier letters treat the Irish absentee tax of 1773. A 1777 letter to Charles James Fox concerns the American war. The letters themselves start beyond what appears here.

For volume seven of Burke's works in the 1887 Nimmo edition, the pages present stop at a contents list of parliamentary speeches. A 1772 speech on the Acts of Uniformity leads. Speeches for relief of Protestant dissenters follow. The Middlesex election and shorter parliaments are also treated. Burke's own speeches do not appear in the pages shown here, only their titles and dates.

Volume eight of Burke's works, in Nimmo's 1887 London edition, shows its contents for a report on India. The ninth report of a Commons select committee fills the volume. Sections cover the East India Company's affairs and Bengal's internal trade. Opium, salt, and saltpetre each get detailed treatment. Silk and piece-goods also appear. The report itself begins past the pages given here.

A contents list for volume nine of Burke's works, Nimmo's 1887 edition, is present here without the text it names. The volume holds articles of charge against Warren Hastings, the late governor-general of Bengal. Charges listed include contracts, presents, and opium deals. One article covers his resignation of office. The impeachment articles themselves do not appear in the pages shown in this record.

Volume ten of Burke's works, Nimmo's 1887 edition, is shown through a contents list of impeachment speeches. Burke prosecuted Warren Hastings, the former governor-general of Bengal. His speech opening the impeachment ran over February days in 1788. A speech on the sixth article of charge followed in 1789. It occupied four days of argument. The speeches themselves begin past what is shown here.

A contents list represents volume eleven of Burke's works in Nimmo's 1887 edition, without the speeches themselves. A Commons report on the Hastings trial journals leads the volume. It dates to 1794 and answers Lord Thurlow's criticisms. Burke's speech in general reply follows, spread over four days. Those days run from late May into June 1794. The report and speeches start beyond the pages shown here.

Volume twelve of Burke's works, the last of Nimmo's 1887 set, appears here as a contents list alone. Burke's speech in general reply against Warren Hastings continues from the prior volume. Its later days run through June 1794. A general table of contents for the whole set follows. An index closes the volume. The speech text itself does not appear in the opening pages provided.
three-at-table-the-lady-of-the-barge-and:
W. W. Jacobs placed Three at Table inside The Lady of the Barge and Other Stories, and the tale opens in a coffee room full of ghost talk. Opinions range from rank unbelief to childlike faith. One believer tangles the Witch of Endor with Jonah.
